▶ Gastrointestinal System Pyloric stenosis 6 questions
Source: 3A #8
A 2-week-old newborn is brought to the emergency department by his parents because of a 2-day history of excessive forceful vomiting after eating. The vomitus is not green or bloody. He continues to breast feed vigorously but has had fewer wet diapers than normal. He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and vaginal delivery. He appears mildly dehydrated. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), and pulse is 135/min. The abdomen is soft, and the patient tolerates deep palpation of the abdomen without crying. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) X-ray of the abdomen B) X-ray of the chest C) Barium enema D) Ultrasonography of the abdomen E) CT scan of the abdomen
Correct Answer: D) Ultrasonography of the abdomen
Pyloric stenosis is caused by hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter, leading to gastric outlet obstruction and vomiting. It commonly presents with non-bloody, non-bilious emesis after feedings and begins around 3 to 6 weeks of age, though it can present earlier as in this case. It is more common in male infants. Symptoms may begin with occasional vomiting, then progress to projectile emesis after every feed, dehydration, and malnutrition as the stenosis worsens. Repeated bouts of vomiting cause metabolic and electrolyte derangements, classically a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis caused by the loss of hydrochloric acid and volume contraction. On physical examination, an ovoid lump may be palpated in the upper abdomen, correlating with the hypertrophied pylorus. Diagnosis of pyloric stenosis is definitively made by abdominal ultrasonography demonstrating thickened pyloric musculature. Treatment is with surgical pyloromyotomy. Choice A (X-ray of the abdomen): May show distention of the stomach in pyloric stenosis and can evaluate other intra-abdominal pathology such as bowel obstruction, but would not clearly outline hypertrophy of the pylorus. Choice B (X-ray of the chest): Used in evaluation of chest pain, shortness of breath, and cough to assess for intrathoracic pathology. Upright chest x-ray is used in suspected bowel perforation. It is not commonly used to evaluate recurrent emesis in the absence of suspected complications, although it could demonstrate a hiatal or diaphragmatic hernia if present. It plays no role in the diagnosis of pyloric stenosis. Choice C (Barium enema): Used to examine for abnormalities in the large intestine, such as colon cancer. In children, it can evaluate for Hirschsprung disease and intestinal malrotation. It is not useful in the diagnosis of pyloric stenosis. Choice E (CT scan of the abdomen): Would likely demonstrate the hypertrophic pyloric musculature. However, it is associated with much greater radiation exposure than ultrasonography, making it a less appropriate next step in diagnosis, especially in a pediatric patient. Educational Objective: Pyloric stenosis presents at several weeks of life and is characterized by repeated non-bilious vomiting after feeds, leading to dehydration and a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Diagnosis is made with ultrasonography, and treatment is with surgical pyloromyotomy.
Source: 9A #20
A 6-week-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of nonbilious, projectile vomiting shortly after feedings. His pulse is 120/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Capillary refill time is normal. Examination shows mild dehydration and decreased subcutaneous fat. Abdominal examination shows a 2-cm, hard, nontender mass deep in the right epigastrium. Serum studies are most likely to show which of the following electrolyte concentrations in this patient? A) Abnormally decreased sodium, potassium, and chloride with decreased bicarbonate B) Normal sodium, potassium, and chloride with decreased bicarbonate C) Normal sodium, potassium, and chloride with high bicarbonate D) Normal sodium and potassium with decreased chloride and high bicarbonate E) Normal sodium and potassium with decreased chloride and bicarbonate
Correct Answer: D) Normal sodium and potassium with decreased chloride and high bicarbonate
This 6-week-old patient with nonbilious, postprandial projectile vomiting and a palpable mass in the right epigastrium has pyloric stenosis. Pyloric stenosis is caused by hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter, leading to gastric outlet obstruction and vomiting. It typically presents in male infants around 3 to 6 weeks of age with nonbloody, nonbilious emesis after feedings. Symptoms may progress from occasional vomiting to projectile emesis after every feed, accompanied by dehydration and malnutrition. Definitive diagnosis is via abdominal ultrasonography. Repeated vomiting of gastric contents causes characteristic electrolyte imbalances: hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. This occurs because the stomach loses hydrochloric acid (HCl), a major component of gastric secretions. Loss of HCl leads to decreased chloride and metabolic alkalosis (increased bicarbonate). Metabolic alkalosis develops secondary to dehydration and volume contraction, which results in relative bicarbonate excess and causes activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS). RAAS activation stimulates renal tubule bicarbonate reabsorption and new bicarbonate generation. Volume depletion, metabolic alkalosis, and increased aldosterone concentrations lead to renal potassium excretion, causing hypokalemia. Notably, sodium concentration typically remains normal or only mildly decreased unless dehydration is severe, as sodium is largely reabsorbed in response to volume depletion. Choice A is incorrect because sodium and bicarbonate are not both decreased in pyloric stenosis; sodium is typically normal and bicarbonate is elevated. Choice B is incorrect because it suggests normal electrolytes with acidosis, which could occur in nonanion gap metabolic acidosis but not in pyloric stenosis. Choice C is incorrect because it suggests all electrolytes are normal with elevated bicarbonate, which would not explain the significant chloride losses from gastric outlet obstruction. Choice E is incorrect because while chloride is appropriately decreased, potassium is typically low in moderate to severe pyloric stenosis, not normal. Treatment includes fluid and electrolyte correction followed by definitive pyloromyotomy.
Source: 7A #33
A 1-month-old male newborn is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of forceful, nonbilious vomiting. His mother reports that the vomiting has been getting worse and that he now seems irritable and acts hungry afterward. He was born at term and weighed 2948 g (6 lb 8 oz). There were no prenatal or perinatal complications. He has not had any sick contacts and does not attend day care. His mother underwent pyloromyotomy as an infant. The patient's current weight is 2835 g (6 lb 4 oz). His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 180/min, respirations are 36/min, and blood pressure is 60/40 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 99%. On physical examination, the anterior fontanel is sunken and mucous membranes are dry. Which of the following sets of electrolyte findings is most likely in this patient? A) Na+ 136 mEq/L, K+ 3 mEq/L, Cl- 84 mEq/L, HCO3- 38 mEq/L B) Na+ 136 mEq/L, K+ 2 mEq/L, Cl- 84 mEq/L, HCO3- 38 mEq/L C) Na+ 138 mEq/L, K+ 4 mEq/L, Cl- 100 mEq/L, HCO3- 24 mEq/L D) Na+ 145 mEq/L, K+ 4 mEq/L, Cl- 105 mEq/L, HCO3- 38 mEq/L E) Na+ 150 mEq/L, K+ 5 mEq/L, Cl- 108 mEq/L, HCO3- 24 mEq/L
Correct Answer: B) Na+ 136 mEq/L, K+ 2 mEq/L, Cl- 84 mEq/L, HCO3- 38 mEq/L
Pyloric stenosis is caused by hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter, leading to gastric outlet obstruction and vomiting. It commonly presents with nonbloody, nonbilious emesis after feedings beginning around 3 to 6 weeks of age and is more common in male infants. Symptoms may begin with occasional vomiting, then progress to projectile emesis after every feed, dehydration, and malnutrition as the stenosis worsens. Repeated bouts of vomiting cause characteristic metabolic and electrolyte derangements: hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis caused by losses of hydrochloric acid, a major component of stomach secretions. Metabolic alkalosis occurs secondary to dehydration and subsequent volume contraction plus relative excess of bicarbonate. Volume depletion leads to activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, which stimulates kidney tubule bicarbonate reabsorption and new bicarbonate generation. Metabolic alkalosis, volume depletion, and increased aldosterone concentrations lead to renal potassium excretion and hypokalemia. Hypokalemia also contributes to metabolic alkalosis via transcellular exchange of extracellular sodium and protons for potassium ions. Choice A demonstrates isolated hypochloremia with a potassium of 3 mEq/L, which is not as low as typically seen in pyloric stenosis. Choice C demonstrates a normal basic metabolic panel, which would not be present in a patient with significant vomiting and dehydration from pyloric stenosis. Choice D demonstrates isolated metabolic alkalosis with increased bicarbonate but normal electrolytes. However, patients with pyloric stenosis lose chloride and potassium through gastric secretions and renal excretion, making hypochloremia and hypokalemia essential features alongside metabolic alkalosis. Choice E shows evidence of dehydration with normal bicarbonate and increased values of sodium, potassium, and chloride, suggesting relative intravascular water depletion. However, patients with pyloric stenosis despite being dehydrated have low concentrations of potassium and chloride because of their loss in gastric secretions and through the kidney, not high concentrations. Choice B correctly demonstrates hypochloremic (Cl- 84 mEq/L), hypokalemic (K+ 2 mEq/L) metabolic alkalosis (HCO3- 38 mEq/L) with mild hyponatremia (Na+ 136 mEq/L), representing the classic electrolyte abnormality pattern in pyloric stenosis. Diagnosis is made with abdominal ultrasonography showing thickened pyloric musculature, and treatment requires surgical pyloromyotomy.
Source: 8A #32
A 5-week-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of vomiting immediately after each feeding. During this time, he has had only two wet diapers. He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery and weighed 3317 g (7 lb 5 oz). He was exclusively breast-fed during his first 3 weeks of life; for the past 2 weeks, his diet has consisted of a cow milk-based formula. He has been on 4 to 5 oz feedings and, until yesterday, had minimal spitting up after each feeding. At his most recent examination 1 week ago, he weighed 4.22 kg; examination shows no other abnormalities. After the examination, he is given a bottle of formula, drinks 4 oz, and vomits a large amount. This patient most likely has an obstruction at which of the following locations? A) Duodenum B) Gastroesophageal junction C) Jejunum D) Midesophagus E) Pylorus
Correct Answer: E) Pylorus
Pyloric stenosis is a disorder of the pyloric sphincter that occurs in young infants and can result in partial or complete gastric outlet obstruction. It is caused by hypertrophy of the pylorus and an inability to relax the pyloric sphincter. Infants classically present within the first 1 to 2 months of life with forceful nonbilious emesis. Physical examination is notable for a characteristic ovoid mass in the epigastric region. The recurrent emesis, if severe, may result in signs of volume depletion and malnutrition. Laboratory studies typically show a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis as a result of the loss of gastric hydrochloric acid and potassium ions. Additionally, the resultant volume depletion causes activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, resulting in renal losses of potassium and protons. Confirmatory diagnosis is made by ultrasound imaging to evaluate the thickness and length of the pyloric muscle. Patients are treated with surgical pyloromyotomy to relieve the stenosis. Choice A (Duodenum) is the location of obstruction in patients with duodenal atresia, which is caused by failure of recanalization of the duodenal lumen. Duodenal atresia presents with vomiting and abdominal distension within the first few days after birth in complete atresia. Choice B (Gastroesophageal junction) is the location of obstruction in achalasia. Achalasia is an esophageal dysmotility disorder resulting from deficient peristalsis as a result of impaired neuromuscular transmission and impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter. It manifests as dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, halitosis, and regurgitation of undigested food. It is typically diagnosed between ages 25 and 65 years and is rare in children. Choice C (Jejunum) may undergo atresia in a fetus secondary to an ischemic event, which may have various causes, such as maternal cocaine use, malrotation with volvulus, or other idiopathic causes. Patients may present with vomiting and abdominal distension on the first day of life, similar to patients with duodenal atresia. Choice D (Midesophagus) is the location of obstruction in patients with a vascular ring. A vascular ring is a congenital malformation of the aortic arch and/or great vessels that encircles the trachea and midesophagus. In addition to dysphagia, vomiting, and feeding problems, patients may present with stridor and respiratory difficulties. Educational Objective: Pyloric stenosis presents at several weeks of life and is characterized by repeated nonbilious vomiting after feeds leading to dehydration and a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Diagnosis is made with ultrasonography, and treatment is with surgical pyloromyotomy.
Source: 8A #44
A previously healthy 7-week-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents because of a 3-day history of progressive vomiting. Her symptoms began with spitting up after every feeding; now she has forceful vomiting. Her mother says that she has seemed hungry during this period. She has not had fever or diarrhea. She is alert and appears well hydrated. Her temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 120/min, and respirations are 28/min. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 9 g/dL White blood cell count 8500/mm³ Segmented neutrophils 50% Lymphocytes 45% Monocytes 5% Platelet count 360,000/mm³ Serum Na+ 138 mEq/L Cl- 90 mEq/L K+ 3.6 mEq/L HCO3- 36 mEq/L Urea nitrogen 25 mg/dL Glucose 70 mg/dL Creatinine 0.3 mg/dL Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Acute hyperammonemia B) Acute viral gastroenteritis C) Gastroesophageal reflux D) Hemolytic-uremic syndrome E) Malrotation of the intestine F) Porphyria G) Pyloric stenosis
Correct Answer: G) Pyloric stenosis
Pyloric stenosis is a disorder of the pyloric sphincter that occurs in young infants and can result in partial or complete gastric outlet obstruction. It is caused by hypertrophy of the pylorus and an inability to relax the pyloric sphincter. Infants classically present within the first 1 to 2 months of life with forceful, nonbilious emesis. Physical examination is notable for a characteristic ovoid mass in the epigastric region. The recurrent emesis, if severe, may result in signs of volume depletion and malnutrition. Laboratory studies typically show a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis caused by the loss of gastric hydrochloric acid and potassium ions. Additionally, the resultant volume depletion causes activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, resulting in renal losses of potassium and protons. Confirmatory diagnosis is made with ultrasonography to evaluate the thickness and length of the pyloric muscle. Patients are treated with surgical pyloromyotomy to relieve the stenosis. This patient's presentation is consistent with pyloric stenosis: age 7 weeks (within classic range of 1-2 months), forceful nonbilious vomiting after feedings, hunger despite vomiting, and laboratory findings of hypochloremic (Cl- 90), hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis (HCO3- 36). Incorrect answers: Choice A (Acute hyperammonemia): Often caused by underlying genetic metabolic abnormalities (e.g., ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency). While hyperammonemia can present with somnolence and vomiting, this patient lacks the expected neurological findings and metabolic profile. Choice B (Acute viral gastroenteritis): Often presents with vomiting and diarrhea with or without fever. This patient with progressive forceful emesis occurring only after feeding has a presentation more consistent with gastric outlet obstruction, and notably has no diarrhea. Choice C (Gastroesophageal reflux disease): Caused by acid reflux into the lower esophagus. In an infant, GERD presents with frequent regurgitation without excessive irritability, not the forceful postprandial vomiting seen here. Choice D (Hemolytic-uremic syndrome): Typically associated with infection from enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli O157:H7. It classically presents with bloody diarrhea accompanied by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury—none of which are present in this patient. Choice E (Malrotation of the intestine): Results from incomplete rotation of the midgut during embryonal development. Can present with bilious vomiting (not nonbilious as in this case), abdominal distension, and pain. Choice F (Porphyria): May present with abdominal pain, polyneuropathy, psychological symptoms, and port-wine-colored urine—not the clinical picture here. Educational Objective: Pyloric stenosis presents at several weeks of life and is characterized by repeated nonbilious vomiting after feedings, leading to dehydration and a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Diagnosis is made with ultrasonography, and treatment is with surgical pyloromyotomy.
Source: 3A #21
Over the past 48 hours, an 8-week-old boy has been vomiting continuously after each meal. The emesis is projectile and does not contain bile. The infant appears lethargic and has dry mucous membranes. Palpation of the abdomen shows a small olive-sized mass in the epigastric region. Which of the following profiles is most likely in this infant? A) Cl⁻ 106 mEq/L, K⁺ 2.8 mEq/L, pH 7.48 B) Cl⁻ 106 mEq/L, K⁺ 5.2 mEq/L, pH 7.51 C) Cl⁻ 84 mEq/L, K⁺ 2.8 mEq/L, pH 7.50 D) Cl⁻ 84 mEq/L, K⁺ 2.8 mEq/L, pH 7.25 E) Cl⁻ 84 mEq/L, K⁺ 5.2 mEq/L, pH 7.25
Correct Answer: C) Cl⁻ 84 mEq/L, K⁺ 2.8 mEq/L, pH 7.50
Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS) is a disorder of the pyloric sphincter occurring in young infants, caused by hypertrophy of the pylorus and inability of the pyloric sphincter to relax, resulting in partial or complete gastric outlet obstruction. Infants classically present within the first 1 to 2 months of life with forceful, projectile nonbilious emesis. Physical examination reveals a characteristic ovoid (olive-sized) mass in the epigastric region. The recurrent emesis, if severe, results in signs of volume depletion and malnutrition. Laboratory findings show a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis caused by loss of gastric hydrochloric acid and potassium ions. Additionally, resultant volume depletion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, causing renal losses of potassium and further acid loss, perpetuating the alkalosis (contraction alkalosis). Confirmatory diagnosis is made by ultrasound imaging to evaluate pyloric muscle thickness and length. Treatment is surgical pyloromyotomy. Choice A and B are incorrect because they represent metabolic alkalosis with high chloride concentration (106 mEq/L). Metabolic alkalosis from gastric acid loss typically results in hypochloremia due to chloride ion loss. Choice D and E are incorrect because they represent metabolic acidosis (pH 7.25) rather than alkalosis. Expected pH should reflect alkalosis from high-volume loss of gastric acid and contraction alkalosis. Additionally, choice D has the correct electrolytes but wrong pH, and choice E has hyperkalemia which does not occur in this condition. Choice C correctly demonstrates hypochloremia (84 mEq/L), hypokalemia (2.8 mEq/L), and metabolic alkalosis (pH 7.50), consistent with the pathophysiology of IHPS.
▶ Cardiovascular System Ventricular Septal Defect 5 questions
Source: 6A #11
A 2-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of sweating and fatigue during feedings. His mother has also noticed that he seems to breathe fast and has a pounding heart rate at rest. He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. He is at the 50th percentile for length and 5th percentile for weight. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 145/min, respirations are 70/min, and blood pressure is 92/40 mm Hg. Examination shows prominence of the left precordium and a palpable parasternal lift. A blowing holosystolic murmur is heard best over the lower left sternal border. A chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascular markings. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's symptoms? A) Anomalous pulmonary blood return B) Increased peripheral vascular resistance C) Increased systemic vascular resistance D) Intermittent supraventricular tachycardia E) Left-to-right shunt
Correct Answer: E) Left-to-right shunt
A left-to-right shunt from a large ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the most likely explanation for this patient's clinical presentation. VSDs are among the most common congenital heart malformations with heterogeneous genetic causes, including associations with Down syndrome, DiGeorge syndrome, and Holt-Oram syndrome, but may also occur in isolation via de novo mutations. VSDs are characterized by a holosystolic murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border and may have an associated palpable thrill. The left-to-right shunt increases pulmonary blood flow, leading to pulmonary vascular remodeling and smooth muscle hypertrophy. This results in concentric narrowing of pulmonary arterioles and pulmonary arterial hypertension. If severe and progressive, this causes increased right ventricular pressures and myocardial hypertrophy, potentially reversing the shunt and leading to Eisenmenger syndrome with cyanosis. Increased pulmonary blood flow also causes increased blood return to the left atrium, leading to left atrial enlargement. These mechanisms explain the patient's cardiomegaly, increased pulmonary vascular markings, failure to thrive (5th percentile weight), tachycardia, tachypnea, and sweating during feedings. Choice A (Anomalous pulmonary blood return): Total anomalous pulmonary venous return involves oxygenated blood returning to the right atrium instead of the left atrium and requires a second shunt. It does not present with a holosystolic murmur. Choice B (Increased peripheral vascular resistance) and Choice C (Increased systemic vascular resistance): These represent normal compensatory responses to decreased cardiac output to maintain peripheral perfusion pressure. They do not explain the holosystolic murmur or the patient's clinical presentation. Choice D (Intermittent supraventricular tachycardia): SVT presents with arrhythmias originating above the ventricles (e.g., multifocal atrial tachycardia, atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia) with narrow QRS complexes on ECG. A holosystolic murmur is not characteristic of this condition. Educational Objective: VSDs are common cardiac malformations resulting in left-to-right intracardiac shunts that may form in isolation or with other malformations. While the majority are asymptomatic and self-resolve, severe disease can progress to pulmonary hypertension and Eisenmenger syndrome if untreated.
Source: 3A #47
A 2-month-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. He is feeding well. Growth and development are appropriate for age. Immunizations are up-to-date. His vital signs are within normal limits. The lungs are clear to auscultation. A grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the lower left sternal border with radiation throughout the precordium. A systolic thrill is palpated at the lower left sternal border. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities. Femoral pulses are equal. An ECG shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the chest shows an enlarged left atrium. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Aortic stenosis B) Atrial septal defect C) Pulmonary valve stenosis D) Tetralogy of Fallot E) Ventricular septal defect
Correct Answer: E) Ventricular septal defect
Ventricular septal defects (VSD) are among the most common congenital heart malformations and may occur in isolation or in association with complex structural abnormalities. The genetic cause is heterogeneous and includes associations with syndromes such as Down, DiGeorge, or Holt-Oram syndrome, as well as isolated de novo mutations. VSDs are characterized by a holosystolic murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border with an associated palpable systolic thrill, as demonstrated in this patient. VSDs result in a left-to-right shunt, which increases pulmonary blood flow. This leads to remodeling of the pulmonary vasculature with smooth muscle hypertrophy and concentric narrowing of pulmonary arterioles, resulting in pulmonary arterial hypertension. If severe and progressive, increased right ventricular pressures and myocardial hypertrophy can reverse the shunt, causing shortness of breath and cyanosis. Increased pulmonary blood flow results in increased blood return to the left atrium, causing left atrial enlargement as seen on this patient's chest x-ray. Aortic stenosis (Choice A) presents with a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur best heard at the upper right sternal border radiating to the carotid arteries. It typically occurs secondary to age-related fibrotic and calcific changes but can occur earlier with bicuspid aortic valve or rheumatic heart disease. Atrial septal defect (Choice B) is a common congenital malformation resulting in a left-to-right shunt but typically presents with a fixed, widely split S2 caused by increased blood flow through the pulmonic valve, not a holosystolic murmur. Pulmonary valve stenosis (Choice C) presents with a systolic murmur best heard in the second left intercostal region that is crescendo-decrescendo in nature, quieter than aortic stenosis with less radiation. Tetralogy of Fallot (Choice D) consists of pulmonary infundibular stenosis, overriding aorta, VSD, and right ventricular hypertrophy, resulting in a right-to-left shunt with cyanosis first noted in infancy. While it includes a VSD component, this otherwise healthy patient without cyanosis or other findings more likely has an isolated VSD. Educational Objective: VSDs are common cardiac malformations resulting in a left-to-right intracardiac shunt that may form in isolation or with other malformations. The majority are asymptomatic and self-resolve, but severe disease can result in pulmonary hypertension and Eisenmenger syndrome if untreated.
Source: 9A #8
A 2-week-old female newborn is brought to the office for a well-child examination. She was born at term following spontaneous vaginal delivery to a 23-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1. Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. She was at the 50th percentile for weight at birth. Prior to discharge at 1 day of age, pulse oximetry on room air showed an oxygen saturation of 95%, and examination showed no abnormalities. The mother says the patient has been breast-feeding well every 2 to 3 hours. She has six to eight wet diapers and four stools daily. She receives no medications. Today, she is alert and appears to be in no distress. She is at the 55th percentile for length and weight and 50th percentile for head circumference. Her pulse is 148/min, respirations are 34/min, and blood pressure is 82/53 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 96%. On cardiac examination, a grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard best at the lower left sternal border. No diastolic murmurs are heard. S1 and S2 are normal. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following changes since birth is the most likely explanation for this patient's current cardiac findings? A. Closing of a ductus arteriosus B. Decreased pulmonary vascular resistance C. Increased pulmonary vascular resistance D. Increased systemic vascular resistance E. Opening of a ductus arteriosus
Correct Answer: B. Decreased pulmonary vascular resistance
This patient has a holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border, which is classic for a ventricular septal defect (VSD). The key to understanding why this murmur may not have been detected at birth but is now apparent at 2 weeks of life relates to changes in pulmonary vascular resistance during the transition from intrauterine to extrauterine life. At birth, as the pediatric lungs expand with air and physiologic venoarterial shunts close, pulmonary vascular resistance falls progressively over the first days to weeks of life. This decline in pulmonary vascular resistance increases left-to-right shunting across the VSD, allowing high-pressure blood flow from the left ventricle to the right ventricle, producing the audible holosystolic murmur. The murmur becomes more apparent as pulmonary vascular resistance continues to decrease. VSDs are among the most common congenital heart malformations, characterized by a holosystolic murmur best heard at the lower left sternal border and may have an associated palpable thrill. They result in a left-to-right shunt, which increases pulmonary blood flow and are acyanotic lesions. Up to 2% of newborns have a detectable VSD, most of which will close without intervention. VSDs should be evaluated by echocardiography to characterize the location, size, and hemodynamic effects of the lesions, which determines the need for repair or ongoing monitoring. Physiologic or isolated VSDs may close on their own or have no hemodynamic significance, in which case no specific treatment is needed, while large, hemodynamically significant defects may require surgical closure.
Source: 5A #28
A 1-month-old boy is brought for a well-child examination. He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy. Fifteen minutes after delivery, a very soft systolic murmur was heard along the left sternal border. He appears well today. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 76/54 mm Hg. He is at the 50th percentile for length and weight. A grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard best at the middle left sternal border. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely physiologic mechanism for the change in intensity of this patient's murmur? A) Closed ductus arteriosus B) Decreased pulmonary vascular resistance C) Improved atrial natriuretic factor functioning D) Improved myocardial contractility E) Increased circulating blood volume
Correct Answer: B) Decreased pulmonary vascular resistance
The correct answer is B. Decreased pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) most likely explains the increased intensity of this patient's holosystolic murmur, which is consistent with a ventricular septal defect (VSD). In fetal circulation, oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein is shunted from the right atrium to the left atrium via the foramen ovale, bypassing the fetal lungs. The fetal lungs are filled with amniotic fluid in utero, resulting in high pulmonary vascular resistance. This elevated PVR effectively prevents left-to-right shunting of blood from the left ventricle (LV) to the right ventricle (RV) through the VSD. At birth, amniotic fluid is cleared from the lungs and expands, causing the PVR to decrease dramatically over the first several weeks of life. As PVR decreases, the pressure gradient between the LV and RV increases, allowing blood to shunt left-to-right across the VSD during systole, producing the characteristic holosystolic murmur that becomes more prominent as PVR continues to drop. Choice A is incorrect. While the ductus arteriosus normally closes within several days of delivery in healthy newborns, continued patency produces a continuous 'machinery' murmur, not a holosystolic murmur. Choice C is incorrect. Atrial natriuretic factor (ANF) is a substance released by the atria in response to increased circulating volume to induce natriuresis in the kidneys. It does not explain changes in murmur intensity or severity. Choice D is incorrect. Improved myocardial contractility would increase contractility equally in both ventricles and would not create a sufficient pressure gradient between the LV and RV to explain the change in murmur intensity. Choice E is incorrect. While large VSDs may eventually cause right ventricular overload and right heart failure with volume overload later in life, increased circulating blood volume alone does not account for the acute change in murmur intensity observed in this patient. Educational Objective: In fetal circulation, elevated pulmonary vascular resistance prevents left-to-right shunting through a VSD from the LV to the RV. At birth, the rapid physiologic decrease in PVR creates a substantial pressure gradient between the two ventricles, allowing development of a left-to-right shunt and producing an audible holosystolic murmur. The continued gradual decrease in PVR over the following weeks and months accounts for the progressive increase in murmur intensity.
Source: 7A #38
A 10-year-old girl is brought to the physician for her first well-child examination. She was recently adopted from an orphanage in Eastern Europe. Her parents were informed that she has an unrepaired congenital heart defect, but further details are not available. Growth and development are appropriate for age. Her pulse is 96/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 102/66 mm Hg in the right upper extremity and 114/72 mm Hg in the right lower extremity. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 93%. Cardiac examination shows a hyperdynamic precordium with a right ventricular impulse. There is a loud, narrowly split S2. A grade 2/6 early to mid-systolic murmur is heard over the lower left sternal border. The liver edge is palpated 2 cm below the right costal margin. Brachial and femoral pulses are normal. An ECG shows right ventricular hypertrophy. The most likely mechanism of this patient's condition is an increase in which of the following? A) Central venous pressure B) Left ventricular end-diastolic pressure C) Pulmonary vascular resistance D) Systemic cardiac output E) Systemic vascular resistance
Correct Answer: C) Pulmonary vascular resistance
This patient presents with clinical and laboratory findings consistent with a ventricular septal defect (VSD) with secondary pulmonary hypertension. VSDs are among the most common congenital heart malformations and can occur in isolation or as part of genetic syndromes such as DiGeorge syndrome, Down syndrome, or Holt-Oram syndrome. VSDs are characterized by a holosystolic murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border, sometimes with an associated palpable thrill. The defect results in a left-to-right shunt, which increases pulmonary blood flow. This chronic volume overload leads to remodeling of the pulmonary vasculature with smooth muscle hypertrophy and concentric narrowing of the pulmonary arterioles. This results in increased pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) and pulmonary arterial hypertension. Persistent elevation of PVR causes increased right ventricular afterload, leading to right ventricular hypertrophy and myocardial remodeling (evident on ECG). The narrowly split S2 reflects the timing of pulmonary valve closure as the right ventricle takes longer to eject. The right ventricular heave (hyperdynamic precordium with right ventricular impulse) and hepatomegaly (2 cm below costal margin) are signs of right heart failure secondary to the increased PVR. The patient's borderline oxygen saturation (93% on room air) suggests possible shunt reversal (Eisenmenger syndrome), which develops when uncorrected VSDs allow right-sided pressures to eventually exceed left-sided pressures. Choice A (Central venous pressure): While central venous pressure may be secondarily elevated due to right-sided heart failure from pulmonary hypertension, this is a consequence rather than the primary mechanism. The CVP elevation would be secondary to increased PVR. Choice B (Left ventricular end-diastolic pressure): LVEDP is initially decreased in VSDs as blood shunts left-to-right. As pulmonary hypertension develops and right-sided pressures increase, shunt reversal eventually occurs and LVEDP may increase, but all these changes are secondary to increased PVR. Choice D (Systemic cardiac output): Systemic cardiac output is not the primary mechanism. While left heart stroke volume may be reduced due to shunting to the right side, this is compensated by increased heart rate to maintain overall cardiac output. Additionally, increased preload from the volume-overloaded right heart partially offsets this decrease. Choice E (Systemic vascular resistance): SVR may increase secondarily in response to decreased cardiac output or hypoxia but does not cause the pathophysiology seen in this patient. The primary problem is pulmonary, not systemic, vascular resistance. Educational Objective: VSDs cause left-to-right shunting and increased pulmonary blood flow, which leads to progressive pulmonary hypertension from pulmonary vascular remodeling. The resulting increase in pulmonary vascular resistance causes right ventricular hypertrophy, narrowly split S2, right ventricular heave, and right heart failure signs such as hepatomegaly. If uncorrected, severe increases in right-sided pressures can lead to shunt reversal and cyanosis (Eisenmenger syndrome).
▶ Endocrine System Congenital hypothyroidism 5 questions
Source: 6A #47
A 2-week-old girl is brought for her first well-child examination. Newborn screening showed an increased thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentration. Her mother takes propylthiouracil for hyperthyroidism. The patient is active and eating well. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient? A) Reassurance and follow-up examination in 1 month B) Measurement of serum growth hormone concentration C) Measurement of serum thyroid-binding globulin concentration D) Measurement of serum thyroxine (T4) and TSH concentrations E) Thyroid scan F) Levothyroxine therapy
Correct Answer: D) Measurement of serum thyroxine (T4) and TSH concentrations
In this patient with elevated TSH at birth in the context of maternal antithyroid medication use (propylthiouracil), repeat serum measurement of T4 and TSH concentrations is the most appropriate next step. Elevated TSH in newborns can result from either transient congenital hypothyroidism (caused by placental transmission of maternal antithyroid medication or iodine deficiency) or congenital primary hypothyroidism (from embryological thyroid dysgenesis or defective thyroid hormone synthesis). Congenital hypothyroidism is typically asymptomatic at birth due to placental transfer of maternal thyroid hormone, but if left untreated can manifest with lethargy, hypothermia, feeding problems, hoarse cry, myxedematous facies, macroglossia, hypotonia, umbilical hernia, prolonged jaundice, dry skin, and intellectual disability in childhood. Thyroid function in newborns typically recovers from maternal antithyroid medication within 2 weeks, making repeat serum testing at 2 weeks after birth essential to distinguish between transient and primary hypothyroidism. If persistent hypothyroidism is confirmed (decreased T4 with elevated TSH), thyroid scans and thyroid-binding globulin measurements help determine the etiology. Choice A (Reassurance and follow-up in 1 month) is inappropriate because elevated TSH of unclear etiology requires prompt investigation to prevent long-term neurological disability. Choice B (Growth hormone measurement) would be indicated for central hypothyroidism with suspected pituitary insufficiency, but elevated TSH indicates primary thyroid dysfunction. Choice C (Thyroid-binding globulin measurement) and Choice E (Thyroid scan) may ultimately be needed to elucidate the cause of hypothyroidism but should only be ordered after confirming persistent hypothyroidism with repeat T4/TSH testing. Choice F (Levothyroxine therapy) may be necessary if repeat testing confirms persistent hypothyroidism, but initiating treatment without confirming the diagnosis would be inappropriate if transient hypothyroidism resolves spontaneously. Educational Objective: Congenital hypothyroidism requires early detection and differentiation between transient (secondary to maternal antithyroid medications) and primary (from thyroid dysgenesis or hormone synthesis defects) etiologies. Repeat serum T4 and TSH measurement at 2 weeks of life allows confirmation of persistent hypothyroidism before initiating levothyroxine therapy and determines whether further diagnostic testing is warranted.
Source: 9A #48
A 5-day-old male infant is brought to the physician by his mother after his newborn screening results become available. His mother reports that he breast-feeds every 4 to 5 hours and that he seems to sleep much more than her 2-year-old nephew slept at the same age. The patient passes one stool every other day. His temperature is 35.8°C (96.4°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 55/30 mm Hg. Results of newborn screening show: Test Result Normal Range Hemoglobinopathy FAS FA Biotinidase (U/L) 20 >16 Serum thyroxine (T4) (µg/dL) 13 >7 Serum galactose (mg/dL) 12 <15 Immunoreactive trypsin (µg/L) 76 <120 Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Reassure the mother that these findings are normal for a breast-fed newborn B) Inform the mother that the patient is a carrier of cystic fibrosis C) Advise the mother to discontinue breast-feeding D) Measure serum thyroxine (T4) and thyroid-stimulating hormone concentrations at this visit E) Measure serum thyroxine (T4) and thyroid-stimulating hormone concentrations in 2 months F) Begin prophylactic penicillin therapy
Correct Answer: D) Measure serum thyroxine (T4) and thyroid-stimulating hormone concentrations at this visit
This infant is presenting with signs and symptoms of congenital hypothyroidism. The clinical presentation includes lethargy (sleeping much more than expected), constipation (one stool every other day), and hypothermia (35.8°C). The newborn screening shows decreased serum T4 (13 µg/dL, which is below the normal range of >7 but concerning given the clinical context). The most appropriate next step in management is immediate measurement of serum thyroxine (T4) and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) concentrations at this visit to confirm the diagnosis. Congenital hypothyroidism commonly presents in the first few months of life with symptoms including feeding difficulties, lethargy, constipation, myxedematous facies, macroglossia, large fontanelles, hypotonia, and hypothermia. Thyroid dysfunction can be caused by thyroid dysgenesis, resistance to TSH, abnormalities in thyroid hormone transport, iodine deficiency, maternal antibodies, or antithyroid medications. Early diagnosis and treatment is critical as congenital hypothyroidism is one of the most preventable causes of intellectual disability. Management includes oral levothyroxine. Choice A is incorrect: Reassuring the mother that these findings are normal for a breast-fed newborn is inappropriate. The patient has decreased serum T4 and clinical symptoms concerning for hypothyroidism, requiring further evaluation. Choice B is incorrect: While the immunoreactive trypsin is slightly elevated at 76 µg/L (normal <120), this is not diagnostic of cystic fibrosis. The pertinent findings are the decreased serum T4 and clinical symptoms of hypothyroidism. Choice C is incorrect: Discontinuing breast-feeding is not appropriate. Breast-feeding provides optimal nutrition and maternal antibodies. The clinical concern is thyroid dysfunction, not a contraindication to breast-feeding. Further thyroid evaluation is needed. Choice E is incorrect: Waiting 2 months to measure thyroid function is inappropriate. Prompt diagnosis and treatment of congenital hypothyroidism is essential to prevent intellectual disability. These measurements should be obtained at this visit. Choice F is incorrect: Prophylactic penicillin therapy is not indicated. This infant does not have findings consistent with infection or a condition requiring penicillin prophylaxis. The clinical presentation is consistent with congenital hypothyroidism. Educational Objective: Recognize the clinical presentation of congenital hypothyroidism (lethargy, constipation, hypothermia, decreased T4) and understand that prompt confirmation with TSH and T4 measurements at the time of diagnosis is critical to initiate early treatment and prevent intellectual disability.
Source: 4A #11
A 2-month-old infant has a large posterior fontanelle, a large tongue, and hypotonia. He was born at 38 weeks' gestation; pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. Apgar scores were 7 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of disease? A) Anterior horn cell degeneration B) Connective tissue disorder C) Cortical dysfunction D) Electrolyte imbalance E) Myopathy F) Peripheral neuropathy G) Spinal cord dysfunction H) Thyroid dysfunction
Correct Answer: H) Thyroid dysfunction
Congenital hypothyroidism is the correct diagnosis. Congenital thyroid dysfunction that leads to hypothyroidism is typically asymptomatic at birth because maternal thyroid hormone crosses the placenta, keeping the newborn in a euthyroid state. However, congenital hypothyroidism commonly presents in the first few months of life with the classic triad of findings seen in this patient: macroglossia (large tongue), large fontanelles, and hypotonia. Additional presentations include feeding difficulties, lethargy, constipation, myxedematous facies, and hypothermia. Thyroid dysfunction can result from thyroid dysgenesis, resistance to thyroid-stimulating hormone, abnormalities in thyroid hormone transport, iodine deficiency, maternal antibodies, or antithyroid medications. Early diagnosis via routine newborn screening is critical, as treatment with thyroid hormone supplementation (levothyroxine) prevents intellectual disability and neurologic complications such as hearing loss and ataxia. Incorrect answers: - Choice A (Anterior horn cell degeneration): Seen in spinal muscular atrophy, which presents with weakness, weak cry, feeding difficulties, and respiratory failure—not the constellation of findings in this case. - Choice B (Connective tissue disorder): Conditions like Ehlers-Danlos and Marfan syndrome manifest later with hyperflexibility, skin elasticity, or tall stature; they are not associated with macroglossia or large fontanelles at 2 months. - Choice C (Cortical dysfunction): Would present more broadly with intellectual disability, developmental delay, and neuromuscular abnormalities such as unilateral weakness or spastic paralysis. - Choice D (Electrolyte imbalance): Can cause cardiac irritability, skeletal abnormalities, altered mental status, or neuromuscular weakness, but would not present with large posterior fontanelle and macroglossia. - Choice E (Myopathy): Congenital myopathies present with muscle weakness and may include respiratory failure or scoliosis, but not the characteristic large fontanelle and macroglossia seen here. - Choice F (Peripheral neuropathy): Typically presents with paresthesias, numbness, or weakness in extremities; would not cause large fontanelle or macroglossia. - Choice G (Spinal cord dysfunction): Could cause weakness, numbness, or autonomic instability, but would be unlikely to cause anatomic changes superior to the area of dysfunction such as macroglossia and large fontanelle. Educational Objective: Recognize that congenital hypothyroidism presents in the first few months of life with feeding difficulties, lethargy, constipation, myxedematous facies, macroglossia, large fontanelles, and hypotonia. Early identification through newborn screening and treatment with thyroid hormone supplementation are essential to prevent long-term neurologic and developmental complications.
Source: 8A #27
A 2-month-old boy is brought to the physician for an initial examination because of persistent jaundice. He is described as a "good" baby, who breast-feeds reasonably well but often needs to be awakened to feed. Examination shows an umbilical hernia, mild jaundice, and cool extremities. Growth is appropriate for age. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Karyotype analysis B) Measurement of sweat chloride concentration C) Thyroid function tests D) CT scan of the head E) CT scan of the liver
Correct Answer: C) Thyroid function tests
Congenital hypothyroidism typically presents without symptoms in the neonatal period due to placental crossing of maternal thyroid hormone. However, if left untreated, infants develop characteristic findings including lethargy, hypothermia, feeding problems, hoarse cry, myxedematous facies, macroglossia, hypotonia, umbilical hernia, prolonged jaundice (caused by impaired feeding and decreased bilirubin conjugation), and dry skin. Intellectual disability in childhood may develop if untreated. This 2-month-old presents with persistent jaundice, requires awakening for feeds (lethargy), cool extremities (hypothermia), and umbilical hernia—all classic signs of congenital hypothyroidism. Diagnosis requires evaluation of thyroid function tests, which typically show increased TSH and decreased thyroxine (T4) concentrations. In patients with decreased thyroid hormone concentrations on serum testing, thyroid scans and thyroid-binding globulin concentrations help elucidate the cause of hypothyroidism (e.g., distinguishing between thyroid dysgenesis and defective thyroid hormone synthesis). Management requires proactive newborn screening and levothyroxine therapy. Choice A (Karyotype analysis) would be helpful in diagnosing chromosomal diseases such as Turner syndrome, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, or trisomy 21, which do not fit this clinical presentation. Choice B (Measurement of sweat chloride concentration) is used in the diagnosis of cystic fibrosis, a hereditary chloride channelopathy resulting in thickened bronchial and gastrointestinal mucous secretions, leading to chronic infection, inflammation, and malabsorption. This clinical presentation is not consistent with cystic fibrosis. Choice D (CT scan of the head) can help evaluate structural brain abnormalities such as intracranial hemorrhage or congenital malformations but has no role in diagnosing congenital hypothyroidism. Choice E (CT scan of the liver) would not be helpful in evaluating congenital hypothyroidism. Jaundice secondary to biliary obstruction can be evaluated with ultrasonography of the right upper quadrant of the abdomen. Educational Objective: Congenital hypothyroidism in infants presents with lethargy, hypothermia, feeding problems, hoarse cry, myxedematous facies, macroglossia, hypotonia, umbilical hernia, prolonged jaundice caused by impaired feeding and decreased bilirubin conjugation, and dry skin. Evaluation of thyroid function tests is necessary for early diagnosis and treatment to prevent complications and intellectual disability.
Source: 4A #30
A 3-month-old infant is inactive and slow in feeding and has constipation. Her serum thyroxine (T4) concentration is decreased and serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration is increased. Which of the following is the most likely cause? A) Deficiency in T4-binding globulin B) Hypopituitarism C) Lymphocytic thyroiditis D) Thyroid dysgenesis E) Unresponsiveness to thyroid hormone
Correct Answer: D) Thyroid dysgenesis
Thyroid dysgenesis involves the underdevelopment or complete absence of thyroid tissue and is the most common cause of congenital hypothyroidism. It is commonly caused by mutations in PAX8, encoding a paired box transcription factor crucial for proper embryologic development of thyroid tissue. Paired box transcription factors are essential for proper tissue development throughout the body, and mutations in paired box genes cause various diseases including Waardenburg syndrome, aniridia, ocular coloboma, optic nerve hypoplasia, oligodontia, and kidney hypoplasia. Thyroid dysgenesis presents in infancy with classic symptoms of hypothyroidism including lethargy, poor feeding, and constipation. The characteristic laboratory pattern shows increased serum TSH concentration with decreased or absent serum thyroid hormone concentrations, reflecting primary thyroid failure with appropriate pituitary response. Choice A (Deficiency in T4-binding globulin) is a rare inherited condition that is usually asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on thyroid laboratory studies. It does not cause symptomatic hypothyroidism. Choice B (Hypopituitarism) may cause secondary hypothyroidism due to inadequate TSH production. However, TSH concentrations would be decreased in this scenario, which contradicts the patient's laboratory findings of elevated TSH. Choice C (Lymphocytic thyroiditis/Hashimoto disease) is the most common form of thyroiditis in the general population but primarily affects middle-aged women. Although teens and rarely children can be affected, Hashimoto disease is extremely rare in infancy, making thyroid dysgenesis the more likely diagnosis in this age group. Choice E (Unresponsiveness to thyroid hormone) is a rare disorder characterized by peripheral tissue unresponsiveness to thyroid hormone receptor binding. Serum T4 concentrations are characteristically increased (not decreased) to overcome tissue unresponsiveness, which does not match this patient's presentation. Educational Objective: Recognize thyroid dysgenesis as the most common cause of congenital hypothyroidism presenting in infancy with lethargy, poor feeding, and constipation. Understand the characteristic laboratory findings of primary hypothyroidism (elevated TSH with decreased thyroid hormone) and differentiate from secondary hypothyroidism and other thyroid conditions.
▶ Renal Urinary System Poststreptococcal Glomerulonephritis 5 questions
Source: 3A #29
An 11-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 1-day history of lethargy, mild abdominal pain, and dark urine. He had a sore throat and an upper respiratory tract infection 10 days ago that resolved spontaneously. His pulse is 90/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Examination shows slight swelling around the eyes. Urinalysis shows light brown urine with RBC and granular casts. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism for these findings? A) Antigen-antibody immune complex B) Bacterial infiltration of the basement membrane C) Bacterial infiltration of the epithelial cells D) Destruction of tubular epithelial cells E) Renal ischemia
Correct Answer: A) Antigen-antibody immune complex
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is a type of nephritic syndrome that presents with peripheral and periorbital edema, dark-colored urine (due to hematuria), hypertension, acute kidney injury, and proteinuria following infection with Streptococcus pyogenes (group A). The pathogenesis of PSGN involves streptococcal antigens complexing with antibodies to form immune complexes that deposit in the glomerular basement membrane. This triggers complement activation and inflammatory responses, with neutrophilic infiltration of the glomerular tuft. The typical urinalysis findings include granular (muddy brown) casts and RBCs, consistent with this patient's presentation. Choice B and C are incorrect because PSGN does not involve direct bacterial infiltration of the basement membrane or epithelial cells; rather, it is an immune-mediated process. Choice D describes acute tubular necrosis (ATN), which involves destruction of tubular epithelial cells and occurs following ischemic or nephrotoxic injury. Choice E (renal ischemia) may be a precipitant of ATN but is not the primary mechanism in PSGN. Management of PSGN is primarily supportive, focusing on treating complications such as volume overload and hypertension with diuretics and antihypertensive medications, with kidney replacement therapy reserved for severe cases.
Source: 4A #12
An 18-year-old man has had nausea, fatigue, and periorbital swelling for 4 days; the swelling is worse in the morning. He had tonsillitis 2 weeks ago that resolved after treatment with penicillin. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 170/95 mm Hg. There is periorbital edema bilaterally and trace ankle edema. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Serum Urea nitrogen: 60 mg/dL Serum Creatinine: 4 mg/dL Urine Protein: 1+ Urine WBC: few Urine RBC: many RBC casts: 1/hpf Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Acute renal failure B) Biventricular heart failure C) Cirrhosis of the liver D) Inferior vena cava obstruction E) Nephrotic syndrome
Correct Answer: A) Acute renal failure
This patient presents with acute renal failure following a tonsillar infection, consistent with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), a nephritic syndrome. PSGN typically occurs 2-4 weeks following an acute infection with Streptococcus pyogenes (group A), commonly presenting after impetigo, streptococcal pharyngitis, or tonsillitis. Importantly, appropriate antibiotic treatment of the streptococcal infection does not reduce the likelihood of developing PSGN. The pathophysiology involves a Type III hypersensitivity reaction with kidney deposition of immune complexes and complement activation. Clinical presentation includes dark-colored urine, hypertension, and peripheral/periorbital edema. Laboratory findings reveal elevated serum creatinine (4 mg/dL) and BUN (60 mg/dL) indicating renal dysfunction, with urinalysis showing hematuria, proteinuria, and characteristically RBC casts. Kidney biopsy (diagnostic gold standard) shows enlarged glomeruli on light microscopy, bumpy irregularity of the glomerular basement membrane on immunofluorescence, and subepithelial immune complex deposits on electron microscopy. Treatment is supportive, including diuretics and antihypertensive agents. Biventricular heart failure (Choice B) may occur in severe myocarditis or rheumatic heart disease but would not cause hematuria and RBC casts characteristic of nephritic syndrome. Cirrhosis of the liver (Choice C) is caused by alcoholic and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and presents with ascites, anasarca, jaundice, elevated transaminases, decreased albumin, and impaired hepatic synthetic function. It does not develop following streptococcal infections and does not typically present with hypertension or hematuria. Inferior vena cava obstruction (Choice D) prevents venous drainage from lower body regions, typically associated with underlying malignancy, thrombosis from indwelling catheters, or compression by a gravid uterus. This patient lacks historical features suggestive of IVC obstruction. Nephrotic syndrome (Choice E) presents with proteinuria, edema, hyperlipidemia, and hypercoagulability. PSGN is primarily a nephritic process resulting in mild, sub-nephrotic range proteinuria, not true nephrotic syndrome. Educational Objective: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis causes acute renal failure 2-4 weeks following Group A Streptococcus infection (impetigo, pharyngitis, tonsillitis). Patients present with dark urine, hypertension, periorbital and peripheral edema, elevated creatinine/BUN, and characteristic RBC casts on urinalysis.
Source: 5A #35
A 10-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of swelling of the eyelids and feet for 3 days. Over the past week, she has had decreased urinary frequency. Two weeks ago, she had a sore throat that resolved spontaneously. Her temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 140/85 mm Hg. Examination shows periorbital, pretibial, and pedal edema. Urinalysis shows pH 6, specific gravity 1.015, blood large, protein 3+, RBC too numerous to count, WBC 5-10/hpf, and RBC casts 10-20/hpf. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the hypertension? A) Catecholamine excess B) Idiopathic hypertension C) Mineralocorticoid excess D) Stimulation of the parasympathetic system E) Volume overload
Correct Answer: E) Volume overload
This clinical presentation is consistent with acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (APSGN), a type of nephritic syndrome characterized by dark-colored urine, hypertension, acute kidney injury, hematuria, and proteinuria following infection with group A streptococcus. The key features present in this case include: a recent streptococcal throat infection (2 weeks prior), periorbial/pretibial/pedal edema, hypertension, decreased urinary frequency, and urinalysis findings of hematuria (RBCs too numerous to count), proteinuria (3+), and RBC casts. Glomerular injury involves immune complex formation in the glomerulus with C3 and IgG deposits on light microscopy. The hypertension in APSGN is caused by salt and fluid retention resulting in volume overload. This fluid retention leads to generalized edema and can cause complications such as heart failure, pulmonary edema, and respiratory distress. Choice A (Catecholamine excess) occurs in pheochromocytoma, presenting with episodic headaches, sweating, palpitations, tremors, agitation, tachycardia, and tachypnea, but would not cause hematuria and proteinuria. Choice B (Idiopathic hypertension) is a diagnosis of exclusion when no underlying cause is identified; however, this patient has a clear preceding cause—poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Choice C (Mineralocorticoid excess) occurs in hyperaldosteronism with increased aldosterone secretion from adrenal adenoma or hyperplasia, presenting with hypertension, normal or decreased potassium, and metabolic alkalosis. It would not present with hematuria and proteinuria characteristic of nephritic syndrome. Choice D (Parasympathetic stimulation) results in cholinergic toxicity with excessive salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, and altered mental status. Increased sympathetic (not parasympathetic) activation causes hypertension; parasympathetic stimulation would not cause the hypertension seen here. Educational Objective: Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is a nephritic syndrome occurring after group A streptococcal infection. Hypertension in APSGN results from salt and fluid retention causing volume overload, not from endocrine dysfunction or sympathetic activation.
Source: 8A #17
A 12-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 6-day history of occasional headache, fatigue, and poor appetite and a 2-day history of brown urine. She vomited yesterday morning but has not had abdominal pain, diarrhea, or painful urination. Her father reports that she had a sore throat and fever 2 weeks ago that resolved spontaneously. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her growth and development have been appropriate for age. She appears mildly pale but is in no distress. She is at the 50th percentile for height and 75th percentile for weight. Her temperature is 36.7°C (98°F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 138/88 mm Hg. The pharynx is erythematous, but no exudate is present. The lungs are clear to auscultation. On cardiac examination, a grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur is heard; there is no rub or gallop. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities. The extremities are warm; there is 1+ edema. Laboratory studies show: Serum Na+ 132 mEq/L, K+ 5.2 mEq/L, Cl- 100 mEq/L, HCO3- 15 mEq/L, Urea nitrogen 42 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL. Urine pH 5, Specific gravity 1.020, Blood 2+, Protein 1+, RBC casts too numerous to count, Gram stain no organisms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Serum C3 concentration B) Serum antinuclear antibody assay C) Urine culture D) Echocardiography E) Renal ultrasonography
Correct Answer: A) Serum C3 concentration
Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is a type of nephritic syndrome characterized by dark-colored urine, hypertension, acute kidney injury, hematuria, and proteinuria following an infection with group A streptococcus. The pathogenesis of PSGN involves streptococcal antigens complexing with antibodies, deposition of immune complexes in the glomerular basement membrane, and triggering of complement activation and inflammation. Light microscopy shows deposits of C3 and IgG in the glomerulus and mesangium. The deposition of C3 in the glomerulus and mesangium leads to decreased concentrations of serum C3, making this the most appropriate diagnostic test. Urinalysis shows hematuria and variable proteinuria, with or without red blood cell casts. Hypertension associated with PSGN is caused by salt and fluid retention resulting in volume overload. Fluid retention can lead to generalized edema including periorbital, pretibial, and pedal edema, and can lead to complications involving heart failure, pulmonary edema, and respiratory distress. Choice B (Serum antinuclear antibody assay): Shows increased antinuclear antibodies in many autoimmune and inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus but is neither sensitive nor specific for PSGN. Choice C (Urine culture): While urinalysis can be helpful in the diagnosis of acute PSGN, demonstrating hematuria and proteinuria, a urine culture would not be helpful. A urine culture can help in the diagnosis of urinary tract infections such as cystitis or pyelonephritis. Choice D (Echocardiography): Can evaluate for the presence of heart failure, which is another potential complication of streptococcal pharyngitis in the setting of rheumatic heart disease. However, this patient's lungs are clear to auscultation, indicating heart failure is less likely as a cause of her apparent hypervolemic state. Choice E (Renal ultrasonography): Can help with the diagnosis of diseases that alter the size, shape, or tissue of kidneys, such as cysts in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, tumors, abscesses, or urinary tract obstructions. Immune complex deposition in acute PSGN is a microscopic change seen on light microscopy, not ultrasonography of the kidneys. Educational Objective: Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is a type of nephritic syndrome characterized by dark-colored urine, hypertension, hematuria, and proteinuria following an infection with group A streptococcus. Immune complex deposition within the glomerulus and mesangium leads to decreased concentrations of serum C3.
Source: 9A #12
A 9-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother because of a 2-day history of generalized swelling, especially around her eyes. This morning, she also had one episode of bloody urine. Two weeks ago, she had a sore throat, fever, and nonproductive cough that resolved spontaneously after 3 days. She has no history of serious illness and receives no medications. Her temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 154/88 mm Hg (systolic: above the 90th percentile for age and height). Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 96%. Examination shows mild, diffuse edema and moderate periorbital edema. Basilar crackles are heard in the posterior aspect of the lungs. An S3 gallop is heard. Urinalysis is most likely to show which of the following findings? A) Increased protein, eosinophils, cellular casts B) Increased protein, red blood cells, brownish granular casts C) Increased protein, red blood cells, red blood cell casts D) Minimal protein, red blood cells, red blood cell casts E) Minimal protein, white blood cells, cellular casts
Correct Answer: C) Increased protein, red blood cells, red blood cell casts
This patient presenting with periorbital edema and hematuria following a sore throat and upper respiratory infection 2 weeks prior has poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). PSGN is a type III (immune complex-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction that occurs because of antibody formation against group A streptococcus proteins after acute infection. Inflammatory deposition of the antibody-antigen complex into the glomeruli results in damage to the glomerular filtration barrier, allowing abnormal passage of protein and red blood cells into the urine. The clinical presentation of periorbital edema, pulmonary edema (evidenced by basilar crackles and S3 gallop), and hypertension confirms significant proteinuria and active glomerulonephritis. PSGN is characterized by the presence of increased protein, red blood cells, and red blood cell (RBC) casts in the urine. Antibiotic treatment of the initial streptococcal infection does not fully prevent PSGN but may decrease its risk. Choice A (eosinophils, cellular casts) is incorrect as this pattern is characteristic of acute interstitial nephritis, which typically follows allergic exposure to medications such as NSAIDs, beta-lactam antibiotics, or proton pump inhibitors, not streptococcal infection. Choice B (brownish granular casts) is incorrect as this pattern is characteristic of acute tubular necrosis, which follows nephrotoxic or ischemic events such as shock, rhabdomyolysis, or nephrotoxic drugs, not post-infectious glomerulonephritis. Choice D (minimal protein) is incorrect. While some mild presentations of PSGN may show only minimal proteinuria, this patient's significant periorbital and pulmonary edema indicates severe proteinuria, not minimal protein loss. Choice E (white blood cells, cellular casts) is incorrect as this pattern is characteristic of pyelonephritis, kidney parenchymal infection, which would not result in significant proteinuria or the edema and pulmonary manifestations seen in this patient.
▶ Endocrine System Diabetic ketoacidosis 5 questions
Source: 7A #28
A 12-year-old girl has had cramping abdominal pain, nausea, and four episodes of vomiting over the past 24 hours. Over the past 2 months, she has been drinking large quantities of fluids and has had urinary frequency; she has had a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight loss during this period. She appears tired but is alert and answers questions appropriately. There is diffuse abdominal tenderness and a fruity odor to her breath. Which of the following is the most likely additional finding in this patient? A) Exophthalmos B) Hypertension C) Increased tidal volume D) Neutropenia E) Thrombocytopenia
Correct Answer: C) Increased tidal volume
This patient with nausea, abdominal pain, and a fruity odor to her breath has a presentation consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). DKA occurs most commonly in the setting of type 1 diabetes mellitus and may be the initial presentation in a patient who has not yet been diagnosed. It is caused by accumulation of serum ketones such as beta-hydroxybutyric acid, acetoacetic acid, and acetone in the setting of insulin deficiency or acute catabolic stressors such as infection. Dysregulated fatty acid degradation and ketone synthesis occurs because of the relative state of starvation created by absent insulin signaling. Patients with DKA may present with fatigue, polyuria, polydipsia, shortness of breath or tachypnea, and diffuse abdominal discomfort. Vital signs may show tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypotension due to severe hypovolemia, which occurs secondary to osmotic diuresis from hyperglycemia. Kussmaul respiration, a rapid and deep breathing pattern, is a classic physical examination finding due to respiratory compensation for the underlying metabolic acidosis. This increased depth and rate of respiration results in increased tidal volume. Patients may demonstrate physical examination signs of hypovolemia (eg, dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor) along with a sweet breath odor secondary to ketones. Laboratory analysis typically show increased serum glucose and ketones, metabolic acidosis, and a high anion-gap due to the accumulation of unmeasured anions in serum. A metabolic acidosis is accompanied by a decreased bicarbonate concentration in the serum, as bicarbonate is consumed in the neutralization of increased acidic molecules (hydrogen ions) in the blood. Choice A (Exophthalmos) is classically seen in association with hyperthyroidism secondary to Graves disease. In addition to exophthalmos, patients with hyperthyroidism may experience weight loss, tachycardia, and tremors. Polyuria, polydipsia, and a fruity odor to the breath would not be expected in a patient with hyperthyroidism. Choice B (Hypertension) would not be expected in this patient. Patients with DKA may be hypotensive due to volume depletion in the setting of osmotic diuresis. Choice D (Neutropenia) and Choice E (Thrombocytopenia) would not be expected in this patient. Patients with DKA may have a normal white blood cell count, or it may be increased due to an underlying infection or demargination. Platelet count can be normal or may be slightly increased as it is an acute phase reactant. Initial management of DKA should focus on volume repletion with isotonic fluids, which is crucial to hemodynamically stabilize the patient, restore tissue perfusion, and clear ketones. Volume repletion should be followed by insulin, correction of electrolyte abnormalities, and treatment of any precipitating conditions. Educational Objective: Diabetic ketoacidosis occurs most often in the setting of type 1 diabetes mellitus and may be the initial presentation in an otherwise undiagnosed patient. Patients may present with nausea, vomiting, vague abdominal pain, polyuria, and polydipsia. Laboratory evaluation will show a metabolic acidosis with high anion gap. Treatment includes volume resuscitation and electrolyte management followed by intravenous insulin.
Source: 4A #50
A 4-year-old boy has had fatigue, decreased appetite, and a 2.3-kg (5-lb) weight loss over the past 2 months. He appears listless. His pulse is 80/min while supine and 105/min while standing, and his blood pressure is 85/60 mm Hg while supine and 75/45 mm Hg while standing. Serum glucose concentration is 465 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows 3+ ketones, 4+ glucose, and 1 to 2 WBC/hpf. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Urine culture B) Oral glucose tolerance test C) Measurement of hemoglobin A1c D) Administration of insulin, subcutaneously E) Administration of 0.9% saline, intravenously
Correct Answer: E) Administration of 0.9% saline, intravenously
This pediatric patient presents with classic findings of type 1 diabetes mellitus complicated by diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). The clinical features include fatigue, decreased appetite, weight loss, hyperglycemia (glucose 465 mg/dL), ketonuria (3+ ketones), and glucosuria (4+ glucose). Critically, the patient demonstrates orthostatic vital signs with a pulse increase of 25/min and systolic blood pressure decrease of 10 mm Hg from supine to standing position, indicating significant dehydration. DKA results from deficient insulin signaling, leading to dysregulated fatty acid degradation, ketone accumulation, and osmotic diuresis. The osmotic diuresis from hyperglycemia and glucosuria causes significant fluid losses, resulting in dehydration and orthostatic hypotension. In the acute management of DKA, fluid resuscitation with intravenous isotonic saline is the first priority before other interventions. Choice A (Urine culture) is incorrect because urinary tract infection is unlikely without symptoms of dysuria, urgency, or frequency. The urinalysis findings of ketones and glucose are consistent with DKA, not infection (WBC count <5-10/hpf). Choice B (Oral glucose tolerance test) is inappropriate as this test is used to evaluate type 2 diabetes or gestational diabetes, not acute DKA. A random glucose >200 mg/dL with associated symptoms already establishes the diabetes diagnosis. Choice C (Hemoglobin A1c) is useful for diagnosis and long-term management of diabetes but is not the immediate priority in acute DKA management. Choice D (Subcutaneous insulin) may eventually be necessary, but insulin administration should be intravenous and only after appropriate fluid resuscitation has begun. In a dehydrated, orthostatic patient, intravenous fluid resuscitation must be the first intervention. Educational Objective: Type 1 diabetes mellitus and diabetic ketoacidosis cause significant dehydration through hyperglycemia-induced osmotic diuresis. The first step in acute DKA management is intravenous fluid resuscitation with isotonic saline to correct hypovolemia and restore perfusion.
Source: 3A #37
A 9-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department because of lethargy, labored breathing, and seven episodes of vomiting over the past 6 hours. Her skin is flushed and warm and she appears severely dehydrated. There is a fruity odor to her breath. She is at the 75th percentile for height and 25th percentile for weight. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Capillary refill time is 4 seconds, and capillary blood glucose concentration is greater than 500 mg/dl. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management? A) Intravenous administration of 20 ml/kg of 5% dextrose in water B) Intravenous administration of 20 ml/kg of 0.9% saline C) Intravenous administration of 20 ml/kg of lactated Ringer solution with 40 mEq/L of potassium chloride D) Intravenous administration of 0.1 U/h of regular insulin E) Continuous intravenous administration of 0.1 U/h of regular insulin
Correct Answer: B) Intravenous administration of 20 ml/kg of 0.9% saline
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) occurs as a result of the accumulation of serum ketones such as β-hydroxybutyric acid, acetoacetic acid, and acetone in the setting of deficient insulin signaling. Dysregulated fatty acid degradation and ketone synthesis occur due to the relative state of starvation created through absent insulin signaling. Extracellular hyperglycemia creates an osmotic effect resulting in the shift of fluid from the intracellular to the extracellular space with accompanying profuse osmotic diuresis and intracellular volume loss. Patients present with signs and symptoms including tachycardia, tachypnea, fatigue, polyuria, shortness of breath, Kussmaul respiration, and diffuse abdominal discomfort. Laboratory evaluation typically shows increased concentrations of glucose, ketones, and a high anion-gap metabolic acidosis caused by the accumulation of unmeasured anions (ketones, lactic acid) in serum. Treatment consists of the replacement of insulin, volume repletion, correction of electrolyte abnormalities, and treatment of any precipitating conditions. Volume resuscitation with 0.9% saline is essential to restore intracellular fluid volume, lower the extracellular glucose concentration, and is the initial step in the management of DKA even prior to insulin administration. Administering insulin prior to knowing the serum potassium concentration can result in life-threatening hypokalemia.
