Insulin is typically repleted at an initial dose of 0.1 U/kg/hour by intravenous infusion only after potassium status is clarified. Choice A (5% dextrose in water) would worsen the patient's profound hyperglycemia and is inappropriate. Choice C (lactated Ringer solution with potassium chloride) may be acceptable once the patient's potassium concentration is known; however, in DKA, derangements in potassium can include either hypo- or hyperkalemia. Infusing a fluid with potassium may result in worsening of unknown derangements with potentially life-threatening dysrhythmias. Choices D and E (insulin administration at 0.1 U/h) are not adjusted for the patient's weight (should be 0.1 U/kg/h) and should not be given before potassium status is established, making volume resuscitation with 0.9% saline the appropriate initial step. Educational Objective: Extracellular hyperglycemia in the setting of diabetic ketoacidosis creates an osmotic effect resulting in the shift of fluid from the intracellular to the extracellular space with accompanying diuresis and intracellular volume loss. Restoration of fluid balance is an essential step in the emergent management of diabetic ketoacidosis and is best accomplished with the intravenous administration of 0.9% saline.
Source: 9A #34
A child is brought to the emergency department by her father because of a 3-day history of moderate abdominal pain and nonbilious vomiting. The father reports that during the past 2 weeks, the patient has seemed tired and has drunk large volumes of fluid and voided frequently. She has not eaten much during this time, resulting in a 3-kg weight loss. She has not had blood or mucus in her stool, chest pain, or cough. She has no history of serious illness and receives no medications. She appears tired. She is 112 cm tall and weighs 19 kg; BMI is 15 kg/m². Temperature is 37.0°C, pulse is 140/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 95%. Physical examination shows dry lips and mucous membranes. Pulmonary examination discloses deep inspiration and clear lungs. Abdominal examination discloses diffuse tenderness without rebound. Intravenous access is established in the dorsum of the right hand. Capillary blood gas analysis on room air shows a pH of 7.1. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 37%, Leukocyte count 12,100/mm³, Platelet count 190,000/mm³, Serum Na⁺ 132 mEq/L, K⁺ 4.5 mEq/L, Cl⁻ 103 mEq/L, HCO₃⁻ 11 mEq/L, Glucose 350 mg/dL, Urine specific gravity 1.030, positive glucose, positive protein, and large ketones. Administration of which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Subcutaneous insulin glargine B) Subcutaneous intermediate-acting insulin C) Intravenous 0.9% saline bolus (10 mL/kg) D) Intravenous short-acting insulin E) Intravenous sodium bicarbonate
Correct Answer: C) Intravenous 0.9% saline bolus (10 mL/kg)
This patient is presenting with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). The clinical presentation includes fatigue, polyuria, polydipsia, abdominal pain, vomiting, weight loss, dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, tachypnea, and metabolic acidosis (pH 7.1). Laboratory findings confirm DKA with elevated serum glucose (350 mg/dL), large urine ketones, hyponatremia (132 mEq/L), and metabolic acidosis with low HCO₃⁻ (11 mEq/L). DKA occurs due to accumulation of serum ketones (β-hydroxybutyric acid, acetoacetic acid, and acetone) in the setting of insulin deficiency. Dysregulated fatty acid degradation and ketone synthesis result from the relative state of starvation created through absent insulin signaling. The most appropriate initial step in management of DKA is fluid repletion with an intravenous bolus of 0.9% saline (10 mL/kg). Volume repletion addresses hypovolemia, improves tissue perfusion, dilutes serum glucose, and promotes renal ketone clearance. After initial fluid administration and correction of electrolyte abnormalities (especially potassium), intravenous insulin can be initiated. Management also includes addressing underlying triggers such as infection. Choice A and B (Subcutaneous insulin glargine and intermediate-acting insulin): These are incorrect because fluid replacement is the most appropriate initial step in management. Subcutaneous insulin administration may be considered in mild cases of DKA or if safe intravenous access cannot be established, but it is not the first-line management. Choice D (Intravenous short-acting insulin): This is incorrect because intravenous insulin is administered after fluids have been given and electrolytes (particularly potassium) have been corrected. Administering insulin before adequate hydration and potassium correction can precipitate hypokalemia and worsening metabolic derangements. Choice E (Intravenous sodium bicarbonate): This is incorrect because sodium bicarbonate is not recommended in the treatment of DKA in the pediatric population. Sodium bicarbonate therapy has been associated with development of hypokalemia, cerebral injury, and hyperventilation. The metabolic acidosis typically resolves with appropriate fluid administration and insulin therapy.
Source: 4A #3
A 7-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes mellitus has had fever, cough, and rhinorrhea for 1 week and lethargy for 3 days. His pulse is 100/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 100/65 mm Hg. He appears lethargic; no other abnormalities are noted. Serum studies show: Na+ 120 mEq/L, Cl- 95 mEq/L, K+ 7.5 mEq/L, HCO3- 10 mEq/L, Glucose 690 mg/dl, Urea nitrogen 23 mg/dl. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the hyperkalemia? A) Adrenal insufficiency B) Cellular shift C) Excessive potassium intake D) Hemolysis E) Respiratory acidosis
Correct Answer: B) Cellular shift
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) typically occurs in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus as a result of increased insulin requirements during times of physiologic stress (e.g., infection) or insulin nonadherence. DKA results from the accumulation of serum ketones in the setting of deficient insulin signaling, with dysregulated fatty acid degradation and ketone synthesis occurring due to the relative state of starvation created through absent insulin signaling. The clinical presentation includes fatigue, polyuria, shortness of breath, and diffuse abdominal discomfort, with vital signs showing tachycardia and tachypnea. Laboratory studies typically show increased glucose and ketone concentrations, metabolic acidosis, and a high anion-gap from the accumulation of unmeasured anions in serum. In metabolic acidosis, excess hydrogen ions are transported into the cell in exchange for potassium ions to maintain electroneutrality. Insulin promotes intracellular potassium entry; in DKA, insulin deficiency contributes to an excess cellular shift of potassium to the extracellular space, resulting in hyperkalemia despite decreased total body potassium concentrations from excess urinary excretion. Choice A (Adrenal insufficiency) refers to insufficient production of adrenal cortex hormones including aldosterone and cortisol. Primary adrenal insufficiency can present with deficiencies in both, while secondary and tertiary forms primarily affect cortisol. Insufficient aldosterone leads to hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. However, DKA is more likely given the patient's history of type 1 diabetes, metabolic acidosis, and severe hyperglycemia. Choice C (Excessive potassium intake) would be unlikely to cause hyperkalemia in this patient. While kidney potassium filtration typically regulates serum potassium within normal range (though this can be impaired in end-stage kidney disease), in DKA the kidney excretion of potassium is actually increased due to osmotic diuresis. The hyperkalemia in this case results from the extracellular shift of potassium and deficient insulin signaling. Choice D (Hemolysis) can result in hyperkalemia through release of intracellular potassium into the serum. However, DKA is unlikely to cause hemolysis, and hemolytic anemia would present with jaundice and increased bilirubin. Choice E (Respiratory acidosis) would be the opposite of what is expected in DKA. In DKA, metabolic acidosis leads to compensatory respiratory alkalosis. Kussmaul respirations (rapid and deep) are a classic physical examination finding in DKA. Treatment of DKA involves insulin replacement, volume repletion, correction of electrolyte abnormalities, and treatment of any precipitating conditions. Educational Objective: DKA typically occurs in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus as a result of increased insulin requirements during physiologic stress or insulin nonadherence. In metabolic acidosis, excess hydrogen ions move intracellularly in exchange for potassium ions to maintain electroneutrality, resulting in hyperkalemia.
▶ Respiratory System Bordetella pertussis Pneumonia 5 questions
Source: 6A #34
A previously healthy 1-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of cough and difficulty breast-feeding. Her mother is concerned because the patient's face turns red when she coughs. She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy, labor, and delivery. She is otherwise healthy. Her mother has had a similar cough for 3 weeks. The patient appears thin. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 110/min, and respirations are 45/min. Examination shows moist mucous membranes and clear rhinorrhea. During the examination, she has a long series of single coughs ending with a loud, high-pitched inhalation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Acute bronchiolitis B) Chlamydial pneumonia C) Foreign body aspiration D) Pertussis E) Viral laryngotracheobronchitis
Correct Answer: D) Pertussis
Episodes of severe paroxysmal coughing in the setting of a respiratory illness is concerning for pertussis. Pertussis occurs as a result of infection from Bordetella pertussis and classically presents in three stages. The catarrhal stage is first, presenting with fever, rhinorrhea, and a mild cough. This progresses to the paroxysmal stage after 1-2 weeks, in which patients experience violent bouts of extreme coughing, sometimes violent enough to cause secondary traumatic injury such as rib fractures, urinary incontinence, and pneumothorax. Coughing fits are often accompanied by cyanosis and may be followed by syncope, emesis, or apnea. The characteristic loud, high-pitched inhalation at the end of the cough is responsible for the colloquial name 'whooping cough'. The paroxysmal stage can last for weeks to months, followed by the convalescent stage lasting 1-4 weeks. Pertussis toxin is a major virulence factor that inactivates the Gi subunits of G protein-coupled receptors in the respiratory epithelium and systemically, leading to uninhibited adenylyl cyclase activity and increased intracellular cAMP concentrations. In neutrophils and macrophages, this results in impaired recruitment, migration, and production of inflammatory mediators. Pertussis can be prevented with immunization in the form of acellular pertussis, typically administered with tetanus and diphtheria vaccines (DTaP), but the first dose is not given until 2 months of age. This patient likely acquired the infection from her mother who has had a similar cough for 3 weeks. Choice A (Acute bronchiolitis) is often the result of infection with respiratory syncytial virus and presents with fever, tachypnea, rhinorrhea, and wheezing. Patients may display apneic episodes, but severe paroxysms of coughing would be atypical. Choice B (Chlamydial pneumonia) is commonly preceded by neonatal conjunctivitis and classically presents in infants with a staccato cough, in which each cough is separated by a brief inspiration. Physical examination may show tachypnea and crackles. Choice C (Foreign body aspiration) symptoms depend on the size of the aspirated item and its location in the bronchial tree. It can present with respiratory distress and stridor, a high-pitched sound caused by turbulent airflow through obstructed or narrowed upper airway structures such as the pharynx, larynx, or trachea. Choice E (Viral laryngotracheobronchitis/Croup) typically presents with fever, rhinorrhea, a barking cough, and inspiratory stridor. It is commonly secondary to viral infection from parainfluenza virus. Educational Objective: Pertussis, caused by Bordetella pertussis, may lead to severe paroxysmal coughing accompanied by cyanosis and followed by syncope, emesis, or apnea. The characteristic 'whoop' is the high-pitched inhalation after paroxysms of coughing. Pertussis can be prevented with DTaP immunization, but patients younger than 2 months are too young to receive vaccination and may acquire infection from contacts such as family members.
Source: 3A #48
A 2-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of coughing spells that have progressively worsened over the past 10 days and are frequently followed by vomiting. On examination, he is afebrile and appears healthy until he spontaneously has a coughing spell. Coughing continues for 20 seconds, at which time he appears cyanotic for 10 seconds. No crackles are heard on auscultation of the chest. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Aspiration due to gastroesophageal reflux B) Chlamydial pneumonia C) Congestive heart failure D) Pertussis E) Respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis
Correct Answer: D) Pertussis
Pertussis is caused by Bordetella pertussis infection and classically presents with severe paroxysmal coughing episodes. The disease progresses through three stages: (1) Catarrhal stage presents with fever, rhinorrhea, and mild cough lasting 1-2 weeks; (2) Paroxysmal stage features violent bouts of extreme coughing that can cause secondary traumatic injury (rib fractures, urinary incontinence, pneumothorax) and is often accompanied by cyanosis, syncope, emesis, or apnea, lasting weeks to months; (3) Convalescent stage involves symptom resolution lasting 1-4 weeks. The pathophysiology involves pertussis toxin inactivating Gi subunits of G protein-coupled receptors, leading to uninhibited adenylyl cyclase activity and increased intracellular cAMP, which impairs neutrophil and macrophage recruitment and inflammatory mediator production. This case presents with the characteristic paroxysmal coughing with cyanosis of the paroxysmal stage. Pertussis is prevented through DTaP immunization and treated with macrolide antibiotics and supportive care. Choice A (Aspiration from gastroesophageal reflux) more commonly presents with symptoms associated with feeding, recurrent bacterial pneumonia, and fever. Choice B (Chlamydial pneumonia) may follow neonatal conjunctivitis and classically presents with a staccato cough (individual coughs separated by brief inspiration), tachypnea, and crackles on examination—not the severe paroxysmal coughing described. Choice C (Congestive heart failure) in infants is typically preceded by signs of cardiac malformations or dysfunction in the neonatal period. While congenital heart defects may cause cyanosis, severe paroxysmal coughing is atypical. Choice E (Respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis) typically presents with fever, tachypnea, rhinorrhea, and wheezing. While apneic episodes may occur, severe paroxysmal coughing is atypical for RSV bronchiolitis.
Source: 8A #36
A 5-week-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents in the fall because of a 2-week history of progressive cough. He often coughs uncontrollably until he is struggling to breathe and vomits. He has not had fever. He had moderate nasal congestion for the first 5 days of his illness. He was born following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. The patient's father also has had a cough for 3 weeks. During the examination, the patient is not in distress except when he is coughing. He is at the 25th percentile for length, weight, and head circumference. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 148/min, and respirations are 40/min. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 95%. The lungs are clear to auscultation. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 28,000/mm³ (N=6000-14,000), Segmented neutrophils 14%, Bands 1%, Lymphocytes 80%, Monocytes 5%. A chest x-ray shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism? A) Bordetella pertussis B) Influenza virus C) Mycoplasma pneumoniae D) Respiratory syncytial virus E) Streptococcus pneumoniae
Correct Answer: A) Bordetella pertussis
Episodes of severe paroxysmal coughing in the setting of a respiratory illness is concerning for pertussis. Pertussis occurs as a result of infection from Bordetella pertussis and classically presents in three stages. The catarrhal stage is first, presenting with fever, rhinorrhea, and a mild cough. This progresses to the paroxysmal stage after 1 to 2 weeks, in which patients experience violent bouts of extreme coughing, sometimes violent enough to cause secondary traumatic injury such as rib fractures, urinary incontinence, and pneumothorax. Such coughing fits are often accompanied by cyanosis and may be followed by syncope, emesis, or apnea. The paroxysmal stage can last for weeks to months. Symptoms resolve during the convalescent stage, which lasts 1 to 4 weeks. The clinical presentation in this case is classic: the 2-week history of progressive cough with paroxysmal episodes causing vomiting, initial mild upper respiratory symptoms, exposure from father who also has prolonged cough, and the characteristic lymphocytosis (80%) with normal chest x-ray. Influenza virus (Choice B) is a common cause of viral pneumonia during winter months, presenting with respiratory, gastrointestinal, and systemic symptoms including cough, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, chills, headache, myalgias, and arthralgias. It typically lasts less than 1 week and does not have a paroxysmal stage. This patient's lack of fever and prolonged cough are inconsistent with influenza. Mycoplasma pneumoniae (Choice C) is a common cause of atypical pneumonia presenting with acute cough, fever, chills, and shortness of breath. Chest x-ray typically shows multifocal infiltrates, which this patient does not have. Respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis (Choice D) is more likely to present with fever, tachypnea, rhinorrhea, and wheezing. Patients may display apneic episodes, although severe paroxysms of coughing would be atypical. Streptococcus pneumoniae (Choice E) is a common bacterial cause of pneumonia, but patients tend to present with focal lung findings indicating lobar pneumonia typically seen on chest x-ray, which this patient does not demonstrate. Educational Objective: Pertussis caused by Bordetella pertussis may lead to severe paroxysmal coughing accompanied by cyanosis and followed by syncope, emesis, or apnea. Pertussis can be prevented with immunization (acellular pertussis vaccine) and is treated with antibiotics, typically macrolides, and supportive care.
Source: 5A #23
A 4-month-old girl is admitted to the hospital because of severe coughing for 2 days. The cough is episodic and staccato-like and often followed by vomiting. One week ago, she developed rhinorrhea. On admission, she appears well when not coughing. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 120/min, and respirations are 34/min. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 95%. Examination shows a few petechiae on the face and thick nasal secretions. An x-ray of the chest shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention to prevent nosocomial transmission? A) Antiviral therapy for all health care workers B) Contact isolation C) Droplet isolation D) Erythromycin therapy for all health care workers E) Intravenous immune globulin therapy for all health care workers F) Intravenous immune globulin therapy for the patient G) Pertussis vaccination for all health care workers H) Pertussis vaccination for the patient I) No intervention
Correct Answer: C) Droplet isolation
Droplet isolation (droplet precautions) is the most effective way to prevent nosocomial spread of Bordetella pertussis. The infection is transmitted via respiratory droplets, requiring that all individuals who come into contact with infected patients wear a mask and eye protection covering the eyes, nose, and mouth. Pertussis presents classically in three stages: (1) Catarrhal stage with fever, rhinorrhea, and mild cough; (2) Paroxysmal stage after 1-2 weeks characterized by violent paroxysmal coughing bouts that can cause secondary traumatic injury (rib fractures, urinary incontinence, pneumothorax, facial petechiae), cyanosis, syncope, emesis, or apnea, lasting weeks to months; (3) Convalescent stage lasting 1-4 weeks with symptom resolution. Pertussis can be prevented with DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus, acellular pertussis) vaccination. Choice A (Antiviral therapy) is incorrect because B. pertussis is a bacterial infection not treated with antivirals like oseltamivir. Choice B (Contact isolation) is reserved for pathogens like Clostridium difficile and MRSA transmitted through skin contact, involving gloves and gowns, not appropriate for respiratory droplet transmission. Choice D (Erythromycin therapy) could be considered in pertussis outbreaks but is not necessary as a primary intervention in this case; antibiotics may shorten symptom duration but do not prevent transmission as effectively as droplet precautions. Choice E (IVIG for health care workers) is not used for B. pertussis post-exposure prophylaxis. Choice F (IVIG for patient) is occasionally used after exposure to certain pathogens like rabies but is not standard for pertussis. Choice G (Pertussis vaccination for health care workers) is not correct. While all adults should receive Tdap every 10 years, infection can occur even in recently vaccinated individuals; droplet precautions are the best prevention method. Choice H (Pertussis vaccination for patient) will not change her acute disease course, though vaccination is recommended at 4 months, 6 months, 15 months, and age 4. Choice I (No intervention) is inappropriate as failure to contain infection exposes other patients and staff to transmission. Educational Objective: Pertussis caused by B. pertussis presents with paroxysmal coughing potentially followed by post-tussive syncope or emesis. While antibiotics can shorten symptom duration, the most appropriate intervention is prevention of transmission through immediate institution of droplet precautions including masks and eye protection, since the bacteria transmit via respiratory droplets.
Source: 5A #30
A 2-year-old child with sickle cell hemoglobinopathy has a 2-week history of a paroxysmal cough followed by vomiting. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 32,000/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 10%, Lymphocytes 85%, Monocytes 5%. An x-ray of the chest shows perihilar infiltrates. Which of the following vaccines could have prevented this condition? A) Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis B) Haemophilus influenzae type b-protein conjugate C) Influenza virus D) Measles-mumps-rubella E) Pneumococcal
Correct Answer: A) Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis
The clinical presentation of severe paroxysmal coughing in this patient is classic for pertussis caused by Bordetella pertussis infection. The disease progresses through three stages: the catarrhal stage (fever, rhinorrhea, mild cough), the paroxysmal stage (violent bouts of extreme coughing lasting weeks to months, accompanied by cyanosis, syncope, emesis, or apnea), and the convalescent stage (1-4 weeks of symptom resolution). The marked lymphocytosis (85%) in this patient is characteristic of pertussis, which occurs because pertussis toxin impairs recruitment and migration of phagocytes. Pertussis is prevented by the diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis (DTaP) vaccine, administered as a multiple-dose series beginning at two months of age per CDC recommendations. Treatment includes macrolide antibiotics and supportive care. Haemophilus influenzae type b causes various mucosal infections and epiglottitis but does not cause paroxysmal coughing. Influenza virus causes fever, chills, myalgias, and may lead to pneumonia but does not typically present with paroxysmal coughing. Measles, mumps, and rubella cause various viral syndromes but none cause paroxysmal coughing. Pneumococcal vaccine prevents Streptococcus pneumoniae infections, which cause pneumonia and meningitis but not paroxysmal coughing.
▶ Immune System HIV Type 1 4 questions

A ?-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 3-day history of fever and cough. She was born at term following an uncomplicated delivery. She was treated for acute otitis media at 5 months of age. She takes no medications. Immunizations are up-to-date. She appears ill. She is at the 50th percentile for length and 25th percentile for weight. Her temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 80/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 80%. Several 0.5- to 1.5-cm, mobile lymph nodes are palpated in the anterior cervical chain, axillae, and groin. Examination shows white plaques on the buccal mucosa. Diffuse crackles are heard bilaterally. The spleen tip is palpated 2 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 10,500/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 66%, Lymphocytes 30%, Monocytes 4%. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows Pneumocystis jiroveci (formerly P. carinii). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Chediak-Higashi syndrome B) Chronic granulomatous disease C) Complement deficiency D) HIV infection E) Hyperimmunoglobulinemia E syndrome F) Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) G) Thymic-parathyroid dysplasia (DiGeorge syndrome) H) Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome I) X-linked agammaglobulinemia
Correct Answer: D) HIV infection
HIV infection acquired via vertical transmission in the perinatal period is the most likely diagnosis in this patient. The clinical presentation is classic for pediatric HIV/AIDS with oral thrush (white plaques on buccal mucosa), diffuse lymphadenopathy (cervical, axillary, and inguinal nodes), splenomegaly (spleen tip 2 cm below costal margin), and Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia confirmed on bronchoalveolar lavage. HIV transmission may occur at any time during gestation but is most commonly acquired at or around the time of delivery and in the immediate postpartum period when children are breastfeeding. Transmission is uncommon if the mother is taking antiretroviral therapy with a low HIV viral load. Most patients present within the first few months of birth with recurrent pneumonia or opportunistic infections. P. jiroveci pneumonia is an AIDS-defining illness in children. Initial evaluation should include measurement of HIV viral load with concomitant testing for mutations. Treatment should include therapy for P. jiroveci pneumonia and thrush along with antiretroviral therapy once HIV infection is confirmed. Incorrect answers: Chediak-Higashi syndrome (Choice A) is caused by LYST gene mutations affecting lysosomal formation and transportation, presenting with frequent bacterial infections, oculocutaneous albinism, peripheral neuropathy, and progressive neurologic dysfunction. Chronic granulomatous disease (Choice B) results from NADPH oxidase deficiency causing impaired intracellular pathogen killing, presenting with recurrent pyogenic infections by catalase-positive organisms like Staphylococcus aureus with normal leukocyte and immunoglobulin concentrations. Complement deficiency (Choice C), particularly terminal cascade deficiency, typically presents with recurrent Neisseria species infections. Hyperimmunoglobulinemia E syndrome (Choice E) involves JAK-STAT signaling mutations impairing Th17 cell development, presenting with recurrent skin infections, noninflamed (cold) abscesses, and diffuse atopic dermatitis. Severe combined immunodeficiency (Choice F) results from failed B and T lymphocyte activity causing impaired cellular and humoral immunity, often from adenosine deaminase deficiency, presenting with recurrent viral, bacterial, and fungal infections from birth. Thymic-parathyroid dysplasia or DiGeorge syndrome (Choice G) presents with thymic hypoplasia/aplasia, impaired immunity, conotruncal cardiac defects, hypocalcemia from parathyroid hypoplasia, and craniofacial abnormalities. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (Choice H) involves WAS gene mutations affecting actin cytoskeleton rearrangement during lymphocyte interactions, presenting with eczema, thrombocytopenia, and infections with encapsulated bacteria and opportunistic pathogens. X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Choice I) results from BTK gene mutations affecting tyrosine kinase essential for B lymphocyte development, causing absent functioning B lymphocytes and recurrent infections from impaired humoral immunity. Educational Objective: Pediatric HIV/AIDS should be suspected in patients presenting with recurrent bacterial pneumonia or AIDS-defining illnesses such as disseminated mycobacterial and nonmycobacterial tuberculosis infection, or Pneumocystis jiroveci infection. Treatment for the presenting infection in conjunction with initiation of antiretroviral therapy is required.
Source: 4A #17
A previously healthy 17-year-old boy comes to the physician because of fever and enlarged lymph nodes for 3 weeks. He has had a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss over the past 2 months. He has had six to eight loose stools daily for 4 weeks. His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 80/min, and respirations are 30/min. Examination shows dry skin. There are bilateral 2-cm lymph nodes in the neck, axillae, and groin. The lungs are clear to auscultation. The liver edge is palpated 1 cm below the right costal margin; the spleen tip is palpated 7 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 10 g/dL, Leukocyte count 2100/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 80%, Lymphocytes 18%, Monocytes 2%, Platelet count 180,000/mm³, Serum IgA 340 mg/dL, IgG 2300 mg/dL, IgM 390 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Common variable immunodeficiency B) HIV infection C) Selective IgA deficiency D) Severe combined immunodeficiency E) Thymic-parathyroid dysplasia (DiGeorge syndrome) F) X-linked agammaglobulinemia
Correct Answer: B) HIV infection
This patient with generalized lymphadenopathy, fever, weight loss, diarrhea, and hepatosplenomegaly with leukopenia most likely has acute HIV infection, known as acute retroviral syndrome. The presentation of primary HIV infection can vary significantly between patients, with some experiencing a mild febrile illness while others experience a severe, mononucleosis-like viral syndrome. The time between infection and onset of symptoms is variable, with incubation time lasting several weeks to months. During acute infection, there is a high degree of viral replication followed by widespread infection of CD4+ T lymphocytes. While the T-lymphocyte count may decrease transiently, it is often within reference ranges in early HIV infection unless patients present with signs of opportunistic infection. Initial laboratory studies include the use of a fourth generation HIV test, which tests for HIV p24 antigen and antibodies, combined with direct measurement of the HIV viral load using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction testing. It is common in early infection for patients to have a negative fourth generation test but a high viral load; this is known as the window period. Once the diagnosis is made, laboratory studies should be sent for mutational analysis and genotyping, but this should not delay immediate treatment with antiretroviral therapy. Therapy typically includes a combination of at least three different medications from at least two different antiretroviral classes. Choice A (Common variable immunodeficiency) classically presents between the ages of 20 to 40 years as multiple, recurrent sinus or pulmonary infections, including pneumonia, bronchitis, and sinusitis. Testing will disclose low immunoglobulin concentrations. Choice C (Selective IgA deficiency) describes an absence of IgA with normal concentrations of IgG, and normal or increased concentrations of IgM. Many patients are asymptomatic and do not demonstrate a history of recurrent infections. The classic presentation is anaphylaxis after transfusion of blood products, which occurs as the result of pre-formed anti-IgA antibodies. Choice D (Severe combined immunodeficiency) results from a variety of different mutations and commonly presents with recurrent bacterial, viral, and fungal infections as a result of severe impairment in both B- and T-lymphocyte function in infancy. This patient's age and absence of prior recurrent infections essentially rules out this diagnosis. Choice E (Thymic-parathyroid dysplasia/DiGeorge syndrome) is caused by a 22q11 deletion that leads to failure of the third and fourth branchial pouches to develop. These structures give rise to the thymus and parathyroid glands, and their absence leads to thymic aplasia and hypocalcemia in cardiac and craniofacial defects. Patients are susceptible to viral and fungal infections. The definitive diagnosis requires fluorescence in-situ hybridization to detect the missing DNA segment. Choice F (X-linked agammaglobulinemia) occurs as a result of mutations in the BTK gene that encodes a tyrosine kinase essential for all stages of B lymphocyte development and proliferation. Patients lack functioning B lymphocytes and therefore lack normal concentrations of immunoglobulins. This patient exhibits normal concentrations of all immunoglobulins. Educational Objective: Acute retroviral syndrome, or acute HIV infection, commonly presents with diffuse lymphadenopathy, diarrhea, malaise, fever, and weight loss. Patients may also present with opportunistic infections or may be entirely asymptomatic. Diagnosis in patients who do not meet classical risk criteria requires a high degree of clinical suspicion. Testing with a fourth-generation antigen/antibody test in addition to assessment of the HIV viral load is requisite.
Source: 8A #26
A child presents with a history of recurrent acute otitis media over the past year. The mother has a history of persistent oral candidiasis and chronic diarrhea and has had a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss. The patient is at a low percentile for weight. On examination, the oral mucous membranes are covered with white plaques. Examination shows 2-cm, nontender, axillary lymph nodes. The spleen is palpated below the left costal margin, and the liver is palpated below the right costal margin. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count: 3,000/mm³ Segmented neutrophils: 60% Lymphocytes: 35% Platelet count: 95,000/mm³ Serum quantitative immunoglobulins: IgA: 420 mg/dL (N=14-159) IgG: 2200 mg/dL (N=345-1236) IgM: 400 mg/dL (N=43-207) Which of the following mechanisms of disease is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms? A) Chédiak-Higashi syndrome B) Chronic granulomatous disease C) Common variable immunodeficiency D) Cystic fibrosis E) HIV infection F) Severe combined immunodeficiency disease G) Terminal complement deficiency H) Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
Correct Answer: E) HIV infection
HIV infection acquired via vertical transmission in the perinatal period is the most likely diagnosis. The clinical presentation includes recurrent oral thrush (candidiasis), recurrent otitis media, and bacterial pneumonia, along with cervical lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly on examination. The mother's history of persistent oral candidiasis and chronic diarrhea is also suggestive of maternal HIV infection. HIV transmission may occur at any time during gestation but is most commonly acquired at or around the time of delivery and in the immediate postpartum period during breast-feeding. Transmission is uncommon if the mother is taking antiretroviral therapy and has a low HIV viral load. As a result of universal screening for HIV in most developed countries, the incidence of perinatal and pediatric HIV has decreased. Most patients present within the first few months of birth with recurrent pneumonia or opportunistic infections, though in some cases, symptoms and AIDS-defining conditions may not develop until many years later. Initial evaluation should include measurement of the HIV viral load with concomitant testing for mutations. Chédiak-Higashi syndrome (Choice A) is caused by mutations in the lysosomal trafficking regulator gene (LYST) essential for normal formation and transportation of lysosomes within the cell. It presents with frequent bacterial infections, oculocutaneous albinism, peripheral neuropathy, and progressive neurologic dysfunction. Chronic granulomatous disease (Choice B) is caused by a deficiency in NADPH oxidase, an enzyme used to generate hydrogen peroxide and hypochlorous acid. These molecules are typically used to kill bacteria intracellularly. Patients present with recurrent pyogenic infections with catalase-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus, with normal concentrations of leukocytes and immunoglobulins. Common variable immunodeficiency (Choice C) classically presents in the second to fourth decades of life as multiple, recurrent sinus or pulmonary infections, including pneumonia, bronchitis, and sinusitis. Testing will show low immunoglobulin concentrations. Cystic fibrosis (Choice D) is associated with recurrent pulmonary infections as a result of impaired clearance of mucous, microbes, and debris from the airways. Other findings include bronchiectasis, pancreatic insufficiency, diarrhea, malnutrition, and weight loss. Severe combined immunodeficiency disease (Choice F) results from a variety of different mutations and commonly presents with recurrent bacterial, viral, and fungal infections as a result of severe impairment in both B- and T-lymphocyte function in infancy. Terminal complement deficiency (Choice G) typically presents with recurrent infections with Neisseria species. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (Choice H) is caused by a mutation in the WAS gene on the X-chromosome that encodes a protein essential for actin cytoskeleton rearrangement. Patients present with eczema, thrombocytopenia, and infections with encapsulated bacteria and opportunistic pathogens. Educational Objective: Pediatric HIV/AIDS should be suspected in patients who present with recurrent bacterial pneumonia or AIDS-defining illnesses such as disseminated mycobacterial and nonmycobacterial infection, or Pneumocystis jiroveci infection.
Source: 8A #34
A 2-year-old boy who is HIV positive is brought to the family clinic by his mother for a follow-up examination. He is currently taking three antiretroviral drugs. His mother is also taking multiple antiretroviral drugs; she has chronic cryptosporidiosis and has had a 5-kg (11-lb) weight loss during the past 2 months. The father is not in contact with the family. The child's growth and development are appropriate for age, and immunizations are up-to-date. Examination shows two small, nontender, mobile lymph nodes in the right axilla. Laboratory studies show: Child: Leukocyte count 12,800/mm3, Segmented neutrophils 55%, Lymphocytes 35%, Monocytes 10%, CD4+ T-lymphocyte count 1852/mm3 (Normal >1000), Plasma HIV viral load undetectable, Serum hepatitis C antibody negative Mother: Segmented neutrophils 80%, Lymphocytes 10%, Monocytes 10%, CD4+ T-lymphocyte count 4/mm3 (Normal >500), Plasma HIV viral load 38,000 copies/mL, Serum hepatitis C antibody positive Which of the following is the most appropriate topic to discuss at this visit? A) The advantages of three-drug versus four-drug antiretroviral regimens B) Plans for the child's care in the event of the mother's death C) The child's immunization schedule D) Hand-washing techniques to prevent HIV transmission E) Long-term complications of HIV infection
Correct Answer: B) Plans for the child's care in the event of the mother's death
Based on the laboratory results, the child has well-controlled HIV with a normal CD4+ count (1852/mm3) and an undetectable viral load. However, his mother has a dangerously low CD4+ count (4/mm3) and persistently elevated viral load (38,000 copies/mL), placing her at high risk of dying from AIDS-related complications. With an absent father, it is critical for the pediatrician to initiate discussions about guardianship and long-term care planning for the child. As an HIV-positive child requiring lifelong antiretroviral medications and ongoing specialty care coordination, the patient will need an aware and committed caregiver. Although difficult, these psychosocial conversations are essential to ensure the child's welfare. Choice A (three-drug versus four-drug antiretroviral regimens): While important for overall HIV management, this is not the most pressing issue given the mother's critical status. Choice C (immunization schedule): The patient's immunizations are already up-to-date, and this is not the most urgent topic at this visit. Choice D (hand-washing techniques to prevent HIV transmission): Hand-washing has not been demonstrated to reduce HIV transmission. HIV is transmitted through blood, vaginal fluid, and semen, primarily via sexual intercourse and needle sharing, not through hand contact. Choice E (long-term complications of HIV infection): While important to discuss at some point, the more pressing concern is ensuring the child has appropriate care planning given his mother's imminent risk of mortality. Educational Objective: Pediatricians must balance medical management with psychosocial care. An essential role includes ensuring that children have adequate guardianship and care planning in place, particularly when parents are facing life-threatening illnesses. Early discussion of these sensitive topics allows for proper resource allocation and legal planning to protect the child's welfare.
▶ Male Reproductive Sexually Transmitted Infections 4 questions
Source: 5A #5
A previously healthy 17-year-old girl comes to the physician 4 days after her sexual partner was diagnosed with gonorrhea. Examination shows no abnormalities. Tests for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis are ordered. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Intramuscular ceftriaxone therapy only B) Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline C) Oral azithromycin therapy only D) Oral azithromycin and intramuscular penicillin therapy E) No treatment indicated because the patient is asymptomatic
Correct Answer: B) Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline
Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a Gram-negative diplococcus that causes vaginitis, cervicitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). Vaginitis presents with mucopurulent discharge and pruritus, while cervicitis presents with similar discharge, erythematous friable cervix, and cervical motion tenderness. When infection spreads to the fallopian tubes and ovaries, PID develops with purulent cervical discharge, uterine and adnexal tenderness, and systemic symptoms including fever. Untreated PID can progress to tubo-ovarian abscess or intraabdominal abscess causing infertility. Gonorrhea can also disseminate causing tenosynovitis, dermatitis, and polyarthralgia, or trigger reactive arthritis. Risk factors include multiple sexual partners, new partners, receptive anal intercourse, young age, substance abuse, and inconsistent condom use. Coinfection with Chlamydia trachomatis is common, so empiric treatment covering both organisms is appropriate following high-risk exposure while confirmatory tests are pending. The standard regimen is ceftriaxone for N. gonorrhoeae and doxycycline for C. trachomatis. Choice A (ceftriaxone only) treats gonorrhea but misses the high risk of concurrent chlamydial infection. Choice C (azithromycin only) covers chlamydia but fails to treat the documented gonorrhea exposure and is insufficient. Choice D (azithromycin and penicillin) covers chlamydia but penicillin is inadequate for gonorrhea due to widespread resistance; ceftriaxone provides superior coverage. Choice E (no treatment) is inappropriate as untreated infection risks serious complications including reactive arthritis, disseminated gonococcal infection, and PID with infertility. Educational Objective: N. gonorrhoeae presents with vaginitis, cervicitis, and pelvic inflammatory disease. Following high-risk gonorrhea exposure, empiric treatment with ceftriaxone and doxycycline is appropriate while tests are pending, with doxycycline covering possible concurrent C. trachomatis infection.
Source: 8A #45
A 17-year-old girl comes to the office because of a 5-day history of a nontender lesion on her vagina. She is sexually active with three male partners, and they use condoms inconsistently. Vital signs are normal with blood pressure 106/68 mm Hg. Examination shows a 2 x 2-cm ulcerated lesion with raised borders over the right labium majus. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism? A) Gram-negative bacillus B) Gram-negative diplococcus C) Obligate intracellular bacterium D) Protozoan E) Virus
Correct Answer: E) Virus
The clinical presentation of a painless genital ulcer with raised borders in a sexually active adolescent is classic for primary syphilis caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum. Syphilis is a sexually transmitted disease that presents in multiple stages. Primary syphilis characteristically manifests as a painless chancre (ulcer) of the genitalia with typically no systemic signs or symptoms at this stage. Dark-field microscopy of fluid from the chancre is the most sensitive test for diagnosis of primary syphilis. RPR (Rapid Plasma Reagin) can be falsely negative in the primary stage. Treatment is a single dose of benzathine Penicillin G intramuscular injection. Testing for additional sexually transmitted infections is appropriate as coinfections are common. Incorrect answers: Choice A: Haemophilus ducreyi is a gram-negative bacillus that causes chancroid, which presents with painful (not painless) genital ulceration and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Choice B: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative diplococcus that causes cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and urethritis presenting with dysuria and mucopurulent discharge rather than a painless ulcer. Choice C: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular bacterium causing cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, epididymitis, and urethritis. While it causes genital infections, a painless genital ulcer is more consistent with syphilis. Choice D: Trichomonas vaginalis is an anaerobic flagellated protozoan causing trichomoniasis with pruritus, dysuria, dyspareunia, cervical erythema, and green, frothy, malodorous discharge with motile organisms on wet mount. Choice F: Herpes simplex virus causes painful genital lesions (not painless) that begin as erythematous areas, erupt as clear fluid-filled vesicles, and evolve to crusted ulcerations that heal without scarring. Educational Objective: Syphilis is caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum and presents in multiple stages. Primary syphilis features a painless chancre (ulcerative lesion) of the genitalia with no systemic symptoms. Secondary syphilis includes fever, lymphadenopathy, and condylomata lata. Tertiary syphilis presents with tabes dorsalis, aortitis, and gummas. The painless nature of the chancre in primary syphilis is a key distinguishing feature from other sexually transmitted infections causing genital ulcers.
Source: 8A #48
A 16-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother for a health maintenance examination. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Immunizations are up-to-date. Menses occur at irregular 28- to 35-day intervals. Her last menstrual period was 3 weeks ago. She does not smoke cigarettes, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. She has been sexually active with one male partner for 1 year; they do not use condoms. Her mother was diagnosed with breast cancer at the age of 40 years. The patient is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 65 kg (143 lb); BMI is 25 kg/m². Vital signs are within normal limits. Breast examination shows no masses or discharge. The external genitalia appear normal; there is no vaginal discharge. Breast and pubic hair development are sexual maturity rating stage 5. Which of the following is the most appropriate screening test to administer at this time? A) Mammography B) Measurement of fasting serum glucose concentration C) Measurement of hemoglobin concentration D) Nucleic acid amplification testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae E) Pap smear
Correct Answer: D) Nucleic acid amplification testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
For this healthy, adolescent female patient who is sexually active, preventive measures should primarily address her sexual health. The US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends screening all sexually active women under age 25 years for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. C. trachomatis is a common sexually transmitted infection that can cause various infections, including cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, epididymitis, and urethritis. In many cases it is asymptomatic, making screening of asymptomatic patients important for finding and treating active infections before long-term sequelae develop. C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae commonly coinfect the same patient, and nucleic acid amplification testing is the preferred diagnostic method. Mammography (Choice A) is recommended for breast cancer screening every 1 to 2 years for patients over age 40 years, not for a 16-year-old. Measurement of fasting serum glucose concentration (Choice B) is used for diabetes screening, which is recommended for asymptomatic adolescents who are overweight and have particular risk factors such as evidence of insulin resistance. This patient has a BMI of 25 kg/m² (normal range) with no other noted risk factors for diabetes. Measurement of hemoglobin concentration (Choice C) screens for anemia. The USPSTF does not recommend routine screening for iron deficiency anemia for children, as evidence for benefit is lacking. Screening for sexually transmitted infection is more important for this patient. Pap smear (Choice E) is recommended for cervical cancer screening in women aged 21 to 29 years every 3 years (or every 5 years with HPV cotesting for women aged 30 to 65 years). At age 16, this patient is not yet at the recommended age for Pap smear screening. Educational Objective: The US Preventive Services Task Force recommends screening all sexually active women under age 25 years for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. Early identification of these often asymptomatic infections prevents development of long-term sequelae.
Source: 8A #49
A 17-year-old girl comes to the office because she has had a burning sensation at the beginning of urination for the last 24 hours. She has no history of similar symptoms. Examination shows no abnormalities. Urinalysis shows marked pus and no bacteria. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Sitz baths B) Testing for sexually transmitted infections C) Wet mount preparation with KOH D) X-ray screening for urinary anomaly E) No intervention
Correct Answer: B) Testing for sexually transmitted infections
The clinician should offer testing for sexually transmitted diseases, or sexually transmitted infections (STIs), at this time. STIs including chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis are a major public health concern as they are often asymptomatic and can cause significant complications if left untreated. Adolescents are an at-risk demographic, especially as stigma regarding sexual activity and concerns about confidentiality may make individuals uncomfortable in disclosing any exposures or concerns regarding STIs. Urinary symptoms are a common presenting complaint for sexually active patients, and urinary tract infections (UTIs) often occur concurrently with STIs. Patients presenting with clinical findings of infection, such as dysuria and pyuria in this case, should be evaluated for both urinary tract infections and sexually transmitted infections, and appropriate treatment based on the results should be prescribed. Choice A (Sitz baths) can help alleviate symptoms of a UTI but should not replace appropriate diagnostic testing and antimicrobial therapy. Sitz baths are more commonly used for perianal pathologies, such as hemorrhoids. Choice C (Wet mount preparation with KOH) is useful in diagnosing Candida vulvovaginitis, which typically presents with pain, pruritis, dysuria, and dyspareunia with vulvar and/or vaginal erythema and thick, white discharge. This patient's clinical findings are more consistent with UTI or STI. Choice D (X-ray screening for urinary anomaly) is not indicated at this time. Patients presenting with recurrent urinary tract infections may have an underlying anatomic abnormality causing obstruction and stasis. However, ultrasound, CT imaging, or fluoroscopic studies are generally more sensitive for detecting structural urinary anomalies than plain film x-ray. Choice E (No intervention) is not appropriate as untreated STIs may have severe complications including upper genitourinary tract infection, pelvic inflammatory disease, abscess, and infertility. Educational Objective: There is a high prevalence of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) among adolescents and significant overlap in the clinical presentation of urinary tract infections and STIs. Patients presenting with suggestive findings, including dysuria and pyuria, should be offered diagnostic evaluation for both.
▶ Cardiovascular System Paroxysmal Tachycardias 4 questions
Source: 7A #4
An infant boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of progressively decreasing activity level and oral intake. His parent reports that he has had fewer wet diapers today. He has not had vomiting. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 245/min and regular, respirations are 32/min and shallow, and blood pressure is 60/40 mm Hg. He appears gray and poorly perfused; pulse oximetry is not obtainable. He is lethargic but responsive to pain. Lungs are clear to auscultation. Abdominal examination shows no abnormalities. Administration of supplemental oxygen is begun. He is placed on a cardiorespiratory monitor. An ECG rhythm strip is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Intramuscular injection of ceftriaxone B) Administration of a bolus of 0.9% saline C) Chest compressions D) Cardioversion E) Endotracheal intubation
Correct Answer: D) Cardioversion
Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) commonly occurs in children and infants and is characterized by paroxysmal episodes of rapid, narrow-complex tachycardia. Infants often present with pallor, irritability, poor feeding, and cyanosis. SVT is often idiopathic and paroxysmal but may occur secondary to accessory pathways in some children with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. Diagnosis is made by electrocardiogram, although some children may require cardiac monitoring to capture a paroxysmal event. Arteriovenous (AV) nodal blockade with adenosine is the first-line treatment for narrow-complex SVT in a hemodynamically stable patient. In the AV node, binding of the adenosine receptor leads to reduced transmission of supraventricular action potentials. If adenosine fails, additional AV nodal blockers or synchronized cardioversion may be attempted. Synchronized cardioversion is the first-line treatment in unstable SVT, as seen in this patient and suggested by the presence of hypotension and decreased end-organ perfusion (decreased urine output, lethargy, mottled skin). Children who are old enough may be trained to use vagal maneuvers to naturally induce AV nodal blockade. A similar vagal maneuver may be attempted by placing an ice bag over the eyes and face for approximately 30 seconds. Choice A: Intramuscular injection of ceftriaxone may be used to treat an underlying infection that could have triggered SVT, such as pneumonia. However, this patient has no signs of infection and is hemodynamically unstable. Therefore, treatment with synchronized cardioversion is the best choice. Choice B: Administration of a bolus of 0.9% saline may be warranted given this patient's recent decreased oral intake and reduced number of wet diapers. However, the decrease in urine output is more likely caused by decreased organ perfusion in the setting of SVT and conversion to normal sinus rhythm may improve it without the additional administration of fluid. This patient is hemodynamically unstable and requires immediate cardioversion. Choice C: Chest compressions are not warranted in this patient. In infants, chest compressions are started for cardiac arrest. This patient has a heart rate and blood pressure, although the latter is inadequate for end-organ perfusion caused by SVT. Performing chest compressions in a patient with organized cardiac activity can be harmful. Cardioversion is the more appropriate first step. Choice E: Endotracheal intubation is not necessary currently as this patient appears to be adequately protecting his airway, and his lungs are clear to auscultation. Pulse oximetry is difficult to obtain solely given his rapid heartbeat, and cardioversion would improve this. Additionally, giving this patient sedation to allow optimal intubating conditions may worsen his hypotension and cause cardiac arrest. Educational Objective: Supraventricular tachycardia, or paroxysmal episodes of rapid, narrow-complex tachycardia, presents in infants with pallor, irritability, poor feeding, and cyanosis. Diagnosis is made with electrocardiogram. Stable SVT is treated with adenosine, arteriovenous nodal blockade, or vagal maneuvers, whereas unstable SVT, characterized by hypotension and end-organ dysfunction, requires immediate synchronized cardioversion.
Source: 4A #33
A 2-week-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents because of a 30-minute history of her chest "fluttering." Thirty minutes ago, she vomited after breast-feeding. She was born at 40 weeks' gestation following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. She weighed 3402 g (7 lb 8 oz) at birth. On arrival, she is awake and appears alert. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is too rapid to count, respirations are 48/min, and blood pressure is 74/48 mm Hg. The extremities are pink and warm; capillary refill time is less than 2 seconds. The lungs are clear to auscultation. No murmurs are heard on cardiac examination. An ECG shows a regular heart rate of 240/min, a QRS complex duration of 0.05 seconds, and no discernible P waves. Application of an ice bag to the face for 5 seconds does not change the heart rate. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Administration of adenosine B) Administration of digoxin C) Administration of procainamide D) Administration of verapamil E) Catheter ablation F) Unsynchronized cardioversion
Correct Answer: A) Administration of adenosine
Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) commonly occurs in children and infants and is characterized by paroxysmal episodes of rapid, narrow-complex tachycardia. SVT is often idiopathic and paroxysmal but may occur secondary to accessory pathways in some children with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. Diagnosis is made by ECG, and this patient's presentation is classic: narrow QRS complex (0.05 seconds), regular rhythm at 240/min, and absent P waves. AV nodal blockade with adenosine is the first-line treatment for narrow-complex SVT. Adenosine is a purine analogue that acts on the adenosine A1 receptor, a G protein-coupled receptor. In the AV node, binding of the adenosine A1 receptor leads to cellular hyperpolarization and reduced transmission of supraventricular action potentials. If adenosine fails, synchronized cardioversion may be attempted. Children may also use vagal maneuvers (such as ice bag application for 30 seconds) to naturally induce AV nodal blockade; the attempted 5-second ice bag application in this case was insufficient duration. Choice B (Digoxin) is useful in managing congestive heart failure and atrial fibrillation/flutter but is not indicated for SVT treatment. Choice C (Procainamide), a sodium channel blocker, may be useful for chemical cardioversion in atrial fibrillation and is commonly used in arrhythmia management in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome (especially antidromic reentrant tachycardia), but is not first-line for acute narrow-complex SVT. Choice D (Verapamil), a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, is useful for chronic control of SVT but is not a first-line agent for aborting the acute arrhythmia. It may be used as adjunctive therapy if adenosine is ineffective. Choice E (Catheter ablation) is reserved for treatment of accessory pathways in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome and is not acute management. Choice F (Unsynchronized cardioversion) delivers an electrical shock at any point within the cardiac cycle and is reserved for pulseless ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation. For SVT patients failing adenosine therapy, synchronized cardioversion is the appropriate choice. Educational Objective: Supraventricular tachycardia is the most common tachyarrhythmia in infants. AV nodal blockade with adenosine is first-line treatment, working by adenosine A1 receptor-mediated cellular hyperpolarization in the AV node, reducing transmission of supraventricular action potentials.
Source: 9A #17
A previously healthy 1-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of progressively rapid breathing during the past 2 days. Her oral intake has decreased. She had an upper respiratory tract infection 3 days ago. She has received no medications. She is responsive and easily consoled. Her temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F), pulse is 190/min, respirations are 56/min, and blood pressure is 78/55 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities. Peripheral pulses are normal. Examination of the abdomen shows no abnormalities. Capillary refill time is 1 second, and a fingerstick blood glucose concentration is 120 mg/dL. Administration of oxygen by face mask is begun, and intravenous access is established. An ECG shows a narrow complex tachycardia without discernible P waves at a rate of approximately 260 to 300 beats per minute. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Intravenous administration of adenosine B) Intravenous administration of lidocaine C) Intravenous administration of propranolol D) Defibrillation E) Electrical cardioversion
Correct Answer: A) Intravenous administration of adenosine
This patient presents with tachypnea, tachycardia, decreased oral intake, and low-grade fever following an upper respiratory infection. The ECG demonstrates a narrow complex tachycardia without discernible P waves at a rate of 260-300 beats per minute, consistent with reentrant supraventricular tachycardia (SVT), most likely atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT). SVT should be suspected when tachycardia exceeds 180-200 beats per minute in children, and the narrow complex morphology on ECG confirms the supraventricular origin. The patient is hemodynamically stable with normal vital signs for a 1-year-old (normal heart rate 120-160 bpm, normal systolic BP >72-82 mm Hg). Initial management of stable SVT/AVNRT consists of vagal maneuvers, adenosine, calcium channel blockers, or cardio-specific beta-adrenergic blockers. Adenosine is first-line therapy because it has rapid onset and short duration of action, making it ideal for acute termination of SVT. AVNRT occurs due to a functional reentry circuit and can be provoked by stress, dehydration, and illness—all present in this case. Choice B (Lidocaine) is incorrect because lidocaine is used for ventricular arrhythmias such as ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation, not for SVT. Choice C (Propranolol) is not optimal because while beta-blockers can treat SVT, propranolol is not cardio-selective and has a longer duration of action than adenosine. Additionally, propranolol is more commonly used for thyroid storm. Choice D (Defibrillation) is inappropriate because defibrillation is reserved for ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia, not for SVT. Choice E (Electrical cardioversion) is reserved for hemodynamically unstable patients with SVT, which this patient is not. It is critical to recognize that normal vital sign ranges differ by age; this patient's blood pressure and perfusion are adequate for a 1-year-old, making adenosine the appropriate next step rather than cardioversion.
Source: 5A #12
A 1-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of increasing irritability and difficulty breathing over the past 6 hours. She has a 3-day history of nasal congestion, cough, and rectal temperatures to 37.5°C (99.5°F). Over the past 2 days, she has been given an over-the-counter cough and cold preparation every 4 hours without improvement, and her parents have been suctioning her nose after applying saline nose drops. She has only breast-fed once in the past 6 hours. Her rectal temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 260/min, respirations are 65/min, and blood pressure is 102/68 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. The liver edge is palpated 2 cm below the right costal margin, and the spleen is not palpable. An ECG is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Atrial fibrillation B) Long QT interval syndrome C) Sinus tachycardia D) Supraventricular tachycardia E) Ventricular tachycardia
Correct Answer: D) Supraventricular tachycardia
Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) refers to an abnormally rapid heart rate and rhythm originating from above the ventricles, typically with a regular rhythm and a narrow QRS complex on ECG. Patients with SVT can manifest with acute symptoms of lightheadedness, palpitations, diaphoresis, and syncope. In infants, signs and symptoms include pallor, irritability, poor feeding, and cyanosis. Infants presenting with SVT typically have a pulse between 220 and 280/min, consistent with this patient's pulse of 260/min. SVT may be caused by structural defects in the His-Purkinje system (e.g., Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome) or provoked by alcohol, nicotine, caffeine, or psychological stress. In this case, SVT was likely provoked by infection or use of an over-the-counter cough and cold preparation containing pseudoephedrine, a sympathomimetic drug that causes adverse reactions including tachycardia, anxiety, and palpitations. For hemodynamically stable patients, management includes vagal maneuvers (e.g., ice or cold water over the face) or adenosine. For hemodynamically unstable patients, cardioversion is indicated. Atrial fibrillation (Choice A) typically presents with irregular tachycardia and occurs more often in patients with structural heart disease. SVT is more likely in a previously healthy patient with regular tachycardia. Long QT interval syndrome (Choice B) is a disorder of prolonged ventricular depolarization and repolarization appearing on ECG with a prolonged QT interval, and can be complicated by polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or torsades de pointes. Sinus tachycardia (Choice C) would be unlikely to produce a pulse of 260/min, as the maximal pulse from the sinus node is typically lower than 220/min. On ECG, sinus tachycardia shows P waves prior to every QRS complex. SVT can achieve higher pulse rates due to a reentrant rhythm that bypasses the atrioventricular node. Ventricular tachycardia (Choice E) shows wide QRS complex tachycardia on ECG, occurring when an abnormal electrical focus or reentry circuit causes rapid ventricular contraction. The general morphology shows wide QRS complex tachycardia in either monomorphic or polymorphic forms. Educational Objective: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) refers to an abnormally rapid pulse and rhythm originating from above the ventricles, typically with a narrow QRS complex on ECG and a regular rhythm. In infants, SVT presents with irritability, poor feeding, and pulse rates of 220-280/min.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Obesity 3 questions
Source: 6A #3
An asymptomatic 10-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. His parents both have essential hypertension and hyperlipidemia. He has an active lifestyle and plays several sports. He consumes a wide variety of foods, including meat, fruit, and vegetables, and drinks two to three glasses each of whole milk and fruit juice daily. He is currently at the 75th percentile for height and above the 97th percentile for weight and BMI. Vital signs are within normal limits. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current weight? A) Excessive intake of carbohydrates B) Excessive intake of fat C) Excessive intake of total calories D) Inadequate intake of fruits and vegetables E) Inadequate physical activity
Correct Answer: C) Excessive intake of total calories
In children, overweight is defined as a BMI at or above the 85th percentile and below the 95th percentile for age and gender, while obesity is defined as a BMI at or above the 95th percentile. This obese child consumes a balanced diet but one that most likely contains excessive total calories. The key to understanding this case is recognizing that regardless of the macronutrient composition, total caloric intake is the fundamental driver of weight gain. Choice A (Excessive intake of carbohydrates) and Choice B (Excessive intake of fat) are both partially correct as this child likely consumes excess carbohydrates and fat, evidenced by drinking two to three glasses each of whole milk and fruit juice daily. However, these are not as comprehensive as excessive total calories, which encompasses all macronutrients and is the underlying mechanism. Choice D (Inadequate intake of fruits and vegetables) is incorrect because this child does consume a wide variety of foods including fruit and vegetables. While inadequate fruits and vegetables may indirectly lead to obesity by causing children to substitute unhealthy, fatty, or salty foods, this is not the primary issue here. Choice E (Inadequate physical activity) is incorrect because this child has an active lifestyle and plays several sports. Although physical inactivity is a common cause of childhood obesity, this patient's diet is the more likely cause of his obesity. Common causes of childhood obesity include consuming excessive total calories, a diet rich in unhealthy, calorie-rich foods, and lack of sufficient exercise. Children with obesity are at increased risk for comorbidities such as hypertension and diabetes mellitus.
Source: 9A #5
A 9-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because of a 1-month history of shortness of breath with exercise. His mother says he is unable to play sports with other children because he "becomes winded" and "breathes hard" after 5 minutes and has to sit down. His shortness of breath resolves after 5 minutes of rest. His mother says she encourages him to be more active and spend less time sitting on the couch and playing video games. He has no history of serious illness and receives no medications. He is at the 65th percentile for height and 95th percentile for weight and BMI. His pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 100/62 mm Hg (systolic and diastolic: 50th percentile for age and height). Examination, including cardiopulmonary examination, shows no other abnormalities. Results of serum lipid studies and a serum chemistry profile are within the reference ranges. Pulmonary function testing shows no abnormalities. A bronchodilator is administered, and repeat pulmonary function testing shows no significant change in baseline results. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Coronary insufficiency syndrome B) Deconditioning C) Exercise-induced asthma D) Gastroesophageal reflux disease E) Restrictive kyphoscoliotic lung disease
Correct Answer: B) Deconditioning
Pediatric obesity is most often caused by unbalanced diets, caloric excess, and lack of sufficient exercise. This patient most likely has deconditioning, which can lead to poor exercise tolerance and further exacerbate lack of activity. The patient is at the 95th percentile for BMI, meeting the diagnostic criteria for pediatric obesity (BMI ≥95th percentile for age and sex). His sedentary lifestyle (spending significant time on the couch and playing video games) combined with inability to sustain physical activity for more than 5 minutes before dyspnea and fatigue occur is classic for deconditioning. His normal cardiopulmonary examination, normal serum lipid studies and chemistry profile, normal pulmonary function tests, and lack of response to bronchodilators help exclude primary cardiopulmonary pathology. Choice A (Coronary insufficiency syndrome) is incorrect. Although it can manifest with chest pain, fatigue, and shortness of breath with exertion, the absence of chest pain, normal vital signs, normal cardiac examination, and normal lipid studies make this unlikely. Deconditioning from pediatric obesity is a more probable diagnosis than cardiovascular disease in this clinical context. Choice C (Exercise-induced asthma) is incorrect. While it may present with dyspnea and exertional symptoms, it is characterized by reversible airflow obstruction. The patient's normal baseline pulmonary function tests and lack of response to inhaled beta-adrenergic agonist (bronchodilator) exclude asthma as the diagnosis. Choice D (Gastroesophageal reflux disease) is incorrect. Although it can occur with increased intra-abdominal pressure (as in obesity), the patient has no associated symptoms such as heartburn, abdominal pain, or sour regurgitation. GERD symptoms are typically associated with large meals or specific trigger foods (acidic beverages, fatty foods, coffee, chocolate, tomato), which are not mentioned in this case. Choice E (Restrictive kyphoscoliotic lung disease) is incorrect. While severe spinal deformities restrict chest cavity volume and impair respiratory function, manifesting as restrictive pulmonary disease on testing (normal or increased FEV1:FVC ratio, decreased total lung capacity, decreased DLCO), this patient's pulmonary function tests are entirely normal. Furthermore, there is no mention of spinal deformity on examination. Pediatric obesity causes health consequences across nearly every organ system including cardiovascular (hypertension, dyslipidemia), endocrine (diabetes mellitus), gastrointestinal (NAFLD), musculoskeletal, and pulmonary (obesity-hypoventilation syndrome, obstructive sleep apnea). Prevention involves education on healthy diet and active lifestyle. Treatment includes diet and lifestyle modification as first-line therapy, with adjunctive options such as GLP-1 inhibitors or bariatric surgery if needed.
Source: 4A #41
An asymptomatic 10-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a health maintenance examination. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. His parents both have essential hypertension and hyperlipidemia. He has an active lifestyle and plays several sports. He consumes a wide variety of foods, including meat, fruit, and vegetables, and drinks two to three glasses each of whole milk and fruit juice daily. He is currently at the 90th percentile for height and above the 97th percentile for weight and BMI. Vital signs are within normal limits. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate dietary recommendation at this time? A) Avoid low-fat diets B) Begin dietary supplementation with a multivitamin C) Continue his current diet D) Decrease his intake of milk and fruit juice E) Increase his intake of fruit and vegetables
Correct Answer: D) Decrease his intake of milk and fruit juice
This 10-year-old boy displays signs concerning for obesity given his BMI over the 97th percentile. Pediatric obesity causes health consequences in nearly every organ system including cardiovascular (hypertension, dyslipidemia), endocrine (diabetes mellitus, hyperandrogenism, early menarche), gastrointestinal (nonalcoholic fatty liver disease), musculoskeletal (slipped capital femoral epiphysis), and pulmonary (obesity hypoventilation syndrome, obstructive sleep apnea). This patient is at further increased risk given his family history of hypertension and dyslipidemia. The first step in weight management in this patient is to decrease his caloric intake. His dietary history discloses that he is drinking an excessive amount of highly caloric beverages including whole milk and fruit juice. While milk contains beneficial nutrients such as calcium and vitamin D, whole milk contains approximately 100 calories per 8 oz serving. In contrast, fruit juice has little nutritional value and also contains approximately 100 calories per 8 oz serving. This simple dietary intervention is the most appropriate first step in managing this patient's weight. Choice A (Avoid low-fat diets) will encourage continued weight gain in this patient rather than help to decrease his weight. By simply decreasing whole milk and fruit juice intake, this patient may not need to pursue any specific diet. Choice B (Begin dietary supplementation with a multivitamin) is not indicated as there is no evidence that this patient does not have adequate vitamins and minerals in his diet. Furthermore, beginning a multivitamin would not affect the patient's weight, which is the primary concern in this otherwise well child. Choice C (Continue his current diet) will continue to perpetuate weight gain and promote eating habits which will negatively impact his adolescent and adult years. By improving his eating habits, he will be better prepared to manage his weight in the future. Choice E (Increase his intake of fruit and vegetables) would be a healthy dietary intervention, but it will not improve his weight. However, replacing high calorie, processed snacks with fruits and vegetables is another healthy habit to encourage in children and adolescents. Educational Objective: Childhood and adolescent obesity is becoming increasingly present in resource-rich countries. Obesity in this age group is associated with numerous health detriments. Patients and their parents should be taught healthy eating habits early in life.
▶ Musculoskeletal System Septic arthritis 3 questions
Source: 3A #15
A previously healthy 5-year-old girl is brought to the physician 24 hours after the onset of fever and increasingly severe left knee pain and swelling. She was unable to sleep last night because of the pain. She appears uncomfortable and is unable to bear weight on her left leg. Her temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 96/56 mm Hg. On examination, the left knee is swollen, red, warm, and exquisitely tender. She holds the knee in 45 degrees of flexion. She refuses to move the knee and resists passive extension and flexion. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities.
