A) Chondromalacia of the patella B) Discitis C) Growing pains D) Hypermobility syndrome E) Iliotibial band syndrome F) Ligamentous injury G) Osgood-Schlatter disease H) Osteoid osteoma I) Osteomyelitis J) Patellofemoral compression K) Referred pain from the hip L) Reflex sympathetic dystrophy M) Rheumatoid arthritis N) Septic arthritis O) Subluxation of the patella P) Toxic synovitis
Correct Answer: N) Septic arthritis
Septic arthritis is the correct answer. This patient presents with the classic clinical features of septic arthritis: acute onset fever (38.7°C), severe joint pain and swelling of the knee, refusal to bear weight, inability to move the joint, and signs of systemic illness (tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension suggesting sepsis). The joint appears erythematous and warm. Septic arthritis commonly occurs in children and is an orthopedic emergency. Risk factors include trauma to the joint and procedures causing transient bacteremia. Patients present with systemic signs and symptoms of illness (fever, chills, myalgias, arthralgias, nausea) along with a painful, erythematous, swollen joint with limited range of motion, commonly affecting the knee or hip. Serum laboratory values typically show leukocytosis and increased ESR and C-reactive protein. Synovial fluid aspiration demonstrates high white blood cell concentration and may disclose bacteria, commonly Staphylococcus aureus. Treatment includes antibiotics and surgical washout of the affected joint. Incorrect answers: Choice A (Chondromalacia of the patella) is a cartilaginous injury causing anterior knee pain, typically from overuse in athletes, without systemic signs. Choice B (Discitis) is intervertebral disc infection presenting with back pain and refusal to walk, not knee arthritis. Choice C (Growing pains) are idiopathic, bilateral, nocturnal, nonarticular, without abnormal examination findings. Choice D (Hypermobility syndrome) presents with joint hypermobility and pain without fever or systemic illness. Choice E (Iliotibial band syndrome) is lateral knee pain from overuse in athletes. Choice F (Ligamentous injury) is acute sports injury with abrupt pain and swelling but no fever. Choice G (Osgood-Schlatter disease) is tibial tubercle apophysitis in adolescent athletes with anterior knee pain, not systemic illness. Choice H (Osteoid osteoma) is a benign bony tumor with pain and refusal to bear weight but without fever or sepsis signs. Choice I (Osteomyelitis) is bone and bone marrow infection with pain and overlying erythema, but this presentation is more suggestive of joint space infection. Choice J (Patellofemoral compression) presents with knee pain on stairs or sitting, not systemic illness. Choice K (Referred pain from the hip) is unilateral pain with limping and refusal to bear weight but no fever or joint findings. Choice L (Reflex sympathetic dystrophy) is chronic burning pain with skin changes, not acute sepsis. Choice M (Rheumatoid arthritis/juvenile RA) occurs before age 16 with joint inflammation and extra-articular findings (uveitis, lymphadenopathy, rash), but typically more insidious onset. Choice O (Subluxation of the patella) is acute knee pain from partial dislocation in young athletes. Choice P (Toxic synovitis) is transient synovial inflammation in children <10 years with inability to bear weight but without signs of sepsis. Educational Objective: Septic arthritis is a common orthopedic emergency in the pediatric population presenting with acute onset joint pain, erythema, swelling, refusal to bear weight, and signs and symptoms of sepsis. Prompt diagnosis via joint aspiration and imaging, followed by antibiotics and surgical washout, is critical to prevent permanent joint damage.
Source: 7A #41
A previously healthy 10-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after the onset of pain in her right knee. She also has had a decreased appetite for 12 hours. There is no history of trauma to the knee or hip. Her temperature is 38.9°C (102°F). Examination shows erythema, swelling, and warmth of the right knee. Passive range of motion of the knee is limited by pain; the associated muscles are in spasm. She walks with an obvious limp. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Juvenile idiopathic arthritis B) Osteomyelitis C) Septic arthritis D) Transient synovitis of the hip E) Transient synovitis of the knee
Correct Answer: C) Septic arthritis
This patient presents with acute onset of a painful, erythematous, swollen knee with limited range of motion, fever, and systemic symptoms (decreased appetite), which is classic for septic arthritis. Septic arthritis results from bacterial infection of the synovial joint space, most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Pathways include direct inoculation, hematogenous spread, or extension from adjacent infection. Clinical presentation includes joint pain worsened with movement and weight-bearing, swelling, overlying erythema, palpable effusion, fever, and tachycardia. Laboratory findings typically show leukocytosis with elevated ESR and CRP. Arthrocentesis is essential for diagnosis and reveals synovial fluid with WBC count >50,000/mm³ that is predominantly neutrophilic, along with positive culture and Gram stain. Treatment consists of broad-spectrum antibiotics and often arthrocentesis with operative irrigation and debridement. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (Choice A) is an autoimmune condition with joint inflammation and extra-articular manifestations (uveitis, lymphadenopathy, rash), but typically lacks the acute fever and systemic toxicity seen here. Osteomyelitis (Choice B) is a bone and bone marrow infection presenting with pain, difficulty bearing weight, and overlying erythema, but this patient's presentation is more consistent with joint space infection rather than bone involvement. Transient synovitis of the hip (Choice D) and transient synovitis of the knee (Choice E) typically follow a preceding viral infection and present with pain on weight-bearing and antalgic gait. However, vital signs and laboratory studies are generally normal in transient synovitis, unlike this patient who has fever and systemic symptoms. Educational Objective: Septic arthritis is a bacterial infection of the joint space, most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Patients present with a painful, swollen, erythematous joint with decreased active and passive range of motion, fever, and systemic symptoms. Arthrocentesis is required for diagnosis, showing markedly elevated synovial fluid WBC count with positive culture.
Source: 6A #12
A 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 3-day history of severe pain and swelling in her right sternoclavicular joint. Ten days ago, the patient had a sore throat. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. Her temperature is 40°C (104°F). Examination shows erythema, swelling, and tenderness of the right sternoclavicular joint. Aspiration of the affected joint yields thick, yellow, purulent fluid. A Gram stain of the fluid shows numerous segmented neutrophils and numerous gram-negative diplococci. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Culture of the aspirate fluid B) Chest x-ray C) Echocardiography D) CT scan of the left sternoclavicular joint E) Indium-labeled leukocyte scan
Correct Answer: A) Culture of the aspirate fluid
This patient with monoarticular septic arthritis of the sternoclavicular joint from disseminated infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae should undergo culture of the aspirate fluid. Septic arthritis commonly occurs in children as a result of trauma permitting translocation of cutaneous organisms (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus) and may also occur in adolescents as a result of dissemination of Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a sexually transmitted bacterium that initially causes cervicitis, urethritis, or pharyngitis and may hematogenously disseminate to cause septic arthritis. Septic arthritis classically presents with a painful, erythematous, swollen joint along with systemic signs such as fever, chills, myalgia, arthralgia, and nausea. Gonococcal arthritis may present with monoarticular or asymmetric polyarticular disease and may feature adjacent tenosynovitis and dermatitis. The most common sites are the knee, ankle, wrist, and elbow, though the sternoclavicular joint may also be affected. In all causes of septic arthritis, serum laboratory values typically show leukocytosis along with increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein concentrations. Diagnosis requires arthrocentesis, which typically demonstrates purulent aspirate with increased neutrophil-predominant white blood cells. In gonococcal arthritis, culture of the aspirate fluid discloses gram-negative diplococci. Management requires antibiotic therapy with ceftriaxone and azithromycin along with source control. Choice B (Chest x-ray) may detect late findings of underlying osteomyelitis (e.g., erosions) in patients with septic arthritis caused by translocation of cutaneous organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus; however, osteomyelitis is less likely to result from gonococcal arthritis. Choice C (Echocardiography) would be helpful in diagnosing gonococcal endocarditis, a rare complication of disseminated Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. However, this patient with symptoms localized to a joint most likely has gonococcal arthritis. Choice D (CT scan of the left sternoclavicular joint) may assist in visualization of a joint effusion, especially in difficult-to-examine joints such as the hip. However, joint aspiration is the preferred method for definitively diagnosing septic arthritis. Choice E (Indium-labeled leukocyte scan) is a nuclear medicine procedure that assists in localizing sites of infection and inflammation and is often used in patients with fever of unknown origin. This patient possesses a clear source of infection. Educational Objective: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a sexually transmitted bacterium that initially causes cervicitis, urethritis, or pharyngitis, and may hematogenously disseminate to cause septic arthritis. Gonococcal arthritis may present with monoarticular or asymmetric polyarticular erythema, edema, and tenderness. Diagnosis requires culture of the aspirate synovial fluid, which typically demonstrates gram-negative diplococci and an increased concentration of neutrophil-predominant white blood cells.
▶ Renal Urinary System Lupus Nephritis 3 questions
Source: 6A #42
Four days after admission to the hospital for evaluation of a high-grade fever, a 12-year-old girl has decreased urine output. Her urine output has been 2 mL/h during the past 12 hours. She has a 4-week history of temperatures to 40.6°C (105°F), facial rash, and diffuse joint pain. On admission, a diagnosis of hypertensive encephalopathy was made, and antihypertensive therapy was begun. Her current temperature is 39.8°C (103.6°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 45/min, and blood pressure is 168/98 mm Hg. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Serum Na+ 129 mEq/L, K+ 9 mEq/L, urea nitrogen 130 mg/dL, creatinine 10.2 mg/dL; Urine RBC >100/hpf, RBC casts occasional. An ECG is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Bolus of methylprednisolone B) Intravenous administration of calcium chloride C) Intravenous administration of 0.9% sodium chloride D) Plasmapheresis E) Hemodialysis
Correct Answer: B) Intravenous administration of calcium chloride
This case presents a 12-year-old girl with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) complicated by lupus nephritis, which has progressed to acute kidney injury (AKI) with severe hyperkalemia. The clinical presentation includes a 4-week history of fever, malar rash (sparing the nasolabial folds), and diffuse joint pain—classic SLE features. The laboratory findings confirm acute renal failure with markedly elevated creatinine (10.2 mg/dL), elevated blood urea nitrogen (130 mg/dL), and severely elevated serum potassium (9 mEq/L). Lupus nephritis commonly affects younger women and can present with hypertension, hematuria, and renal dysfunction. The presence of hematuria and RBC casts on urinalysis supports the diagnosis of lupus nephritis. The ECG changes shown (though not explicitly detailed in the stem) are consistent with severe hyperkalemia, which can cause peaked T waves, PR interval prolongation, loss of P waves, widened QRS complex, and bradycardia—all manifestations of decreased myocardial excitability and repolarization abnormalities. Severe hyperkalemia causing ECG changes is a medical emergency requiring immediate stabilization of the cardiac membrane to prevent dysrhythmias and cardiac arrest. Calcium gluconate or calcium chloride is the first-line emergent intervention, as it stabilizes the myocardial cell membrane by opposing hyperkalemia's effects on membrane potential, reducing the risk of life-threatening arrhythmias. This must be administered before attempting to shift potassium intracellularly or remove it from the body. Choice A (methylprednisolone bolus): While immunosuppressive therapy with corticosteroids may be appropriate for managing the underlying SLE and lupus nephritis, it is not the immediate next step. The acute hyperkalemia with ECG changes requires emergent stabilization first. Choice C (0.9% sodium chloride): Although the patient has mild hyponatremia (129 mEq/L), likely from renal failure and volume overload, administering hypertonic saline would not address the life-threatening hyperkalemia. Moreover, the patient may have volume overload from renal failure, making fluid administration potentially harmful. The immediate priority is cardiac stabilization. Choice D (plasmapheresis): This procedure is used to remove circulating immune complexes or pathogenic antibodies (such as in conditions like thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura) but does not significantly affect serum potassium concentration. It would not address the acute hyperkalemia and would delay necessary treatment. Choice E (hemodialysis): While hemodialysis is an important treatment for severe or refractory hyperkalemia and for managing AKI, it is not the first step. Dialysis takes time to initiate and arrange, whereas calcium must be administered immediately to stabilize the myocardium before potassium-lowering interventions are attempted. After calcium administration, additional measures such as insulin with glucose, beta-adrenergic agonists, bicarbonate, loop diuretics, or sodium polystyrene sulfonate may be used. If hyperkalemia is severe or refractory to these measures, dialysis may then be necessary. Educational Objective: Acute renal failure can lead to hypertension and severe hyperkalemia. Severe hyperkalemia resulting in ECG changes requires the emergent administration of calcium gluconate or calcium chloride to induce cardiac cell membrane stabilization. This is the critical first step before attempting to lower potassium concentrations with medications or dialysis, preventing potentially fatal cardiac arrhythmias.
Source: 5A #44
A 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of a facial rash and fatigue. She has a 9-day history of stiffness and swelling of her fingers on awakening in the morning. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She appears tired and has mild chest pain with deep inspirations. Her temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 94/min and regular, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 112/76 mm Hg. Examination shows a bright red rash over the cheeks and nose. Diffuse 1- to 2-cm lymph nodes are palpated in the anterior and posterior cervical chains. There are three nontender ulcers on the soft palate. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Heart sounds are normal. Examination of the extremities shows mild erythema, tenderness, and swelling of the proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints, knees, and metatarsophalangeal joints. Urinalysis shows 2+ protein and 1+ blood. Which of the following is most appropriate in determining appropriate management for this patient? A) X-rays of the knees B) Echocardiography C) MRI of the brain D) Cerebral angiography E) Renal biopsy
Correct Answer: E) Renal biopsy
This patient presents with multiple criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), a systemic autoimmune connective tissue disease. Her clinical features include: malar rash (bright red rash over cheeks and nose), painless oral ulcers (three nontender ulcers on soft palate), arthritis (symmetric swelling and tenderness of PIP, MCP, knee, and MTP joints with morning stiffness), serositis (pleuritic chest pain), and renal impairment (proteinuria and hematuria on urinalysis). These findings satisfy the diagnostic criteria for SLE (four of eleven criteria required). The most pressing complication evident in this patient is lupus nephritis, indicated by the presence of hematuria and proteinuria. Renal biopsy is the gold standard for determining the type and extent of renal involvement in lupus nephritis, which is essential for optimizing treatment decisions. Different histological patterns (such as diffuse proliferative versus mesangial involvement) have different prognoses and treatment implications. Immunosuppressive therapy is warranted for active diffuse or focal proliferative lupus nephritis but not for mild mesangial or mesangial proliferative disease. Choice A (X-rays of the knees): While knee pain evaluation typically begins with X-rays, this patient's arthritis of SLE is characteristically non-erosive and non-deforming. X-rays will likely be normal and will not change arthritis management, which relies on NSAIDs, antimalarials, or glucocorticoids. This choice does not address the more serious renal manifestation. Choice B (Echocardiography): While the patient has pleuritic chest pain suggestive of pleuritis, she is hemodynamically stable with normal cardiac examination findings. Echocardiography is useful for detecting pleural and pericardial effusions, but the more pressing complication requiring diagnostic evaluation is lupus nephritis. Choice C (MRI of the brain) and Choice D (Cerebral angiography): These neuroimaging modalities are used to evaluate neuropsychiatric manifestations of SLE, such as seizures or psychosis. This patient has no evidence of neuropsychiatric symptoms, making these investigations unwarranted at this time. Educational Objective: SLE is an autoimmune connective tissue disease with multiple potential organ system manifestations. Lupus nephritis is a common and serious complication, particularly in younger female patients. Hematuria and proteinuria with rising creatinine are characteristic findings of lupus nephritis. Renal biopsy is necessary to accurately determine the histological type and extent of renal involvement, which directly informs treatment decisions and prognostication.
Source: 8A #13
A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of dark-colored urine for 5 days and a facial rash for 1 day. She has a history of diffuse joint pain treated with acetaminophen. Her blood pressure is 115/70 mm Hg. She appears pale and thin. Examination shows a prominent, erythematous, butterfly-shaped macular eruption over the face. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely to be decreased? A) Eosinophil count B) Factor D C) Factor P D) Serum C4 concentration E) Serum C9 concentration
Correct Answer: D) Serum C4 concentration
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disorder with a wide range of presentations. Cutaneous manifestations include an erythematous rash over the malar cheeks that spares the nasolabial folds after sun exposure or discoid lesions with hyperpigmented edges and pink, atrophic centers. Painless oral ulcers and nonspecific hair loss may also occur. Fatigue, joint pain, and fever are also common presenting signs. Lupus nephritis is a common complication of SLE, particularly in younger women. Patients with lupus nephritis typically present with evidence of active SLE and may additionally display oliguria or anuria, signs and symptoms of hypertension (e.g., headache, visual disturbance), uremia (e.g., fatigue, nausea, vomiting, pruritus, altered mental status), hyperkalemia (e.g., peaked T waves on ECG), and hypervolemia with peripheral edema. Lupus nephritis involves glomerular deposition of antibodies, including IgG, IgM, and IgA, as well as activation of the classical complement pathway. Laboratory studies therefore generally show hypocomplementemia with decreased serum concentrations of early classical pathway components such as C1q, C2, C3, C4, and CH50, as well as increased creatinine. Kidney biopsy is useful for disease staging and may show a range of histologic patterns from mesangial glomerulonephritis to diffuse proliferative or membranous glomerulonephritis. Choice A (Eosinophil count) is typically normal in patients with lupus nephritis. Increased eosinophil concentrations may be observed in the setting of acute interstitial nephritis. Choice B (Factor D) and Choice C (Factor P) are components of the alternative complement pathway, which is not antibody dependent. The alternative complement pathway is typically not dysregulated in the setting of SLE, and serum concentrations of these components are normal. Choice E (Serum C9 concentration), as well as other late complement components, are typically normal in patients with SLE and lupus nephritis. Educational Objective: Lupus nephritis is a common complication of systemic lupus erythematosus and may present with oliguria or anuria, hypertension, uremia, hyperkalemia, and hypervolemia with peripheral edema. Lupus nephritis involves glomerular deposition of antibodies, including IgG, IgM, and IgA, as well as activation of the classical complement pathway. Laboratory studies therefore generally show hypocomplementemia with decreased serum concentrations of early classical pathway components such as C1q, C2, C3, C4, and CH50, as well as increased creatinine.
▶ Blood Lymphoreticular System Hodgkin lymphoma 3 questions
Source: 3A #18
A 16-year-old girl comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of a mass in the right side of the neck, progressive axillary and inguinal adenopathy, and generalized pruritus. She has had a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight loss during this period. Examination shows no other abnormalities. An x-ray of the chest shows a mediastinal mass. Laboratory studies show anemia with a normal leukocyte count and differential, increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and increased serum ferritin concentration. A node biopsy specimen is most likely to show which of the following? A) Cytomegalovirus infection B) Hodgkin disease C) Sarcoidosis D) Thymoma E) Tuberculosis
Correct Answer: B) Hodgkin disease
Hodgkin disease is a type of lymphoma, predominantly B-cell in origin, that occurs commonly in patients who are 20 to 30 and 55 to 65 years old (bimodal age distribution). Patients typically present with lymphadenopathy as well as nonspecific constitutional symptoms such as fever, night sweats, weight loss, and pruritus. The most common sites of lymphadenopathy are the neck and mediastinum. Laboratory values typically demonstrate a normal leukocyte count, anemia, increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and increased serum ferritin concentration, which are related to the underlying systemic inflammation. Initial evaluation commonly includes a chest x-ray or CT scan, which will potentially outline the extent of the patient's mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy. Definitive diagnosis requires excisional lymph node biopsy, which will disclose Reed-Sternberg cells (atypical cells with bilobed nuclei), a large inflammatory infiltrate with eosinophilic predominance, and fibrosis. Hodgkin cells are typically CD15- and CD30-positive. The most common subtype is nodular sclerosing, whereas the worst prognosis occurs in the setting of the lymphocyte-depleted subtype. Risk factors for its development include Epstein-Barr infection, immunosuppression, and a family history of Hodgkin disease. Treatment includes chemotherapy and radiation therapy. Choice A (Cytomegalovirus infection) is often asymptomatic but can cause a short febrile, flu-like illness in healthy patients. It can cause severe infections in immunocompromised patients but does not present with generalized pruritus. Choice C (Sarcoidosis) is a chronic granulomatous inflammatory condition that can affect multiple organ systems, especially the lungs and lymphatic system. It typically presents with cough, dyspnea, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and potentially with anterior uveitis, erythema nodosum, and arthralgias, not the constellation of findings in this patient. Choice D (Thymoma) is a benign or malignant tumor of the thymus. It presents with an anterior mediastinal mass, which can cause chest pain or shortness of breath. It is commonly associated with myasthenia gravis but does not often present with lymphadenopathy. Choice E (Tuberculosis) is spread via airborne transmission and can present with a primary, latent, or reactivation pattern. Primary disease demonstrates subacute fever, weight loss, night sweats, cough, and malaise, whereas latent tuberculosis is commonly asymptomatic. Reactivation presents similarly to primary disease but occurs after a period of latency, typically affecting the lung apices or resulting in miliary disease. The clinical presentation and laboratory findings are most consistent with Hodgkin disease rather than tuberculosis.
Source: 9A #26
A patient presents with a right-sided neck mass, fever, and an increased ESR that did not respond to antibiotic therapy. What is the most likely diagnosis? A) Acute lymphocytic leukemia B) Cat-scratch disease C) Cervical adenitis D) Histoplasmosis E) Hodgkin lymphoma F) Tuberculosis
Correct Answer: E) Hodgkin lymphoma
The patient presents with classic features of Hodgkin lymphoma: localized lymphadenopathy (right-sided neck mass), B-symptoms (fever), elevated inflammatory markers (increased ESR), and lack of response to antibiotic therapy. Hodgkin lymphoma is a predominantly B-lymphocyte malignancy with a bimodal age distribution (peaks at 20-30 years and 55-65 years). Definitive diagnosis requires core or excisional lymph node biopsy demonstrating Reed-Sternberg cells. Staging with CT or PET scan follows biopsy. Markers of cell turnover (lactate dehydrogenase) and inflammatory markers (ESR) are often elevated. Risk factors include immunosuppression, prior Epstein-Barr virus infection, and HIV. Treatment with chemotherapy and radiation is often curative with favorable prognosis. Choice A (Acute lymphocytic leukemia) is incorrect because it is primarily a malignancy of childhood with characteristic cytopenias and circulating blasts on peripheral smear, not localized lymphadenopathy in an adult. Choice B (Cat-scratch disease) is incorrect because while caused by Bartonella henselae from cat scratches or bites, it typically causes localized lymphadenitis in the drainage pattern of the scratch without systemic B-symptoms or elevated ESR in this presentation. Choice C (Cervical adenitis) is incorrect because while it can present with neck lymphadenopathy from various infections, autoimmune disease, or malignancy, the combination of persistent fever unresponsive to antibiotics, elevated ESR, and a nontender mass is more consistent with Hodgkin lymphoma than simple adenitis. Choice D (Histoplasmosis) is incorrect because it typically presents with pulmonary symptoms (cough, hemoptysis) and mediastinal/hilar lymphadenopathy rather than isolated cervical lymph node enlargement, and is endemic to specific geographic regions. Choice F (Tuberculosis) is incorrect because it would typically present with pulmonary symptoms, constitutional symptoms over a longer time course, and is more common in endemic areas or patients with significant travel history to high-risk regions.
Source: 9A #27
An 11-year-old boy is brought to the office because of cough, fever, and swelling on the right side of the neck for 3 weeks. The cough awakens him from sleep. He just completed a 1-week course of antibiotic therapy with no change in symptoms. His temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse is 80/min, and respirations are 20/min. A 2x4-cm, firm, nontender mass is palpated in the right supraclavicular region; there is no other adenopathy. The lungs are clear to auscultation. The liver and spleen are not palpable. A complete blood count is within normal limits, erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 80 mm/h. An x-ray of the chest shows a mediastinal mass. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Acute lymphocytic leukemia B) Cat-scratch disease C) Cervical adenitis D) Histoplasmosis E) Tuberculosis
Correct Answer: D) Histoplasmosis
This clinical presentation is most consistent with histoplasmosis, a fungal infection that commonly presents with mediastinal lymphadenopathy and supraclavicular lymph node enlargement. The patient's symptoms of persistent cough, fever, and significantly elevated ESR (80 mm/h) with a normal CBC are classic for histoplasmosis. The presence of a mediastinal mass on chest x-ray is a hallmark finding of disseminated histoplasmosis, particularly in children. The failure to respond to antibiotic therapy is an important clue that this is a fungal rather than bacterial infection. Choice A (Acute lymphocytic leukemia): While ALL can present with lymphadenopathy and mediastinal mass, the CBC would typically show abnormal white blood cell counts or blasts, which are absent here. The normal CBC makes ALL less likely. Choice B (Cat-scratch disease): Though this can cause regional lymphadenopathy, it typically causes more localized adenitis at the site of inoculation and does not characteristically produce mediastinal masses. The prolonged course without response to antibiotics and the significant systemic findings make this less likely. Choice C (Cervical adenitis): Cervical adenitis describes inflammation and swelling of cervical lymph nodes from various infectious causes (usually bacterial). However, cervical adenitis would not typically present with a mediastinal mass, and the normal CBC with only elevated ESR suggests a chronic systemic process rather than acute bacterial infection. Choice E (Tuberculosis): Primary tuberculosis infection presents with subacute fevers, weight loss, night sweats, cough, and malaise. While TB can cause mediastinal lymphadenopathy and may be in the differential, histoplasmosis is more common in this clinical context, particularly with the acute presentation and significant lymphadenopathy without systemic symptoms of advanced disease. TB would more typically show hilar rather than supraclavicular involvement as the primary finding.
▶ Behavioral Health Developmental Delay Undefined 3 questions
Source: 3A #30
A 2370-g (5-lb 3-oz) newborn is delivered at term to a 37-year-old primigravid woman who had limited prenatal care. The mother drank one to two beers daily but did not use any illicit drugs. The newborn appears vigorous and is not cyanotic. Examination shows a prominent occiput, narrow palpebral fissures, a small recessed mandible, and a short sternum. The hands are clenched with the index finger folded over the middle finger and the small finger folded over the ring finger. There is a grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur that is heard best at the lower left sternal border. The abdomen is prominent and soft; there is no hepatosplenomegaly. Peripheral pulses are normal. There is generalized hypertonia. Deep tendon reflexes are present. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this newborn's low birth weight? A) Arthrogryposis B) Congenital infection C) Exposure to alcohol in utero D) Trisomy 18 E) Uteroplacental insufficiency
Correct Answer: D) Trisomy 18
Trisomy 18, also known as Edwards syndrome, is the second most common trisomy in infants and presents with characteristic physical features that match this clinical presentation: prominent occiput, micrognathia (small recessed mandible), clenched overlapping fingers (index finger folded over middle finger, small finger folded over ring finger), low-set ears, intellectual disability, and feet with prominent calcanei and convexly rounded soles. The holosystolic murmur indicates congenital heart disease, which is common in this condition. Low birth weight is typical. It is associated with decreased serum PAPP-A and human chorionic gonadotropin concentrations in the first trimester. The incidence increases with increasing maternal age, relevant to this 37-year-old primigravid woman. Most cases result from meiotic nondisjunction, where two chromatids fail to separate, resulting in a single haploid gamete containing two copies of a chromosome. Most patients die within the first 6 months of age, and treatment involves correction or management of life-threatening abnormalities. Arthrogryposis (Choice A) describes congenital joint contractures that result in impaired joint movement and muscle atrophy, but does not explain the facial features or cardiac findings. Congenital infection (Choice B) with viruses such as CMV, HSV, rubella, measles, or parvovirus each produce different abnormalities. HSV causes cutaneous herpetic lesions and systemic manifestations like meningoencephalitis. CMV manifests with hearing loss, seizures, petechial rash, intracranial calcifications, organomegaly, and lymphadenopathy. Congenital rubella presents with cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and congenital heart disease. However, the specific pattern of facial and hand deformities is not consistent with these infections. Exposure to alcohol in utero (Choice C) results in fetal alcohol syndrome, which causes intellectual disability, microcephaly, facial abnormalities (thin vermillion border, small palpebral fissures), and heart defects. While some features overlap, the specific hand positioning with overlapping fingers and the prominent occiput are characteristic of trisomy 18, not fetal alcohol syndrome. Uteroplacental insufficiency (Choice E) describes insufficient blood flow to the placenta or inability to deliver adequate nutrients to the fetus, resulting in fetal hypoglycemia, oligohydramnios, intrauterine growth restriction, or maternal complications including preeclampsia, miscarriage, or stillbirth. This would not produce the specific congenital abnormalities seen in this infant. Educational Objective: Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome) presents with characteristic physical features including a prominent occiput, low-set ears, micrognathia, clenched overlapping fingers, intellectual disability, and feet with prominent calcanei and convexly rounded soles. Maternal age increases the risk of meiotic nondisjunction.
Source: 8A #7
A 4-year-old boy is brought to the office for a well-child visit. He can imitate a straight line, but he cannot copy a circle. He combines words, and only half his speech can be understood. He can jump but cannot balance on one foot. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most accurate assessment of this patient's development? Gross Motor | Fine Motor | Language Development A) Delayed | Delayed | Delayed B) Delayed | Normal | Normal C) Delayed | Delayed | Normal D) Normal | Delayed | Normal E) Normal | Delayed | Delayed F) Normal | Delayed | Normal G) Normal | Normal | Delayed H) Normal | Normal | Normal
Correct Answer: A) Delayed | Delayed | Delayed
Global developmental delay is defined as significant delay in two or more domains of development. This patient demonstrates delays across multiple developmental domains. By age 4 years, most children should be able to: (1) Gross motor: hop on one foot and throw a ball overhand—this patient cannot balance on one foot, indicating gross motor delay; (2) Fine motor: draw a square and simple stick figure—this patient can only imitate a straight line and cannot copy a circle, indicating fine motor delay; (3) Language: tell complex stories, identify colors and numbers, and speak in sentences that are understood by others—this patient's speech is only half understandable, indicating language delay. Screening for developmental milestone achievement across gross motor, fine motor, cognitive, social, and language domains is an important element of the pediatric well-child examination. Patients delayed in meeting developmental milestones should be evaluated for underlying causes and referred for early childhood intervention where they have access to speech therapists, physical therapists, and occupational therapists. All other answer choices are incorrect because they do not accurately capture the delays this patient demonstrates across all three domains assessed (gross motor, fine motor, and language).
Source: 8A #25
A 3-year-old girl is brought to the office for a follow-up examination. She has a seizure disorder and strabismus. Her only medication is valproic acid. She is at the 25th percentile for height and weight and 3rd percentile for head circumference. She appears happy, has an excitable demeanor, and frequently smiles and laughs. Examination shows a flattened posterior aspect of the head, prominent jaw, and widely spaced teeth. She flaps her hands repeatedly. She has a stiff-legged gait and cannot climb stairs without assistance. Her attention span is short. She uses some gestures and sounds to communicate but has not spoken any words. Which of the following is the most likely genetic defect in this patient? A) Chromosome 7 deletion B) Chromosome 15 deletion, maternally inherited C) Chromosome 15 deletion, paternally inherited D) Mutation of MECP2 gene E) Trisomy 15 F) Trisomy 21
Correct Answer: B) Chromosome 15 deletion, maternally inherited
Angelman syndrome is a genetic disorder caused by microdeletion of the maternally inherited chromosome region 15q11-13, which contains the gene for the ubiquitin pathway protein UBE3A. The syndrome is characterized by abnormal development of particular brain areas (hippocampus, cortex, cerebellum) in which the paternally inherited copy of UBE3A is inactivated through imprinting—an epigenetic process involving selective gene inactivation through DNA and histone methylation. This creates a reliance on the maternally inherited copy for normal development. In contrast, microdeletion of paternally inherited UBE3A leads to Prader-Willi syndrome. Children with Angelman syndrome present with characteristic signs and symptoms including severe developmental delay and cognitive disability, seizures, ataxia, speech delay, and microcephaly. Patients typically display a happy, excitable demeanor with uncontrolled laughter and repetitive hand flapping movements. Other findings include characteristic facial features (flat posterior aspect of the head, prominent mandible with widely spaced teeth and protruding tongue), strabismus, sleep disturbances, and fascination with water. Incorrect answers: A) Chromosome 7 deletion at 7q11.23 causes Williams syndrome, characterized by atypically friendly demeanor, emotional dysregulation, intellectual delay, elfin facies, short stature, vascular and cardiac valve abnormalities from elastin dysfunction, urinary tract structural abnormalities, and endocrine abnormalities. C) Chromosome 15 deletion, paternally inherited, causes Prader-Willi syndrome, presenting with hyperphagia and potential obesity, short stature, impaired cognition, motor delays, and hypogonadism. D) Mutation of MECP2 gene on the X chromosome results in Rett syndrome, presenting in females with microcephaly, cognitive and language impairment, loss of motor skills, seizures, repetitive hand wringing movements, and scoliosis. Patients may display autism spectrum disorder-like features with lack of social interest and eye contact. E) Trisomy 15 is a rare cause of Angelman syndrome in the setting of uniparental disomy with paternal nondisjunction of chromosome 15 followed by maternal loss of 15q11-13. However, microdeletion of 15q11-13 without uniparental disomy is more common. Complete trisomy 15 is typically lethal in utero. F) Trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome, presenting with characteristic physical features including broad, flat facial features with prominent epicanthal folds and a single palmar crease. Patients also present with cognitive impairment, cardiac abnormalities (atrial septal defect), gastrointestinal abnormalities (duodenal atresia, imperforate anus), ophthalmologic abnormalities (refractive errors), and hearing loss. Educational Objective: Recognize that Angelman syndrome results from microdeletion of the maternally-inherited chromosome region 15q11-13 containing UBE3A, leading to abnormal brain development due to epigenetic imprinting-mediated inactivation of the paternally inherited copy, and distinguish it from Prader-Willi syndrome (paternally inherited deletion) and other chromosomal disorders.
▶ Gastrointestinal System Intussusception 3 questions
Source: 3A #31
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of intermittent severe abdominal cramping over the past 3 days. He has had no vomiting but has passed three stools during this period; the third stool had reddish discoloration. He is currently alert and resting comfortably. His temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft with normal bowel sounds. There is no organomegaly or masses. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Gastritis B) Intussusception C) Juvenile polyp D) Peptic ulcer E) Viral gastroenteritis
Correct Answer: B) Intussusception
Intussusception occurs when a segment of bowel telescopes into an adjacent segment, resulting in colicky abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and potential bloody, mucoid stools. It classically presents in an infant or young child with recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain often punctuated by asymptomatic periods. Intussusception typically occurs as a result of the presence of a pathologic lead point, often lymphoid hyperplasia, lymphadenopathy, Meckel diverticulum, stricture, or malignancy, which acts to draw one segment of bowel into an adjacent segment during peristalsis. If the intussusception self-resolves, there may be no symptoms. If it does not resolve, traction on mesenteric vessels can result in hypoperfusion of the segment with resultant inflammation, hemorrhage, obstruction, and pain. It may be detected on physical examination as an elongated mass, often in the right upper quadrant. Diagnosis consists of clinical history and physical examination and is supported by imaging. Ultrasonography evaluation is preferred in young children and will show telescoping interposed bowel segments in longitudinal orientation or a targetoid appearance in transverse orientation. Treatment of an ileocolic intussusception requires the administration of a contrast enema, which decreases the intussusception. Contrast enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic in this setting. Surgery may be required in cases where there is repetitive failure of the enema to decrease the intussusception or if the patient presents with symptoms concerning for bowel necrosis or perforation. Choice A (Gastritis) can be caused by a viral illness or use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). It is characterized by epigastric discomfort, nausea, vomiting, or if severe, hematemesis. The associated pain is typically constant, not colicky as seen in this patient. Choice C (Juvenile polyps) are benign hamartomas that can present with painless rectal bleeding. Abdominal pain would be uncommon. In a patient with severe abdominal cramping followed by bloody stool, intussusception is more likely. Choice D (Peptic ulcer disease) is uncommon in children and can be related to NSAIDs or Helicobacter pylori infection. Patients typically present with epigastric discomfort, nausea, and vomiting, typically after eating. PUD can be complicated by hemorrhage or perforation but does not present with the colicky pattern seen here. Choice E (Viral gastroenteritis) is a common, typically self-limiting illness in children characterized by nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and mild abdominal discomfort. It would usually not cause bloody stools. Bloody diarrhea in children should raise suspicion for bacterial gastroenteritis by Escherichia coli O157:H7, not viral causes. Educational Objective: Intussusception occurs when a segment of bowel telescopes into an adjacent segment, resulting in colicky abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and potential bloody, mucoid stools. It is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children between 6 months and 3 years of age and requires urgent evaluation with ultrasonography and treatment with contrast enema.
Source: 7A #19
A previously healthy 10-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of a 10-hour history of bloody, mucoid stools. He also has vomited three times during this time. His mother says that he cries and draws up his legs during the episodes of vomiting. Between episodes, he appears comfortable. He is playful and is not in distress. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows mild distention. A 4-cm, tender, elongated mass is palpated in the right upper quadrant. There is no hepatosplenomegaly. Rectal examination shows bloody mucoid stool in the rectal vault. Results of a contrast enema are shown. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings? A) Bleeding diverticulum B) Intussusception C) Malrotation volvulus D) Peptic ulcer E) Pyloric stenosis
Correct Answer: B) Intussusception
Intussusception occurs when a segment of bowel telescopes into an adjacent segment, resulting in colicky abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and potential bloody, mucoid stools. This case presents the classic presentation of intussusception in an infant with recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain punctuated by asymptomatic periods, bloody mucoid stools, and an elongated mass in the right upper quadrant on physical examination. Intussusception typically occurs due to a pathologic lead point, often lymphoid hyperplasia, lymphadenopathy, Meckel diverticulum, stricture, or malignancy, which acts to draw one segment of bowel into an adjacent segment during peristalsis. When the intussusception does not self-resolve, traction on mesenteric vessels results in hypoperfusion of the segment with inflammation, hemorrhage, obstruction, and pain. Diagnosis is supported by imaging, with ultrasound being preferred in young children, showing telescoping interposed bowel segments in longitudinal orientation or a targetoid appearance in transverse orientation. A contrast enema can also demonstrate intussusception and is both diagnostic and therapeutic, as it can reduce the intussusception. Surgery may be required if there is repetitive failure of enema reduction or concerns for bowel necrosis or perforation. Choice A: Bleeding diverticulum is a common cause of painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding in older adults. While a Meckel diverticulum can bleed in children, it would not present with signs of obstruction as seen in this case. Choice C: Malrotation volvulus occurs secondary to incomplete rotation of bowel during embryonic development, placing newborns at risk for midgut volvulus presenting with bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and pain. In severe cases, intestinal necrosis, hematochezia, perforation, and peritonitis may occur. However, the classic presentation and physical examination findings of an elongated mass in the right upper quadrant are not typical of malrotation volvulus. Choice D: Peptic ulcer disease is uncommon in children and typically presents with epigastric discomfort, nausea, and vomiting after eating. It can result in melena or perforation but does not present with colicky abdominal pain, an abdominal mass, or bloody mucoid stools as in this case. Choice E: Pyloric stenosis typically presents at several weeks of life with repeated nonbilious vomiting after feeds, leading to dehydration and hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. The patient in this case is 10 months old with bloody mucoid stools, which is inconsistent with pyloric stenosis. Educational Objective: Intussusception occurs when a segment of bowel telescopes into an adjacent segment, resulting in colicky abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and potential bloody, mucoid stools. A contrast enema (or barium enema) is useful in both the diagnosis and treatment of intussusception.
Source: 7A #50
A 14-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of intermittent vomiting for 12 hours. During this period, her playing and sleeping have been interrupted by episodes of crying and fretfulness that last 20-30 minutes. Over the past hour she has had two bowel movements, one containing blood. Examination shows no abdominal distention. A noncontrast x-ray of the abdomen shows no evidence of bowel obstruction. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Appendicitis B) Dysentery C) Intussusception D) Viral gastroenteritis E) Volvulus
Correct Answer: C) Intussusception
Intussusception occurs when a segment of bowel telescopes into an adjacent segment, resulting in colicky abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and potentially bloody, mucoid stools. Classically, it presents in an infant or young child with recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain often punctuated by asymptomatic periods. Intussusception typically occurs because of a pathologic lead point, often lymphoid hyperplasia, lymphadenopathy, Meckel diverticulum, stricture, or malignancy, which acts to draw one segment of bowel into an adjacent segment during peristalsis. If the intussusception does not self-resolve, traction on mesenteric vessels can result in hypoperfusion of the segment with resultant inflammation, hemorrhage, obstruction, and pain. It may be detected on physical examination as an elongated mass, often in the right upper quadrant. Diagnosis consists of clinical history and physical examination and is supported by imaging. Ultrasound evaluation is preferred in young children and will show telescoping interposed bowel segments in longitudinal orientation, or a targetoid appearance in transverse orientation. A contrast enema can also show intussusception with appearance of a mass prolapsing into the lumen and an inability of the contrast to reach the proximal bowel. Treatment of an ileocolic intussusception requires the administration of a contrast enema, which reduces the intussusception. Contrast enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic in this setting. Surgery may be required in cases where there is repetitive failure of the enema to reduce the intussusception or if the patient has symptoms concerning for bowel necrosis or perforation. Choice A (Appendicitis) typically presents with loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, and right lower quadrant pain, and is often associated with fever and leukocytosis. It does not typically cause bloody stools. Choice B (Dysentery) is characterized by bloody diarrhea, typically caused by bacteria such as Shigella and enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli. This patient has no risk factors for bacterial diarrhea. Intermittent episodes of abdominal pain and vomiting in a young child is more suspicious for intussusception. Choice D (Viral gastroenteritis) is a common, typically self-limiting illness in children characterized by nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and mild abdominal discomfort. It would usually not cause bloody stools. Choice E (Midgut volvulus) typically occurs in the setting of malrotation secondary to the incomplete rotation of bowel during embryonic development. This presents with bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and pain, and when severe, intestinal necrosis, hematochezia, perforation, and peritonitis. Educational Objective: Intussusception occurs when a segment of bowel telescopes into an adjacent segment resulting in colicky abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and potentially bloody, mucoid stools. A contrast enema is useful in the diagnosis as well as treatment for intussusception.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Congenital Cytomegalovirus Infection 3 questions
Source: 9A #7
A 23-year-old primigravid woman at term delivers a growth-restricted newborn. Her pregnancy had been uncomplicated, and she does not recall any illness. Examination of the newborn shows hydrops, microcephaly, chorioretinitis, hepatosplenomegaly, and intracranial calcifications. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the newborn's findings? A. Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) B. Fetal alcohol syndrome C. Herpes simplex D. Maternal syphilis E. Varicella-zoster virus infection
Correct Answer: A. Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV)
The constellation of findings—hydrops, microcephaly, chorioretinitis, hepatosplenomegaly, and intracranial calcifications—is consistent with congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection. CMV, also known as human herpesvirus 5, is an opportunistic pathogen that commonly causes symptomatic illness in immunocompromised patients. Infections in immunocompetent mothers are often mild or unnoticed, which is likely in this case given the patient's uncomplicated pregnancy and lack of recalled illness. Congenital CMV manifests with chorioretinitis, hearing loss, seizures, petechial rash, intracranial calcifications, organomegaly, and lymphadenopathy. Newborns with congenital CMV generally have developmental delay, and most effects of the infection are irreversible. Choice B (Fetal alcohol syndrome) is incorrect because it is caused by in utero alcohol exposure and presents with intellectual disability, microcephaly, and distinctive facial abnormalities (thin vermillion border, small palpebral fissures) and heart defects, which are not described here. Choice C (Herpes simplex) is incorrect because congenital herpes simplex typically presents with rash or meningoencephalitis in the newborn period. Intracranial calcifications and chorioretinitis would be atypical features. Choice D (Maternal syphilis) is incorrect because congenital syphilis presents with syphilitic rhinitis (mucopurulent nasal discharge), rhagades, dental malformations (notched teeth and irregularly shaped molars), and hepatosplenomegaly with lymphadenopathy. Features may not be fully apparent until infancy or early childhood. Choice E (Varicella-zoster virus infection) is incorrect because congenital varicella is rare in infants born to vaccinated mothers. While it may present with intrauterine growth restriction, microcephaly, cataracts, chorioretinitis, seizures, and developmental delays, the classic presentation would be different from this case.
Source: 7A #32
A female newborn is admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit because of diffuse jaundice and petechial rash noted at birth. She was born at 35 weeks' gestation following spontaneous vaginal delivery to a 23-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1. Pregnancy was complicated by fetal growth restriction. There is no family history of serious illness. There are no pets in the home. The patient is below the 3rd percentile for length, weight, and head circumference. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows diffuse jaundice and a petechial rash over the head, trunk, and all extremities. No murmurs are heard. The liver edge is palpated 5 cm below the right costal margin. The spleen tip is palpated 3 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 16 g/dL (N=15-24), Leukocyte count 8300/mm3 (N=9100-34,000), Platelet count low, Direct bilirubin 7.3 mg/dL. A CT scan of the head shows intracranial calcifications. Brain stem auditory evoked potential testing shows sensorineural hearing loss bilaterally. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the diagnosis? A) Bone marrow aspiration and analysis B) Chromosomal microarray C) Lymphocyte enumeration by flow cytometry D) MRI of the brain E) Serum rubella IgM titer F) Serum Toxoplasma gondii IgM titer G) Urine viral culture
Correct Answer: G) Urine viral culture
This neonate presents with classic findings of congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection, also known as human herpesvirus 5 (HHV-5). The clinical presentation includes intrauterine growth restriction, microcephaly, intracranial calcifications with characteristic periventricular distribution, sensorineural hearing loss (the most common cause of nonhereditary sensorineural hearing loss in neonates), hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, and petechial rash. The diagnosis is confirmed with viral culture or polymerase chain reaction amplification from urine or blood within the first week of life. Urine viral culture is the most practical confirmatory test. Choice A (Bone marrow aspiration and analysis) is used for diagnosing lymphoproliferative or lymphodepletive disorders such as lymphoma, leukemia, and aplastic anemia, not congenital CMV infection. Choice B (Chromosomal microarray) detects chromosomal copy number variants and is useful for syndromic abnormalities with suspected genetic causes, not infectious syndromes. Choice C (Lymphocyte enumeration by flow cytometry) is used to diagnose primary immune deficiencies. While immune-deficient infants may have recurrent infections, the specific constellation of congenital findings suggests an infectious rather than immune etiology. Choice D (MRI of the brain) is unnecessary given that intracranial calcifications have already been identified on CT scan. While intracranial findings may help distinguish CMV from other congenital infections, they are not diagnostic. Choice E (Serum rubella IgM titer) is incorrect because congenital rubella presents with the classic triad of cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and congenital heart disease—a different clinical pattern than this patient. Choice F (Serum Toxoplasma gondii IgM titer) is incorrect because congenital toxoplasmosis presents with chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and ring-enhancing intracranial calcifications. This patient's periventricular calcifications without hydrocephalus is more consistent with CMV. Educational Objective: Congenital CMV infection presents with intrauterine growth restriction, microcephaly, periventricular intracranial calcifications, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, seizures, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, and petechial rash. Primary maternal CMV infection carries high risk for vertical transmission to the fetus via the placenta. Diagnosis is confirmed with viral culture or polymerase chain reaction from urine or blood obtained within the first week of life. CMV is the most common cause of nonhereditary sensorineural hearing loss, with hearing loss being the most common sequela in initially asymptomatic neonates and potentially the only manifestation in about 10% of cases. Treatment involves antiviral agents such as ganciclovir or valganciclovir.
Source: 8A #8
A female newborn is admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit because of diffuse jaundice and petechial rash noted at birth. She was born at 35 weeks' gestation following spontaneous vaginal delivery to a 23-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1. Pregnancy was complicated by fetal growth restriction. There is no family history of serious illness. There are no pets in the home. The patient is below the 3rd percentile for length, weight, and head circumference. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows diffuse jaundice and a petechial rash over the head, trunk, and all extremities. No murmurs are heard. The liver edge is palpated 5 cm below the right costal margin. The spleen tip is palpated 3 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 16 g/dL (N=15-24), Leukocyte count 8300/mm3 (N=9100-34,000), Platelet count 78, Direct bilirubin 7.3 mg/dL. CT scan of the head shows periventricular intracranial calcifications. Brain stem auditory evoked potential testing shows sensorineural hearing loss bilaterally. Congenital infection with which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition? A) Cytomegalovirus B) Listeria monocytogenes C) Parvovirus B19 D) Rubella E) Streptococcus agalactiae (group B) F) S. intermedius G) Toxoplasma gondii
Correct Answer: A) Cytomegalovirus
This newborn presents with findings consistent with congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection. CMV, also known as human herpesvirus 5, belongs to the family of herpesviruses and possesses a large, double-stranded DNA genome. Pregnant women most often contract CMV through exposure from young children, often through daycare centers. A primary maternal infection has a high risk for vertical transmission via the placenta to the fetus. Congenital CMV infection presents with intrauterine growth restriction, microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, hearing loss, seizures, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, and petechial rash. Congenital CMV infection is the most common cause of nonhereditary sensorineural hearing loss. In about 10% of cases, hearing loss may be an isolated finding without other symptoms of infection present. Hearing loss is also the most common sequela of an initially asymptomatic newborn. Fetal hydrops is a potential complication of CMV infection, although less common than in congenital parvovirus B19 infection. Intracranial calcifications have a characteristic periventricular distribution and may be detected by ultrasonography or CT scan. The diagnosis is confirmed with viral culture or polymerase chain reaction amplification from urine or blood within the first week of life. Treatment is with antiviral agents such as ganciclovir or valganciclovir. Choice B (Listeria monocytogenes): A gram-positive, facultative anaerobic bacillus that may cause neonatal listeriosis via the transplacental route or through ascending vaginal infection with chorioamnionitis. Newborns may present with sepsis, meningitis, or pneumonia, and a characteristic rash known as granulomatosis infantiseptica consisting of diffuse, pale, granulomatous cutaneous nodules. Does not typically cause periventricular intracranial calcifications or sensorineural hearing loss. Choice C (Parvovirus B19): Typically occurs in the second or third trimester and presents with fetal anemia caused by viral tropism for bone marrow and infection of erythroid progenitor cells. Fetal and neonatal anemia may result in tachycardia, hydrops, high-output heart failure, and death. Does not explain the intracranial calcifications or hearing loss. Choice D (Rubella): Causative agent of congenital rubella syndrome, which exhibits a classic triad of cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and congenital heart disease. Newborns also typically display a diffuse purpuric rash. However, rubella does not cause intracranial calcifications as seen in this patient. Choice E (Streptococcus agalactiae/group B): An important cause of neonatal sepsis, typically acquired from the vaginal canal during delivery. Does not typically result in intracranial calcifications or sensorineural deafness. Choice F (S. intermedius): A member of the Streptococcus anginosus group that exhibits a tendency to form abscesses, including hepatic and intracranial abscesses. However, it is not a common cause of congenital or neonatal infection and does not present with intracranial calcifications. Choice G (Toxoplasma gondii): An apicomplexan that may be acquired through transplacental infection. Congenital toxoplasmosis presents with the classic triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications with characteristic ring-enhancing appearance. The absence of hydrocephalus and the presence of periventricular calcifications is more consistent with congenital CMV infection. Educational Objective: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection presents with intrauterine growth restriction, microcephaly, intracranial calcifications with characteristic periventricular distribution, hearing loss, seizures, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, and petechial rash. A primary maternal infection has a high risk for vertical transmission via the placenta to the fetus. Intracranial calcifications may be detected by ultrasonography or CT scan.
▶ Blood Lymphoreticular System Acute lymphoblastic leukemia 3 questions
Source: 9A #3
A 7-year-old girl is brought to the office because of fever for 1 month. She has a history of intermittent fevers, weight loss, and scattered petechiae. There is no family history of serious illness. She is at the 50th percentile for height and 10th percentile for weight. Her temperature is 38.5°C. Examination shows generalized lymphadenopathy and scattered petechiae. Breath sounds are decreased. The spleen is palpated 2 cm below the left costal margin. A chest x-ray shows findings concerning for leukemia. Which of the following mechanisms of disease is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms? A. Abnormal leukocyte adhesion B. Abnormal leukocyte degranulation C. Bone marrow infiltration D. Hypersplenism E. Impaired leukocyte chemotaxis F. Impaired leukocyte microbicidal activity
Correct Answer: C. Bone marrow infiltration
This patient presents with a 1-month history of intermittent fever, weight loss (10th percentile), scattered petechiae, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly, which raises concern for acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). Bone marrow infiltration is the mechanism of disease most likely causing this patient's symptoms. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is a common pediatric malignancy of B or T lymphocytes that may present with malaise, fatigue, weight loss, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, anemia, bone pain, and thrombocytopenia. It is the most common hematologic malignancy of childhood, arising from lymphoid progenitor cells. Diagnosis is made with evaluation of peripheral blood, bone marrow, and/or lymph nodes. Treatment is guided by immunophenotype identified on laboratory study, along with management of infections and cytopenias. Choice A (Abnormal leukocyte adhesion) is incorrect. Leukocyte adhesion deficiency is characterized by impaired leukocyte adhesion to vascular endothelium in response to infection, preventing migration to sites of infection or inflammation, though phagocytic ability is retained. Choice B (Abnormal leukocyte degranulation) is incorrect. Increased mast cell and basophil degranulation occurs in anaphylaxis, resulting in acute multisystem inflammation and vasodilation. Infiltration of the bone marrow is the mechanism involved in ALL. Choice D (Hypersplenism) is not the most likely mechanism. While hypersplenism can result from infection, myeloproliferative neoplasms, or cirrhosis with portal hypertension, erythrocytes in an enlarged spleen may have slower transit times and premature removal from circulation. However, bone marrow infiltration is the more likely mechanism in this case. Choice E (Impaired leukocyte chemotaxis) is incorrect. Impaired chemotaxis occurs in Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, presenting with albinism, peripheral neuropathy, and recurrent pyogenic infections, not the clinical picture seen here. Choice F (Impaired leukocyte microbicidal activity) is incorrect. Chronic granulomatous disease exemplifies impaired microbicidal activity from defects in the NADPH oxidase complex, impairing reactive oxygen species production and the respiratory burst in neutrophils, increasing susceptibility to catalase-positive pathogens.
Source: 4A #42
A previously healthy 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 1-week history of intermittent fever. During the past 3 days, he has had decreased activity and joint pain. Yesterday he developed a red rash on his chest. He attends day care. He appears pale and is not in acute distress. His temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), pulse is 140/min, and respirations are 24/min. Examination shows a petechial rash over the chest. The conjunctivae are pale. There is diffuse adenopathy in the cervical chain. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard. The spleen is palpated 1 cm below the left costal margin. There is no swelling or redness of the joints. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 6.4 g/dL, leukocyte count of 50,000/mm³, and platelet count of 10,000/mm³. For each patient with anemia, select the most likely diagnosis. A) Acute lymphoblastic leukemia B) Anemia of chronic disease C) Autoimmune hemolytic anemia D) Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency E) Hemolytic uremic syndrome F) Hereditary spherocytosis G) Lead poisoning H) Red blood cell aplasia (acquired) I) Sickle cell disease J) Thalassemia K) Uremia of chronic renal failure
Correct Answer: A) Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most likely diagnosis in this pediatric patient presenting with anemia due to diffuse bone marrow infiltration by malignant blast cells with subsequent displacement of normal erythroid progenitor cells. The clinical presentation strongly supports leukemia: fever, petechial rash, diffuse lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and significant leukocytosis to 50,000/mm³. The severe anemia (hemoglobin 6.4 g/dL) and thrombocytopenia (10,000/mm³) reflect bone marrow involvement. Peripheral blood smear evaluation would show malignant circulating blasts of lymphoid lineage. B-lymphocyte malignancies are more common than T-lymphocyte malignancies, with flow cytometry and mutational analyses used for specific classification. Treatment involves chemotherapy with many patients achieving remission, and bone marrow transplant can be curative in many cases. Incorrect options: Anemia of chronic disease (Choice B) results from increased hepcidin decreasing iron absorption and increasing storage in the reticuloendothelial system, preventing iron use by erythrocyte precursors, but does not explain the marked leukocytosis or thrombocytopenia. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (Choice C) presents with positive antiglobulin (Coombs) test, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, low haptoglobin, and spherocytes/reticulocytes on smear, but would not produce such elevated WBC. Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (Choice D) causes hemolysis upon exposure to oxidative stressors like sulfa medications, but lacks systemic symptoms and lymphadenopathy. Hemolytic uremic syndrome (Choice E) is classically associated with E. coli O157:H7 infection, presents with bloody diarrhea, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure, but the constellation of fever, adenopathy, and massive leukocytosis is atypical. Hereditary spherocytosis (Choice F) shows spherocytes on smear and is treated with splenectomy, but does not explain the clinical presentation. Lead poisoning (Choice G) inhibits ferrochelatase and ALA dehydratase causing decreased heme synthesis, presenting with encephalopathy, cognitive dysfunction, peripheral neuropathy, and anemia, but the acute presentation and leukocytosis are inconsistent. Red blood cell aplasia (acquired) (Choice H) is an autoimmune process destroying erythroid progenitors resulting in anemia with low reticulocyte count but normal other cell lines, inconsistent with the leukocytosis and thrombocytopenia. Sickle cell disease (Choice I) involves HbS polymerization causing sickling, but the acute presentation and laboratory findings are atypical. Thalassemia (Choice J) results from globin gene deletions or mutations causing reduction in globin chain production with a spectrum of severity, but presentation and lab values are inconsistent. Uremia of chronic renal failure (Choice K) interferes with platelet activity and can predispose to bleeding with usually normal platelet counts, not explaining the clinical picture. Educational Objective: ALL is a common pediatric malignancy of B or T lymphocytes presenting with malaise, fatigue, weight loss, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, anemia, and thrombocytopenia, with circulating leukemic blasts on peripheral blood smear. The mechanism of anemia is secondary to bone marrow infiltration by malignant cells with obliteration of erythroid precursors.
Source: 8A #38
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 4 hours after the onset of irritability and temperatures to 40°C (104°F). He received a diagnosis of polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis 2 months ago. He is inconsolable. Examination shows scattered petechiae over the trunk and extremities, a distended abdomen, and diffuse lymphadenopathy. The liver edge and spleen tip are palpated 5 cm below the costal margins. There is bilateral knee and ankle swelling with effusions. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 23.4%, Leukocyte count 21,000/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 20%, Bands 10%, Lymphocytes 70%, Platelet count 45,000/mm³, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 12 mm/h, Serum AST 235 U/L, ALT 337 U/L, C-reactive protein 3.5 mg/L (N=0.08-3.1). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Abdominal CT scan B) Bone scan C) Gallium scan D) Bone marrow biopsy E) Liver biopsy
Correct Answer: D) Bone marrow biopsy
This patient presents with fever, petechiae, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and laboratory findings of pancytopenia, which are classic findings concerning for acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). ALL is a common pediatric malignancy of B- or T-lymphocytes that typically presents with malaise, fatigue, weight loss, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, anemia, and thrombocytopenia, with circulating leukemic blasts potentially visible on peripheral blood smear. Diagnosis is confirmed with bone marrow biopsy showing >20% lymphoblasts. B-lymphocyte malignancies are more common than T-lymphocyte malignancies. Evaluation with flow cytometry is necessary to determine the specific type of malignant cell, followed by mutational analyses. Treatment typically involves chemotherapy, and many patients with ALL will enter remission. Bone marrow transplant can be curative in many cases. Choice A (Abdominal CT scan) can identify intra-abdominal tumors such as neuroblastoma and nephroblastoma (Wilms tumors), but this patient's hepatosplenomegaly is likely secondary to leukemia rather than primary intra-abdominal pathology. Choice B (Bone scan) uses technetium 99m methyl diphosphonate to evaluate for osteoblastic osseous metastases, most commonly in breast and prostate cancer, and is not indicated here. Choice C (Gallium scan) uses gallium-67 as a tracer to identify areas of inflammation, infection, or malignancy. This has been largely replaced by PET/CT scan for the evaluation and staging of malignancy. Choice E (Liver biopsy) is useful for diagnosing conditions such as cirrhosis, hepatitis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and hepatic metastatic disease, but is not the first diagnostic step in suspected leukemia. Educational Objective: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is a common childhood malignancy that often presents with malaise, fatigue, weight loss, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Diagnosis is confirmed with bone marrow biopsy showing >20% lymphoblasts.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Cystic Fibrosis 3 questions
Source: 9A #30
A 1-year-old boy is admitted to the hospital because of a 3-month history of chronic abdominal distention and diarrhea. His mother reports that his stools contain mucus but no blood. He was adopted from Russia at the age of 3 months. He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. He weighed 3515 g (7 lb 12 oz) at birth. He passed meconium at the age of 36 hours. He has a history of slow height gain despite maintaining a high-calorie diet. Since adoption, he has been hospitalized three times for treatment. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows decreased subcutaneous fat. Abdominal examination shows mild distention and no tenderness. Bowel sounds are increased. Flatulence is noted. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following mechanisms is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms? A. Sensitivity to gluten in diet B. Autoimmune-mediated patchy inflammation of the colon C. Blunting of colonic villi D. Pancreatic enzyme deficiency E. Parasitic infestation
Correct Answer: D) Pancreatic enzyme deficiency
This patient most likely has cystic fibrosis, an autosomal recessive defect of the CFTR gene, leading to abnormally viscous mucus in the pulmonary and gastrointestinal tracts. This results in obstruction and destruction of the airways and pancreatic duct, causing recurrent pulmonary infections, bronchiectasis, and intestinal malabsorption secondary to pancreatic enzyme deficiency. Malabsorption can be mitigated with exogenous supplementation of pancreatic enzymes. Pancreatic enzyme deficiency in cystic fibrosis results from destruction of the pancreatic duct by abnormally viscous mucus. The absence of digestive enzymes made by the pancreas leads to malnutrition (cachexia, muscle wasting), weight loss, vitamin deficiencies, and frequent, loose, foul-smelling, sometimes oily stools (steatorrhea). Cystic fibrosis may also present with meconium ileus. Cystic fibrosis is caused by a deficiency in a chloride channel that secretes chloride in the lungs and gastrointestinal tract and reabsorbs chloride in sweat glands. This abnormal chloride transport causes decreased chloride and water secretion and increased water reabsorption, leading to abnormally viscous mucus. In the gastrointestinal tract, the thick mucus contributes to pancreatic insufficiency, steatorrhea, flatulence, and malabsorption, leading to deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K. Choice A is incorrect. Celiac disease, or gluten-sensitive enteropathy, causes inflammatory infiltration of the proximal small bowel with characteristic intraepithelial lymphocytosis, villous atrophy, and crypt hyperplasia. This leads to malabsorption presenting as chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, and nutritional deficiencies, but does not include pulmonary infections as seen in this patient. Choice B is incorrect. Autoimmune-mediated patchy inflammation is most often seen in Crohn disease, which presents with chronic abdominal cramping, bloody diarrhea, and weight loss. Onset usually occurs in adulthood, not infancy. Choice C is incorrect. The colon does not have villi; villi are primarily found in the small intestine where they expand surface area for nutrient absorption. Blunting of small intestinal villi is a feature of celiac disease, not the pattern seen in cystic fibrosis. Choice E is incorrect. Small bowel parasitic overgrowth, such as Giardia lamblia infection, can cause malabsorption of fats and carbohydrates presenting as foul-smelling, fatty diarrhea with abdominal pain, bloating, cramping, and weight loss. However, it does not cause pulmonary manifestations. This patient's history of recurrent pulmonary infections, chronic abdominal distention, diarrhea, malnutrition, and weight loss despite high-calorie diet is most consistent with cystic fibrosis. Complications including malnutrition can be mitigated with early diagnosis through routine newborn screening; children adopted from countries without routine screening may be at risk for missed early diagnosis.
Source: 7A #2
A 22-month-old girl with recurrent cough and shortness of breath is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination. She was born at term and weighed 3200 g (7 lb 1 oz). Pregnancy was uncomplicated. Recurrent episodes of wheezing with cough began after the age of 6 months and were successfully treated with combinations of oral antibiotics and β-adrenergic agonists.
