She was admitted to the hospital for treatment of lobar pneumonia at the ages of 9, 12, and 16 months. She was treated for rectal prolapse 2 months ago. There is a family history of childhood-onset asthma of varying severity persisting into adulthood. She is alert and acyanotic. She weighs 10.4 kg (23 lb). Her temperature is 37.3°C (99.2°F), pulse is 115/min, and respirations are 32/min. Examination shows mild subcostal and intercostal retractions. Diffuse inspiratory crackles are heard with hyperresonance to percussion. There is minimal clubbing of the nail beds. An x-ray of the chest shows generalized hyperinflation, bronchial thickening in the upper lobes, and patchy atelectasis throughout the lungs. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Measurement of serum IgE concentration B) PPD skin test C) Sweat chloride test D) Methacholine bronchial challenge test E) Nasal mucosal biopsy
Correct Answer: C) Sweat chloride test
Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the CFTR gene, leading to a deficiency in a chloride channel that secretes chloride in the lungs and gastrointestinal tract, and reabsorbs chloride in sweat glands. This abnormal chloride transport causes decreased chloride and water secretion and increased water reabsorption, leading to abnormally viscous mucous. The thick mucus in the gastrointestinal tract contributes to pancreatic insufficiency, steatorrhea, and malabsorption, leading to a deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K. In the lungs, the disease manifests as recurrent pneumonia, especially with Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Repeat antibiotic exposure increases the risk for colonization with resistant organisms. Obstruction and destruction of the airways leads to hypoxemia, air trapping, and bronchiectasis. Physical examination may show hypertrophic osteoarthropathy (clubbing), cyanosis, rales and rhonchi, and hyperresonance to percussion of the chest. Imaging findings include hyperinflation, bronchiectasis with peribronchial cuffing, and diffuse nonspecific inflammatory changes. Diagnosis is made using the sweat chloride test. Choice A (Measurement of serum IgE concentration) is useful in the diagnosis of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), a hypersensitivity reaction caused by Aspergillus fumigatus. While cystic fibrosis and ABPA share the feature of bronchiectasis, and having cystic fibrosis is a risk factor for developing ABPA, this patient's clinical presentation is more consistent with a diagnosis of cystic fibrosis. Choice B (PPD skin test) is useful for diagnosing tuberculosis. Primary infection presents with subacute fevers, weight loss, night sweats, cough, and malaise. Suspicion would be higher in endemic areas or for patients who have spent significant time in high-risk areas. Choice D (Methacholine bronchial challenge test) can be used to diagnose asthma, which is characterized by reversible obstruction to airflow caused by spasm of smooth muscle in the bronchi and small airways. Symptoms include dyspnea, wheezing, and/or chronic nonproductive cough. Recurrent pneumonia would be unusual for asthma. Choice E (Nasal mucosal biopsy) is the gold standard for diagnosis of primary ciliary dyskinesia. Clinical manifestations vary, though most patients will experience recurrent upper and lower respiratory infections. Other manifestations include chronic rhinosinusitis, otitis media, and infertility. Half of patients with primary ciliary dyskinesia will have situs inversus. This patient's symptoms are more consistent with cystic fibrosis, making the sweat chloride test a more appropriate next step in diagnosis. Educational Objective: Cystic fibrosis is associated with recurrent pulmonary infections caused by the impaired clearance of mucous, microbes, and debris from the airways. Recurrent infection may lead to chronic inflammatory changes in the lung parenchyma and chronic cyanosis. It is typically diagnosed using the sweat chloride test.
Source: 4A #21
An 8-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 3-day history of fever, progressive cough, and sputum production. Examination at birth showed no abnormalities, but she has a history of respiratory problems since infancy. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 100/min, and respirations are 32/min. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 84%. Examination shows clubbing, circumoral cyanosis, and a hyperexpanded chest. There are diffuse rhonchi bilaterally with end-expiratory wheezing. An x-ray of the chest shows hyperinflation, scattered atelectasis, and chronic interstitial changes. A) Asthma B) Bronchopulmonary dysplasia C) Congenital heart disease with right-to-left shunt D) Cystic fibrosis E) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy F) Idiopathic pulmonary hypertension G) Methemoglobinemia H) Patent foramen ovale I) Persistent pulmonary hypertension J) Pneumococcal pneumonia K) Respiratory distress syndrome
Correct Answer: D) Cystic fibrosis
Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the CFTR gene, leading to a deficiency in a chloride channel that secretes chloride in the lungs and gastrointestinal tract and reabsorbs chloride in sweat glands. This abnormal chloride transport causes decreased chloride and water secretion and increased water reabsorption, leading to abnormally viscous mucous. The thick mucus in the gastrointestinal tract contributes to pancreatic insufficiency, steatorrhea, and malabsorption, leading to a deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K. In the lungs, the disease manifests as recurrent pneumonia, especially with Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Repeat antibiotic exposure increases the risk for colonization with resistant organisms. Obstruction and destruction of the airways leads to hypoxemia, air trapping, and bronchiectasis. Physical examination may disclose hypertrophic osteoarthropathy (clubbing), cyanosis, rales and rhonchi, and hyperresonance to percussion of the chest. X-ray findings include hyperinflation, bronchiectasis with peribronchial cuffing, and diffuse nonspecific inflammatory changes. Choice A (Asthma) is characterized by reversible obstruction to airflow caused by the spasm of smooth muscle in the small airways, often triggered by an allergen, exercise, or temperature change. Choice B (Bronchopulmonary dysplasia) is a neonatal lung disorder associated with oxygen exposure and mechanical ventilation in preterm infants, where the lungs fail to mature properly and patients develop chronic lung disease characterized by decreased lung volumes, hyperinflation, and atelectasis. Choice C (Congenital heart disease with right-to-left shunt) may be caused by tetralogy of Fallot, transposition of the great arteries, tricuspid atresia, total anomalous pulmonary venous return, or Eisenmenger syndrome; however, a right-to-left shunt would be noted on examination at birth if present. Choice E (Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) is a congenital heart condition characterized by myocardial thickening and left outflow tract obstruction, with patients typically presenting with a murmur. Choice F (Idiopathic pulmonary hypertension) is a rare pulmonary disorder with an unknown cause characterized by progressive pulmonary vascular hypertension. Choice G (Methemoglobinemia) is the accumulation of hemoglobin with an oxidized iron atom that is unable to transport oxygen, resulting in hypoxia, with infants being more susceptible than adults and association with exposure to an oxidizing agent. Choice H (Patent foramen ovale) is a common form of atrial septal defect that is typically asymptomatic but can result in a left-to-right shunt and potential for systemic embolization of venous thromboses. Choice I (Persistent pulmonary hypertension) with any cause may result in right heart failure, with patients typically presenting with exertional dyspnea. Choice J (Pneumococcal pneumonia) is a common infection of the lung parenchyma presenting with fever, cough, increased sputum production, and consolidation on chest x-ray. Choice K (Respiratory distress syndrome) presents with acute dyspnea and bilateral infiltrates on chest x-ray, associated with numerous causes such as infection, sepsis, trauma, pancreatitis, chemical pneumonitis, and shock. Educational Objective: Cystic fibrosis is associated with recurrent pulmonary infections caused by the impaired clearance of mucous, microbes, and debris from the airways. Recurrent infection may lead to chronic inflammatory changes in the lung parenchyma and chronic cyanosis. The clinical presentation of a child with lifelong respiratory symptoms, clubbing, cyanosis, hyperinflation with scattered atelectasis, and chronic interstitial changes on imaging is classic for cystic fibrosis.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Lyme Disease 3 questions
Source: 9A #45
A previously healthy 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of pain and swelling of the left knee and generalized fatigue for 3 weeks. Four months ago, she returned from a camping trip with her father and noticed a rash on her lower leg. The lesion became larger, cleared in the center, and then resolved. She then had an intermittent red rash for 3 weeks. She has had generalized muscle pain and intermittent swelling and pain of the left knee and left elbow since then; her school performance has declined during this period. She is sexually active with one male partner, and they do not use condoms. Examination shows swelling, erythema, and warmth of the left knee; flexion is limited by pain. Which of the following is most likely to have prevented this patient's condition? A) Condom use B) Insect repellent C) Topical antibiotic therapy D) Antihistamine therapy E) Corticosteroid therapy
Correct Answer: B) Insect repellent
Lyme disease is a tick-borne illness caused by infection with Borrelia burgdorferi after being bitten by an ixodid (hard) tick. These ticks are common in the Northeastern United States with transmission most often occurring between May and October. This patient presents with classic features of Lyme disease progressing through stages: early localized disease with erythema chronicum migrans (the expanding rash that cleared in the center), flu-like symptoms (fatigue), and disseminated/late disease manifestations including neurologic dysfunction (declined school performance), myalgias (muscle pain), and arthritis (swelling and pain of the left knee and left elbow). Lyme disease may be prevented by avoidance of tick bites in endemic areas through use of insect repellent. Early stages of Lyme disease can be treated with doxycycline, while later stages affecting the heart or central nervous system are treated with parenteral ceftriaxone. Choice A (Condom use) is incorrect because barrier contraception prevents sexually transmitted infections, not tick-borne illnesses like Lyme disease. Choice C (Topical antibiotic therapy) is incorrect because topical antibiotics are used for superficial soft-tissue infections and would not have prevented Lyme disease acquisition. Choice D (Antihistamine therapy) is incorrect because antihistamines prevent or diminish allergic responses, not tick-borne infections. Insect repellent would be more appropriate for prevention. Choice E (Corticosteroid therapy) is incorrect because corticosteroids may diminish allergic responses but would not prevent Lyme disease. Insect repellent is the appropriate preventive measure for tick-borne illnesses in endemic areas.
Source: 5A #47
An 8-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of rash and a 1-week history of low-grade fever and a mild headache. The rash began as a small red bump on the right thigh and now measures 12 cm. His temperature is 38.1 °C (100.6°F). Examination shows no other abnormalities except for the rash shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Atopic dermatitis B) Cellulitis C) Folliculitis D) Herpes simplex E) Herpes zoster F) Impetigo G) Juvenile melanoma H) Lyme disease I) Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease) J) Neurofibromatosis K) Nevus flammeus L) Poison ivy dermatitis
Correct Answer: H) Lyme disease
Lyme disease is a tick-borne disease caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, endemic in the Northeastern United States. In its early stages, it causes erythema chronicum migrans, which is an expanding rash with a central ring-like clearing—exactly as shown in this case. It is often accompanied by a flu-like illness (fever and headache), consistent with this patient's presentation. Early-stage Lyme disease is treated with doxycycline, which prevents the attachment of aminoacyl-tRNA to ribosomes. Adverse effects of tetracycline antibiotics include gastrointestinal distress, photosensitivity, and in children, discoloration of teeth and inhibition of bone growth, making it contraindicated in pregnancy. Later stages of Lyme disease can be characterized by carditis, atrioventricular heart block, facial nerve palsy (often bilateral), migratory arthralgias, and if left untreated, encephalopathy and chronic arthritis. Later stages affecting the heart or central nervous system are generally treated with parenteral ceftriaxone. Incorrect Answers: Choice A (Atopic dermatitis/eczema) is characterized by pruritus, flexural distribution, a history of asthma or hay fever, and dry skin. The rash presents with erythematous papules and vesicles with exudates and crusting, progressing to dry, scaly, excoriated skin (lichenification) with chronic scratching—not an expanding targetoid lesion. Choice B (Cellulitis), Choice C (Folliculitis), and Choice F (Impetigo) are superficial bacterial skin infections. Cellulitis presents with a warm, erythematous patch or plaque without central clearing. Folliculitis presents with follicle-centric pustules on hair-bearing areas. Impetigo presents with honey-colored crust typically around the mouth or nose in children. None present with an expanding, targetoid, erythematous patch with central clearing. Choice D (Herpes simplex) typically begins with vesicle formation, which lyse and progress to shallow, painful ulcers with an erythematous border, often accompanied by fever, chills, and lymphadenopathy. The presentation does not include a characteristic expanding rash with central clearing. Choice E (Herpes zoster) commonly presents as a unilateral, dermatomal erythematous patch with overlying clear to yellow grouped vesicles. Caused by varicella-zoster virus (human herpesvirus-3), it can be associated with neuropathic pain that both precedes and outlasts the rash, though this is more common in elderly patients. It does not present with an expanding rash and central clearing. Choice G (Juvenile melanoma) is suggested by a single lesion with asymmetry, irregular borders, variable coloration, diameter greater than 6 mm, and rapid evolution—not by an expanding rash with central clearing. Choice I (Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome/Kawasaki disease) is a multisystemic inflammatory disease in children characterized by fever for at least 5 days, bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, polymorphous rash, lymphadenopathy, erythema and edema of hands and feet, and erythema of mucous membranes with dry, cracked lips. This patient does not present with these criteria. Choice J (Neurofibromatosis) is a genetically inherited disorder characterized by neurofibromas, plexiform neurofibromas, café-au-lait macules, and axillary freckling—none of which are present in this patient. Choice K (Nevus flammeus) is a common red patch present on the forehead or posterior neck at birth, representing a benign capillary malformation that fades or resolves over time—not an expanding rash in an 8-year-old. Choice L (Poison ivy dermatitis) is characterized by linearly arranged vesicles and eczematous patches—not by an expanding targetoid lesion. Educational Objective: Lyme disease is a tick-borne disease caused by B. burgdorferi, endemic in the Northeastern United States. Erythema chronicum migrans, an expanding rash with a central ring-like clearing, is often the first manifestation and is the key diagnostic finding in this patient.
Source: 4A #32
Two weeks after a camping trip in New England, a 5-year-old boy develops a 3-cm, red, circular lesion with a clear center, lymphadenopathy, conjunctivitis, myalgia, and nausea. Antibodies to Proteus vulgaris Ox-19 are negative. Which of the following is the most likely causal agent? A) Bacterium B) Fungus C) Rickettsia D) Spirochete E) Virus
Correct Answer: D) Spirochete
Lyme disease is a tick-borne disease caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, which is endemic in the Northeastern United States and commonly transmitted by the Ixodes scapularis tick. The clinical presentation in this case is highly characteristic of early Lyme disease. The pathognomonic rash is erythema chronicum migrans, which is an expanding rash that may have a central ring-like clearing (described as a circular lesion with a clear center in this patient). The systemic manifestations of flu-like illness including myalgia, nausea, and lymphadenopathy are consistent with early Lyme disease. The negative Proteus vulgaris Ox-19 antibodies help exclude Rocky Mountain spotted fever, which would be positive in this test. Early-stage Lyme disease is treated with amoxicillin or doxycycline, with amoxicillin preferred in pediatric patients. Doxycycline, which acts by preventing the attachment of aminoacyl-tRNA to ribosomes, has adverse effects including gastrointestinal distress, photosensitivity, and in children, discoloration of teeth and inhibition of bone growth, making it contraindicated in children under 8 years old. Later stages of Lyme disease affecting the heart or central nervous system are treated with parenteral ceftriaxone. Late manifestations can include carditis, atrioventricular heart block, facial nerve palsy (which may be bilateral), migratory arthralgias, encephalopathy, and chronic arthritis. Choice A (Bacterium): While bacterial infections can cause a wide variety of skin infections including impetigo, cellulitis, and folliculitis caused by organisms like Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, these are not characteristic of the circular lesion with central clearing pattern seen here, nor are they typically associated with this constellation of systemic findings. Choice B (Fungus): Fungal infections of the skin such as tinea corporis (ringworm), tinea capitis, and tinea pedis present with pruritic circular lesions with central clearing. However, these lesions are typically scaly and are not associated with systemic findings such as lymphadenopathy, myalgia, and conjunctivitis. Choice C (Rickettsia): Rickettsial infections include Rocky Mountain spotted fever and typhus. Rocky Mountain spotted fever is transmitted by ticks but presents with a vasculitic rash affecting the palms and soles, not a single circular lesion with central clearing. Typhus presents with a generalized rash on the trunk that spreads outward while sparing the palms and soles. Neither produces the characteristic erythema chronicum migrans pattern. Choice E (Virus): Viral skin infections such as varicella zoster virus and herpes simplex virus present with vesicular rashes rather than a single circular lesion with central clearing. Educational Objective: Lyme disease is a tick-borne disease caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi and characteristically causes erythema chronicum migrans, an expanding rash that may have a central ring-like clearing. Early-stage disease is treated with doxycycline or amoxicillin, with amoxicillin preferred in pediatric patients. Ceftriaxone is indicated for late-stage or disseminated cases.
▶ Gastrointestinal System Gastroenteritis 3 questions
Source: 5A #1
A 1-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of low-grade fever and watery diarrhea. She has had 8 to 10 watery stools daily that contain mucus but no blood; she has had fewer wet diapers than usual. She has not had vomiting or symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection, but her father reports that she became very fussy earlier today. She has been drinking juice and children's electrolyte supplement but not eating much food. Her older brother had a mild upper respiratory tract infection and diarrhea last week. On arrival, she appears lethargic. She is at the 25th percentile for length and weight. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 160/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 70/40 mm Hg. The mucous membranes are dry. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination shows a grade 1/6 systolic ejection murmur with no rub or gallop. The abdomen is soft, and there is no hepatosplenomegaly. The extremities are cool, and capillary refill time is 3 to 4 seconds. Laboratory studies show: Serum Na+ 134 mEq/L, K+ 3.2 mEq/L, Cl- 105 mEq/L, HCO3- 8 mEq/L, Urea nitrogen 25 mg/dL, Glucose 88 mg/dL, Creatinine 0.5 mg/dL. Urine pH 5, Specific gravity 1.025, Glucose negative, Protein negative, Ketones 3+, Gram stain no organisms. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Celiac disease B) Diabetic ketoacidosis C) Inflammatory bowel disease D) Lactic acidosis E) Renal tubular acidosis
Correct Answer: D) Lactic acidosis
This infant presents with tachycardia, hypotension, delayed capillary refill, and acute-onset diarrhea consistent with gastroenteritis with associated volume depletion. Children with gastroenteritis are at increased risk for volume depletion compared to adults. Clinical signs of volume depletion include tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor, and prolonged capillary refill. Children may present with irritability or lethargy. Laboratory studies show perturbations in serum sodium and potassium concentrations. Volume depletion secondary to diarrhea is usually accompanied by significant stool loss of bicarbonate, which in combination with hypoperfusion of end organs results in lactic acidosis and metabolic acidosis. Urinalysis shows aciduria (pH 5) and increased urinary specific gravity (1.025). Treatment includes repletion of fluids and electrolytes. Choice A (Celiac disease): Gluten-sensitive enteropathy presents with diarrhea and malabsorption caused by gliadin hypersensitivity. It does not present with acute onset and rarely leads to significant volume depletion. Choice B (Diabetic ketoacidosis): While DKA may present with volume depletion and metabolic acidosis, in an infant this is most commonly caused by type 1 diabetes mellitus, which presents with polyuria and glucosuria. This child's history of acute onset diarrhea and a sick contact are more suggestive of gastroenteritis. Poor feeding in an acutely ill child may lead to starvation ketoacidosis with mild ketonuria, but glucose is normal (88 mg/dL) here. Choice C (Inflammatory bowel disease): Presents with abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. It is rare in infancy and does not typically present with this acute picture. Choice E (Renal tubular acidosis): A family of disorders causing metabolic acidosis. While RTA may present with metabolic acidosis, aciduria, and electrolyte disturbances, it does not typically present with acute onset diarrhea and does not explain the acute clinical picture of volume depletion. Educational Objective: Gastroenteritis may lead to volume depletion with associated lactic acidosis. Clinical signs of volume depletion include tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor, and prolonged capillary refill. Children may present with irritability or lethargy. Treatment includes repletion of fluids and electrolytes.
Source: 7A #14
A previously healthy 15-month-old boy is brought to the physician in late winter by his mother because of persistent vomiting followed by fever and diarrhea. His symptoms began 2 days ago after a large family gathering. His mother tried to give him apple juice, but he vomited the juice after drinking only 4 ounces. The patient is crying and appears alert. His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 36/min, and blood pressure is 88/56 mm Hg. Capillary refill time is normal. Examination shows tear production and slightly dry mucous membranes. The abdomen is nontender; bowel sounds are hyperactive. Test of the stool for occult blood is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient? A) Oral bismuth subsalicylate B) Oral hydration solution C) Oral loperamide D) Rectal prochlorperazine E) Intravenous 5% dextrose in water
Correct Answer: B) Oral hydration solution
Acute-onset fever, emesis, and diarrhea is consistent with a likely diagnosis of gastroenteritis. Though this is typically a self-limiting illness, children with gastroenteritis are at increased risk for volume depletion in comparison to adults, and this patient should be treated initially with oral hydration solution. Clinical signs of volume depletion include tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor, and prolonged capillary refill. Children may present with irritability or lethargy. Laboratory evaluation may show perturbations in serum sodium, bicarbonate, and potassium concentrations. Volume depletion secondary to diarrhea is usually accompanied by a significant stool loss of bicarbonate, which in combination with the hypoperfusion of end organs, may result in metabolic acidosis. Urinalysis shows aciduria and a high urinary specific gravity. Treatment includes the repletion of fluids and electrolytes. Choice A (Oral bismuth subsalicylate) is a nonantibiotic treatment option for adults with acute gastroenteritis but should be avoided in infants and pregnant women because of the risk for salicylate toxicity. Choice C (Oral loperamide) and other antidiarrheal agents are generally not recommended for treatment of acute gastroenteritis in children. The condition is usually self-limiting, and there is little known benefit of using these agents with significant risk for side effects. Choice D (Rectal prochlorperazine) is an antipsychotic and effective antiemetic typically reserved for severe, refractory nausea and vomiting, chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, and intractable migraine in children. Choice E (Intravenous 5% dextrose in water), or any isotonic intravenous fluid, is indicated for severe volume depletion in children, though when feasible and tolerated, oral rehydration therapy is preferred. Severe volume depletion is characterized by delayed capillary refill time (greater than 3 seconds), cold and mottled extremities, lethargy, and hypovolemic shock. This patient has normal capillary refill time and mild-to-moderate signs of dehydration, making oral rehydration therapy appropriate. Educational Objective: Acute gastroenteritis is a common, typically self-limiting illness in children characterized by nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. Compared to adults, pediatric patients are at increased risk for volume depletion. Oral rehydration therapy is preferred for mild and moderate cases of hypovolemia, while isotonic intravenous fluids should be used for severe hypovolemia.
Source: 7A #29
A 2-month-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother for a well-child examination. Six weeks ago, she had watery diarrhea with blood in her stool. At that time, she was switched from a cow milk-based formula, which she had been fed since birth, to a soy-based formula, and the diarrhea resolved. She appears well. She is at the 50th percentile for length, weight, and head circumference. Examination shows no abnormalities. The mother should be counseled about which of the following regarding this patient's diet? A) She will likely have lifelong lactose intolerance B) She will likely have lifelong milk protein intolerance C) She will likely outgrow her lactose intolerance D) She will likely outgrow her milk protein intolerance
Correct Answer: D) She will likely outgrow her milk protein intolerance
This patient's presentation is consistent with cow's milk protein intolerance (CMPI), a hypersensitivity reaction to non-native antigens in cow's milk mediated by both IgE-dependent and non-IgE-dependent mechanisms. CMPI presents in infants with colic, regurgitation, diarrhea, hematochezia, urticarial rash, atopic dermatitis, and iron deficiency anemia. Severe cases may rarely present with failure to thrive, wheezing, or anaphylaxis. The diagnosis is clinical and confirmed with improvement in symptoms following elimination of cow's milk from the diet. Importantly, CMPI resolves in approximately half of children by 1 year of age and in nearly all children by 5 years of age. Choice A (lifelong lactose intolerance) is incorrect. Lactose intolerance is a distinct entity from CMPI, caused by inadequate lactase expression and is typically lifelong. While both present similarly with cramping abdominal pain, bloating, flatulence, and diarrhea, lactose intolerance typically presents after 2-3 years of age, contrasting with CMPI's presentation in infancy. Choice B (lifelong milk protein intolerance) is incorrect. The great majority of children will outgrow CMPI by 5 years of age, making lifelong milk protein intolerance rare. Choice C (outgrow lactose intolerance) is incorrect. Outgrowing lactose intolerance is atypical, as lactose intolerance is typically a lifelong condition. Educational Objective: CMPI occurs due to hypersensitivity to antigens in cow's milk and is mediated by IgE-dependent and non-IgE-dependent mechanisms. It is fundamentally distinct from lactose intolerance and resolves in nearly all children by 5 years of age, making it important to counsel families that this is a transient condition.
▶ Human Development Routine vaccinations in infancy and childhood 3 questions
Source: 7A #15
A 4-month-old girl is brought to the physician for a well-child examination in October. Pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. Immunizations are up-to-date. Growth and development are appropriate for age. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities. Immunization against which of the following is most appropriate at this time? A) Chickenpox B) Influenza C) Measles-mumps-rubella D) Rotavirus E) Shingles
Correct Answer: D) Rotavirus
Rotavirus is a double-stranded RNA virus that causes infectious diarrhea in children and is the most common cause of diarrheal illness in children worldwide. The virus is transmitted fecal-orally and is highly contagious, with viral shedding in stool occurring prior to symptom development, allowing asymptomatic patients to become disease vectors. The diarrhea caused by rotavirus is watery, profuse, and often foul-smelling, and is typically not bloody. While most cases are self-resolving, severe infections can produce dehydration, which may be life-threatening, particularly in low-resource and developing countries. Rotavirus vaccine is available in live-attenuated formulations and is recommended for all children, given in a two or three dose series between age 2 and 6 months. At 4 months of age, this patient is within the appropriate window for rotavirus vaccination. Chickenpox (Choice A) vaccine against varicella is administered in a two-dose series at age 12 months and between age 4 to 6 years, making it inappropriate at 4 months. Influenza (Choice B) vaccine is recommended beginning at age greater than 6 months, so it is not yet appropriate for this 4-month-old. Measles-mumps-rubella vaccine (Choice C) prevents measles, mumps, and rubella infection and is recommended by the CDC beginning at age 1 year, not at 4 months. Shingles (Choice E) is caused by varicella virus infection and presents in elderly patients as a painful, unilateral, dermatomal erythematous patch with overlying clear to yellow grouped vesicles. CDC recommends shingles vaccination beginning at age 60 years, making it inappropriate for a 4-month-old. Educational Objective: Rotavirus vaccine is a live-attenuated vaccine recommended for all children and should be administered in a two or three dose series between age 2 and 6 months.
Source: 7A #48
A 7-year-old boy is brought to the office in the fall for a routine examination. He has mild intermittent asthma and gastroesophageal reflux disease. His medications are albuterol and ranitidine. Immunizations were up-to-date when he entered kindergarten. He is at the 75th percentile for height and 50th percentile for weight. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate vaccine to administer? A) Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis (DTaP) B) Haemophilus influenzae type b C) Influenza D) Meningococcal E) Pneumococcal
Correct Answer: C) Influenza
Influenza is a respiratory viral illness caused by influenza virus, an orthomyxovirus transmitted via respiratory droplets that causes seasonal pandemics. Symptoms include fever, chills, myalgias, malaise, headaches, nausea, and vomiting, with potential pneumonia development. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends annual influenza virus vaccination beginning at age greater than 6 months. The influenza vaccine is available as a trivalent or quadrivalent intramuscular injection of inactivated virus or as a nasal spray of live attenuated virus. Influenza is a seasonal illness affecting patients typically in winter and early spring months. This 7-year-old boy presenting in the fall for routine examination is the ideal candidate for annual influenza vaccination. Choice A (DTaP) is incorrect because DTaP vaccine is given as a three-dose series at ages 2, 4, and 6 months, followed by booster injections between age 15 to 18 months and between age 4 to 6 years. Since this patient's immunizations were up-to-date when he entered kindergarten, he would have already completed the DTaP series. Choice B (Haemophilus influenzae type b) is incorrect. While H. influenzae vaccine is indicated for all children for prevention of infection with Haemophilus influenzae (which can cause conjunctivitis, otitis media, bronchitis, pneumonia, and was the leading cause of epiglottitis in children prior to widespread immunization), the vaccine is administered in a two or three-dose series between ages 2 and 6 months, followed by a booster at age 12 to 15 months. This patient's immunizations are already up-to-date. Choice D (Meningococcal) is incorrect. Meningococcal vaccine is indicated for all children and is typically administered prior to age 23 months. An additional serogroup B vaccine is indicated for all children over age 10 years at increased risk for meningococcal disease. This patient has already received the meningococcal vaccination series. Choice E (Pneumococcal) is incorrect. Pneumococcal vaccine is indicated for all adults over age 65 years and in patients with high-risk conditions such as chronic heart, kidney, and liver disease or chronic smokers. This 7-year-old child without such risk factors does not require pneumococcal vaccination at this time. Educational Objective: Annual influenza virus vaccination is recommended for the prevention of influenza beginning at age greater than 6 months. Influenza is a seasonal illness affecting patients typically in winter and early spring months. Patients should be administered influenza vaccine annually in the fall, making this the most appropriate choice for a routine fall office visit in a 7-year-old with up-to-date immunizations.
Source: 8A #20
A 12-month-old girl is scheduled for discharge 7 days after admission for treatment with intravenous antibiotics. This is her third admission to the hospital for treatment of staphylococcal infections in 9 months. She has received no immunizations. Examination shows no abnormalities. Serum studies show a decreased T-lymphocyte count. Additional serum studies show: IgA 50 mg/dL (N=11-106) IgG 200 mg/dL (N=172-1069) IgM 50 mg/dL (N=41-173) CD4+ T-lymphocyte count 100/mm³ (N>1000) Which of the following vaccines should be administered at this time? A) BCG B) Haemophilus influenzae type b C) Rotavirus D) Varicella E) No vaccines can be safely administered
Correct Answer: B) Haemophilus influenzae type b
T-lymphocyte function is an essential component of host defense and is impaired in this patient, leading to recurrent bacterial infections. Haemophilus influenzae type b is an encapsulated gram-negative bacterium that can result in various mucosal infections, such as conjunctivitis, otitis media, bronchitis, and pneumonia. It was the leading cause of epiglottitis in children prior to widespread immunization. The Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccination uses conjugated capsular polysaccharide to provoke an adaptive immune response. Vaccination is a form of active immunity designed to prevent disease by stimulating the immune system to develop and maintain the ability to respond to a foreign antigen. In a patient with recurrent bacterial pneumonia, a vaccine against Haemophilus influenzae type b should be administered as it is a frequent cause of bacterial pneumonia. Choice A (BCG) protects against tuberculosis, which can also cause pulmonary infections. However, it is much less common and is not routinely given to children, except in countries with a high prevalence of tuberculosis. Choice C (Rotavirus) is a double-stranded RNA virus that causes infectious diarrhea in children. It does not cause bacterial pneumonia, thus a vaccine against Haemophilus influenzae type b is a higher priority for a patient with recurrent bacterial pneumonia. Choice D (Varicella) defense relies on T-lymphocyte function, which is impaired in the setting of T-lymphocyte immunodeficiency. Infants with deficient T-lymphocyte function are at increased risk for severe infection with varicella. A vaccination against Haemophilus influenzae type b is a higher priority for a patient with recurrent bacterial pneumonia. Choice E (No vaccines) would be inappropriate, as vaccines will help protect against bacterial and viral infections in this patient with T-lymphocyte immunodeficiency. Educational Objective: Haemophilus influenzae type b is a common cause of bacterial pneumonia. A vaccine against Haemophilus influenzae type b can help prevent recurrent bacterial pneumonia in patients with T-lymphocyte immunodeficiency.
▶ Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Atopic Dermatitis 2 questions
Source: 6A #4
A 10-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 5-day history of a rash over the cheeks and diaper area that she constantly rubs. Her mother says that for the past 24 hours, she has been unwilling to stand. She is afebrile and otherwise healthy. Her mother and 6-year-old brother have asthma. Examination shows erythematous lichenified papules and plaques, and excoriations on the diaper area. She has red lichenified plaques on the cheek and chin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Atopic dermatitis B) Candidiasis C) Food allergy D) Tinea corporis E) Toxic epidermal necrolysis
Correct Answer: A) Atopic dermatitis
Atopic dermatitis (eczema) is a chronic pruritic inflammatory skin disease common in children that is suggested by pruritus and recurrent eczematous rashes. The rash is initially characterized by erythematous papules and vesicles with exudates and crusting and, with chronic scratching, becomes dry, scaly, and excoriated in a process called lichenification. Flexural dermatitis is a common pattern in children and adults with atopic dermatitis, but infants demonstrate a unique pattern that primarily involves bilateral cheeks and diaper area, as these areas are both frequently moist and subject to irritation. This patient's presentation is classic for infantile atopic dermatitis. Additionally, the family history of asthma supports an atopic diathesis. Treatment begins with gentle skin care: minimizing long baths in warm water (which causes skin drying), avoiding fragrant products, and using bland moisturizers such as petroleum jelly daily. In infants, keeping cheeks dry and frequent diaper changes are important. Flares are treated with mild- to moderate-potency topical corticosteroids such as triamcinolone. In children, moderate-potency topical corticosteroids should not be used consistently for over 2-3 weeks due to risk of systemic absorption, particularly in the diaper area. Choice B (Candidiasis) presents with thick, white plaques on mucous membranes that can be scraped off, or red macerated thin plaques with satellite papules on skin. While candidiasis is a common cause of diaper rash, the additional facial findings make atopic dermatitis more likely. Choice C (Food allergy) rarely contributes to atopic dermatitis. Patients with diaper dermatitis caused or worsened by food allergy demonstrate gastrointestinal symptoms including diarrhea, which are absent here. Specific food avoidance diets play no role in treating pediatric atopic dermatitis. Choice D (Tinea corporis) is caused by superficial dermatophyte infection, most often Trichophyton tonsurans. The classic appearance is a round, annular patch with a scaly border, and potassium hydroxide preparation would disclose hyphae. Choice E (Toxic epidermal necrolysis) is a life-threatening adverse cutaneous drug reaction characterized by skin pain, sloughing, and mucosal involvement. The lichenified papules and plaques in this case are consistent with atopic dermatitis, not toxic epidermal necrolysis. Educational Objective: Atopic dermatitis is a chronic pruritic inflammatory skin disease common in children suggested by pruritus and recurrent eczematous rashes. In infants, atopic dermatitis primarily involves bilateral cheeks and diaper area due to increased moisture and irritation in these regions.
Source: 4A #6
A 6-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a scaly, pruritic rash on intertriginous areas of her elbows and knees that worsens in the spring and the fall; it often appears in conjunction with episodes of respiratory distress and wheezing. Treatment with which of the following is the most effective short-term treatment of the rash? A) Clotrimazole B) Coal tar C) Griseofulvin D) Lindane E) Triamcinolone
Correct Answer: E) Triamcinolone
Atopic dermatitis, or eczema, is a chronic pruritic inflammatory skin disease common in children. The diagnosis is made based on clinical symptoms where pruritus must be present in addition to three of the following: current or past flexural eczema, history of asthma or hay fever, or presence of dry skin within the past year. The rash is initially characterized by erythematous papules and vesicles with exudates and crusting. With chronic scratching, they become dry, scaly, and excoriated in a process called lichenification. This patient's flexural dermatitis and apparent asthma and hay fever suggest a diagnosis of atopic dermatitis, which forms part of the atopic triad. Treatment of atopic dermatitis begins with gentle skin care: minimizing long baths in warm water which causes drying of the skin, avoiding products with fragrance, and use of bland moisturizers such as petroleum jelly daily. Flares of eczema are treated with mild to moderate potency topical corticosteroids, such as triamcinolone. In children, moderate potency topical corticosteroids should not be used consistently for over 2 to 3 weeks because of the potential of systemic absorption. Clotrimazole (Choice A) is a topical antifungal used to treat superficial dermatophyte infections such as tinea pedis and tinea corporis, not eczema. Griseofulvin (Choice C) is a systemic antifungal used to treat tinea capitis in children. While the bacterial and fungal microbiome do play a role in the development and treatment of atopic dermatitis, triamcinolone is a more effective short-term treatment. Coal tar (Choice B) is a topical remedy used in psoriasis, not eczema. Its mechanism is not fully elucidated, but it is thought to be anti-inflammatory and anti-proliferative to the epidermis. Lindane (Choice D) is an antiparasitic agent which in the past has been used to treat lice infestation but is no longer used given the relatively high incidence of neurologic toxicity, which is especially concerning in young children who have a lower body surface area to volume ratio.
▶ Gastrointestinal System Volvulus 2 questions
Source: 6A #6
A 3-week-old boy is brought to the physician 4 hours after the onset of vomiting watery, green material. His mother says that he has been drawing up his legs as if in pain while vomiting. He appears uncomfortable. He is afebrile. The abdomen is tender but not distended. An abdominal x-ray shows dilated loops of small bowel and air-fluid levels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Appendicitis B) Congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung disease) C) Duodenal atresia D) Foreign body ingestion E) Gastroesophageal reflux disease F) Hepatitis G) Intussusception H) Pancreatitis I) Pyloric stenosis J) Volvulus
Correct Answer: J) Volvulus
Volvulus occurs when a portion of the gastrointestinal tract twists, leading to bowel obstruction. Midgut volvulus usually occurs in children who have intestinal malrotation, a congenital anomaly in which the midgut incompletely rotates during development, and typically presents within the first year of life. The most common initial symptom in infants is vomiting, which becomes bilious as a result of the blockage of the small bowel and the retrograde flow of bile. In older children, abdominal pain is the most common presenting symptom. The diagnosis can be confirmed with imaging. Plain x-rays are acquired first to screen for perforation. Once perforation has been excluded, an upper gastrointestinal contrast series is obtained. Imaging studies may show evidence of malrotation with a small bowel obstruction including air-fluid levels and dilated loops of bowel. If not recognized quickly, volvulus can lead to vascular compromise with subsequent intestinal necrosis, perforation, and peritonitis. Choice A (Appendicitis) typically presents with right lower quadrant abdominal pain that is often periumbilical at onset, along with nausea, anorexia, fever, leukocytosis, and tenderness to palpation in the right lower quadrant on examination. It does not cause bowel obstruction or bilious vomiting. Choice B (Congenital megacolon/Hirschsprung disease), caused by the congenital absence of the distal portion of the myenteric plexus, often leads to an inability to pass meconium within the first few days of life and may result in a large bowel obstruction. An explosive expulsion of feces on rectal examination is a classic clinical finding. Choice C (Duodenal atresia) is caused by failure of recanalization of the duodenal lumen. It presents with vomiting and abdominal distension, as well as gaseous dilation of the stomach and duodenum on an abdominal x-ray. Choice D (Foreign body ingestion) may cause intestinal obstruction and bilious vomiting. However, it is more common in older infants and toddlers who tend to put items in their mouths, not 3-week-old newborns. Choice E (Gastroesophageal reflux disease) in an infant presents with frequent regurgitation without excessive irritability. Bilious vomiting is a warning sign of a structural cause of vomiting. Choice F (Hepatitis) can be caused by viral infections, autoimmune diseases, or medications. Hyperbilirubinemia with jaundice or icterus is often present. It is not a cause of small bowel obstruction or bilious vomiting. Choice G (Intussusception) occurs when an intestinal lead point causes the small or large intestine to telescope on itself. It presents with episodic, crampy abdominal pain accompanied by crying, vomiting, and bloody, mucoid stool. Choice H (Pancreatitis) presents with epigastric abdominal pain that radiates to the back, along with nausea and emesis. Acute pancreatitis can be complicated by necrosis, hemorrhage, abscess, or the formation of pseudocysts, but generally not a small bowel obstruction. Choice I (Pyloric stenosis) is caused by hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter, leading to gastric outlet obstruction and vomiting. It commonly presents with non-bloody, nonbilious emesis after feedings, and begins around 3 to 6 weeks of age. Educational Objective: Congenital malrotation of the intestines predisposes to midgut volvulus, which presents with signs of small bowel obstruction including bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. X-ray findings of small bowel obstruction include dilated loops of bowel with air-fluid levels.
Source: 9A #46
A previously healthy 2-week-old female newborn is brought to the emergency department by her parents because of a 6-hour history of forceful vomiting and lethargy that began after cow milk-based formula feeding. She initially vomited formula; after several episodes of vomiting, the emesis was green. Her parents say she then became less responsive and refused her next feeding. She has not had fever, diarrhea, or other symptoms. She appears lethargic. Her temperature is 38°C, pulse is 150/min, respirations are 40/min and shallow, and blood pressure is 60/40 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. The extremities are cool to the touch. The abdomen is mildly distended and diffusely tender to palpation; there is mild rebound. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Cow milk protein allergy B) Duodenal atresia C) Galactosemia D) Midgut volvulus E) Streptococcus agalactiae (group B) infection
Correct Answer: D) Midgut volvulus
Midgut volvulus is the most likely diagnosis in this patient. The clinical presentation is highly suggestive of an acute intestinal obstruction rather than a congenital defect present from birth. Definition and Pathophysiology: Midgut volvulus is a dangerous complication of intestinal malrotation that typically occurs in infants within the first few months of life. Malrotation results from incomplete rotation of the midgut during embryonal development, leaving the midgut attached to a thin stalk of mesentery at the base of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) instead of the normally broad-based mesenteric stalk. This anatomical derangement leaves the small intestine at risk for volvulus at the base of the SMA. Volvulus can lead to bilious vomiting, abdominal distention, and vascular compromise of the small bowel with potential consequent intestinal necrosis, hematochezia, perforation, and peritonitis. Key Clinical Features: Infants with midgut volvulus present with abdominal bloating, distention, failure to tolerate oral intake, nausea, vomiting, and signs of dehydration/volume depletion. This patient demonstrates classic findings: forceful vomiting, bilious (green) emesis, abdominal distention, diffuse tenderness, lethargy, hypotension (60/40 mm Hg), tachycardia (150/min), and signs of hypovolemic shock (cool extremities). The acute onset after feeding and absence of symptoms at birth suggest a new obstruction rather than a congenital condition. Evaluation: Upper gastrointestinal series is the diagnostic test of choice, which outlines the small bowel anatomy and demonstrates the characteristic corkscrew appearance of volvulus with displaced bowel and obstruction. Treatment involves emergent exploratory laparoscopy for confirmed or suspected volvulus with unstable vital signs, as in this case. Incorrect Answers: Choice A - Cow milk protein allergy: While this patient was fed cow milk-based formula, cow milk protein allergy typically presents with diarrhea (which may be bloody) and difficulty feeding. It would not cause hypotension, abdominal distention, and persistent forceful bilious vomiting. Choice B - Duodenal atresia: Although duodenal atresia is a differential diagnosis of midgut volvulus and can present with bilious vomiting, symptoms typically occur earlier and closer to birth. This patient's abrupt and acute presentation suggesting a new obstruction that was not present from birth is more consistent with midgut volvulus rather than a congenital anomaly. Choice C - Galactosemia: Galactosemia is an inborn error of metabolism in which patients lack enzymes necessary for conversion of galactose to glucose. Symptoms manifest from birth with systemic findings such as cataracts, hepatomegaly, cirrhosis, or renal failure. This patient's acute presentation after 2 weeks of normal feeding is inconsistent with galactosemia. Choice E - Streptococcus agalactiae (group B) infection: While S. agalactiae (GBS) can cause severe infections in newborns, it typically presents with fever and variable symptoms depending on the site of infection (meningoencephalitis, endocarditis, pneumonia, bacteremia/sepsis). Gastrointestinal infection from GBS is uncommon. More importantly, this patient's presentation is suggestive of mechanical obstruction rather than infection.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Beckwith-Wiedemann Syndrome 3 questions
Source: 6A #13
A 5000-g (11-lb 1-oz) male infant is born at term to a 35-year-old woman following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. Initial examination shows that he is large for gestational age and has macroglossia, visceromegaly, and an omphalocele. This infant most likely has which of the following associated conditions? A) Congenital heart disease B) Hypoglycemia C) Imperforate anus D) Polycythemia E) Renal tubular acidosis
Correct Answer: B) Hypoglycemia
Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is a genetic disorder involving mutations of genes located at the 11p15.5 locus that may result from defects of imprinting or uniparental disomy. The syndrome is characterized by cellular overgrowth and predisposition to malignancy. Clinical presentation commonly includes above-average birth weight, macrosomia, macroglossia, visceromegaly, renal malformations, omphalocele, or umbilical hernia. The key associated condition in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is neonatal hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia, which affects approximately half of affected children due to poorly understood mechanisms. Children with this syndrome are also at increased risk for Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma. Choice A (Congenital heart disease): While congenital heart defects may occur with various syndromes such as trisomy 21, they are not commonly associated with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. Choice C (Imperforate anus): Although imperforate anus may occur as a sporadic defect or as part of VACTERL association (vertebral anomalies, anorectal malformations, cardiovascular anomalies, tracheoesophageal fistula, esophageal atresia, renal anomalies, and limb defects), it is not commonly observed in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. Choice D (Polycythemia): While polycythemia may rarely occur in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, it is uncommon compared to hypoglycemia. Neonatal polycythemia more commonly occurs in post-term infants and infants of mothers with gestational diabetes mellitus. Choice E (Renal tubular acidosis): This family of disorders causes hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis and inability to absorb HCO3- or excrete titratable acid as NH4+. It is not commonly associated with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. Educational Objective: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is a heterogenous genetic disorder involving the 11p15.5 locus characterized by above-average birth weight, macrosomia, macroglossia, visceromegaly, renal malformations, omphalocele, umbilical hernia, and increased risk for malignancy such as Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma. Approximately half of affected children develop neonatal hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia. Diagnosis is confirmed with cytogenetic testing.
Source: 9A #15
A 1-month-old boy is admitted to the hospital for management of presumed sepsis. He has had a 6-hour history of listlessness and poor feeding. In the emergency department, he had a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. He was delivered at term by vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery and weighed 4224 g (9 lb 5 oz) at birth. Today, he is at the 90th percentile for length and 95th percentile for weight. His temperature is 35.6°C (96°F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 50/min, and blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg. A photograph of the patient is shown. The liver edge is palpated 4 cm below the right costal margin; the liver span is 12 cm. The spleen tip is palpated 2 cm below the left costal margin. Examination shows bilateral nephromegaly. Which of the following is the most likely underlying diagnosis? A) Alagille syndrome B) Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome C) Congenital adrenal hyperplasia D) Congenital hypothyroidism E) Cushing disease
Correct Answer: B) Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) is a heterogenous genetic disorder involving the 11p15.5 locus characterized by above-average birth weight, macrosomia, macroglossia, visceromegaly, renal malformations, omphalocele, umbilical hernia, and increased risk for malignancy including nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor) and hepatoblastoma. This patient presents with key features consistent with BWS: macrosomia (95th percentile for weight), organomegaly (hepatomegaly with 12 cm span, splenomegaly), bilateral nephromegaly, and seizures. BWS results from mutations at the 11p15.5 locus through various mechanisms including imprinting defects or uniparental disomy. Patients have cellular overgrowth and predisposition to malignancy. Approximately half of BWS patients experience neonatal hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia, which can manifest as seizures in severe cases. Additionally, BWS patients have increased risk for recurrent urinary tract infections and urosepsis. Diagnosis is confirmed with cytogenetic testing, and management includes multidisciplinary care, early diagnosis and treatment of infections, and regular malignancy surveillance. Choice A (Alagille syndrome) is incorrect. This autosomal dominant disorder causes ductal and vascular dysplasia leading to hepatic cholestasis from insufficient bile ducts, cardiac defects, and facial and skeletal abnormalities. The constellation of macrosomia, organomegaly, and nephromegaly is not typical of Alagille syndrome. Choice C (Congenital adrenal hyperplasia) is incorrect. CAH causes adrenal hypofunction resulting in decreased cortisol with variable effects on mineralocorticoids and androgens. While hypovolemic shock can occur in adrenal crisis or severe salt wasting, this patient's physical examination findings of macrosomia and visceromegaly are most consistent with BWS, not adrenal insufficiency. Choice D (Congenital hypothyroidism) is incorrect. Although congenital hypothyroidism can present with feeding difficulties, lethargy, myxedematous facies, macroglossia, and hypothermia in early infancy, the findings of macrosomia, organomegaly, and bilateral nephromegaly are more characteristic of BWS. Choice E (Cushing disease) is incorrect. Cushing syndrome from a corticotroph adenoma causes abnormally elevated serum cortisol with manifestations including hypertension, hyperglycemia, weight gain, facial fat deposition, truncal obesity, abdominal striae, hirsutism, and menstrual irregularities. Cushing disease presenting in infancy is uncommon, and this patient's clinical presentation is not consistent with hypercortisolemia.
Source: 8A #40
A 6-month-old girl with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is brought to the physician because of a firm mass in the right upper quadrant. She receives no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows macroglossia and right-sided hypertrophy. On palpation, a firm mass is palpated in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory studies show: B-hCG: 0 mIU/mL α-Fetoprotein: 15,678 ng/mL (N<10) Urine Homovanillic acid/creatinine: 10 mg/g Cr (N=0-42) Vanillyimandelic acid/creatinine: 5.6 mg/g Cr (N=0-27) Abdominal ultrasonography is ordered. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's mass? A) Germ cell tumor B) Hepatoblastoma C) Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor) D) Neuroblastoma E) Spina bifida occulta
Correct Answer: B) Hepatoblastoma
Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is a genetic disorder involving mutations of genes located at the 11p15.5 locus that may result from defects of imprinting or uniparental disomy. It is characterized by cellular overgrowth and predisposition to malignancy, with presentation including above-average birth weight, macrosomia, macroglossia, visceromegaly, kidney malformations, omphalocele, or umbilical hernia. Children with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome are at increased risk for Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma. The markedly elevated α-fetoprotein (15,678 ng/mL) is the key finding pointing to hepatoblastoma, as α-fetoprotein concentrations are markedly increased in most patients with hepatoblastoma. The right upper quadrant location is consistent with a hepatic mass. Choice A (Germ cell tumor): Would not present as a firm upper abdominal mass. Yolk sac tumors may present as a pelvic mass in young children and are associated with increased serum α-fetoprotein, but the upper quadrant location and clinical context make this unlikely. Choice C (Nephroblastoma/Wilms tumor): The most common pediatric kidney malignancy, characterized by a large, often palpable, unilateral flank mass. While patients with Beckwith-Wiedemann are at increased risk for Wilms tumor, these are not associated with increased α-fetoprotein, making this less likely given the markedly elevated α-fetoprotein in this case. Choice D (Neuroblastoma): A malignancy of neuroendocrine cells of the sympathetic nervous system commonly affecting the adrenal glands. It may be differentiated by its tendency to cross the midline, nodular texture, association with paraneoplastic opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome, and increased serum and urine catecholamine metabolites. The catecholamine metabolites in this patient are normal, ruling out neuroblastoma. Choice E (Spina bifida occulta): Caused by failure of the caudal neuropore to close. Patients may have a tuft of hair or skin dimple at the affected vertebral level. This is not associated with increased α-fetoprotein or an abdominal mass. Educational Objective: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is a heterogenous genetic disorder characterized by above-average birth weight, macrosomia, macroglossia, visceromegaly, kidney malformations, omphalocele, umbilical hernia, and increased risk of malignancy such as Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma. Markedly increased serum α-fetoprotein concentrations are characteristic of hepatoblastoma in these patients.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Inhalation Injury from Gases, Vapors, and Smoke 2 questions
Source: 6A #16
A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after the onset of confusion, decreased awareness, headache, weakness, and dyspnea. When his mother returned home from work, she found him sitting in front of the television with the space heater on and an open package of cookies and glass of milk nearby. The most appropriate treatment is administration of which of the following? A) Acetylcysteine B) Amyl nitrite C) Atropine D) Deferoxamine E) Dimercaprol (BAL) F) Methylene blue G) Naloxone H) Oxygen I) Vitamin K
Correct Answer: H) Oxygen
Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning occurs as a consequence of inhaling the gas, often due to its generation in poorly ventilated areas such as garages with running cars, space heaters in poorly ventilated rooms, or malfunctioning furnaces. CO is a byproduct of combustion. When inhaled, it avidly crosses the pulmonary capillary membrane and tightly binds hemoglobin with an affinity hundreds of times greater than that of oxygen, readily displacing oxygen from heme and inducing a conformational change that prevents oxygen binding. CO also has affinity for the mitochondrial electron transport chain, so in addition to hypoxemia from impaired oxygen-carrying capacity, cells may not be able to utilize the oxygen they receive via aerobic metabolism. This results in anaerobic metabolism dominance and lactic acidosis. Symptoms include headache, loss of consciousness, dizziness, vomiting, and fatigue; severe cases may present with seizures, dysrhythmias, coma, and death. Examination may show red skin. Treatment begins with administration of 100% oxygen regardless of pulse oximetry readings, and if neurologic symptoms or signs of end-organ dysfunction are present, hyperbaric oxygen therapy may be indicated. Incorrect Answers: Acetylcysteine (Choice A) is the principal antidote for acetaminophen toxicity, which causes glutathione depletion and production of the toxic metabolite N-acetyl-P-benzoquinoneimine. Amyl nitrite (Choice B) is an antidote for cyanide poisoning by inducing methemoglobin formation, which sequesters cyanide as cyanomethemoglobin. Atropine (Choice C) is a cholinergic antagonist used for organophosphate poisoning, reversing cholinergic excess effects on the heart and lungs. Deferoxamine (Choice D) is an antidote for iron toxicity, which causes hepatic failure and profound metabolic acidosis. Dimercaprol/BAL (Choice E) is used to treat arsenic and mercury poisoning and can also chelate lead and gold in serum. Methylene blue (Choice F) is an antidote for methemoglobinemia, decreasing iron in methemoglobin to Fe²⁺ to restore oxygen binding and transport. Naloxone (Choice G) is an opioid receptor antagonist used for opiate overdose presenting with bradypnea and miosis, and can also treat clonidine overdose. Vitamin K (Choice I) is used to reverse warfarin and coumarin overdoses. Educational Objective: CO has an affinity for hemoglobin that is hundreds of times greater than that of oxygen, readily displacing oxygen from heme. Treatment for CO poisoning begins with the administration of 100% oxygen.
Source: 9A #35
An 8-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a headache, lethargy, and abdominal pain for 12 hours. Several family members have similar symptoms. The family recently moved to a home that is heated by a woodstove. They have not smelled any unusual odors in the home. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 95/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. Exposure to which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Carbon dioxide B) Carbon monoxide C) Cyanide D) Organophosphate E) Radon
Correct Answer: B) Carbon monoxide
Carbon monoxide (CO) is the most likely cause of this patient's presentation. CO has an affinity for hemoglobin that is hundreds of times greater than that of oxygen, readily displacing oxygen from heme. When inhaled, CO avidly crosses the pulmonary capillary membrane and tightly binds hemoglobin, inducing a conformational change that prevents oxygen binding. Additionally, CO has affinity with the mitochondrial electron transport chain, so in addition to hypoxemia due to interference with oxygen-carrying capacity, cells cannot efficiently utilize oxygen via aerobic metabolism. This results in anaerobic metabolism dominance and lactic acidosis. Symptoms of CO poisoning include headache, lethargy, dizziness, vomiting, fatigue, and abdominal pain. In severe cases, seizures, dysrhythmias, coma, and death may occur. Importantly, pulse oximetry readings may be falsely normal because oximeters measure the saturation of hemoglobin without distinguishing between oxyhemoglobin and carboxyhemoglobin. The patient's exposure to an indoor woodstove in poor ventilation is a classic risk factor, as CO is a byproduct of combustion. Treatment begins with administration of 100% oxygen regardless of pulse oximetry readings. If neurologic symptoms or signs of end-organ dysfunction are present (as in this patient), hyperbaric oxygen therapy may be indicated. Carbon dioxide (Choice A) is incorrect. While environmental CO2 exposure can occur, it is relatively rare compared to CO exposure. Acute hypercapnia typically results from respiratory insufficiency rather than environmental exposure. Cyanide (Choice C) is incorrect. Although cyanide also inhibits the electron transport chain and causes lactic acidosis, it produces mydriasis (whereas CO does not), causes bradycardia (this patient has normal heart rate), and does not improve with 100% oxygen administration. Additionally, residential woodstove heating is a risk factor for CO poisoning, not cyanide poisoning. Organophosphate (Choice D) is incorrect. Organophosphate poisoning from pesticide exposure causes characteristic cholinergic agonist effects including vomiting, diarrhea, diaphoresis, salivation, lacrimation, bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, seizures, and muscle weakness. This patient's presentation and risk factors are more consistent with CO poisoning. Radon (Choice E) is incorrect. While radon exposure typically occurs in the home and basement, radon poisoning is a chronic process from repeated inhalation that promotes mutations leading to bronchogenic lung cancer over time. Given that this family recently moved to their new home, acute CO exposure is far more likely than radon-related illness.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Examination of liveborn at admission to hospital 2 questions
Source: 6A #18
A 2807-g (6-lb 3-oz) newborn has a strong cry immediately after delivery. She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and a spontaneous vaginal delivery complicated by a few decelerations. The newborn was suctioned at the perineum and placed on the warmer/resuscitation table. After 10 seconds of warming, the newborn's pulse is greater than 100/min, and respirations are 20/min. Examination shows peripheral cyanosis and minimal movement of the upper and lower extremities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Tactile stimulation and oxygen therapy B) Naloxone therapy C) Subcutaneous epinephrine therapy D) Positive-pressure ventilation via face mask E) Immediate intubation
Correct Answer: A) Tactile stimulation and oxygen therapy
The initiation of breathing following delivery is crucial for newborns. A substantial portion of neonates require assistance with the initiation of breathing. Initial universal steps after delivery include assessment of the newborn's heart and respiratory rates, muscle tone, reflexes, and color, along with immediate warming, drying, and tactile stimulation—all of which are helpful for stimulating spontaneous respirations. This newborn has adequate heart rate (>100/min) and some respiratory effort (20/min), indicating the need for noninvasive support initially. Neonates who fail to respond to gentle tactile stimulation should then be supported with more invasive techniques such as bag-mask ventilation or endotracheal intubation. Choice B (Naloxone therapy) may be useful for reversal of opioid toxicity in neonates, but this infant has no known risk factors for opioid exposure, making tactile stimulation a more appropriate initial step. Choice C (Subcutaneous epinephrine therapy) is useful for anaphylaxis treatment. This newborn has no exposure to agents likely to cause anaphylaxis; epinephrine is reserved for neonates with bradycardia during resuscitation, which is not present here. Choices D (Positive-pressure ventilation via face mask) and E (Immediate intubation) are appropriate interventions if the newborn remains apneic and does not respond to initial efforts of tactile stimulation. However, these invasive methods are not appropriate as first-line measures. Educational Objective: Many neonates require assistance with spontaneous respiration initiation. Tactile stimulation and oxygen therapy are noninvasive approaches that decrease neonatal morbidity and mortality and should be attempted before more invasive interventions.
Source: 8A #3
Five minutes after delivery, a full-term newborn shows peripheral cyanosis, decreased muscle tone, and decreased reflex activity. His pulse is 80/min, and respirations are irregular. Which of the following is the most likely Apgar score? A) 0-1 B) 2-3 C) 4-6 D) 7-8 E) 9-10
Correct Answer: C) 4-6
Apgar scoring is performed at 1 and 5 minutes after birth to assess the status of the newborn and need for possible resuscitation. The Apgar score consists of points given in five different categories: appearance, pulse, grimace or reflex irritability, activity/muscle tone, and respiratory effort. Each category is given 0, 1, or 2 points, with 0 points for absent function, 1 for diminished or irregular function, and 2 for a normal, expected presentation. For this patient: - Appearance (peripheral cyanosis): 1 point - Pulse (80/min, less than 100/min): 1 point - Grimace/reflex irritability (decreased reflex activity): 1 point - Activity/muscle tone (decreased muscle tone): 1 point - Respiratory effort (irregular respirations): 1 point Total Apgar score = 5 (falls within 4-6 range) Newborns with lower scores, especially below 7, may require further evaluation and/or intervention. This score indicates the potential need for further resuscitation. Choice A (0-1) and Choice B (2-3) would require extreme deficiency in several assessed categories (absent pulse, general cyanosis, absent muscle tone, absent respirations, and/or no response to stimulation). This patient has objective, scorable neonatal Apgar features, even if suboptimal. Choice D (7-8) and Choice E (9-10) would be more reassuring and would require the newborn to have a pink acyanotic appearance, pulse greater than 100/min, active response to stimulation, normal muscle tone with active movement, and vigorous cry. Apgar scores are not necessarily associated with later functional or developmental abnormalities.
▶ Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Hemangioma 2 questions
Source: 6A #19
A 2-week-old female newborn is brought to the physician because of bruising on her arms and legs for 2 days. She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy. The delivery was precipitous, but the newborn fed well soon after birth. Examination shows petechiae over the face and trunk, scattered ecchymoses over the extremities, and an erythematous, fleshy irregular mass on the thigh. A bruit is heard over the hepatic area. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 13 g/dL, leukocyte count of 5000/mm³, and platelet count of 15,000/mm³. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings? A) Cutaneous lymphoma B) Cystic hygroma C) Hemangioma D) Juvenile xanthogranuloma E) Lymphangioma F) Mastocytoma G) Neurofibroma
Correct Answer: C) Hemangioma
Kasabach-Merritt syndrome is a consumptive coagulopathy associated with large vascular neoplasms, including tufted angioma and kaposiform hemangioendothelioma (both types of hemangiomas). These lesions present as red or purple subcutaneous tumors and may be present at or shortly after birth. The increased blood flow causes the affected area to be warm and swollen and can produce a bruit when located over vascular organs like the liver. The large, convoluted vascular architecture causes platelet adhesion and trapping within the lesion, leading to consumption of fibrinogen and activation of fibrinolysis. This results in severe thrombocytopenia and other coagulation factor deficiencies, presenting clinically with mucocutaneous bleeding (petechiae and ecchymoses) that cannot be explained by trauma alone. Laboratory findings show profound thrombocytopenia (platelet count of 15,000/mm³ in this case). Treatment includes supportive measures to maintain hemostasis and management of the underlying vascular neoplasm. Cutaneous lymphoma (Choice A) is rare in newborns and typically presents with scaly patches in sun-protected areas, primarily in adults. Cystic hygroma (Choice B) and lymphangioma (Choice E) are lymphatic malformations that may present as subcutaneous masses but are not associated with Kasabach-Merritt syndrome or thrombocytopenia. Juvenile xanthogranuloma (Choice D) is a benign histiocytic proliferation presenting as an orange-pink papule; it is not a vascular neoplasm and does not cause consumptive coagulopathy. Mastocytoma (Choice F) is a benign mast cell proliferation presenting as an orange-brown leathery plaque that may cause anaphylaxis but does not produce thrombocytopenia. Neurofibroma (Choice G) is associated with neurofibromatosis and presents with neurofibromas, café-au-lait macules, and axillary freckling; thrombocytopenia is not a typical finding.
Source: 3A #13
A 1-month-old infant has had a 12 x 8-cm, red, raised, well-defined lesion that is lobulated and compressible overlying the buttocks since birth. Examination also shows multiple petechiae and bruises. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings? A) Disseminated intravascular coagulation B) High-output congestive heart failure C) Impaired tissue growth due to altered vascular supply D) Increased tissue growth due to increased vascular supply E) Thrombocytopenia from platelet sequestration
Correct Answer: E) Thrombocytopenia from platelet sequestration
This clinical presentation is consistent with Kasabach-Merritt syndrome, a complication of vascular tumors such as tufted hemangiomas and kaposiform hemangioendotheliomas. The syndrome presents with bleeding, ecchymoses, and petechiae resulting from platelet sequestration by the tumor and an associated coagulopathy. Typical findings include rapid enlargement of the tumor, thrombocytopenia, hypofibrinogenemia, and increased D-dimer concentration. The altered vasculature of these tumors sequesters and activates platelets, leading to thrombocytopenia and consumptive coagulopathy. Treatment options include steroids, chemotherapy (e.g., vincristine), and immunomodulators (e.g., sirolimus). Disseminated intravascular coagulation (Choice A) presents with similar bleeding manifestations and coagulopathy (increased PT/PTT, decreased fibrinogen, increased D-dimer), but is typically associated with trauma, severe sepsis, or malignancy. It is less likely in this otherwise healthy patient with a localized vascular tumor. High-output congestive heart failure (Choice B) presents with shortness of breath, weight gain, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and peripheral edema, typically in the setting of arteriovenous fistula, cirrhosis, sepsis, or severe anemia. It does not present with bruising and petechiae. Choices C and D regarding impaired or increased tissue growth are incorrect, as the altered vascular supply of the tumor does not affect tissue growth but rather results in platelet sequestration and consumptive coagulopathy. Educational Objective: Recognize that vascular tumors such as tufted hemangiomas and kaposiform hemangioendotheliomas can be complicated by Kasabach-Merritt syndrome, characterized by sequestration and activation of platelets by the tumor, leading to thrombocytopenia and consumptive coagulopathy.
▶ Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Tinea Capitis 2 questions
Source: 6A #20
A previously healthy 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of progressive hair loss over the past 4 weeks. Examination shows a swollen and purulent area on the scalp. A photograph is shown. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Topical corticosteroid therapy B) Oral antibacterial therapy C) Oral antifungal therapy D) Surgical excision E) No intervention necessary
Correct Answer: C) Oral antifungal therapy
Tinea capitis is a fungal infection of the scalp that is common in children. The most common presentation is scaly patches with alopecia, which may demonstrate black dots representing broken hairs. When a significant inflammatory response to the fungal infection occurs, a kerion develops—a boggy and swollen lesion on examination. Tinea capitis is caused by dermatophytes including Trichophyton rubrum, Epidermophyton floccosum, and Microsporum canis.
