Delayed puberty is defined as the absence of testicular enlargement or secondary sexual characteristics by age 14. The most common cause of delayed puberty is constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP), a normal variant accounting for approximately 50% of cases. CDGP results from transient deficient gonadotropin-releasing hormone production, reducing pituitary FSH and LH stimulation, and is often familial. In this patient, gonadarche is present (Tanner stage 2 genitalia) and pubarche has occurred (pubic hair noted 6 months ago), indicating appropriate progression through puberty stages despite delayed timing. He has not yet reached adrenarche (facial/axillary hair), which explains lack of shaving need. His development will continue appropriately, so reassurance is the most appropriate management. Choice B (Serum testosterone measurement) is unnecessary when puberty is progressing in correct sequence; it would be indicated only if progression stopped. Choice C (Urine toxicology) would only be relevant if drug-induced gynecomastia (e.g., marijuana use) were suspected; mild bilateral gynecomastia is normal in early puberty from relative estrogen excess. Choice E (Breast biopsy) is indicated for suspicious nodules or masses, not benign gynecomastia. Choice D (CT head) is inappropriate; MRI would be considered only if neurologic findings or suspected intracranial pathology (pituitary adenoma) were present. Neither imaging is warranted here. Educational Objective: Puberty in boys follows an orderly sequence of gonadarche, pubarche, adrenarche, and growth spurt. Delayed puberty is most commonly caused by constitutional delay of growth and puberty, a benign variant. Reassurance is appropriate when secondary sexual characteristics are developing in proper sequence, even if timing is delayed.
Source: 5A #26
An asymptomatic 15-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. He is concerned because he is the shortest student in his class. Review of his records from the age of 8 years to today shows a consistent pattern of height at the 3rd percentile and weight at the 25th percentile. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. His last routine examination 2 years ago showed no abnormalities. His mother is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) tall, and his father is 178 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall. He says his parents are always nagging him to eat better, but he thinks his diet is okay. Genital and pubic hair development is Tanner stage 2. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's short stature? A) Adrenal insufficiency B) Constitutional growth delay C) Familial short stature D) Growth hormone deficiency E) Insufficient caloric intake
Correct Answer: B) Constitutional growth delay
Constitutional growth delay is a normal variant of growth and the most likely diagnosis in this case. The patient demonstrates the classic features of constitutional growth delay: parents with normal stature, slow but consistently decreased growth velocity (remaining at 3rd percentile from age 8 to 15), delayed puberty (Tanner stage 2 at age 15), and absence of other pathologic signs or symptoms. Key distinguishing features: Constitutional growth delay is independent of parental stature, has consistently decreased growth velocity, and bone age is younger than chronological age. Patients typically reach normal adult height with more rapid growth during puberty. Familial short stature (Choice C) presents in patients with both parents of short stature, normal growth velocity, and bone age consistent with chronological age. This patient has parents of normal height, making this less likely. Growth hormone deficiency (Choice D) is rare and presents with severe growth delay, rapid decline in height-for-age curve crossing percentiles, and bone age younger than chronological age. This patient has slow but consistent growth velocity without crossing percentiles. Adrenal insufficiency (Choice A) typically presents with fatigue, nausea, fasting hypoglycemia, muscle weakness, and morning headaches. Patients may show mineralocorticoid deficiency (urinary salt wasting) and androgen deficiency (decreased body hair). This patient lacks these symptoms and signs. Insufficient caloric intake (Choice E) results in abnormally low weight and signs of malnutrition such as dry skin and hair loss. This patient has normal weight and no signs of malnutrition. Educational Objective: Constitutional growth delay is a normal growth variant in patients with parents of normal stature who present with short stature, delayed pubertal development, slow but consistent growth velocity, and bone age less than chronological age. These patients achieve normal development and stature once they complete puberty.
▶ Nervous System Special Senses Neurofibromatosis 2 questions
Source: 3A #35
A 2-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because she has developed several brown spots on the skin since birth. Her 28-year-old mother has similar spots as well as several 1-cm subcutaneous lumps and scoliosis. Examination of the girl shows four 1-cm flat brown spots on the back. Which of the following is the most likely pattern of inheritance in this patient? A) Autosomal dominant B) Autosomal recessive C) Mitochondrial D) Multifactorial E) X-linked recessive F) Unknown
Correct Answer: A) Autosomal dominant
Neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1) is an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder that typically results from an inherited mutation of the NF1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 17. The clinical presentation in this patient—café-au-lait spots (brown macules) on the skin and subcutaneous neurofibromas in the mother—is classic for NF1. The inheritance pattern shows vertical transmission from mother to daughter, consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance. NF1 is inherited with complete penetrance and variable expressivity, meaning all individuals carrying the mutation express some feature of the disease, but the severity and specific manifestations vary. The disorder presents with cutaneous neurofibromas (benign neoplasms derived from neural crest cells), café-au-lait spots, axillary or inguinal freckling, pigmented iris hamartomas (Lisch nodules), optic gliomas, and/or pheochromocytomas. Diagnosis is typically based on physical examination findings, though genetic testing may be used to confirm ambiguous cases. Treatment includes surgical debulking of tumors, management of seizures and neurological complications, and genetic counseling. Choice B (Autosomal recessive): Autosomal recessive neurocutaneous disorders such as ataxia-telangiectasia present with oculocutaneous telangiectasias, progressive cerebellar ataxia, immune deficiency, and neurologic abnormalities. Autosomal recessive inheritance requires two affected parents or two carrier parents; however, this patient's mother is clearly affected with overt manifestations, making recessive inheritance unlikely. Choice C (Mitochondrial): Mitochondrially inherited disorders rarely include neurocutaneous findings. Mitochondrial diseases typically present with muscle weakness, encephalopathy, and incoordination. Additionally, mitochondrial disorders show maternal inheritance with all offspring of affected mothers being affected, which is not the typical pattern seen with variable expressivity in NF1. Choice D (Multifactorial): The inheritance pattern of neurofibromatosis 1 is not multifactorial. It is a single-gene disorder with a known monogenic inheritance pattern. Choice E (X-linked recessive): X-linked recessive neurocutaneous disorders include Menkes disease, a congenital X-linked disorder that causes a defect in intestinal copper absorption leading to copper deficiency. Menkes disease presents with progressive neurologic symptoms, hypopigmentation of the skin, bony abnormalities, and kinked hair. The mother's affected status and transmission to both sons and daughters rules out X-linked recessive inheritance. Choice F (Unknown): The inheritance pattern of neurofibromatosis 1 is well-established as autosomal dominant with complete penetrance and variable expressivity, not unknown. Rarely, the mutation in the NF1 gene occurs sporadically in a patient without a family history.
Source: 8A #23
An asymptomatic 17-year-old boy comes to the physician for a routine examination prior to participation in school sports. Examination shows no abnormalities except for approximately 10 light brown hyperpigmented lesions over the trunk and extremities; the lesions vary in size from 0.6 to 2 cm in diameter. There are also some freckle-like lesions over both axillae. Compared to the general population, this patient is at increased risk for which of the following? A) Arteriovenous malformation B) Cerebral aneurysm C) Craniopharyngioma D) Medulloblastoma E) Optic nerve glioma
Correct Answer: E) Optic nerve glioma
The clinical presentation of light brown hyperpigmented lesions (café-au-lait spots) and freckle-like lesions in the axillae is classic for Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1), an autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder (phakomatosis) resulting from a mutation of the NF1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 17. NF1 is inherited with complete penetrance and variable expressivity, though mutations can occur sporadically. The disorder presents with cutaneous neurofibromas (benign neural crest-derived neoplasms), plexiform neurofibromas, hyperpigmented maculae, axillary or inguinal freckling, pigmented iris hamartomas (Lisch nodules), cognitive disability, and seizures. Patients with NF1 have a significantly increased risk for optic nerve glioma and pheochromocytoma. Optic nerve gliomas are typically indolent, low-grade pilocytic astrocytomas that may involve one or both optic nerves or the optic chiasm. They present with insidious vision loss, proptosis, and optic nerve atrophy. Diagnosis is based on physical examination findings, with genetic testing used for ambiguous cases. Management includes surgical debulking, seizure management, and genetic counseling. Children with NF1 require regular annual ophthalmic screening for early detection of optic nerve glioma. Arteriovenous malformations (Choice A) are characteristic of Wyburn-Mason syndrome (Bonnet-Dechaume-Blanc syndrome), which presents with retinal and midbrain arteriovenous malformations and facial cutaneous angiomas, not NF1. Cerebral aneurysm (Choice B) is associated with intracranial hemorrhage in adults but is not associated with NF1. Craniopharyngioma (Choice C) is a rare pituitary mass derived from Rathke pouch remnants presenting with bitemporal hemianopsia, but it is not associated with increased risk in NF1. Medulloblastoma (Choice D) is the most common malignant pediatric brain tumor, typically presenting in children ages 5-9 with increased intracranial pressure signs and gait ataxia, but it is not associated with NF1. Educational Objective: NF1 is an autosomal dominant phakomatosis presenting with cutaneous neurofibromas, plexiform neurofibromas, hyperpigmented maculae, and Lisch nodules. Patients with NF1 have increased risk for optic nerve glioma and pheochromocytoma and require regular screening examinations including annual ophthalmic evaluation.
▶ Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Measles 2 questions
Source: 3A #38
An 8-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a diffuse rash for 24 hours. She has had cough, congestion, eye discharge, and fever for 4 days. The rash initially began on her face and chest but has spread to involve her abdomen, back, and lower extremities. Her temperature is 38.9°C (102.1°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 115/70 mm Hg. Examination shows a diffuse red, macular and papular rash involving the face, trunk, and extremities; there are no lesions on the palms or soles. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Ehrlichiosis B) Henoch-Schönlein purpura C) Id reaction D) Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease) E) Pityriasis rosea F) Rocky Mountain spotted fever G) Rubeola H) Scabies I) Scarlet fever J) Staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome
Correct Answer: G) Rubeola
Measles (rubeola) is caused by a highly contagious paramyxovirus and is the correct diagnosis for this clinical presentation. The classic triad of findings includes the prodromal symptoms (cough, coryza/congestion, conjunctivitis/eye discharge) followed by fever and a characteristic rash. The rash characteristically starts on the head/neck and spreads to the trunk and extremities while sparing the palms and soles, exactly as described in this case. Physical examination may also reveal Koplik spots (bright red macules with bluish-white centers on the buccal mucosa) and lymphadenopathy. Treatment is supportive care, with vitamin A supplementation particularly important in malnourished children due to the association of vitamin A deficiency with severe disease. Complications include subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (a neurodegenerative disease with intellectual regression, personality changes, motor deterioration, and seizures), encephalitis, and giant cell pneumonia. Incorrect choices: Ehrlichiosis (Choice A) is a tick-borne illness presenting with fever, malaise, myalgia, headache, and rash but lacks the characteristic prodromal respiratory symptoms and conjunctivitis of measles. Henoch-Schönlein purpura (Choice B) presents with gravity-dependent purpura on buttocks and legs, arthralgias, hematuria, and abdominal pain rather than a confluent maculopapular rash with prodromal symptoms. Id reaction (Choice C) is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction manifesting as diffuse eczematous rash triggered by localized skin inflammation, not an acute febrile illness with systemic symptoms. Kawasaki disease (Choice D) requires fever for at least five days with bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, polymorphous rash, lymphadenopathy, and hand/foot edema, but lacks the characteristic cough, coryza, and maculopapular rash pattern of measles. Pityriasis rosea (Choice E) presents with a pruritic herald patch followed by smaller lesions on trunk and proximal extremities without the prodromal respiratory symptoms. Rocky Mountain spotted fever (Choice F) is a tick-borne rickettsial disease with petechial rash starting at ankles and wrists, accompanied by headache and fever but notably without cough, coryza, or conjunctivitis. Scabies (Choice H) is caused by Sarcoptes scabiei mite infestation with intense pruritus and lesions in characteristic locations (finger webs, wrists, axillae), not a systemic febrile illness with respiratory symptoms. Scarlet fever (Choice I) presents with erythematous tongue, rough papular diffuse body rash, and desquamation of hands and feet following streptococcal infection, lacking the cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis prodrome. Staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome (Choice J) features full-body erythematous desquamating rash with accentuation in skin folds caused by Staphylococcus aureus exfoliative toxin, without the prodromal symptoms or characteristic rash distribution of measles.
Source: 7A #30
A 3-year-old girl presents with a 3-day history of low-grade fever, mild generalized itching, and fatigue and a 1-day history of rash that started over her face and now involves her entire body. She also has had mild rhinorrhea. She has not had abdominal discomfort or diarrhea. She recently immigrated to the USA from Central America with her family. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F). Examination shows discrete, maculopapular lesions over the face, extremities, trunk, and back. There are no ocular or oral lesions. Which of the following vaccines is most likely to have prevented this patient's condition? A) Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis B) Haemophilus influenzae type b C) Hepatitis B D) Inactivated poliovirus E) Influenza virus F) Measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) G) Pneumococcal H) Typhoid I) Varicella
Correct Answer: F) Measles-mumps-rubella (MMR)
Measles (rubeola) virus is a highly contagious paramyxovirus that causes measles, which is associated with acute febrile illness and potentially severe sequelae. It is more common in children than adults and characteristically presents with a prodromal fever along with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and a confluent maculopapular rash that starts at the head/neck and spreads to the trunk, excluding the palms and soles. Physical examination may show bright red macules with a bluish-white center on the buccal mucosa (Koplik spots) and lymphadenopathy. This patient's presentation—fever, rhinorrhea, facial rash spreading to trunk—is classic for measles. Treatment is supportive. Complications include subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, which is uniformly fatal. Measles infection may be prevented with the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, which is a live attenuated vaccine. The CDC recommends vaccination with MMR in a two-dose series beginning at age 1 year. Incorrect Answers: Choice A (Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis): DTaP vaccine prevents diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis infections. None of these infections present with a descending maculopapular rash. Choice B (Haemophilus influenzae type b): Hib is indicated for all children for prevention of infection with H. influenzae. H. influenzae can result in various mucosal infections, such as conjunctivitis, otitis media, bronchitis, and pneumonia. It was the leading cause of epiglottitis in children prior to widespread immunization. It does not cause a descending maculopapular rash. Choice C (Hepatitis B): HBV vaccine prevents viral hepatitis caused by hepatitis B virus and is given at birth and at age 2 months and 6 months. Hepatitis B infection presents acutely with right upper quadrant discomfort, fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and increased serum transaminase concentrations. Choice D (Inactivated poliovirus): IPV prevents infection with polio virus, which causes poliomyelitis. IPV is given at age 2, 4, 6 to 18 months, and age 4 through 6 years. Polio does not cause a maculopapular rash. Choice E (Influenza virus): Influenza causes fever, chills, myalgias, malaise, headaches, nausea, and vomiting. It does not generally present with a rash. Choice G (Pneumococcal): Pneumococcal vaccine is indicated for all adults over age 65 years and in patients with high-risk conditions. It does not prevent measles. Choice H (Typhoid): Typhoid vaccine prevents infection with Salmonella typhi, which causes typhoid fever presenting with fever, abdominal pain, rash, and diarrhea—not the characteristic measles presentation. Choice I (Varicella): Varicella vaccination prevents infection with varicella virus, which causes chickenpox. Chickenpox does not typically present with conjunctivitis or coryza. The rash is vesicular and characteristically begins on the trunk, in contrast to the descending, maculopapular rash associated with measles. Educational Objective: Measles (rubeola) is a highly contagious paramyxovirus that characteristically presents with prodromal fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and a confluent maculopapular rash starting at the head/neck and spreading to the trunk, excluding palms and soles. Measles may be prevented with the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, a live attenuated vaccine given in a two-dose series beginning at age 1 year as recommended by the CDC.
▶ Respiratory System Acute Bronchiolitis 2 questions
Source: 3A #45
A previously healthy 4-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department in January because of cough and poor feeding for 2 days. She is still urinating and making tears. She initially had a fever of 38.2°C (100.8°F) but has been afebrile for the past day. She appears mildly ill. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 140/min, and respirations are 56/min. Examination shows pink tympanic membranes with good mobility. There are mild intercostal retractions, and diffuse bilateral crackles and wheezes are heard. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 84%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Arterial blood gas analysis B) Culture of the pharynx for bacteria C) Viral culture of respiratory secretions D) X-rays of the chest E) X-rays of the neck F) Administration of an inhaled bronchodilator G) Administration of oxygen H) Subcutaneous administration of epinephrine
Correct Answer: G) Administration of oxygen
Bronchiolitis is a common cause of lower respiratory tract infection in children under the age of 2 years, typically caused by viral infection, most commonly respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). It presents with a viral prodrome of fever, nasal congestion, and rhinorrhea followed by cough, dyspnea, and lethargy as inflammation progresses to the lower airway. Auscultation may disclose wheezes and crackles. Severe disease is marked by increased respiratory effort (tachypnea, accessory muscle use, intercostal retractions, nasal flaring, grunting), hypoxemia, and apnea. This patient demonstrates signs of severe disease with intercostal retractions, tachypnea (56/min), and significant hypoxemia (SpO2 84% on room air). The initial management of hypoxemia requires immediate administration of supplemental oxygen, regardless of cause. Patients with severe disease should be hospitalized and immediately started on respiratory support with oxygen, nasal suctioning, and advanced airway and ventilatory support if respiratory failure is imminent. Arterial blood gas analysis (Choice A) may confirm hypoxemia but should not delay oxygen administration given the patient's decreased peripheral oxygen saturation. Culture of the pharynx for bacteria (Choice B) is indicated for pharyngitis workup, not lower respiratory tract infection. Viral culture of respiratory secretions (Choice C) may aid in identifying RSV, influenza, parainfluenza, or adenovirus and can inform decisions about isolation and prophylaxis, but oxygen should be administered first. X-rays of the chest (Choice D) and neck (Choice E) may exclude alternative diagnoses such as epiglottitis, bacterial pneumonia, pneumothorax, foreign body aspiration, or heart failure, but securing the airway and treating hypoxemia takes priority. Administration of an inhaled bronchodilator (Choice F) may be considered if there is diagnostic ambiguity regarding reactive airways disease but does not particularly help treat bronchiolitis and should not precede oxygen administration in a hypoxemic patient. Subcutaneous epinephrine (Choice H) is not a currently accepted therapy for bronchiolitis; it may be appropriate for anaphylaxis or reactive airway disease but oxygen administration must come first.
Source: 7A #10
A 3-month-old female infant born at 34 weeks gestation is admitted to the hospital in January because of a 3-day history of copious rhinorrhea, fever, poor feeding, and periods of tachypnea. Her 3-year-old brother was diagnosed with an upper respiratory tract infection 5 days ago. Her temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), respirations are 66/min, and blood oximetry on room air is normal. Physical examination shows intercostal retractions. Wheezes are heard bilaterally. A chest x-ray shows hyperinflation and peribronchial thickening. Which of the following is the most likely pathogen? A) Bordetella pertussis B) Chlamydia trachomatis C) Influenza virus D) Listeria monocytogenes E) Mycoplasma pneumoniae F) Respiratory syncytial virus G) Staphylococcus aureus H) Streptococcus pneumoniae
Correct Answer: F) Respiratory syncytial virus
Bronchiolitis is a common cause of lower respiratory tract infection in children under age 2 years. It is typically caused by a viral infection, most commonly from respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The clinical presentation fits this diagnosis perfectly: viral prodrome with fever, nasal congestion, and rhinorrhea progressing to cough, dyspnea, and lethargy as inflammation extends to the lower airway. Auscultation findings of wheezes and the chest x-ray findings of hyperinflation and peribronchial thickening are classic for bronchiolitis. Severe disease is marked by increased respiratory effort (tachypnea, accessory muscle use, intercostal retractions), which this patient demonstrates with a respiratory rate of 66/min and intercostal retractions. Patients with severe disease require hospitalization and respiratory support including oxygen therapy, suctioning, and consideration of advanced airway management if respiratory failure is imminent. Choice A (Bordetella pertussis) causes pertussis with severe paroxysmal coughing accompanied by cyanosis, syncope, emesis, or apnea. It is preventable by immunization and treatable with antibiotics (typically macrolides). The clinical presentation does not match pertussis. Choice B (Chlamydia trachomatis) is a common cause of neonatal conjunctivitis, presenting within 5-14 days of birth with watery discharge and sexually transmitted infections. This patient's presentation is inconsistent with chlamydial infection. Choice C (Influenza virus) is a common cause of viral pneumonia during winter months, but bronchiolitis is more commonly caused by respiratory syncytial virus, and the clinical and radiographic findings are more consistent with bronchiolitis. Choice D (Listeria monocytogenes) is a common cause of neonatal meningitis or pneumonia. Meningitis typically presents with lethargy, poor feeding, bulging fontanelle, altered mental status, and seizures. Pneumonia from Listeria generally occurs before 1-2 months of age. While this patient is 3 months old, the clinical presentation is more consistent with viral bronchiolitis. Choice E (Mycoplasma pneumoniae) can cause pneumonia in children with fever, cough, and crackles on lung auscultation. However, bronchiolitis is triggered by viral pathogens more frequently, and mycoplasma typically affects older children. Choice G (Staphylococcus aureus) is more commonly associated with skin and soft tissue infections, septic arthritis, and enteritis. While it can cause pneumonia, it does so more frequently in post-viral superinfections, the immunocompromised, or in patients with cystic fibrosis. It would be unlikely in an otherwise healthy child presenting with this clinical picture. Choice H (Streptococcus pneumoniae) is a common bacterial cause of pneumonia, but patients typically present with focal lung findings indicating lobar pneumonia and lobar consolidation on chest x-ray. Diffuse wheezing on examination and peribronchial thickening on chest x-ray are more consistent with bronchiolitis. Educational Objective: Respiratory syncytial virus is one of the most common causes of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in children younger than two years of age.
▶ Gastrointestinal System Malrotation without volvulus 2 questions
Source: 3A #49
A 7-day-old boy is brought to the emergency department 8 hours after the onset of vomiting bilious material. He has passed one bloody stool during this period. He has refused to feed for 12 hours. He was born at 38 weeks' gestation following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. He was initially well except for occasional wet burps after breast-feeding. He appears lethargic. He weighs 3260 g (7 lb 3 oz). His temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 170/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 65/35 mm Hg. Examination shows mottled skin and a supple neck. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Abdominal examination shows mild distention and diffuse tenderness with guarding. Bowel sounds are decreased. On digital rectal examination, there is gross blood. A lateral x-ray of the upper gastrointestinal tract with barium contrast is shown. Which of the following events in utero is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Abnormal exocrine secretions from the pancreas and intestinal glands B) Failure of cannulization of the proximal bowel C) Failure of caudal migration of ganglion cells D) Failure of normal bowel rotation E) Vascular occlusion in a segment of bowel
Correct Answer: D) Failure of normal bowel rotation
Midgut volvulus, a dangerous complication of intestinal malrotation, often occurs in children within the first few months of life. Malrotation results from the incomplete rotation of the midgut during embryonal development and leaves the midgut attached to a thin stalk of mesentery at the base of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) instead of the normally broad-based mesenteric stalk. The cecum also remains in an abnormal position within the mid-upper abdomen instead of the right lower quadrant and is attached to the lateral abdominal wall by fibrous bands which cross over the top of the duodenum and can also cause constriction. This leaves the small intestine at risk for volvulus at the base of the SMA. Volvulus can lead to bilious vomiting, abdominal distention, and vascular compromise of the small bowel with consequent intestinal necrosis, hematochezia, perforation, and peritonitis. The SMA is susceptible to constriction in midgut volvulus because of its anatomical proximity and embryonal relationship to the formation of the midgut. Evaluation of malrotation and midgut volvulus requires an upper gastrointestinal barium study, which will outline the patient's small bowel anatomy and further assess for the presence of an obstructive volvulus. The upper gastrointestinal barium study in this patient demonstrates a spiral appearance of the duodenum with an abnormal position of the duodenojejunal junction on the lateral view, which indicates the presence of malrotation with a midgut volvulus. Treatment requires emergent surgical correction. Choice A (Abnormal exocrine secretions from the pancreas and intestinal glands) can occur in cystic fibrosis, which is caused by a failure of proper chloride channel function. This leads to inspissated stool and meconium ileus, which can present with abdominal distention but more commonly presents with absence of a bowel movement within the first 48 hours of life. It would not be expected to cause peritonitis, as in this patient. Choice B (Failure of cannulization of the proximal bowel) results in duodenal atresia. It typically presents with signs of intestinal obstruction in the newborn, such as recurrent emesis and poor feeding. It is associated with Down syndrome, polyhydramnios in utero, and two adjacent contrast-filled structures on imaging. This patient was previously able to tolerate oral feeding, making this diagnosis less likely. Choice C (Failure of caudal migration of ganglion cells) causes Hirschsprung disease, which classically presents with the failure to pass stool in the first 48 hours of life. Digital rectal examination commonly demonstrates an explosive release of stool, rather than gross blood, as in this patient. Choice E (Vascular occlusion in a segment of bowel) can result in jejunal or ileal atresia. This most commonly occurs in the setting of maternal smoking or use of cocaine. The newborn typically presents with poor feeding and emesis, and on imaging exhibits multiple air-fluid levels in the small bowel proximal to the site of atresia causing obstruction. Educational Objective: Malrotation occurs secondary to the incomplete rotation of bowel during embryonic development. This places the newborn at risk for midgut volvulus, which can present with bilious vomiting, abdominal distention, and pain, and when severe, intestinal necrosis, hematochezia, perforation, and peritonitis.
Source: 5A #31
A 5-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of daily episodes of vomiting after feedings. Her mother reports that the episodes began shortly after birth and that the vomiting is occasionally bilious. Her diet consists of soy-based formula; trials of multiple infant formulas have not stopped the vomiting. Abdominal examination shows no distention or tenderness. There are no masses. Normal bowel sounds are heard. An upper gastrointestinal series is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Cyclic vomiting syndrome B) Gastroesophageal reflux disease C) Hiatal hernia D) Intestinal malrotation E) Pyloric stenosis
Correct Answer: D) Intestinal malrotation
Intestinal malrotation is a congenital anomaly in which the midgut incompletely rotates during development. This leaves the midgut attached to a thin stalk of mesentery at the base of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), instead of the normally broad-based mesenteric stalk. The cecum also remains in an abnormal position within the mid-upper abdomen instead of the right lower quadrant and is attached to the lateral abdominal wall by fibrous bands, which cross over the top of the duodenum and can cause constriction. This leaves the small intestine at risk for volvulus originating at the base of the SMA. While most patients present in the first year of life, some individuals do not present until later childhood or adulthood. In this case, the patient's upper gastrointestinal barium series demonstrates the presence of the small intestine only within the right abdomen. In its usual anatomic position, the duodenum crosses the midline toward the ligament of Treitz and the remaining small intestine courses throughout the abdominal quadrants. These imaging findings suggest malrotation of the small intestine. Malrotation of the intestines predisposes to intestinal obstruction. The persistent vomiting of bilious emesis suggests a partial small bowel obstruction secondary to the patient's malrotation. Choice A (Cyclic vomiting syndrome) is an idiopathic disorder seen in both children and adults characterized by recurrent episodes of vomiting with periods of normal health between episodes. The bilious nature of the vomit suggests a structural cause instead. Choice B (Gastroesophageal reflux disease) is caused by acid reflux into the lower esophagus. This commonly occurs as a result of increased intra-abdominal pressure or diminished closing pressure of the lower esophageal sphincter. In an infant, GERD presents with frequent regurgitation without excessive irritability. Bilious vomiting is a warning sign of a structural cause of vomiting rather than GERD. Choice C (Hiatal hernia) is caused by a defect in the diaphragm at the esophageal hiatus that allows the lower esophageal sphincter and variable amounts of the stomach to be displaced into the thorax. It can cause heartburn, nausea, emesis, dysphagia, regurgitation, and shortness of breath. It does not cause bilious emesis or the radiographic findings seen in this case. Choice E (Pyloric stenosis) is caused by hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter, leading to gastric outlet obstruction and vomiting. It commonly presents with nonbloody, nonbilious emesis after feedings and begins around three to six weeks of age. It is more common in male infants. Symptoms may begin with occasional vomiting, then progress to projectile emesis after every feeding, dehydration, and malnutrition as the stenosis worsens. Educational Objective: Intestinal malrotation is a congenital anomaly in which the midgut incompletely rotates during development, leaving the midgut attached to a thin stalk of mesentery at the base of the SMA, instead of the normally broad-based mesenteric stalk. It can be recognized on imaging by the presence of small intestine in the right abdomen only. Malrotation increases the risk for volvulus of the small bowel at the base of the SMA (midgut volvulus), which causes small bowel obstruction.
▶ Musculoskeletal System Slipped capital femoral epiphysis 2 questions
Source: 9A #2
A 13-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of a 2-day history of a left-sided limp that has worsened during the past day. He reports severe pain in his left knee on weight bearing. Two months ago, he had influenza and diffuse pain in his calves, which resolved after a 2-day course of ibuprofen. His current pain has not resolved with ibuprofen therapy. He has no other history of serious illness and no history of recent falls or trauma. He takes no other medications. The patient is at the 75th percentile for height and has increased weight and BMI. Vital signs: Temperature is 36.6°C (97.9°F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 120/50 mm Hg. Examination shows mild gynecomastia. The patient lies with the left lower extremity externally rotated and the knee flexed; there is no erythema, edema, or tenderness to palpation. Passive inward rotation of the left knee elicits severe pain. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, Hematocrit 44%, Leukocyte count 9500/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 60%, Platelet count 330,000/mm³, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 16 mm/h. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's condition? A) Abnormal collagen formation B) Autoactivation of the immune system C) Gram-positive bacterial infection D) [Option not fully visible] E) Mechanical disruption of the femoral epiphysis relative to the femoral neck
Correct Answer: E) Mechanical disruption of the femoral epiphysis relative to the femoral neck
This patient presents with the classic presentation of slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE). At age 13 with an increased BMI (95th percentile), he is at risk for SCFE, which most commonly occurs between ages 10-15 in overweight children. The key clinical findings are left-sided limp, severe pain with internal rotation of the knee, and external rotation with knee flexion positioning of the affected limb. Pain radiating to the knee is characteristic of SCFE and can initially confound the diagnosis as a primary knee problem. SCFE results in displacement of the femoral epiphysis relative to the femoral neck secondary to anterosuperior movement of the metaphysis due to a fracture of the growth plate. This mechanical disruption is the fundamental pathophysiology of the condition. The diagnosis is confirmed with hip x-rays including frontal and frog-leg views. Treatment requires making the patient non-weight bearing followed by operative stabilization. Choice A (Abnormal collagen formation) is incorrect because osteogenesis imperfecta, caused by mutations in collagen genes like COL1A1 and COL1A2, results in decreased collagen synthesis and impaired bone matrix leading to multiple fractures throughout life, not the presentation described here. Choice B (Autoactivation of the immune system) is incorrect because juvenile idiopathic arthritis, while occurring in children under 16, presents with joint pain and inflammation with extra-articular manifestations such as uveitis, lymphadenopathy, and rash, and would show evidence of systemic inflammation. Choice C (Gram-positive bacterial infection) is incorrect because septic arthritis from bacterial infection (commonly Staphylococcus aureus) presents with fever, leukocytosis, and the affected joint shows pain, swelling, and erythema—none of which are present in this patient. This patient's normal CBC, normal ESR, absence of systemic signs of infection, and absence of joint swelling or erythema exclude infectious etiologies. The mechanical disruption of the femoral epiphysis is the correct mechanism underlying SCFE.
Source: 7A #20
A previously healthy 13-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 4-week history of intermittent left groin pain associated with a limp. He has not had fever. He is not in acute distress. He is at the 50th percentile for height, 97th percentile for weight, and above the 97th percentile for BMI. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 116/75 mm Hg. On examination, internal rotation and abduction of the left hip are limited. Internal and external rotation to 75 degrees produces pain. The left hip externally rotates on passive flexion. Examination of the right hip and both knees shows no abnormalities. AP and cross-table lateral x-rays of the left hip show irregular widening of the epiphyseal plate of the left femur and mild osteopenia of the left femoral neck and head. In addition to analgesic therapy and discussion about weight loss, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Physical therapy B) Abduction bracing C) Traction D) Spica cast immobilization E) Internal fixation
Correct Answer: E) Internal fixation
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) most commonly occurs in overweight children between the ages of 10 to 15. It results in displacement of the femoral epiphysis relative to the femoral neck secondary to anterosuperior movement of the metaphysis because of a Salter-Harris type 1 fracture of the growth plate. SCFE typically presents with a painful limp, and if severe, may result in restricted range of motion of the hip joint (eg, limited abduction and internal rotation of the hip) and inability to bear weight on the affected lower extremity. Diagnosis requires evaluation of both hips in frontal and frog-leg views for comparison. If untreated, complications include avascular necrosis of the femoral head, limited range of motion and gait impairment, and premature osteoarthritis. To prevent these complications, treatment requires surgical fixation of the femoral epiphysis. Physical therapy (Choice A) would be appropriate in the setting of muscle or ligament strain or sprain. This patient does not present following an injury, and sprains of hip joint ligaments are less common. Abduction bracing (Choice B) and spica cast immobilization (Choice D) are used in the management of developmental dysplasia of the hip, which can present with limited hip range of motion, palpable hip instability, unequal leg lengths, and asymmetric thigh skinfolds. Traction (Choice C) is used to pull to length any shortening caused by traumatic fractures of extremity bones. This patient has not sustained any trauma or fractures. Educational Objective: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis results in displacement of the femoral epiphysis relative to the femoral neck, and management involves surgical fixation of the femoral epiphysis.
▶ Nervous System Special Senses Bacterial Meningitis 2 questions
Source: 9A #4
A 4-year-old girl with congenital hydrocephalus and myelomeningocele is brought to the physician because of a 4-day history of progressively worsening headache and a 1-day history of vomiting. She is irritable. Her temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 110/min, and respirations are 20/min. Examination shows mild nuchal rigidity. Cerebrospinal fluid aspirated from the shunt is cloudy. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows: Leukocyte count 250/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 90%, Lymphocytes 10%, Glucose 35 mg/dL, Protein 100 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings? A. Enteroviral infection B. Herpes encephalitis C. Latex reaction D. Meningococcal meningitis E. Shunt infection
Correct Answer: E. Shunt infection
Shunt infections are a critical complication that may occur insidiously weeks to months after shunt placement or manipulation, typically from intraoperative contamination with organisms such as coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus aureus, or Cutibacterium acnes. This patient presents with classic signs of shunt infection progressing to meningitis: headache, vomiting, irritability, fever (38°C), nuchal rigidity, and a cloudy CSF sample indicating biofilm formation. The CSF analysis demonstrates neutrophilic pleocytosis (90% segmented neutrophils), decreased glucose (35 mg/dL), and elevated protein (100 mg/dL)—findings consistent with bacterial meningitis secondary to shunt infection. Diagnosis is confirmed by CSF analysis and culture obtained from the shunt or ventricle. Management requires removal of the infected hardware and initiation of appropriate antibiotic therapy. Recent shunt manipulation is a major risk factor for infection. Choice A (Enteroviral infection) is incorrect because enteroviral meningitis typically presents with lymphocytic pleocytosis (not neutrophilic), mildly increased protein, and normal glucose levels. Choice B (Herpes encephalitis) is incorrect because while herpes encephalitis can present with fever and altered mental status, it typically includes focal neurologic deficits such as seizures, aphasia, hemiparesis, or cranial nerve abnormalities, which this patient does not demonstrate. The history of shunt revision is a much stronger risk factor for shunt infection than for herpes encephalitis. Choice C (Latex reaction) is incorrect because latex reactions present with systemic symptoms ranging from mild urticaria to anaphylaxis. Central nervous system manifestations such as meningitis would be atypical and do not explain the CSF findings. Choice D (Meningococcal meningitis) is incorrect because while bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status, meningococcal disease typically follows a prodrome of upper respiratory tract infection symptoms. Risk factors include adolescence and communal living environments. This patient lacks these risk factors and prodromal symptoms. Most importantly, recent shunt manipulation makes shunt infection the most likely diagnosis. Educational Objective: Recognize that shunt infections may develop weeks to months after shunt placement or manipulation and can progress to meningitis. Understand that CSF analysis may show neutrophilic pleocytosis, decreased glucose, and increased protein concentrations. Recognize the importance of considering shunt infection in any patient with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt presenting with headache, fever, and meningeal signs, particularly following shunt manipulation.
Source: 4A #20
A 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of fever and increasingly severe headache and malaise. He has a history of recurrent pneumonia; the last episode was 2 years ago. His family recently immigrated to the USA from Mexico. On arrival, he is somnolent but arousable. His temperature is 39.3°C (102.8°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 34/min, and blood pressure is 146/94 mm Hg. Examination shows nuchal rigidity. Crackles are heard over the left lower lung field. On mental status examination, he is oriented to person but not to place or time. A lumbar puncture is performed. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows: Opening pressure 340 mm Hg, Glucose 28 mg/dL, Total protein 154 mg/dL, Leukocyte count 8648/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 85%, Lymphocytes 15%, Erythrocyte count 95/mm³. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Cryptococcal meningitis B) Enterovirus meningitis C) Herpes simplex encephalitis D) Neurocysticercosis E) Pneumococcal meningitis F) Tuberculous meningitis
Correct Answer: E) Pneumococcal meningitis
Bacterial meningitis presents acutely with fever, headache, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status, typically following a prodrome of upper respiratory tract infection symptoms, although it can also be concomitant with another infection. Physical examination commonly shows positive Kernig or Brudzinski signs indicative of meningeal irritation and can disclose focal neurologic symptoms or signs of increased intracranial pressure such as hemiparesis or sixth cranial nerve palsy. Laboratory studies show leukocytosis, and coagulation studies can demonstrate signs of disseminated intravascular coagulopathy with thrombocytopenia, decreased fibrinogen, and increased D-dimer. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) evaluation is the initial diagnostic step and will show an increased opening pressure, increased white blood cell count with prominent neutrophils (85% in this case), increased protein concentration, and decreased glucose concentration in bacterial meningitis. Culture of the CSF is utilized to diagnose the specific bacterial cause. The most common cause of bacterial meningitis in children and young adults is Streptococcus pneumoniae, although its incidence has decreased with the pneumococcal vaccine. Risk factors include an immunocompromised state, diabetes mellitus, and chronic heart or lung disease. Treatment involves immediate antibiotic therapy accompanied by glucocorticoids. This patient's presentation with acute fever, headache, nuchal rigidity, altered mental status, and CSF findings of elevated opening pressure (340 mm Hg), elevated protein (154 mg/dL), low glucose (28 mg/dL), and predominance of neutrophils (85%) is classic for pneumococcal meningitis. Choice A (Cryptococcal meningitis) is a fungal meningitis occurring most commonly in immunocompromised patients such as those with lymphoma, leukemia, HIV/AIDS, or solid organ transplantation. However, fungal meningitis shows prominent lymphocytes on CSF evaluation rather than a predominance of neutrophils as in this patient. Choice B (Enterovirus meningitis) more commonly occurs in patients less than one year of age but can present in children and young adults. Viral meningitis is associated with a normal opening pressure, predominance of lymphocytes, and normal protein and glucose concentrations on CSF evaluation, which does not match this patient's CSF profile. Choice C (Herpes simplex encephalitis) presents in patients of all ages with fever, headache, seizures, focal neurologic signs, and confusion. Herpes simplex is commonly associated with a significant amount of red blood cells on CSF evaluation as well as neuroimaging showing inflammation in the temporal lobe, not the neutrophil-predominant picture seen here. Choice D (Neurocysticercosis) is an infection caused by the parasitic pork tapeworm Taenia solium occurring most commonly in endemic rural regions of Latin America, Asia, and Africa. While it can present with findings similar to bacterial meningitis and subcutaneous or muscle nodules, CT scan would show cystic, ring-enhancing, calcified lesions in brain parenchyma, meninges, ventricles, spinal cord, and/or orbit. The CSF findings would not typically show this neutrophil predominance. Choice F (Tuberculous meningitis) typically presents in a more subacute fashion than bacterial meningitis and is more frequently associated with cranial nerve palsies. In children, seizures are common. CSF evaluation shows a predominance of lymphocytes, unlike in this patient. Educational Objective: Bacterial meningitis presents acutely with fever, headache, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status. Cerebrospinal fluid evaluation is the initial diagnostic step and will show an increased opening pressure, increased leukocyte count with prominent neutrophils, increased protein concentration, and decreased glucose concentration. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in children and young adults.
▶ Endocrine System Congenital adrenal hyperplasia 2 questions
Source: 9A #21
A 7-day-old male newborn is brought to the emergency department by his mother because of a 1-day history of vomiting and poor feeding. She says that he seems weak today. He has not had fever or diarrhea. He was born at term to a 30-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 1, following an uncomplicated pregnancy and spontaneous vaginal delivery. He is exclusively breast-fed. He weighed 3000 g (6 lb 10 oz) at birth. Today, he weighs 2850 g (6 lb 5 oz). He is at the 25th percentile for length and head circumference. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 160/min, respirations are 40/min, and blood pressure is 60/30 mm Hg. Examination of the skin shows no rash or jaundice. The anterior fontanel is soft and flat. The genitalia appear normal. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Serum studies show: sodium 110 mEq/L (N=136-145), potassium 6.5 mEq/L (N=3.5-5), glucose 45 mg/dL (N=50-90), and bicarbonate 16 mEq/L (N=22-26). Administration of intravenous fluids is begun. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy? A. Intravenous acyclovir B. Intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin C. Intravenous carnitine D. Intravenous hydrocortisone and oral fludrocortisone E. Oral thyroid hormone
Correct Answer: D. Intravenous hydrocortisone and oral fludrocortisone
This newborn patient presents with vomiting, weakness, and poor feeding with laboratory findings of hyponatremia (sodium 110 mEq/L), hyperkalemia (potassium 6.5 mEq/L), metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate 16 mEq/L), and hypoglycemia (glucose 45 mg/dL), which are classic for congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH). The most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy is intravenous hydrocortisone and oral fludrocortisone. CAH results from a defect in adrenal steroid biosynthesis, particularly of cortisol, with variable effects on mineralocorticoids and androgens. The most common form is due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency, which accounts for approximately 90% of cases and results in increased 17-hydroxyprogesterone, androstenedione, and testosterone as well as decreased aldosterone and cortisol, leading to hypotension, hyperkalemia, and hyponatremia. The salt-wasting form presents in infants with vomiting, poor feeding, weakness, metabolic acidosis, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. Treatment consists of exogenous glucocorticoid (hydrocortisone) and mineralocorticoid (fludrocortisone) supplementation. In addition, fluid resuscitation is indicated given the dehydration present. Choice A (Intravenous acyclovir) is incorrect. Acyclovir is used for neonatal herpes simplex infection, which typically presents with fever, vesicular rash, and systemic manifestations. This patient has findings consistent with CAH, not herpes simplex. Choice B (Intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin) is incorrect. Ampicillin and gentamicin are first-line empiric antibiotics for neonatal sepsis. Patients with neonatal sepsis typically present with fever or hypothermia, altered mental status, lethargy, irritability, jaundice, hypotension, and shock. The electrolyte abnormalities and clinical presentation are consistent with CAH rather than sepsis. Choice C (Intravenous carnitine) is not the most appropriate next step. Carnitine deficiency may present with variable symptoms including hepatic encephalopathy, poor feeding, lethargy, lactic acidosis, hypotonia, weakness, and rhabdomyolysis. While this patient has some overlapping symptoms like poor feeding and weakness, the specific pattern of electrolyte abnormalities (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis) and hypoglycemia are pathognomonic for CAH, not primary carnitine deficiency. Choice E (Oral thyroid hormone) is incorrect. Congenital hypothyroidism presents in the first few months of life with feeding difficulties, lethargy, constipation, myxedematous facies, macroglossia, large fontanelles, hypotonia, and hypothermia. The metabolic derangements (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis) seen in this patient are not characteristic of hypothyroidism and instead point to CAH.
Source: 5A #3
A 10-day-old male newborn is brought to the emergency department because of poor feeding and drowsiness for the past day. He also has had two episodes of vomiting today. He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery and weighed 3600 g (7 lb 15 oz). On arrival, he is lethargic. His skin color is a shade darker than his parents' skin color. His temperature is 36.1°C (97°F), pulse is 180/min, respirations are 70/min, and blood pressure is 58/30 mm Hg. The anterior fontanel is sunken, and the scalp has sparse fine blond hairs. The nipples and scrotum are darkly pigmented. The pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light and accommodation. There is no scleral icterus. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination shows a regular rhythm and no murmurs. S1 and S2 are normal. The abdomen is soft with no masses or organomegaly. Genital development is Tanner stage 1; the penis is 4 cm long. Testes are descended. Serum studies are most likely to show which of the following? A) Na+ decreased, K+ decreased, Glucose decreased B) Na+ decreased, K+ increased, Glucose decreased C) Na+ increased, K+ decreased, Glucose increased D) Na+ increased, K+ increased, Glucose increased E) Na+ normal, K+ decreased, Glucose increased F) Na+ normal, K+ increased, Glucose decreased
Correct Answer: B) Na+ decreased, K+ increased, Glucose decreased
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is a defect in adrenal steroid biosynthesis, particularly of cortisol, with variable effects on mineralocorticoids and androgens. The most common form is 21-hydroxylase deficiency, which presents with salt wasting in newborns, characterized by decreased sodium, increased potassium, and decreased glucose. Because of the enzyme deficiency, concentrations of 17-hydroxyprogesterone, androstenedione, and testosterone are increased, while aldosterone and cortisol are decreased. This leads to hypotension (from sodium loss), hyperkalemia (from potassium retention without aldosterone-mediated excretion), and hypoglycemia (caused by inadequate cortisol). Diffuse hyperpigmentation of the skin, as seen in this newborn, is characteristic and results from increased melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH), a byproduct of proopiomelanocortin (POMC) that also produces adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). In adrenal insufficiency, stimulation of ACTH production simultaneously produces MSH, leading to diffuse hyperpigmentation. The mechanism of electrolyte disturbance: aldosterone normally binds to receptors in the collecting tubule and leads to placement of sodium and potassium channels on the luminal cell membrane, allowing potassium to exit into the lumen and sodium to be reabsorbed. Without aldosterone, potassium does not leave the cell and accumulates in the interstitium and blood (hyperkalemia), while sodium remains in the lumen and is lost in urine (hyponatremia/salt wasting). Choices A, C, and E are incorrect because they show decreased or normal potassium, but without aldosterone, potassium accumulates in the blood causing hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia. Choices D and F are incorrect because they show increased or normal sodium; however, without aldosterone, sodium is lost in the urine causing hyponatremia, not normal or increased serum sodium. Treatment of CAH consists of exogenous glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid supplementation. Educational Objective: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia results from a defect in adrenal steroid biosynthesis. Its most common form, 21-hydroxylase deficiency, presents with salt wasting in infants (decreased sodium, increased potassium, decreased glucose), hypotension, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia. It also causes virilization of XX infants and increased concentrations of 17-hydroxyprogesterone. Treatment includes exogenous administration of mineralocorticoids and glucocorticoids.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Sexual Abuse 2 questions
Source: 9A #22
A 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother for a physical examination prior to participating in school sports. She feels well. Her immunizations are up-to-date. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Her mother leaves the examination room to answer a phone call. The patient reports to the nurse that she is afraid that she has HIV because her stepfather has been coming into her bed while her mother is at work. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A. Encourage the patient to talk to her mother about her concerns B. Inform the mother of the patient's report when the stepfather arrives C. Order an HIV antibody test and do not inform the patient's mother D. Reassure the patient that she does not have HIV infection E. Report the suspected abuse to child protective services
Correct Answer: E. Report the suspected abuse to child protective services
According to the federal Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act of 1974, mandated reporters (including physicians) are required to report suspected child abuse or neglect to child protective services. This applies to physical, psychological, sexual, and financial abuse, as well as neglect. Child protective services is a state agency that investigates reports of child abuse or neglect and formulates steps to keep the child safe, which may include mandating treatment, providing in-home services, or removing the child from the home. Choice A is incorrect because encouraging the patient to talk to her mother neglects the physician's responsibility to report suspicions of abuse to state authorities. Conversations regarding abuse are difficult and may be ignored or postponed if the burden is placed solely on the victim. Moreover, if the mother is participating in or allowing the abuse, this may increase the patient's risk for future harm. Choice B is incorrect because while physicians are required by federal law to report abuse to child protective services, they are not required to disclose these concerns to parents. Additionally, physicians are obligated to protect patient confidentiality, even in the case of adolescents. Informing the mother in the presence of the stepfather may place the patient at risk for further harm. Choice C is incorrect because although laboratory studies for sexually transmitted infections (including HIV antibody/antigen testing, Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and others) should be performed, and physicians can elect to withhold information from a minor's parents in select situations dealing with sexual health, substance use, and trauma, the physician is still required by law to report this concern to child protective services. Choice D is incorrect because it is dismissive and fails to address the patient's legitimate concerns. Patients presenting after sexual assault should undergo standard evaluation including urine pregnancy test and comprehensive screening for sexually transmitted infections (HIV antibody/antigen testing, C. trachomatis, N. gonorrhoeae, Trichomonas vaginalis, hepatitis B, and syphilis). Educational Objective: Physicians and other mandated reporters are required by US law to report suspected child abuse to child protective services. This is the most appropriate next step in management for this patient and applies to physical, psychological, sexual, and financial abuse, as well as neglect.
Source: 7A #31
A 7-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of a 2-day history of a burning sensation during urination. She has been treated with nitrofurantoin for infections on two separate occasions; cultures at the time of the infections were negative. Examination shows a frothy vaginal discharge. The vulva is normal, and there is a small uterus. A wet mount preparation of the discharge shows Trichomonas vaginalis. Urinalysis shows no abnormalities except for occasional T. vaginalis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Evaluation for sexual abuse B) Urine culture C) Clotrimazole therapy D) Intravenous pyelography E) Cystoscopy
Correct Answer: A) Evaluation for sexual abuse
Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by Trichomonas vaginalis that causes vaginitis and cervicitis in women and urethritis in men. The infection commonly presents with vaginal pruritus, dyspareunia, cervical erythema, and abnormal discharge that is characteristically green, frothy, and malodorous. Trichomoniasis can also lead to overactive bladder symptoms including frequency, urgency, and urge incontinence. Critically, because T. vaginalis is transmitted exclusively through sexual contact, a young child with trichomoniasis should be promptly evaluated for sexual abuse, making this the most appropriate next step in management. Choice B (Urine culture) is incorrect because the diagnosis of trichomoniasis has already been established by positive T. vaginalis on wet mount preparation. Urine and vaginal cultures are utilized less frequently than nucleic acid amplification testing and take days to result. Choice C (Clotrimazole therapy) is incorrect because topical clotrimazole is used to treat candidal vulvovaginitis, not trichomoniasis. It is not a recommended treatment for T. vaginalis infection. Choice D (Intravenous pyelography) is incorrect because this imaging modality involves intravenous injection of radiopaque contrast to visualize the kidney collecting system, ureters, and bladder under fluoroscopy. It is used to investigate suspected urinary tract anatomic abnormalities, malignancies, and strictures, but is not helpful for diagnosing trichomoniasis when the diagnosis has already been established. Choice E (Cystoscopy) is incorrect because cystoscopy involves inserting a camera into the urethra and bladder and is typically performed in the evaluation of hematuria. It is not helpful for diagnosing trichomoniasis when the diagnosis has already been confirmed. Educational Objective: Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted infection causing vaginitis, cervicitis, and urethritis. Because Trichomonas vaginalis is sexually transmitted, a young child presenting with trichomoniasis should be evaluated for sexual abuse as part of the management plan.
▶ Human Development Motor developmental stages in infancy and childhood 2 questions
Source: 9A #25
A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because she is concerned about his behavior. He sits for approximately 15 minutes during dinner and fidgets once he finishes eating, wanting to leave the table. He can play quietly with blocks for 30 minutes, but he prefers activities that involve running, jumping, and climbing. He has to be asked several times before he will pick up his toys and cloth it he splashes water "all over the room." He does not like going to bed and often asks for glasses of water, sneaks toys into his bed, or gets up without permission. He is toilet trained but occasionally wets his underwear while playing because he forgets to use the bathroom. His preschool teachers report that they often allow him to do his work while standing so he fidgets less. During the examination, he fidgets but is cooperative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder B. Intellectual developmental disorder C. Oppositional defiant disorder D. Separation anxiety disorder E. Normal development
Correct Answer: E) Normal development
This 4-year-old boy presents with behavioral concerns reported only by his mother at home, while preschool teachers report that his social and academic skills are appropriate for his age. The key clinical distinction is that his symptoms occur primarily in one setting (home) and do not impair functioning across multiple contexts. Normal development of a 4-year-old includes the ability to hop on one foot, play cooperatively with peers or imaginary friends, use complete sentences with prepositions, and demonstrate limited attention spans with occasional difficulty following parental directions immediately. It is developmentally appropriate for this age to express desires and preferences, avoid bedtime, fidget, and have incomplete bladder control during play. The physical and mental examination revealed no abnormalities. Choice A (Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder) is incorrect because ADHD requires chronic symptoms of hyperactivity/impulsivity and/or inattention that occur in multiple settings and significantly impair academic, social, and/or emotional functioning. This child's symptoms are isolated to home and do not cause functional impairment at school. Choice B (Intellectual developmental disorder) is incorrect because the patient has demonstrated normal intellectual ability on mental status examination and is performing appropriately in preschool academically and socially. Choice C (Oppositional defiant disorder) is incorrect because ODD manifests as a persistent pattern of angry mood, defiant behavior, and vindictiveness that causes distress and impaired functioning. While the child is sometimes resistant to parental requests, this reflects normal developmental assertiveness rather than ODD. Choice D (Separation anxiety disorder) is incorrect because while some separation anxiety is normal in childhood development (occurring around 9 months in infancy, 18 months in toddlers, and during preschool years), this child's behavior pattern does not present with the typical manifestations of crying, stress, and anxiety when separated from caregivers. Educational Objective: It is important to distinguish between normal child development and true pathology. Most toddlers and preschool-age children have limited attention spans and may not immediately obey parental directions. They may begin to express themselves and their desires in ways parents may find concerning, but these behaviors often reflect normal development rather than psychiatric illness. Clarifying whether concerning behaviors occur across multiple settings (home, school, peer interactions) is essential in making the diagnosis. Parents should be reassured when their child's behavior is developmentally appropriate, and counseling regarding normal developmental expectations can be helpful. For specific concerns like bedtime avoidance, establishing a consistent nightly bedtime routine is an appropriate intervention.
Source: 7A #21
A 9-month-old boy is brought to the office for a well-child examination. His mother says he is a happy baby. He likes to lie on the floor and can roll from his stomach to his back; he has been trying to roll from his back to his stomach over the past 2 weeks. He can sit with support. His appetite is good, and he likes to feed himself crackers and cereal from the high-chair table. He jabbers, imitates sounds, and says "Dada" and "Mama" to everyone and everything. Immunizations are up-to-date. He is at the 75th percentile for length and 50th percentile for weight. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most accurate assessment of this patient's development? | | Fine Motor Development | Gross Motor Development | Language Development | Social Development | |---|---|---|---|---| | A) | Normal | Delayed | Normal | Normal | | B) | Delayed | Delayed | Normal | Normal | | C) | Normal | Delayed | Delayed | Normal | | D) | Delayed | Normal | Normal | Normal | | E) | Normal | Delayed | Normal | Normal | | F) | Normal | Normal | Delayed | Normal | | G) | Normal | Normal | Normal | Delayed | | H) | Normal | Normal | Normal | Normal |
Correct Answer: E) Normal fine motor development, delayed gross motor development, normal language development, normal social development
Developmental milestones refer to the actions that most infants or children can perform at a given age. By 9 months of age, infants are typically able to initiate and maintain a sitting position without support. This patient can only sit with support, indicating delayed gross motor development. Fine Motor Development: The patient demonstrates normal fine motor skills. By 9 months, infants are expected to rake food toward themselves and move objects between hands. This patient is feeding himself crackers and cereal, demonstrating age-appropriate fine motor abilities. Gross Motor Development: This is delayed. The patient can roll from stomach to back and is attempting to roll from back to stomach, but critically, he can only sit with support. At 9 months, independent sitting without support is an expected milestone. Language Development: This is normal. By 9 months, infants can make various sounds including "mama" and "dada," which this patient demonstrates through jabbering, imitating sounds, and saying these words. Social Development: This is normal. The patient is described as happy and engages appropriately. By 9 months, infants typically display affect, show interest in their environment, and respond to social interaction, all of which are evident here. Incorrect Answers: Choices A, B, C, D, F, G, and H incorrectly classify at least one developmental domain. This patient's only developmental delay is in gross motor function. Educational Objective: Infants are typically able to achieve and maintain a sitting position unsupported by age 9 months. Infants who cannot sit without support at this age demonstrate delayed gross motor development. Screening for developmental delays alerts physicians to the potential need for further medical evaluation and/or early referral to developmental specialists. Early intervention has been demonstrated to improve outcomes.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders IgA Vasculitis 2 questions
Source: 9A #29
A pediatric patient presents with gravity-dependent purpura on the buttocks and lower extremities, arthralgias, hematuria, and abdominal pain following a recent upper respiratory tract infection. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) IgA vasculitis B) Juvenile idiopathic arthritis, systemic C) Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease) D) Polyarteritis nodosa E) Rheumatic fever
Correct Answer: A) IgA vasculitis
IgA vasculitis (formerly Henoch-Schönlein purpura) is an acute, systemic, small-vessel vasculitis that typically presents with gravity-dependent purpura (affecting buttocks, legs, and feet), arthralgias, hematuria, and abdominal pain. This condition usually occurs in children following a viral illness or upper respiratory tract infection. The renal, gastrointestinal, cutaneous, and musculoskeletal systems are most commonly affected. Most cases are self-limited, though patients require monitoring for serious sequelae such as intestinal intussusception or kidney disease. Treatment is primarily supportive care. The causative agents linked to IgA vasculitis include Streptococcus species, coxsackievirus group A, B19 virus, influenzavirus, and Salmonella species. Choice B (Juvenile idiopathic arthritis, systemic) is incorrect. While it is the most common rheumatic disease in children and can present with polyarthralgias, fever, uveitis, lymphadenopathy, and an evanescent pink-colored rash, this patient's subacute onset and extra-articular symptoms are more consistent with IgA vasculitis. Choice C (Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome/Kawasaki disease) is incorrect. This multisystemic vasculitic disease presents with acute arteritis and risk for coronary artery aneurysms. Characteristic features include fever for at least 5 days, bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, polymorphous rash, lymphadenopathy, erythema and edema of hands and feet, and mucosal involvement with dry cracked lips. This patient's lower extremity purpuric rash and abdominal pain are more consistent with IgA vasculitis. Choice D (Polyarteritis nodosa) is incorrect. This systemic medium-vessel necrotizing vasculitis is associated with hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and hematologic malignancies, though many cases are idiopathic. It typically presents with insidious-onset subcutaneous nodules, polyneuropathy, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, abdominal pain, and arthralgias, and most commonly occurs in adults rather than children. Choice E (Rheumatic fever) is incorrect. Acute rheumatic fever presents with migratory polyarthralgia, pancarditis (pericarditis, myocarditis, and/or endocarditis), subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea, fever, increased ESR, and short PR interval following group A streptococcal infection, typically pharyngitis. This clinical picture does not match the presentation of gravity-dependent purpura and hematuria seen in this patient.
Source: 4A #9
A 13-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. He has no history of serious illness. During the past 2 years, he has noticed brown urine whenever he has a cold. He has not had dysuria or urinary urgency or incontinence. Examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Serum: Urea nitrogen 15 mg/dL, Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, C3 90 mg/dL (N=83-177) Urine: Blood 4+, Protein 3+ Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Hemolytic uremic syndrome B) Hemorrhagic cystitis C) IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) D) Nephrotic syndrome E) Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis
Correct Answer: C) IgA nephropathy (Berger disease)
IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) is a type of nephritic syndrome resulting in episodic gross hematuria, often following an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal tract infection. This patient's presentation of brown urine (gross hematuria) following colds over 2 years is classic for IgA nephropathy. Nephritic syndromes typically present with acute kidney injury with associated hematuria, red blood cell casts, and hypertension. On urinalysis, there is a significant quantity of red blood cells (RBCs), possible RBC casts, and sub-nephrotic range proteinuria (as seen with 3+ protein rather than >3 g/day). The key distinguishing feature is that serum complement concentrations, including C3, are typically within reference ranges (90 mg/dL is normal). This differentiates IgA nephropathy from postinfectious glomerulonephritis. Additionally, anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase titers will be negative in IgA nephropathy. Incorrect Answers: Choice A (Hemolytic uremic syndrome) is caused by Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (O157:H7) and is usually accompanied by bloody diarrhea. This is characterized by a classic triad of thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. This patient lacks diarrhea and hemolytic anemia. Choice B (Hemorrhagic cystitis) refers to inflammation of the urinary bladder, which commonly is secondary to acute bacterial urinary tract infection presenting with dysuria, urinary urgency, and frequency. A typical infectious cystitis presents with increased urinary white blood cells with detectable leukocyte esterase and nitrites on urinalysis. This patient explicitly denies dysuria and urinary urgency, making this unlikely. Choice D (Nephrotic syndrome) typically presents with excessive proteinuria (>3 g/day), hyperlipidemia, hypoalbuminemia, and peripheral edema. Notably, nephrotic syndrome does not cause hematuria. The most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children is minimal change disease. This patient has hematuria, ruling out nephrotic syndrome. Choice E (Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis) is a nephritic syndrome presenting with urinary RBCs and RBC casts, typically occurring 2 to 6 weeks after infection with group A β-hemolytic streptococci. The key differential finding is that laboratory studies will show decreased serum C3 concentrations, and anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase titers are positive. This patient has normal C3 (90 mg/dL), which rules out poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Educational Objective: IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) is a type of nephritic syndrome resulting in episodic gross hematuria, often following an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal tract infection. Serum complement concentrations, including C3, are typically within reference ranges, distinguishing it from postinfectious glomerulonephritis.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Septic Shock 2 questions
Source: 9A #39
A previously healthy 3-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after her parents noticed a generalized rash. She has a 1-day history of fever. She was born at 39 weeks' gestation following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. Immunizations are up-to-date. On examination, she is lethargic. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse is 200/min, respirations are 42/min, and blood pressure is 70/50 mm Hg. Examination shows a generalized petechial, purpuric rash. Capillary refill time is prolonged. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A. Adenosine B. Atropine C. Dexamethasone D. Epinephrine E. Intravenous isotonic crystalloid fluid resuscitation
Correct Answer: E. Intravenous isotonic crystalloid fluid resuscitation
