Acute osteomyelitis is more common in children and is most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Risk factors include traumatic inoculating injury, diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, intravenous substance use, and prosthetic devices or indwelling hardware. Patients typically present with pain, difficulty bearing weight, and overlying erythema. Laboratory studies show leukocytosis and increased inflammatory markers. Bone scintigraphy with technetium 99m shows increased uptake in the area of infection. This patient demonstrates the classic presentation: fever (39.4°C), localized pain and swelling over the proximal medial tibia, inability to bear weight, leukocytosis (14,000/mm³), elevated ESR (60 mm/h), and characteristic technetium 99m uptake at the metaphysis. Osgood-Schlatter disease (Choice B) is traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle in adolescent athletes presenting with progressive pain along the anterior proximal tibia exacerbated by kneeling. It does not cause fever, inability to bear weight, or systemic signs. Fracture of the tibia (Choice C) presents with acute pain, inability to bear weight, and localized edema and tenderness but would not explain fever, leukocytosis, elevated inflammatory markers, or positive bone scintigraphy. X-ray or CT would be the initial imaging modality. Prepatellar bursitis (Choice D) is inflammation of the bursa overlying the patella from infection, trauma, or recurrent pressure. A bone scan would show no abnormalities, and systemic signs would be absent. Septic arthritis (Choice E) results from bacterial infection of the synovial joint space, usually by S. aureus. It presents with a tender, erythematous, and edematous joint with purulent synovial fluid containing >50,000 WBC/mm³. This patient's physical examination does not disclose a tender, erythematous, edematous joint, and the bone scan shows metaphyseal uptake rather than joint involvement. Educational Objective: Osteomyelitis is an infection of bone or bone marrow caused by direct local spread or hematogenous seeding. Patients present with fever, localized pain and inflammation, and increased inflammatory markers. Imaging shows inflammatory and destructive bony changes with characteristic technetium 99m uptake on bone scintigraphy.
Source: 8A #11
A 14-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination 3 weeks after a nail punctured his right foot through his shoe. The wound was thoroughly cleaned and bandaged, but he continues to have moderate pain at the site. The patient received the tetanus vaccine at age 5 years and is otherwise healthy. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination of the wound site shows erythema and warmth of the overlying skin with tenderness to palpation. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism? A) Aeromonas hydrophila B) Group A streptococcus C) Klebsiella pneumoniae D) Pseudomonas aeruginosa E) Staphylococcus aureus
Correct Answer: D) Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Osteomyelitis may occur from hematogenous spreading from adjacent skin and soft tissue infection, or direct inoculation in the case of trauma. Osteomyelitis clinically presents with pain at the site, erythema, tenderness to palpation, swelling, decreased range of motion, and fever. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an aerobic, oxidase-positive, gram-negative bacteria that is associated with hospital-acquired infections as well as osteomyelitis following a puncture wound (classically through an athletic shoe). Patients who suffer puncture wounds and diabetic patients are at the highest risk for Pseudomonas-associated osteomyelitis. This patient's presentation of persistent pain, erythema, and tenderness 3 weeks after a puncture wound through his shoe is classic for Pseudomonas osteomyelitis. Choice A: Aeromonas hydrophila is a gram-negative anaerobic bacteria present in water. These organisms may cause diarrhea, opportunistic infections in immunocompromised individuals, and wound infections in patients in contact with contaminated fresh water or soil at the time of injury, but it is not the typical organism associated with puncture wounds through footwear. Choice B: Group A streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) is a gram-positive bacterium that may cause pharyngitis, skin infections such as impetigo, erysipelas, or cellulitis, and life-threatening infections including necrotizing fasciitis or toxic shock syndrome. It is not characteristically associated with osteomyelitis from puncture wounds. Choice C: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a gram-negative bacillus that may cause pneumonia in patients at risk for aspiration pneumonia, such as those with alcohol use disorder. It is a less likely cause of cellulitis or osteomyelitis than Pseudomonas in this case. Choice E: Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of osteomyelitis overall and may be related to direct inoculation or hematogenous spread. However, Pseudomonas aeruginosa is more common specifically in the setting of puncture wounds. Educational Objective: Osteomyelitis may occur from hematogenous spread, spread of existing skin or soft tissue infection, or trauma. The most common organism associated with puncture wounds is Pseudomonas aeruginosa. X-ray or MRI are used to clinically evaluate patients with suspected osteomyelitis, although MRI is more sensitive. Treatment consists of operative debridement to remove necrotic tissue, operative cultures to identify the causative organism, and empiric antibiotic coverage, with modifications based on culture results.
▶ Musculoskeletal System Osteogenesis imperfecta 1 questions
Source: 6A #1
A 20-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 36 weeks' gestation delivers a stillborn infant. She had no prenatal care, and the prenatal course was complicated by maternal cocaine and alcohol use. She also was seen in the emergency department at 20 weeks' gestation after being assaulted by her boyfriend. Examination at the time showed scalp and forearm lacerations and bruising of the abdomen and face. She took phenytoin during the pregnancy for a seizure disorder; she had no seizures during the pregnancy. An autopsy of the fetus shows multiple fractures of thin ribs and multiple fractures of the rather broad and ribbon-shaped tubular bones. Examination of the fetus shows blue sclerae, soft calvaria, a small chest, and bent short extremities. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this condition? A) Abnormality in type I collagen B) Alcohol-induced fetal abnormalities C) Intrauterine trauma resulting from abuse to the mother D) Placental insufficiency from cocaine use E) Teratogenicity of phenytoin
Correct Answer: A) Abnormality in type I collagen
This infant likely died from complications of osteogenesis imperfecta, which results from mutations or posttranslational defects in collagen, type I. Given the presence of collagen, type I, in bone, skin, and connective tissues, pathology results from connective tissue defects ranging in severity from postpubertal fractures to fatal fractures in utero. The presentation of this fetus reflects fragile long bones along with decreased calvarial ossification and thin sclerae (leading to visualization of the choroidal veins). Patients may also present with short stature, scoliosis, basilar skull deformities (leading to nerve compression), hearing loss (likely related to abnormal bone formation in the ossicles and cochlea), opalescent and fragile teeth, and easy bruising (caused by collagen, type I, defects in blood vessel walls). Treatment is primarily supportive, involving possible bisphosphonates along with monitoring for complications, physical therapy, and genetic counseling. Choice B (Alcohol-induced fetal abnormalities) includes intellectual disability, developmental delay, and physical malformations such as microcephaly, facial dysmorphia, limb deformities, and congenital heart disease. Patients with fetal alcohol syndrome may demonstrate abnormal bone development and delayed bone growth, but osseous fragility would be atypical. Choice C (Intrauterine trauma from maternal abuse) may lead to increased fetal cortisol production and stress physiology, but in the absence of direct blunt or penetrating injury to the fetus, mechanical trauma would be unlikely. Choice D (Placental insufficiency from cocaine use) can lead to preterm birth, intrauterine growth restriction, low birth weight, and placental abruption, but osseous fragility would be atypical. Choice E (Teratogenicity of phenytoin) commonly causes orofacial clefts, cardiac malformations, and genitourinary defects. In adults, phenytoin may cause osteomalacia from changes in calcium metabolism, but maternal phenytoin use is unlikely to result in osseous fragility in infants. Educational Objective: In osteogenesis imperfecta, abnormalities of collagen, type I, lead to connective tissue defects and consequent bone fractures, scoliosis, short stature, skull deformities, blue sclera, fragile teeth, hearing loss, and easy bruising. Severe cases lead to death in utero.
▶ Nervous System Special Senses Spinal Muscular Atrophy 1 questions
Source: 6A #2
A previously healthy 1-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 2-month history of increasing weakness and difficulty feeding. He is alert. Examination shows tongue fasciculations and profound hypotonia. Deep tendon reflexes are absent. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Botulism B) Guillain-Barre syndrome C) Myasthenia gravis D) Progressive infantile spinal muscular atrophy E) Transverse myelitis
Correct Answer: D) Progressive infantile spinal muscular atrophy
This patient most likely has progressive infantile spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). SMA commonly involves an autosomal recessive mutation of the SMN protein, resulting in defective mRNA synthesis in motor neurons. The infantile form of SMA typically affects normally developing infants who are several months old. In spinal muscular atrophy, the bilateral lower brainstem motor nuclei and anterior horns degenerate, leading to progressive, symmetric muscular weakness and a lower motor neuron-pattern of dysfunction (e.g., decreased tone, hyporeflexia, fasciculations, early-onset atrophy). The lower extremities are typically more affected than the upper extremities. Dysfunction progresses over the course of months. In severe cases, progressive respiratory insufficiency may develop. The diagnosis can be confirmed with genetic testing. Treatment is supportive and includes promoting nutrition, motor, and respiratory function. Choice A (Botulism) is an acute disease of the neuromuscular junction caused by exposure to Clostridium botulinum toxin. Over hours to days, patients develop symmetric hypotonia and hyporeflexia beginning with cranial nerves and descending to lower extremities, which may mimic SMA. However, this patient's weakness developed over months rather than hours to days. Choice B (Guillain-Barre syndrome) results from autoimmune attack of spinal nerve roots with acute-onset, symmetric, ascending muscle weakness and hyporeflexia. This patient's weakness progressed over months, not acutely. Additionally, many patients demonstrate autonomic dysfunction and/or sensory symptoms atypical in SMA. Choice C (Myasthenia gravis) is an autoimmune disorder of neuromuscular transmission causing focal or generalized muscle weakness and fatigability. It demonstrates bimodal age of onset in young adults (teens to 20s) and older adults (50s-60s). Myasthenia gravis in an infant would be atypical. Choice E (Transverse myelitis) is an acquired condition with inflammation affecting one spinal cord section bilaterally, leading to acute motor, sensory, or autonomic dysfunction. This patient experienced insidious onset of motor dysfunction only. Educational Objective: In spinal muscular atrophy, bilateral lower brainstem motor nuclei and anterior horns degenerate, leading to progressive, symmetric muscular weakness and lower motor neuron-pattern dysfunction (decreased tone, hyporeflexia, fasciculations, early-onset atrophy). Deficits typically progress over months, which differentiates SMA from the acute descending motor weakness of botulism.
▶ Endocrine System Precocious puberty 1 questions
Source: 6A #5
An otherwise healthy 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of the growth of pubic hair over the past 2 years. He is 157 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 50 kg (110 lb). He appears muscular. Pubic hair development is Tanner stage 5. Examination shows a mature penis. Testicular volume is normal for age. Which of the following is the most likely site of excessive hormonal production? A) Adrenal cortex B) Hypothalamus C) Liver D) Pituitary gland E) Testes
Correct Answer: A) Adrenal cortex
Precocious puberty is defined as the onset of pubertal development and secondary sexual characteristics prior to 8 years of age in girls and 9 years of age in boys. This 6-year-old boy presents with secondary sexual characteristics (pubic hair at Tanner stage 5, mature penis) with normal testicular volume for age, indicating peripheral precocious puberty with androgen excess. In peripheral precocious puberty, excess sex hormones from the gonads or adrenal glands cause feedback inhibition of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), FSH, and LH, resulting in age-appropriate testicular size despite virilization. The adrenal cortex is the most likely site because adrenal causes of precocious puberty include congenital adrenal hyperplasia and androgen-secreting tumors, which present with the clinical picture seen in this patient. Choice B (Hypothalamus): Excess hormone production from the hypothalamus would cause central precocious puberty with increased GnRH, FSH, and LH concentrations. Increased FSH would lead to testicular enlargement (increased testicular volume), which is not observed in this patient whose testicular size is normal for age. Choice C (Liver): The liver does not typically produce hormones. While liver cirrhosis can cause hyperestrogenism symptoms (gynecomastia, spider angiomata), liver failure is not a common cause of precocious puberty in children. Choice D (Pituitary gland): Excess hormone production from the pituitary gland (through gonadotropin-secreting tumors) could cause central precocious puberty with increased FSH and LH. However, these tumors are exceedingly rare in children, and age-appropriate testicular size indicates peripheral rather than central pathology. Choice E (Testes): While testicular pathology can cause peripheral precocious puberty, the most common testicular cause (Leydig cell tumor) would present with asymmetric testicular enlargement, not the symmetric age-appropriate testicular size seen in this patient. Educational Objective: Precocious puberty can be classified as central (with increased FSH and LH) or peripheral (with decreased FSH and LH due to feedback inhibition). In young boys presenting with virilization and age-appropriate testicular size, adrenal pathology is the most likely cause of peripheral precocious puberty. Diagnosis involves measuring FSH, LH, and testosterone to differentiate between central and peripheral causes, with peripheral cases further evaluated by adrenal imaging.
▶ Endocrine System SIADH 1 questions
Source: 6A #7
A previously healthy 6-month-old boy is admitted to the hospital because of a 1-day history of fever, lethargy, and vomiting. His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 160/min, and respirations are 34/min. Examination shows nuchal rigidity and a bulging anterior fontanel. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, Leukocyte count 17,300/mm³, Platelet count 262,000/mm³, Serum Na⁺ 121 mEq/L, K⁺ 4.2 mEq/L, Cl⁻ 105 mEq/L, HCO₃⁻ 16 mEq/L, Glucose 150 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's serum sodium concentration? A) Excessive intake of free water B) Factitious hyponatremia due to hyperglycemia C) Increased loss of chloride in the kidneys D) Increased secretion of ADH (vasopressin) E) Insufficient intake of sodium chloride F) Intravascular volume depletion
Correct Answer: D) Increased secretion of ADH (vasopressin)
The clinical presentation of fever, lethargy, vomiting, altered mental status, nuchal rigidity, and a bulging anterior fontanel is classic for meningitis. This patient's hyponatremia (Na⁺ 121 mEq/L) is caused by syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH). Release of ADH (vasopressin) by the posterior pituitary is typically stimulated by an increase in plasma osmolality but can occur without stimulus in SIADH. SIADH can result from adverse effects of medications (e.g., cyclophosphamide), paraneoplastic processes, or secondary to central nervous system disorders including stroke, hemorrhage, infection, trauma, or tumor. In this patient, meningitis is the underlying cause of SIADH. Treatment involves addressing the underlying disease and gradual sodium correction, typically with fluid restriction, at a safe rate of no more than 6 to 12 mEq/day. Rapid correction can lead to central pontine myelinolysis due to osmotic shifts causing demyelination, particularly in the pons. Choice A (Excessive intake of free water) can cause hyponatremia via psychogenic polydipsia but would be unlikely in a patient presenting with acute meningitis, where SIADH is the more likely etiology. Choice B (Factitious hyponatremia due to hyperglycemia) occurs with severe hyperglycemia causing osmotic shifts of water from intracellular to extracellular space. This patient's glucose of 150 mg/dL is insufficient to cause hyponatremia on laboratory evaluation. Choice C (Increased loss of chloride in the kidneys) does not explain hyponatremia. Chloride is typically reabsorbed with sodium in the nephron. The patient's hyponatremia results from increased free water reabsorption due to SIADH, not abnormalities in sodium or chloride reabsorption. The patient's chloride concentration is normal. Choice E (Insufficient intake of sodium chloride) would not cause hyponatremia due to the kidney's ability to reabsorb sodium and water to maintain homeostatic serum osmolarity. SIADH impairs this homeostatic mechanism by causing unregulated free water reabsorption. Choice F (Intravascular volume depletion) would typically lead to hypernatremia, not hyponatremia, as it develops secondary to inadequate free water intake or administration. Educational Objective: SIADH can occur as an adverse effect of medications, a paraneoplastic process, or secondary to central nervous system disorders including infection, and should be considered in patients presenting with meningitis and unexplained hyponatremia.
▶ Nervous System Special Senses Torticollis and Cervical Dystonia 1 questions
Source: 6A #8
A 2-month-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. Pregnancy was uncomplicated. He was born at term following forceps delivery for fetal heart rate decelerations. Apgar scores were 4 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. He is at the 50th percentile for length and 75th percentile for weight. He keeps his head turned to the right and cries when it is moved toward the left. Examination shows flattening of the right posterior part of the skull. A 1.5-cm mass is palpated in the left side of the neck. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Cervical spine hemivertebrae B) Craniosynostosis C) Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy D) Left clavicle fracture E) Prenatal stroke F) Right clavicle fracture G) Sternomastoid injury H) Syringobulbia
Correct Answer: G) Sternomastoid injury
This patient likely experienced an injury of the sternomastoid (sternocleidomastoid, or SCM) muscle as a result of birth trauma, leading to congenital torticollis. Torticollis refers to an abnormal contraction of the neck muscles that results in the head tilting to one side. The clinical presentation is classic: the patient has a preferred head position (turned right), decreased cervical range of motion (cries when head moved toward left), and a palpable mass in the left SCM (the side toward which the head cannot turn). Congenital torticollis typically presents at 2 to 4 weeks of age. The hypothesized mechanism involves birth trauma (such as forceps delivery in this case) or intrauterine malposition causing SCM injury with subsequent fibrosis and contracture. The fibrosis manifests as the palpable mass. Birth trauma can also lead to plagiocephaly (flattening of the skull), explaining the flattening of the right posterior skull in this patient. Diagnosis is clinical, and treatment involves physical therapy with SCM stretching, which resolves torticollis in most infants. Cervical spine hemivertebrae (Choice A) is a rare condition of incomplete vertebral ossification that may present with torticollis and cervical scoliosis, but is not associated with birth trauma and would not present with plagiocephaly or SCM mass. Craniosynostosis (Choice B) involves premature fusion of cranial sutures causing asymmetric skull growth. While it can cause skull deformities, torticollis and SCM mass would be atypical presentations. Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (Choice C) presents with nonspecific CNS dysfunction signs such as decreased Apgar scores, abnormal consciousness, weak cry, poor tone, respiratory distress, feeding difficulties, absent primitive reflexes, or seizures. Focal findings like torticollis and plagiocephaly with a discrete SCM mass are not characteristic. Left or right clavicle fractures (Choices D and F) are the most common traumatic birth injuries but present with pain, swelling, and deformity localized to the clavicle. They do not explain torticollis, plagiocephaly, or an SCM mass. Prenatal stroke (Choice E) presents with nonspecific symptoms such as drowsiness, poor feeding, and seizure. Focal deficits with plagiocephaly and SCM mass would be atypical, and it is not associated with birth trauma mechanisms. Syringobulbia (Choice H) is a rare brainstem condition presenting with lower cranial nerve and cerebellar signs and involuntary movements. Plagiocephaly and SCM mass would be atypical. Educational Objective: Congenital torticollis typically presents in newborns starting at 2-4 weeks of age with a preferred head position, decreased cervical range of motion, and a sternocleidomastoid muscle mass. Hypothesized causes include birth trauma (such as forceps delivery) or intrauterine malposition of the head, leading to SCM injury with fibrosis and contracture. Associated findings may include plagiocephaly from the persistent abnormal head positioning.
▶ Respiratory System Histoplasmosis 1 questions
Source: 6A #9
A previously healthy 7-year-old girl is admitted to the hospital because of an 11-day history of fever, fatigue, and progressive nonproductive cough. During the past 2 weeks, she has had a decreased appetite, resulting in a 1.4-kg (3-lb) weight loss. The family lives on a farm in Missouri, and the patient often plays in an abandoned chicken coop. Her direct contact to animals is limited to a pet dog and turtle. She has not travelled outside of the state during the past 9 months and has never been out of the USA. She appears alert. She is at the 50th percentile for height and weight. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 34/min, and blood pressure is 96/57 mm Hg. Mild wheezes are heard bilaterally. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, Leukocyte count 11,300/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 48%, Bands 2%, Lymphocytes 46%, Monocytes 4%, Platelet count 210,000/mm³. A blood culture obtained 4 days ago shows no growth. A PPD skin test performed 3 days ago shows no induration; a mumps control skin test shows 8 mm of induration. A biopsy specimen of a mediastinal lymph node shows necrotizing granulomas. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Acute lymphocytic leukemia B) Acute myelocytic leukemia C) Chlamydia trachomatis infection D) Histoplasmosis E) Q fever F) Salmonella enteritidis infection G) Tuberculosis
Correct Answer: D) Histoplasmosis
Histoplasmosis is an endemic mycosis caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, endemic to the Mississippi and Ohio River valleys in the United States, as well as parts of Central and South America, sub-Saharan Africa, and Southeast Asia. The patient's exposure history is consistent with histoplasmosis, as she frequently played in an abandoned chicken coop on a Missouri farm, where bird droppings are a source of fungal spores. Pulmonary histoplasmosis presents in acute, subacute, or chronic phases with fevers, malaise, myalgia, cough, and hemoptysis, along with small calcified nodules and mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy. The virulence of Histoplasma capsulatum depends on its growth inside nonactivated macrophages, which protect fungal cells from immune detection. Diagnosis is made via detection of histoplasma antigen in serum and/or urine. Histology reveals oval yeast cells within macrophages and caseating (necrotizing) granulomas, as seen in this patient's mediastinal lymph node biopsy. This clinical presentation—with fever, weight loss, cough, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and necrotizing granulomas—is classic for histoplasmosis. Acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL) and acute myelocytic leukemia (AML) are hematologic malignancies with similar presentations (malaise, fever, bleeding, bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy), but neither would demonstrate necrotizing granulomas on lymph node biopsy. Chlamydia trachomatis causes cervicitis, urethritis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and neonatal infections; other Chlamydia species cause atypical pneumonia with diffuse patchy opacities, not granulomas. Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii acquired from cattle or sheep amniotic fluid (no exposure history in this case) and presents as pneumonia or endocarditis. Salmonella enteritidis causes food-borne illness with gastrointestinal symptoms from consumption of raw poultry and eggs, not respiratory disease with granulomas. Tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, would present similarly but is excluded by the negative PPD skin test with positive mumps control, indicating intact cell-mediated immunity; the mumps control shows the patient's immune system is functioning and can mount a delayed hypersensitivity response. Educational Objective: Histoplasmosis is an endemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum endemic to the Mississippi and Ohio River valleys in the United States. Exposure to bird or bat droppings is the primary risk factor. Pulmonary histoplasmosis presents in acute, subacute, or chronic phases with fevers, malaise, myalgia, cough, and hemoptysis, associated with small calcified nodules and mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy. Necrotizing granulomas on lymph node biopsy are characteristic of histoplasmosis.
▶ Immune System Type 1 Hypersensitivity Reactions 1 questions
Source: 6A #10
A 25-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 20 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She feels well, and her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 20-week gestation. She reports that her first child had bloody diarrhea as an infant when he was fed cow milk-based formula. The diarrhea resolved when the formula was changed to a hypoallergenic type. She states that she avoids dairy products because they upset her stomach. She asks how she can prevent food allergies in her next child. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation? A) Delay the introduction of solid food until the age of 9 months B) Do not feed the infant eggs or peanut-based products until the age of 9 months C) Exclusively breast-feed for at least 6 months D) Use a hypoallergenic formula for at least 6 months E) Use a lactose-free formula exclusively for at least 9 months
Correct Answer: C) Exclusively breast-feed for at least 6 months
Food allergies are a component of the atopic triad, which consists of atopic dermatitis, asthma, and food or environmental allergies. Food allergies may be immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated (e.g., urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis) or non-IgE-mediated (e.g., food protein-induced proctitis, proctocolitis, enterocolitis). Exclusive breast-feeding for at least 6 months is hypothesized to decrease the rate of food allergy in infants. Dietary avoidance of allergenic foods during pregnancy or lactation does not lead to decreased rates of food allergies in children. In actuality, introducing allergenic foods into the diet while lactating may lead to an increased likelihood of tolerance developing in the child and decreased rates of food allergy. Choice A (Delay introduction of solid food until 9 months) and Choice B (Delay allergenic foods including eggs and peanut-based products until 9 months) have not been shown to decrease rates of food allergy. In contrast, early introduction of allergenic foods has been recommended in order to improve tolerance to these foods. Choice D (Hypoallergenic formula for at least 6 months) and Choice E (Lactose-free formula for at least 9 months) are not necessary nor shown to decrease food allergy development. In contrast, exclusive breast-feeding for at least 6 months is recommended. At 6 months, solid foods can begin to be introduced. Educational Objective: Exclusive breast-feeding for at least 6 months is hypothesized to decrease the rate of food allergy in infants.
▶ Renal Urinary System Chronic Kidney Disease 1 questions
Source: 6A #14
A 9-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of headache and dizziness for the past week. She has a history of recurrent urinary tract infections. At the age of 2 years, she received the diagnosis of vesicoureteral reflux and was treated with prophylactic amoxicillin until the age of 6 years. She has been admitted to the hospital twice for treatment of pyelonephritis. Development is appropriate for age, and her immunizations are up-to-date. Her height and weight are below the 5th percentile. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg in all four extremities. Funduscopic examination shows narrowing of the retinal arteries. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Follow-up blood pressure measurement in 1 week B) Blood culture C) Measurement of serum urea nitrogen and creatinine concentrations D) Thyroid function tests E) CT scan of the head
Correct Answer: C) Measurement of serum urea nitrogen and creatinine concentrations
This patient with chronic vesicoureteral reflux and a history of recurrent pyelonephritis presenting with new onset headache, dizziness, and hypertension most likely has hypertensive urgency secondary to chronic kidney disease. Chronic vesicoureteral reflux predisposes patients to recurrent pyelonephritis as urine from the bladder travels in a retrograde fashion to the kidneys. Recurrent pyelonephritis leads to scarring of the renal parenchyma and loss of nephron mass, decreasing the glomerular filtration rate and causing chronic kidney disease. Hypertension in chronic renal disease results primarily from impaired sodium handling leading to expansion of intravascular volume and systolic hypertension. Over time, chronic vascular remodeling and increased systemic vascular resistance increase diastolic blood pressure. Assessment of serum urea nitrogen and creatinine concentrations is the appropriate first step in evaluating kidney function; increases in both are suggestive of kidney injury. Further assessment of urinary protein excretion is also appropriate. Choice A (Follow-up blood pressure measurement in 1 week) is inappropriate as the patient is presenting with symptoms potentially attributed to hypertension. Further workup to determine the cause and initiate treatment is necessary. Choice B (Blood cultures) is unnecessary. The patient is afebrile with no flank pain or dysuria, making acute pyelonephritis unlikely. Choice D (Thyroid function tests) may be part of secondary hypertension evaluation but would not be the first step. Hypothyroidism is more commonly associated with hypertension but typically presents with weight gain, constipation, fatigue, and cold intolerance. Choice E (CT scan of the head) should be considered only in patients with focal neurologic deficits or severe, sudden onset headache to rule out hemorrhagic stroke or subarachnoid hemorrhage. This patient has had a headache for 1 week with no reported neurologic deficits; a CT scan would provide little additional diagnostic information. Educational Objective: Chronic vesicoureteral reflux predisposes patients to recurrent pyelonephritis, which can result in scarring of renal parenchyma and loss of nephron mass leading to chronic kidney disease. Impaired salt handling in chronic renal disease leads to expansion of intravascular volume and subsequent hypertension. Laboratory evaluation should include measurement of serum urea nitrogen and creatinine concentrations.
▶ Gastrointestinal System Meckel diverticulum 1 questions
Source: 6A #15
An 8-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 4-day history of pallor. He has not had cough, rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, or diarrhea. He is alert but pale. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 150/min, respirations are 36/min, and blood pressure is 90/72 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. The stool is maroon, and test for occult blood is positive. His hemoglobin concentration is 8 g/dl. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) X-ray of the abdomen B) Upper gastrointestinal series C) HIDA scan D) Meckel scan E) Anoscopy
Correct Answer: D) Meckel scan
Meckel scan, or technetium 99m pertechnetate scan, is the modality used to confirm a Meckel diverticulum. This is a common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract characterized by a small diverticulum projecting from the terminal ileum that is approximately 2 inches in length and located 2 feet proximal to the ileocecal valve. The diverticulum may contain ectopic gastric mucosa, which secretes gastric acid, leading to erosion of the intestinal mucosa and subsequent painless hematochezia or melena. In this case, the bleeding has caused iron deficiency anemia with hemoglobin of 8 g/dl. Additionally, the diverticulum may act as a lead point for intussusception, obstruction, or volvulus. In a Meckel scan, the pertechnetate is taken up by the metabolically active gastric cells and visualized in the right lower quadrant, corresponding with ectopic gastric mucosa within the diverticulum. Choice A (X-ray of the abdomen) is not sensitive for Meckel diverticulum. It is the first step in identifying a small bowel obstruction or ruling out gastrointestinal perforation but will not provide information about the cause of this patient's gastrointestinal bleeding. Choice B (Upper gastrointestinal series) refers to a series of upper abdominal x-rays taken after the administration of oral contrast to visualize the proximal gastrointestinal tract and assess for conditions such as duodenal atresia, malrotation, and midgut volvulus. A gastrointestinal series is unable to identify a Meckel diverticulum. Choice C (HIDA scan) is a nuclear medicine scan used to diagnose cholecystitis when ultrasound is indeterminate. This patient's symptoms are more consistent with a gastrointestinal bleed secondary to a Meckel diverticulum than cholecystitis. Choice E (Anoscopy) refers to direct visualization of the anus and distal rectum and is used to visualize bleeding hemorrhoids, which is another cause of bright red bleeding per rectum but does not typically cause a significant decrease in hemoglobin. Educational Objective: Meckel scan, or technetium 99m pertechnetate scan, is the modality used to confirm a Meckel diverticulum. A Meckel diverticulum is a small diverticulum projecting from the terminal ileum that may contain ectopic gastric mucosa and lead to painless gastrointestinal bleeding.
▶ Endocrine System Graves disease 1 questions
Source: 6A #17
A previously healthy 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 4-month history of progressive fatigue and nervousness, intermittent blurred vision, and declining school performance. She has had a 3-kg (6.6-lb) weight loss during this period despite an increased appetite. Her sister has hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. The patient's temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 110/80 mm Hg. Examination shows warm flushed skin and fine soft hair. There is mild exophthalmos and lid lag. Funduscopic examination and visual fields show no abnormalities. Examination of the neck shows an enlarged thyroid gland with a bruit. There is a fine tremor when her upper extremities are outstretched. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's findings? A) Levothyroxine overdose B) Lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland C) Malignant infiltration of the thyroid gland D) Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)-producing pituitary tumor E) TSH receptor autoantibodies
Correct Answer: E) TSH receptor autoantibodies
Graves disease is an autoimmune hyperthyroid condition caused by thyroid-stimulating autoantibodies that activate the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) receptor. Hyperstimulation of the TSH receptor leads to overproduction of thyroid hormone and a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland, along with classic signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism including weight loss, insomnia, palpitations, heat intolerance, warm flushed skin, tremor, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and nervousness. TSH-receptor-stimulating antibodies also stimulate orbital fibroblasts, leading to thyroid ophthalmopathy characterized by expansion of orbital fat and connective tissue with resultant exophthalmos, lid lag, and restrictive strabismus. Thyroid ophthalmopathy may progress to diplopia, corneal exposure, and compressive optic neuropathy. Laboratory studies in Graves disease demonstrate primary hyperthyroidism with increased thyroxine and triiodothyronine and decreased TSH. Radioactive iodine uptake nuclear scintigraphy shows diffuse, abnormally increased uptake without discrete nodules. Treatment includes antithyroid drugs such as methimazole and propylthiouracil, or radioactive iodine ablation. Choice A (Levothyroxine overdose) may present with hyperthyroid symptoms including tachycardia, hypertension, tremor, and anxiety, but this patient's progressive 4-month symptom course and orbital findings of exophthalmos and lid lag are not consistent with an acute overdose event. Choice B (Lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland) is characteristic of Hashimoto disease. While Hashimoto disease may present with transient hyperthyroid symptoms during the acute stage, patients progress to hypothyroidism with fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, hyporeflexia, myxedema, and cool skin. Critically, Hashimoto disease does not cause orbital findings of exophthalmos and lid lag. Choice C (Malignant infiltration of the thyroid gland) may cause hyperthyroidism through destruction of thyroid follicular cells with release of thyroid hormone, but this mechanism would not cause the characteristic orbital findings of exophthalmos and lid lag. Choice D (TSH-producing pituitary tumor) would lead to hyperthyroidism with elevated serum TSH and thyroid hormone concentrations, representing secondary hyperthyroidism. This would not produce thyroid eye disease. Educational Objective: Graves disease is an autoimmune hyperthyroid condition caused by thyroid-stimulating antibodies that activate the TSH receptor. The presence of thyroid eye disease (thyroid ophthalmopathy), characterized by exophthalmos, lid lag, and restrictive strabismus, is highly suggestive of Graves disease and distinguishes it from other causes of hyperthyroidism.
▶ Gastrointestinal System Blunt abdominal trauma 1 questions
Source: 6A #21
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of increasingly severe abdominal pain. His parents say that he injured his stomach when he ran into the corner of a table 4 days ago. He cried immediately after the injury but then seemed to feel better. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). Abdominal examination shows a 2 x 2-cm mass at the midline. Serum studies show increased amylase and lipase activities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) X-ray of the abdomen B) Barium enema C) Barium swallow D) CT scan of the abdomen E) Endoscopy
Correct Answer: D) CT scan of the abdomen
Children are more susceptible to intra-abdominal injuries after blunt abdominal trauma compared with adults because of less developed abdominal muscles, less anterior abdominal fat, flexible ribs that transmit force to intra-abdominal structures, and anterior positioning of the liver and spleen. This patient presents after blunt abdominal trauma with a midline mass, raising concern for a duodenal hematoma. Increased amylase and lipase concentrations have been shown to correlate with intra-abdominal injury after blunt trauma to the abdomen. Clinical suspicion for abdominal injuries should be raised when patients present with increasing abdominal pain or tenderness, persistent emesis, increased amylase concentrations, bowel obstruction, or sepsis. The initial imaging of choice to evaluate for a duodenal or pancreatic injury is a CT scan of the abdomen, which may demonstrate a duodenal hematoma, duodenal perforation, pancreatic laceration, bleeding, or other injury pattern. Duodenal hematomas can be complicated by proximal bowel obstruction as a result of the hematoma. Initial management may be nonoperative for smaller injuries or may require exploratory laparotomy for severe or persistent injuries. An x-ray of the abdomen (Choice A) may be used in the evaluation of severe bowel obstruction or perforation but would not be helpful in assessing for the presence of a duodenal hematoma. A barium enema (Choice B) is used to examine for abnormalities in the large intestine, such as colon cancer, and can be used in children to evaluate for Hirschsprung disease and intestinal malrotation, but is not useful in the diagnosis of duodenal hematoma. A barium swallow (Choice C) is used in the evaluation of malrotation and midgut volvulus and outlines small bowel anatomy to assess the presence of an obstructive volvulus. Endoscopy (Choice E) is a procedure involving direct visualization of the upper gastrointestinal tract and can be helpful in pediatrics for the evaluation of swallowed foreign bodies, gastrointestinal bleeding, dysphagia, or inflammatory bowel disease, but does not assess for duodenal hematoma. Educational Objective: A duodenal hematoma can occur after blunt abdominal trauma in children. The initial imaging of choice to evaluate for a duodenal or pancreatic injury is a CT scan of the abdomen.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Peripartum Streptococcus agalactiae Infection 1 questions
Source: 6A #22
A full-term 24-hour-old newborn has respiratory distress and seizures. Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. An x-ray of the chest shows diffuse hazy infiltrates bilaterally. Leukocyte count is 12,500/mm³ (65% segmented neutrophils and 10% bands). Examination of cerebrospinal fluid shows 4 leukocytes/mm³ (90% lymphocytes), a glucose concentration of 75 mg/dL, and a protein concentration of 25 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Group B streptococcal sepsis B) Meconium aspiration C) Pneumococcal meningitis D) Pneumocystis jiroveci (formerly P. carinii) pneumonia E) Respiratory syncytial virus pneumonia
Correct Answer: A) Group B streptococcal sepsis
This 24-hour-old newborn presents with early-onset neonatal sepsis (within 72 hours of birth), characterized by respiratory distress, seizures, diffuse bilateral infiltrates on chest x-ray, and leukocytosis with left shift (bandemia). The cerebrospinal fluid findings suggest meningitis as a complication of sepsis. Early-onset neonatal sepsis typically results from pathogens acquired from the mother during birth, with Group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae), E. coli, Listeria monocytogenes, and coagulase-negative Staphylococcus being the most common causative organisms. The clinical presentation of lethargy, seizures, weak cry, hypotonia, and nonfocal examination findings is consistent with early-onset sepsis. Pneumonia is more common in early-onset sepsis and presents with tachypnea, hypoxia, and diffuse infiltrates as seen on this patient's chest x-ray. Choice B (Meconium aspiration) occurs when fetal meconium is inhaled during labor and delivery and presents with respiratory distress. However, it is generally self-resolving with small amounts of aspiration and would not typically cause seizures or CSF pleocytosis. Choice C (Pneumococcal meningitis) is most common in adults. Neonatal meningitis is more commonly caused by Group B Streptococcus, E. coli, coagulase-negative Staphylococcus, and Listeria monocytogenes rather than Streptococcus pneumoniae. Choice D (Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia) generally occurs in immunocompromised patients, particularly those with advanced HIV, and would be rare in an otherwise healthy neonate. Classic presentation includes perihilar and multifocal infiltrates rather than diffuse infiltrates. Choice E (Respiratory syncytial virus pneumonia) is a common cause of bronchiolitis in children younger than 2 years but is less consistent with bandemia and the CSF findings of meningitis seen in this patient. Bacterial infection is more common than viral infection in the neonatal period and is more consistent with the clinical and laboratory presentation. Educational Objective: The common causes of early-onset neonatal sepsis (within 72 hours of birth) include Group B Streptococcus, E. coli, and Listeria monocytogenes, which are generally acquired from the mother during birth through contact in the birth canal or transplacental spread.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Syncope 1 questions
Source: 6A #27
A previously healthy 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents 1 day after she fainted during soccer practice. Her teammates said that she fell to the ground while running and appeared to be unconscious for approximately 15 seconds; no abnormal movements were noted. There is no prior history of syncope, palpitations, or murmurs. Her parents are concerned because a maternal cousin died suddenly at the age of 22 years of an unknown cause. The patient is alert and oriented. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step? A) Reassurance B) Chest x-ray C) ECG D) EEG E) Admission to the hospital for observation
Correct Answer: C) ECG
An ECG should be obtained in this patient with unexplained exertional syncope. Exertional syncope is a characteristic feature of several high-risk cardiac conditions that must be evaluated urgently, including hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), coronary artery anomalies, valvular aortic stenosis, long QT syndrome, and Brugada syndrome. These can be classified as either structural defects or electrical abnormalities. HCM is one of the more common causes and is generally inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion, which may explain the sudden death in this patient's maternal cousin at age 22. Syncope in HCM occurs as a result of left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction with consequent decrease in cardiac output leading to decreased cerebral perfusion. Decreased perfusion of the coronary arteries can cause angina and increase the risk for ventricular arrhythmias. ECG is mandatory in all patients with unexplained syncope and is a low-cost, noninvasive means of assessing for underlying cardiac defects that should be performed as soon as possible. ECG classically demonstrates left ventricular hypertrophy with nonspecific T wave abnormalities in the precordial leads. Deep, narrow, symmetric Q waves may also be seen in the lateral and inferior leads. ECG can help diagnose conditions such as long QT syndrome or Brugada syndrome. Echocardiography should subsequently be performed to evaluate the underlying cardiac anatomy and assess the degree of LVOT obstruction if present. Choice A (Reassurance) is inappropriate because patients with unexplained exertional syncope are at high risk for sudden cardiac death and require urgent evaluation. Choice B (Chest x-ray) could be considered in patients with exertional shortness of breath, wheezing, or a prodrome suggestive of bacterial pneumonia, but this patient's presentation is more consistent with a cardiac cause of syncope. Choice D (EEG) is not necessary as this patient's syncopal episode was not associated with classic seizure-like activity. Seizures resulting in syncope are typically preceded by an aura, and patients are usually confused upon waking (postictal state). The patient's history is not consistent with a seizure. While convulsions can be seen during syncope, the absence of abnormal movements and the exertional context make this diagnosis unlikely. Choice E (Admission to the hospital for observation) is not necessary at this time. Admission would be appropriate if the patient had not regained consciousness or required cardiopulmonary resuscitation. This patient should be advised not to participate in exercise until a complete evaluation has been undertaken, but this can be performed in the outpatient setting after initial ECG screening.
▶ Musculoskeletal System Dislocation of hip 1 questions
Source: 6A #29
A previously healthy 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 6-week history of right knee pain. She plays volleyball for her school, and the pain is worse after jumping or running. There is no history of trauma. She appears well. Examination shows a tender right knee; there is crepitance with flexion. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Conversion disorder B) Dermatomyositis C) Growing pains D) Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis E) Legg-Calve-Perthes disease F) Neuroblastoma with bone marrow metastases G) Patellofemoral instability H) Septic arthritis I) Transient synovitis
Correct Answer: G) Patellofemoral instability
Patellofemoral instability is a common cause of anterior knee pain caused by an anatomical defect leading to excessive movement of the patella. It is exacerbated by overuse and activities that put weight on a flexed knee, such as running and jumping, which matches this patient's presentation. On examination, passive movement of the patella demonstrates increased sliding of the patella in either the lateral axis or superior-inferior axis. The patella may also be tender to palpation. The mainstay of treatment for patellar instability is activity modification and physical therapy, with the goal of strengthening the surrounding muscles to recruit stability of the patella and improve position and balance of the limb overall. NSAIDs may also be prescribed for use as needed. Conversion disorder (Choice A), or functional neurologic disorder, involves neurologic symptoms such as sensory or motor dysfunction that are not explained by objective findings on physical examination or imaging. This patient's symptoms are not solely neurologic. Dermatomyositis (Choice B) is an autoimmune connective tissue disease that causes pink papules over the dorsal fingers (Gottron papules), heliotrope sign on the eyelids, light pink to lilac patches with telangiectasias on the upper back and sun-exposed chest, dilated capillaries with dropout on the proximal nail folds, and proximal muscle weakness. This patient lacks these characteristic findings. Growing pains (Choice C) are recurrent, self-limited pains in the extremities that occur during childhood and early adolescence with a normal physical examination. This patient has chronic activity-related pain with physical examination findings of tenderness and crepitance. Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (Choice D), or systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, is characterized by fever, arthritis, an evanescent salmon-colored rash, and lymphadenopathy. This patient appears well without these systemic features. Legg-Calve-Perthes disease (Choice E) is an idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head that often presents in young males with slow onset of hip pain worsened by activity and associated with a limp. This patient has knee pain, not hip pain. Neuroblastoma with bone marrow metastases (Choice F) is a malignancy of neuroendocrine cells associated with the sympathetic nervous tissue. Bone marrow metastases classically cause pain at night, and the patient would likely appear ill and cachectic. This patient appears well. Septic arthritis (Choice H) results from bacterial infection of the synovial joint space, most commonly by Staphylococcus aureus. The affected joint demonstrates pain, swelling, and erythema, with arthrocentesis disclosing purulent synovial fluid with >50,000 leukocytes/mm³. This patient appears well and lacks signs of infection. Transient synovitis (Choice I) is a noninfectious arthropathy that presents with joint pain, often the hip, frequently following a viral infection in a child. It is unlikely in this adolescent athlete whose knee pain is chronic and related to activity rather than following viral illness. Educational Objective: Patellofemoral instability is a common cause of anterior knee pain in young athletes, exacerbated by load-bearing activities such as running and jumping. Physical therapy and activity modification are the mainstay of treatment.
▶ Musculoskeletal System Developmental dysplasia of the hip 1 questions
Source: 8A #47
A healthy 16-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of a painless right-sided limp since she began to walk 4 months ago. She was delivered at term by cesarean section because of breech presentation. There is no family history of musculoskeletal disorders. Examination shows a left lower extremity that is shorter than the right; sensation, circulation, and muscle strength are normal. Abduction of the left hip is limited to 30 degrees. Examination of the right hip shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of these findings? A) Acute epiphyseal fracture B) Acute suppurative arthritis C) Avulsion of muscle origin D) Displacement of the capital femoral epiphysis E) Failure of osteoid to mineralize F) Developmental dysplasia of the hip
Correct Answer: F) Developmental dysplasia of the hip
Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) occurs as the result of an abnormal or poorly developed acetabulum in infants, leading to femoral instability. Risk factors include female sex, breech position during delivery, and family history of the condition. This patient presents with classic findings: female, breech delivery history, limb-length discrepancy (left lower extremity shorter than right), and limited hip abduction (30 degrees). In infants, the Barlow and Ortolani maneuvers may be used to test for hip instability and help diagnose DDH. Additional testing including ultrasonography may be useful to diagnose infants younger than age 4 months. If left untreated, DDH may result in functional disability, pain, and early osteoarthritis. The most common treatment for infants with this condition is an abduction splint, most commonly the Pavlik harness. Incorrect choices: Acute epiphyseal fracture (Choice A) could occur with mechanical trauma and would present with pain, ecchymosis, and guarding. Acute suppurative arthritis/septic arthritis (Choice B) results from bacterial infection (commonly Staphylococcus aureus) and presents with fever, joint pain, and decreased range of motion, requiring arthrocentesis and intravenous antibiotics. Avulsion of muscle origin (Choice C) is associated with traumatic injury and may present with a palpable step-off or mass. Displacement of the capital femoral epiphysis/slipped capital femoral epiphysis (Choice D) occurs in adolescents with obesity or during growth spurts and is more common in males. Failure of osteoid to mineralize (Choice E) occurs in rickets and presents with bowed legs or varus deformity, associated with vitamin D deficiency or malabsorption. Educational Objective: Developmental dysplasia of the hip occurs as the result of abnormal acetabular development, which leads to femoral instability. Patients may present with limb-length discrepancy and decreased abduction. Diagnosis can be made with the Barlow and Ortolani maneuvers, as well as ultrasonography. Patients with developmental dysplasia of the hip benefit from an abduction splint to prevent long-term complications, including functional disability.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Mixed Acid-Base Disturbances 1 questions
Source: 6A #30
A 1-day-old, 1400-g (3-lb 2-oz) newborn has tachypnea, expiratory grunting, flaring of the alae nasi, and peripheral edema. He is cyanotic while breathing room air. Laboratory studies show: Serum: Na+ 138 mEq/L, Cl- 100 mEq/L, K+ 4.2 mEq/L, HCO3- 14 mEq/L, Urea nitrogen 12 mg/dL Urine: pH 6.2, Protein 1+, RBC 0-1/hpf, WBC 0-1/hpf Arterial blood gas analysis on room air: pH 7.17, PCO2 50 mm Hg, PO2 40 mm Hg Which of the following is the most likely acid-base disorder? A) Lactic acidosis with respiratory compensation B) Pure metabolic acidosis C) Respiratory acidosis and metabolic compensation D) Respiratory acidosis complicated by renal failure E) Respiratory and metabolic acidosis
Correct Answer: E) Respiratory and metabolic acidosis
This patient demonstrates a mixed respiratory and anion-gap metabolic acidosis. The metabolic acidosis is indicated by a pH less than 7.35 (acidemia) with decreased HCO3- (14 mEq/L). The anion gap is calculated as [Na+] - ([Cl-] + [HCO3-]) = 138 - (100 + 14) = 24, which is elevated (normal is 8-12), indicating an anion-gap metabolic acidosis. In this neonatal case, lactic acidosis secondary to inadequate organ perfusion and forced anaerobic metabolism (resulting from hypoxemia) is the likely cause of the metabolic acidosis. Normally, the respiratory system compensates for metabolic acidosis by increasing minute ventilation to eliminate CO2 (an acid), resulting in a decreased PCO2. However, this patient has an increased PCO2 of 50 mm Hg, indicating that respiratory compensation is not only inadequate but that a concomitant respiratory acidosis is also present. The Winters formula calculates the expected PCO2 with adequate respiratory compensation: 1.5(HCO3-) + 8 ± 2. In this case, the expected range would be 1.5(14) + 8 ± 2 = 27 to 31 mm Hg. The measured PCO2 of 50 mm Hg is well above this predicted range, confirming CO2 accumulation in addition to organic anions. Choice A (Lactic acidosis with respiratory compensation) would show a PCO2 within the Winters formula range; the elevated PCO2 here indicates inadequate compensation. Choice B (Pure metabolic acidosis) similarly would demonstrate appropriate respiratory compensation with a lower PCO2. Choice C (Respiratory acidosis and metabolic compensation) would present with increased PCO2 and increased HCO3-, but this patient has decreased HCO3-. Choice D (Respiratory acidosis complicated by renal failure) would show elevated creatinine and urea nitrogen indicating renal dysfunction, which are not significantly elevated here. Educational Objective: Metabolic acidosis is identified by pH less than 7.35 with decreased HCO3-. The anion gap should be calculated to determine potential causes and differentiate between anion-gap and non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. The Winters formula (1.5(HCO3-) + 8 ± 2) determines the expected respiratory compensation and identifies the presence of a concurrent respiratory acid-base disturbance. When measured PCO2 falls outside the predicted range, a mixed acid-base disorder is present.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Ovarian Cyst 1 questions
Source: 6A #31
A 17-year-old girl comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of pain in the right lower quadrant of her abdomen. She has had no loss of appetite. She was able to attend school today. Her last menstrual period was 24 days ago. She is not sexually active. Her temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows no rebound tenderness. Pelvic examination is difficult to perform because of discomfort but shows a tender right adnexa. A pregnancy test is negative. Ultrasonography shows a 3.5-cm right ovarian cyst that appears to be filled with fluid. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Observation B) Intravenous antibiotic therapy C) Diagnostic laparoscopy D) Ovarian biopsy E) Appendectomy
Correct Answer: A) Observation
The corpus luteum develops from the mature follicle after ovulation during the menstrual cycle and can form a cyst in some instances. Patients may be asymptomatic but can present with abdominal or pelvic pain if the cyst is large. Potential complications include cyst rupture or ovarian torsion. In unruptured corpus luteum cysts, physical examination may demonstrate an adnexal mass and adnexal tenderness, as in this patient. Pelvic ultrasonography will disclose a cystic mass or free fluid in the pelvis if the cyst has ruptured, which may include hemorrhagic components (hemoperitoneum). Corpus luteum cysts are typically managed with observation and supportive therapy unless suspicious for malignancy or causing persistent symptoms. Choice B (Intravenous antibiotic therapy) would be appropriate for a tubo-ovarian abscess, which presents with fever, abdominopelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, and an adnexal mass, commonly in the setting of a sexually transmitted infection. This patient is not sexually active, making a tubo-ovarian abscess unlikely. Choice C (Diagnostic laparoscopy) would be appropriate in management of a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, which commonly presents with vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain or peritonitis, a positive pregnancy test, and hemodynamic instability when severe. This patient's last menstrual period was 24 days ago and pregnancy test is negative, making ectopic pregnancy less likely. Diagnostic laparoscopy would be indicated for ovarian torsion or if the patient's cyst grew or caused persistent symptoms. Choice D (Ovarian biopsy) could be used to diagnose an adnexal mass but is rarely used as it would lead to spilling of contents of cystic structures and seeding of the tract of potentially malignant masses. Pathology for ovarian masses is more commonly dependent on excisional biopsies. Choice E (Appendectomy) would be appropriate for appendicitis, which commonly presents with periumbilical pain that later moves to the right lower quadrant, along with anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and fever. Physical examination may demonstrate rebound tenderness. This patient's ultrasound did not disclose appendicitis and she lacks anorexia and fever. Educational Objective: A corpus luteum cyst may be asymptomatic or present with unilateral abdominopelvic pain if large. Complications include cyst rupture and ovarian torsion. Unless the cyst is suspicious for malignancy or causing persistent symptoms, observation and supportive therapy is appropriate.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Breath-holding Spells with Syncope 1 questions
Source: 6A #32
A 2-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after a syncopal episode. At the time of the episode, she turned blue around the mouth while having a temper tantrum; she then fell down and became unresponsive. Her extremities became rigid and shook and then became limp. After a few seconds, she resumed normal activity. She currently is alert, active, and well hydrated. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 94/52 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. A grade 1/6 systolic ejection murmur is heard at the lower left sternal border with no gallops or rubs. The cranial nerves are intact. Muscle tone is normal, and deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's syncopal episode? A) Atonic seizure B) Breath holding C) Hypochondriasis D) Low cardiac output E) Complex partial seizure
Correct Answer: B) Breath holding
Syncope triggered by emotional distress in this 2-year-old girl was most likely caused by a breath-holding episode. Breath-holding episodes are common paroxysmal events between ages 6 months to 6 years, typically triggered by stress-induced autonomic dysfunction. The classic sequence of events is crying followed by breath-holding and cyanosis, then muscle rigidity and shaking, and finally limpness and loss of consciousness. This sequence perfectly matches the patient's presentation. Episodes may recur daily and typically remit spontaneously. Physicians should assess for iron deficiency anemia, which is commonly associated with breath-holding episodes, and treat with supplemental iron if deficient. Choice A (Atonic seizures) are generalized seizures causing sudden loss of muscle tone and consciousness, but stress-related triggers and cyanosis are more consistent with breath-holding episodes. Choice E (Complex partial seizures) are focal seizures with focal motor or sensory symptoms and impaired consciousness; again, the cyanotic presentation and stress trigger favor breath-holding. In ambiguous cases, seizures should be ruled out using EEG. Choice C (Hypochondriasis/Illness anxiety disorder) involves persistent excessive anxiety about having a serious illness, which is not applicable to a 2-year-old who does not understand serious illness concepts. Choice D (Low cardiac output) may cause syncope but would be atypical in this otherwise healthy child with a physiologic flow murmur. The brief episode with a sequence typical of breath-holding episodes makes cardiac etiology unlikely, though cardiac evaluation should be considered if episodes are frequent, prolonged, or there is a family history of sudden cardiac death. Educational Objective: Breath-holding episodes are common paroxysmal events in infants and toddlers arising from stress-induced autonomic dysfunction. Patients present with breath-holding, acute cyanosis, muscle shaking, atonia, and loss of consciousness following crying. Stress-related triggers and cyanosis differentiate breath-holding episodes from seizures.
▶ Nervous System Special Senses Corneal Abrasion and Ulcer 1 questions
Source: 6A #33
A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 10 minutes after a firecracker accident; he has pain and tearing of the right eye. The right eye appears normal. Both pupils are equally round and accommodate to light. His visual acuity is 20/20. Ocular movements are full. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the eye pain? A) Increased intraocular pressure B) Inflammation of periorbital tissues C) Loss of corneal epithelium D) Obstruction of the lacrimal duct E) Retinal detachment
Correct Answer: C) Loss of corneal epithelium
Loss of corneal epithelium describes the pathogenesis of a corneal abrasion, sustained in this example from debris scattered into the eye from a firecracker explosion. Corneal abrasions classically present with pain, conjunctival injection, tearing, and foreign body sensation. Visual acuity may be diminished, and blurry vision may be reported if the abrasion involves the visual axis. If the abrasion is large enough, it may be grossly visible as a discontinuity in the surface of the cornea, but if it cannot be clearly visualized, the use of fluorescein stain and blacklight or slit lamp may be required to detect the epithelial defect, which will be visible as an area of concentrated fluorescein stain, often in a linear or geometric pattern. Treatment includes irrigation to clear any residual debris, analgesia, and prophylactic ophthalmic antibiotic ointment to prevent superimposed infection. Incorrect Answers: Choice A: Increased intraocular pressure describes a common finding in glaucoma. In children, this may be a result of congenital glaucoma, which presents with characteristic findings including buphthalmos (an enlarged eye), a large cornea which may be edematous and opacified, and increased intraocular pressure. Infants typically present with epiphora, photophobia, and blepharospasm or eye rubbing. Choice B: Inflammation of periorbital tissues describes the pathophysiology of periorbital cellulitis, which presents with erythema, pain, and induration of the eyelids or adjacent skin. The globe itself is not affected. Choice D: Obstruction of the lacrimal duct presents with tearing (epiphora) from the ipsilateral eye, though it is generally not painful unless the obstructed lacrimal duct is also infected (e.g., dacryocystitis). Choice E: Retinal detachment can occur in the setting of ocular trauma; however, it is generally painless and is accompanied by visual symptoms of photopsia, floaters, and often with a visual field defect. Educational Objective: Corneal abrasions arise as a result of injury to the surface epithelium of the cornea and are diagnosed on gross examination or with the use of fluorescein and a blacklight. Treatment includes irrigation, analgesia, and topical antibiotics.
▶ Cardiovascular System Anemia-induced High-output Heart Failure 1 questions
Source: 6A #36
A 10-year-old boy with sickle cell disease is brought to the physician because of a 2-day history of increasing fatigue and shortness of breath. He has had a persistent upper respiratory tract infection for 5 days that has been unresponsive to over-the-counter medications. His temperature is 39.5°C (103.1°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 80/55 mm Hg. Examination shows pale conjunctivae and dry mucous membranes. Cardiac examination shows an active precordium; a grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur is heard along the left sternal border. His hematocrit is 16%. Which of the following is most likely to be increased in this patient? A) Cardiac output B) Central venous pressure C) Peripheral tissue oxygenation D) Pulmonary vascular resistance E) Systemic afterload
Correct Answer: A) Cardiac output
Cardiac output is most likely to be increased in this patient with severe anemia secondary to sickle cell disease. Adequate oxygen delivery to peripheral tissues depends on: (1) oxygenation in the lungs, (2) oxygen binding to hemoglobin, and (3) delivery of oxygenated erythrocytes with adequate cardiac output. Peripheral oxygen delivery is mathematically defined as the product of cardiac output and arterial oxygen content. In severe anemia, arterial oxygen content is significantly reduced due to low hemoglobin concentration. Therefore, cardiac output must increase to maintain adequate oxygen delivery to peripheral tissues. This accounts for the patient's active precordium and grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur. Additionally, the persistent upper respiratory infection and fever suggest a component of sepsis, which further increases cardiac output in early stages to maintain mean arterial pressure. Choice B (Central venous pressure): CVP is likely decreased because this patient has evidence of dehydration (dry mucous membranes, hypotension). CVP serves as a surrogate for preload and correlates with right atrial volume when pulmonary artery pressure is normal. Choice C (Peripheral tissue oxygenation): Peripheral tissue oxygenation will remain the same or decrease further if cardiac output cannot maintain its increased compensatory state and/or if hemoglobin concentration further decreases. Choice D (Pulmonary vascular resistance): PVR is likely normal or low because of this patient's hypovolemia. While chronic high-output cardiac states in older patients with SCD can lead to pulmonary hypertension and increased PVR, acute anemia typically results in normal or low PVR. Choice E (Systemic afterload): Systemic afterload is likely low or normal due to components of both hypovolemic and septic shock. Although hypovolemia typically causes increased systemic vascular resistance to maintain mean arterial pressure, the concurrent sepsis with fever causes cytokine-mediated arterial vasodilation, resulting in low systemic vascular resistance. Educational Objective: Peripheral oxygen delivery depends on hemoglobin concentration and cardiac output. In severe anemia where hemoglobin is markedly low, cardiac output must increase compensatorily to maintain adequate oxygen delivery, resulting in a high-output cardiac state.
▶ Immune System Terminal Component Deficiency (C5b-C9; terminal complement complex) 1 questions
Source: 6A #37
A previously healthy 8-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of fever, rash, and lethargy for 4 hours. She has had one previous episode of similar symptoms. Her brother died of fulminant meningococcemia 4 years ago. Her temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure is 95/42 mm Hg. There are scattered purpuric lesions over the trunk and extremities. Her capillary refill time is 4 seconds. Which of the following is the most likely cause? A) AIDS B) Child abuse C) Complement system immunodeficiency D) Congenital humoral system immunodeficiency E) Frequent exposure to multiple pathogens F) Vitamin A deficiency
Correct Answer: C) Complement system immunodeficiency
Complement system immunodeficiency, specifically late component complement deficiency (C5 to C9), is the most likely diagnosis in this patient presenting with meningococcemia. The family history of fulminant meningococcemia in her brother and her own recurrent infections with purpuric rash are classic presentations of terminal complement deficiency. Terminal complement deficiency impairs the formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC), which is critical for controlling Neisseria meningitidis infections. The complement cascade converges at C3, where C3 convertase cleaves C3 into C3a (a potent chemoattractant) and C3b. C3b is incorporated into C5 convertase, which cleaves C5 into C5a and C5b. C5b then complexes with C6, C7, C8, and C9 to form the MAC—a transmembrane pore that disrupts cellular membrane integrity and leads to cell lysis. Deficiency of terminal complement factors (C5-C9) prevents MAC formation and preferentially predisposes patients to invasive infections with Neisseria species, including fulminant meningococcemia. Choice A (AIDS) typically presents with opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis pneumonia, Mycobacterium avium) or recurrent pneumonia, usually within months of birth, and does not account for the specific family history or clinical presentation. Choice B (Child abuse) is incorrect because purpura on the trunk and extremities with sepsis is classic for meningococcemia, not typical child abuse injury patterns. Abuse-related bruising occurs in atypical locations (back) with atypical appearances (linear marks). Choice D (Congenital humoral system immunodeficiency) such as X-linked agammaglobulinemia causes low or absent immunoglobulin secretion and increased bacterial infection risk, but presents within the first 18 months of life and does not specifically predispose to Neisseria species infection. Choice E (Frequent exposure to multiple pathogens) is incorrect because healthy children are exposed to numerous pathogens daily without developing invasive bacterial infections. There is no history of epidemiologic exposure such as college dormitory or military barracks outbreak. Choice F (Vitamin A deficiency) causes xerophthalmia and other nutritional deficiency signs, not the acute septic presentation with purpuric meningococcemia seen here. Educational Objective: Terminal complement protein deficiency (C5-C9) prevents membrane attack complex formation, impairing bacterial lysis and predisposing to recurrent and invasive Neisseria meningitidis infections. Suspect this diagnosis in patients with recurrent meningococcemia or a family history of fulminant meningococcemia.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia 1 questions
Source: 6A #38
A 4-month-old female infant is brought to the physician by her mother for a routine examination. The patient was born at 27 weeks' gestation to a 26-year-old multiparous woman after premature rupture of the membranes and premature labor. The patient's birth weight was 1200 g (2 lb 10 oz), and she spent the first 3 months of her life in the hospital. During hospitalization, she was treated for sepsis and respiratory distress syndrome that required intubation, mechanical ventilation, and umbilical artery catheterization. She is currently receiving oxygen and diuretic therapy at home. She is at the 5th percentile for length and weight. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure is 78/45 mm Hg. Breath sounds are decreased bilaterally, and wheezing is heard occasionally. Cardiac examination shows a pronounced S2 and a precordial heave. Abdominal examination shows hepatomegaly. An ECG shows right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these cardiac findings? A) Cardiomyopathy B) Intracardiac left-to-right shunting C) Peripheral pulmonary stenosis D) Pulmonary hypertension E) Pulmonary outlet obstruction
Correct Answer: D) Pulmonary hypertension
Pulmonary hypertension is a potential complication of chronic pulmonary disease caused by the response of the pulmonary vasculature to inflammation, hypoxia, and pathologic remodeling. This infant has a history of respiratory distress syndrome requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation and continues to have decreased breath sounds and wheezing, consistent with bronchopulmonary dysplasia (neonatal chronic lung disease), which is a cause of pulmonary hypertension in infants. As the pulmonary circulation is usually a low-pressure system, the right ventricle is not equipped to pump against increased pressures. Thus, pulmonary hypertension causes secondary right ventricular dysfunction, or cor pulmonale. Cor pulmonale is manifested by right-axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy on ECG, with peripheral edema and hepatomegaly (signs of right-sided heart failure). The enlarged right ventricle produces a precordial heave on examination and a pronounced S2 due to increased pressure in the pulmonary system affecting pulmonic valve closure dynamics. Choice A (Cardiomyopathy): While the right ventricle has hypertrophied, this is secondary to pulmonary hypertension rather than a primary disorder of the myocardium. Choice B (Intracardiac left-to-right shunting): Seen in congenital cardiac defects such as atrial septal defect or ventricular septal defect. If severe and untreated, increased blood flow through the pulmonary vasculature can trigger pathologic remodeling leading to pulmonary hypertension and Eisenmenger syndrome. However, in this case, pulmonary hypertension is secondary to bronchopulmonary dysplasia, not intracardiac shunting. Choice C (Peripheral pulmonary stenosis) and Choice E (Pulmonary outlet obstruction): While these are potential causes of pulmonary hypertension and increased right-sided heart pressure, the patient's history is more consistent with bronchopulmonary dysplasia as the underlying etiology. Educational Objective: Pulmonary hypertension may be secondary to bronchopulmonary dysplasia in neonates.
