At high doses, saturation of phase II metabolic pathways leads to excess acetaminophen being metabolized by cytochrome P450-mediated reactions to N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI), which is directly hepatotoxic. Diphenhydramine (Choice B) ingestion results in central nervous system H1-receptor blockade, anticholinergic, and anti-α-adrenergic side effects, causing dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, hallucinations, delirium, ataxia, flushed skin, visual disturbances (cycloplegia), and sedation—not oral ulcerations. Ibuprofen (Choice D) is an NSAID that inhibits cyclooxygenase. In small doses, it can cause gastritis or peptic ulcer disease. In large overdose, it can cause hypotension, hypothermia, and metabolic acidosis, but this is uncommon and does not typically present with oral ulcerations. Organophosphates (Choice E) are found in insecticides and inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing cholinergic excess characterized by vomiting, diarrhea, urination, diaphoresis, salivation, lacrimation, bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, seizures, and muscle weakness—not the oral burns and ulcerations seen here. Pseudoephedrine (Choice F) is a sympathomimetic nasal decongestant. Toxicity causes nausea, vomiting, dizziness, headache, restlessness, and anxiety, not oral ulcerations. Educational Objective: Drain cleaners contain caustic alkali that can cause burns and ulcerations of the tongue, airway, and esophagus, resulting in stridor, hoarseness, vomiting, and drooling. This is a common pediatric poisoning requiring prompt evaluation with endoscopy and supportive care.
▶ Musculoskeletal System Synovitis 1 questions
Source: 3A #26
A 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents because of left hip pain for 2 days and an associated limp for the past 4 hours. One week ago, he had watery stools and temperatures to 37.8°C (100°F); these symptoms resolved within 2 days. There is no history of trauma or recent immunizations. He is otherwise healthy, and his immunizations are up-to-date. He appears alert. His temperature is 36°C (96.8°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 110/75 mm Hg. The left hip is not swollen or erythematous, but there is pain with movement and weight bearing. His erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 28 mm/h. Ultrasonography of the left hip joint shows a small effusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy? A) Oral acyclovir B) Oral clindamycin C) Oral ibuprofen D) Intravenous ceftriaxone E) Intravenous vancomycin
Correct Answer: C) Oral ibuprofen
The most likely diagnosis is transient synovitis of the hip, a noninfectious inflammatory condition affecting the synovial lining of weight-bearing joints. This diagnosis is supported by the clinical presentation: a child recovering from a recent viral infection (gastroenteritis 1 week ago), with pain on weight-bearing, antalgic gait, pain with range of motion, normal vital signs, and mildly elevated inflammatory markers (ESR 28 mm/h). The hip joint shows an effusion but no signs of acute infection. Treatment is supportive and involves rest combined with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications such as oral ibuprofen. Diagnosis also requires exclusion of emergent conditions (cellulitis, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, fracture), which can be accomplished through clinical assessment and imaging as needed. Choice A (Oral acyclovir) is inappropriate as it is used for herpetic infections (herpes labialis, genital herpes, varicella) and acts as a guanosine analog requiring viral thymidine kinase activation to prevent viral genome replication. It has no anti-inflammatory properties and is not indicated for transient synovitis. Choice B (Oral clindamycin) is an antibiotic that inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit and is used for skin and soft-tissue infections with activity against gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic pathogens. It is not indicated for transient synovitis as this is a noninfectious condition. Choice D (Intravenous ceftriaxone), a third-generation cephalosporin with broad-spectrum activity against gram-positive and gram-negative organisms including Neisseria gonorrhoeae, is indicated for serious bacterial infections including meningitis, septic arthritis, and osteomyelitis. It is inappropriate for transient synovitis as the clinical presentation does not suggest bacterial infection. Choice E (Intravenous vancomycin) inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis with activity primarily against gram-positive organisms. It is used for serious infections such as osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, and skin and soft-tissue infections caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Like ceftriaxone, it is not indicated for transient synovitis. Educational Objective: Transient synovitis is a noninfectious arthropathy that presents with pain of weight-bearing joints, often the hip, frequently following a viral infection in a child. Diagnosis involves the exclusion of emergent or urgent conditions such as cellulitis, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, and fracture. It is best managed with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications.
▶ Renal Urinary System Wilms Tumor 1 questions
Source: 3A #28
A 3-year-old boy is brought for a well-child examination. His mother states that his belly seems big. His vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows aniridia. There is a palpable mass in the right flank. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Measurement of serum catecholamine concentration B) Measurement of urine vanillylmandelic acid and homovanillic acid concentrations C) X-ray of the abdomen D) X-ray of the chest E) Ultrasonography of the abdomen
Correct Answer: E) Ultrasonography of the abdomen
Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor) is the most common renal malignancy in childhood, resulting from mutations in tumor suppressor genes WT1 or WT2. It is characterized by a large, often palpable, unilateral flank mass. Patients may be asymptomatic or present with abdominal pain or hematuria. The clinical presentation is classic: a 3-year-old with a palpable right flank mass and aniridia, which is a known congenital association (along with hemihypertrophy and genitourinary abnormalities). The preferred initial diagnostic study is abdominal ultrasonography to evaluate the abdominal mass and differentiate nephroblastoma from other conditions such as hydronephrosis and polycystic kidney disease. If nephroblastoma is diagnosed, further imaging can be performed to evaluate tumor infiltration and extent. Choice A (serum catecholamine concentration) is used to evaluate pheochromocytoma or neuroblastoma, which are catecholamine-secreting tumors, not renal masses. Choice B (urine vanillylmandelic acid and homovanillic acid) is also used for pheochromocytoma evaluation. Pheochromocytoma presents with episodic headaches, sweating, palpitations, tremors, agitation, tachycardia, tachypnea, and treatment-refractory hypertension due to functional secretion of epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine. Choice C (abdominal X-ray) has limited utility for evaluating abdominal masses as it is not sensitive enough. Plain films are better suited for evaluating bowel obstruction, foreign bodies, necrotizing enterocolitis, or constipation. Choice D (chest X-ray) may eventually be needed to evaluate for lung metastases, but the abdominal mass should be characterized first with a more sensitive imaging modality. Educational Objective: Nephroblastoma is the most common pediatric renal malignancy and presents with a large, often palpable unilateral flank mass. Abdominal ultrasonography is the preferred initial diagnostic study for evaluating suspected abdominal masses in children.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Varicella-zoster virus infection in pregnancy 1 questions
Source: 3A #34
A 12-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of chickenpox for 4 weeks. She developed vesicular lesions on her head, trunk, and extremities 2 weeks after her older brother developed lesions, and she has continued to have new lesions since then. She is at the 10th percentile for length, weight, and head circumference. Her temperature is 38°C (100.4°F). Examination shows papules, fluid-filled vesicles, and crusted small ulcers scattered over the head, trunk, and proximal extremities. Indirect fluorescent antibody testing of the material from the base of one of the vesicles is positive for the varicella antigen. Which of the following is the most likely immunologic abnormality? A) Impaired B-lymphocyte function B) Impaired complement function C) Impaired neutrophil adhesion D) Impaired neutrophil chemotaxis E) Impaired T-lymphocyte function F) Neutrophil oxidation burst
Correct Answer: E) Impaired T-lymphocyte function
Varicella zoster (human herpesvirus-3) is transmitted via respiratory secretions and direct contact with infected skin lesions. In immunocompetent children, chickenpox typically presents with a rash persisting for 1 to 2 weeks. However, this patient has had chickenpox for 4 weeks with continued new lesion formation, which is abnormal and suggests an underlying immunodeficiency. The persistence of varicella infection for 1 month is highly suggestive of T-lymphocyte immunodeficiency. T-lymphocyte function is essential for host defense against viral infections, particularly herpesviruses. Varicella is uncommon in infancy and may occur as an opportunistic infection in infants with HIV or other conditions impairing T-lymphocyte function. Infants with T-lymphocyte immunodeficiency are at greater risk for severe consequences of varicella infection, including end organ involvement such as encephalitis and pneumonia. Incorrect Answers: - Choice A (Impaired B-lymphocyte function): Occurs in conditions like X-linked agammaglobulinemia and common variable immunodeficiency. Affected infants demonstrate recurrent infections with both bacterial and viral organisms, but typically not the prolonged single infection seen here. - Choice B (Impaired complement function): Occurs in complement disorders. Patients are at increased risk for infection with encapsulated bacterial organisms, not characteristic of prolonged viral persistence. - Choice C (Impaired neutrophil adhesion): Occurs in leukocyte adhesion deficiency, presenting with recurrent skin and mucosal infections, absent pus, and delayed umbilical cord separation. - Choice D (Impaired neutrophil chemotaxis): Occurs in Chediak-Higashi syndrome, which presents with albinism, peripheral neuropathy, and recurrent pyogenic infections. - Choice F (Neutrophil oxidation burst): Defects occur in chronic granulomatous disease, presenting with recurrent infections with catalase-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus. Educational Objective: Defense against varicella zoster virus relies on T-lymphocyte function, which is impaired in HIV infection and T-lymphocyte immunodeficiency. Infants with deficient T-lymphocyte function are at increased risk for severe infection with varicella, which may manifest as persistent infection or end organ involvement.
▶ Cardiovascular System Myocarditis 1 questions
Source: 3A #36
A 10-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of fever and agitation for 8 hours. She has had an upper respiratory tract infection for 2 days. Her temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse is 160/min, respirations are 40/min, and blood pressure is 60/palpable mm Hg. An S3 gallop is heard on auscultation. S1 and S2 are normal. Scattered crackles are heard bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's findings? A) Bronchiolitis B) Endocarditis C) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy D) Myocarditis E) Valve rupture
Correct Answer: D) Myocarditis
Viral myocarditis is the most likely diagnosis in this 10-month-old girl presenting with fever and agitation following an upper respiratory tract infection, with classic signs of heart failure including tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, S3 gallop, and bilateral crackles indicating pulmonary edema. The S3 gallop is a characteristic heart sound associated with dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure resulting from increased atrial and ventricular end-diastolic volume. Viral myocarditis commonly presents in children with a viral prodrome such as recent respiratory illness, fever, malaise, and myalgia, followed by signs and symptoms of heart failure including volume overload, shortness of breath, and pulmonary edema. Treatment focuses on supportive care including diuretics and mechanical ventilation as needed to maintain hemodynamic stability. Choice A (Bronchiolitis): Bronchiolitis is a respiratory syncytial virus infection that causes respiratory distress from mucous plugging of small airways, but it does not cause volume overload, pulmonary edema, or an S3 gallop. Rhonchi, not crackles, are typically heard on lung auscultation in bronchiolitis. Choice B (Endocarditis): Endocarditis is rare in children and usually associated with underlying congenital heart disease, rheumatic heart disease, or central venous catheter use. While it can present with fever, the typical findings include new murmurs, vegetation on echocardiography, and positive blood cultures. It does not typically present with an S3 gallop or acute heart failure as the primary manifestation. Choice C (Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy): While hypertrophic cardiomyopathy can present with signs of heart failure, syncope on exertion, or exertional chest pain, it typically follows a subacute or chronic course rather than acute presentation. The characteristic murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a systolic murmur from left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. The acute presentation with fever and S3 gallop is more suggestive of myocarditis. Choice E (Valve rupture): Mitral valve rupture can cause pulmonary edema and tachypnea, but it is not commonly associated with fever unless it is a complication of endocarditis. Valve rupture is characterized by a systolic murmur on auscultation, not an S3 gallop. Educational Objective: Viral myocarditis presents in children with fever and signs and symptoms of heart failure, including volume overload, chest pain, shortness of breath, pulmonary edema manifesting as bilateral crackles, and an S3 gallop on physical examination, often following a viral prodrome such as recent upper respiratory infection.
▶ Respiratory System Bronchiectasis 1 questions
Source: 3A #39
A 5-year-old girl with a 1-year history of chronic nonproductive cough is brought for a follow-up examination. The cough occurs during the day and night and is not exacerbated by exercise. She has not had chills, diarrhea, or weight loss. Inhaled β-adrenergic agonists, two courses of oral antibiotics, and a 10-day course of oral prednisone have not relieved her symptoms. She is at the 50th percentile for height and weight. She appears well. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 82/60 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. An x-ray of the chest shows no abnormalities except for a linear consolidation in the right middle lobe. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) α1-Antitrypsin deficiency B) Asthma C) Bronchiectasis D) Congenital emphysema E) Cystic fibrosis
Correct Answer: C) Bronchiectasis
Bronchiectasis refers to dilation and distortion of the bronchi or bronchioles that leads to obstructive lung disease. Numerous causes exist in children, including congenital bronchiectasis from underlying genetic disorders of cartilage or airways, cystic fibrosis, Kartagener syndrome, recurrent aspiration, airway malignancies, immunodeficiency syndromes with recurrent necrotizing pulmonary infections, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, and connective tissue disorders. Children classically present with chronic cough (with or without sputum production) and symptoms of infection (fever, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain) during exacerbations. Exercise intolerance and dyspnea on exertion are usually absent until late disease progression. Chest imaging may show linear atelectasis or scarring, dilated airways with thickened walls, and peripheral opacities related to multifocal mucous plugs. This patient's clinical presentation—chronic nonproductive cough for 1 year without constitutional symptoms, normal growth parameters, absence of systemic illness, and chest x-ray findings of linear consolidation in the right middle lobe—is consistent with bronchiectasis. Choice A (α1-Antitrypsin deficiency) results in early development of panacinar emphysema and cirrhosis from a hereditary defect in α1-antitrypsin misfolding. The lack of functional α1-antitrypsin creates an imbalance of proteases and antiproteases in lung parenchyma, destroying alveolar septa. This would not present as linear consolidation. Choice B (Asthma) is characterized by reversible airflow obstruction from smooth muscle spasm in bronchi and small airways, presenting with dyspnea, wheezing, or chronic nonproductive cough, often triggered by allergens, exercise, or temperature changes. Asthma may progress to reactive airway remodeling. This patient's lack of response to inhaled β-adrenergic agonists and oral prednisone argues strongly against asthma. Choice D (Congenital emphysema) is a rare pulmonary disorder from disrupted embryonic bronchopulmonary development characterized by air trapping and lung hyperinflation visible on chest imaging. Disease severity varies widely, ranging from asymptomatic until adulthood to neonatal respiratory distress. The linear consolidation finding is not consistent with emphysema. Choice E (Cystic fibrosis) results from CFTR gene defects leading to deficiency in a chloride channel that secretes chloride in lungs and gastrointestinal tract and reabsorbs chloride in sweat glands. While cystic fibrosis is associated with bronchiectasis due to recurrent pulmonary infections, the absence of other typical cystic fibrosis findings—such as pancreatic insufficiency, diarrhea, malnutrition, and weight loss—argues against cystic fibrosis as the cause of this patient's bronchiectasis. This patient is at the 50th percentile for height and weight with no gastrointestinal symptoms. Educational Objective: Bronchiectasis is an obstructive lung disease characterized by dilation and thickening of the bronchi or bronchioles with numerous associated causes, including cystic fibrosis, Kartagener syndrome, and immunodeficiencies with recurrent necrotizing pulmonary infections. Chronic cough is a typical presenting symptom in children, and chest imaging may show linear atelectasis or scarring with dilated airways.
▶ Human Development Consent and screening for reproductive coercion in adolescence 1 questions
Source: 3A #40
A 16-year-old girl comes to the physician requesting contraceptive advice. She feels well. She is currently sexually active with two male partners and uses condoms inconsistently. Menarche was at the age of 12 years, and menses occur at regular 35-day intervals and last 5 days. Her last menstrual period was 10 days ago. She is 157 cm (5 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 50 kg (110 lb); BMI is 20 kg/m². Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 68/min, and blood pressure is 105/65 mm Hg. Breast and pubic hair development is Tanner stage 3. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Pelvic examination shows an ectropion on the cervix. The external genitalia, vaginal mucosa, uterus, and adnexa are normal. In addition to initiating a conversation about contraceptive methods and performing a Pap smear, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Human papillomavirus testing B) Testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae C) Measurement of serum follicle-stimulating and luteinizing hormone concentrations D) Measurement of serum thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine concentrations E) Colposcopy
Correct Answer: B) Testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
The US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends screening all sexually active adolescent women under the age of 25 years for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. Chlamydia trachomatis is a common sexually transmitted disease that can cause various infections including cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, epididymitis, and urethritis. However, in most cases it is asymptomatic, making screening of asymptomatic individuals important for identifying and treating active infections before long-term sequelae develop. Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae commonly co-infect the same individual. This patient's cervical ectropion is a normal variant in young women that does not warrant treatment but increases the risk for acquiring sexually transmitted infections such as Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and HIV. Choice A (HPV testing) is not indicated until age 30 years. Prior to that, cytologic study alone is adequate for cervical cancer screening. After age 30, screening may be performed by cytology every 3 years or cytology combined with HPV testing every 5 years. Choice C (FSH and LH testing) is unnecessary as this patient demonstrates no signs of delayed puberty and shows normal pubertal development consistent with age. There are no indications of abnormality in the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Choice D (TSH and free thyroxine testing) is not indicated for screening in an asymptomatic individual. These measurements would only be warranted if the patient presented with signs or symptoms of thyroid dysfunction. Choice E (Colposcopy) is indicated as follow-up to abnormal cervical screening or to evaluate abnormal cervical findings. This patient's ectropion is a common normal variant in adolescents with no indication for colposcopy. Educational Objective: The USPSTF recommends screening all sexually active adolescent women under age 25 for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Early identification of these often asymptomatic infections prevents long-term sequelae. Cervical ectropion is a normal variant that does not require treatment but increases STI acquisition risk.
▶ Nervous System Special Senses Peripheral Nerve Injury 1 questions
Source: 3A #41
A 12-year-old boy falls out of a tree and sustains a fracture of the shaft of his right humerus. He is unable to extend his wrist or fingers. The most likely diagnosis is injury to which of the following? A) Musculocutaneous nerve B) Posterior cord of the brachial plexus C) Median nerve D) Radial nerve E) Ulnar nerve
Correct Answer: D) Radial nerve
The radial nerve is the correct answer. It is a branch of the brachial plexus with contributions from C5-T1 nerve roots. It courses through the axilla, down the posterior shaft of the humerus within the spiral groove, and along the posterolateral aspect of the forearm. The radial nerve provides motor innervation to the extensors of the elbow, wrist, and fingers, as well as sensation to the posterior upper extremity and dorsal hand. Due to its close proximity to the humeral diaphysis within the spiral groove, the radial nerve is particularly vulnerable to injury in midshaft humerus fractures, which explains this patient's inability to extend the wrist and fingers. The musculocutaneous nerve (Choice A) courses along the anterolateral portion of the arm and innervates the elbow flexors and forearm supinators, with sensory distribution over the lateral forearm. It does not supply wrist and finger extensors. The posterior cord of the brachial plexus (Choice B) contributes to multiple nerves including the subscapular, thoracodorsal, lower subscapular, axillary, and radial nerves. While injury to the posterior cord would result in loss of wrist and finger extension, it would also cause deltoid weakness and loss of sensation over the shoulder, presenting with more extensive symptoms than seen in this patient. The median nerve (Choice C) courses along the anteromedial arm and through the carpal tunnel. It innervates wrist flexors, lateral finger flexors, and thumb opposition muscles, with sensory distribution to the volar aspect of the lateral 3½ fingers. The median nerve is most commonly injured in supracondylar fractures of the humerus, not midshaft fractures. The ulnar nerve (Choice E) courses along the medial aspect of the arm and innervates wrist flexors, medial finger flexors, and intrinsic hand muscles. It provides sensation to the volar aspect of the medial 1½ fingers. The ulnar nerve is most commonly injured in medial epicondyle fractures of the humerus, not midshaft fractures. Educational Objective: The radial nerve is commonly injured in midshaft fractures of the humerus as it courses in the spiral groove. Radial nerve injuries typically present with the inability to extend the elbow, wrist, or fingers, along with loss of sensation to the posterior arm and dorsal hand.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Neonatal Jaundice 1 questions
Source: 3A #42
A 4-day-old newborn is brought to the physician because of a 2-day history of progressive jaundice. He was born at 36 weeks' gestation to a 27-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery and weighed 2608 g (5 lb 12 oz). The newborn's blood group is O, Rh-positive, and the mother's blood group is B, Rh-positive. He has been breast-fed since birth and receives 1 to 2 ounces of a supplemental soy milk-based formula every day. His mother says that he has had about seven wet diapers daily, and his stools are yellow and seedy. At discharge 2 days ago, his weight was 2495 g (5 lb 8 oz); he now weighs 2608 g (5 lb 12 oz). His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 138/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure is 65/40 mm Hg. Examination shows scleral icterus and jaundice from the face to the lower abdomen. The liver edge is palpated 2 cm below the right costal margin. Laboratory studies at 36 hours of age and now show: At 36 Hours of Age / Now: Hematocrit (%): 54 / 52 Serum Bilirubin, total (mg/dl): 8.2 / 12.5 Direct (mg/dl): 0.1 / 0.3 Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings? A) ABO isoimmunization B) Biliary obstruction C) Dehydration D) Erythrocyte enzyme defect E) Physiologic jaundice F) Polycythemia
Correct Answer: E) Physiologic jaundice
This case presents with physiologic jaundice, the most common cause of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia. Neonatal jaundice is defined as an increased bilirubin concentration greater than 5 mg/dl, resulting from increased hemolysis or decreased bilirubin conjugation or excretion. Physiologic jaundice (benign neonatal hyperbilirubinemia) has characteristic features: development after 24 hours of life, a rate of bilirubin rise of less than 0.5 mg/dl daily, a maximum peak of 14-15 mg/dl, and predominance of indirect bilirubin (>90%). This patient fits these criteria perfectly—jaundice appeared at 2 days of life, bilirubin rose from 8.2 to 12.5 mg/dl over approximately 2 days (rate of ~0.65 mg/dl daily, borderline but acceptable), and direct bilirubin remains minimal (0.1 to 0.3 mg/dl, indicating indirect predominance). The mechanism involves increased breakdown of red blood cells generating bilirubin, immature hepatic metabolism of bilirubin, and increased enterohepatic circulation. The infant shows good clinical indicators of adequate intake (seven wet diapers daily, yellow seedy stools) and is gaining weight appropriately. Choice A (ABO isoimmunization) occurs when maternal IgG antibodies to fetal RBC antigens cause hemolysis. While this produces indirect hyperbilirubinemia, it presents with pathologic features including early presentation (within first 24 hours) and rapid rate of rise—neither of which are present here. The blood type compatibility (mother B, baby O) makes isoimmunization less likely than if the baby were type B and mother O. Choice B (Biliary obstruction) from biliary atresia causes direct hyperbilirubinemia, not the indirect predominance seen here. The direct bilirubin is only 0.3 mg/dl, ruling out this diagnosis. Choice C (Dehydration) is the mechanism behind breastfeeding jaundice, which occurs when inadequate milk transfer leads to dehydration, increased enterohepatic circulation, and indirect hyperbilirubinemia. However, this infant demonstrates seven wet diapers daily and yellow seedy stools, which are signs of adequate hydration and milk intake. Choice D (Erythrocyte enzyme defect) such as glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency causes increased RBC hemolysis and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with early presentation and rapid rise. Additionally, it would present with a substantial decrease in hematocrit, but this infant's hematocrit remained stable at 54-52%. Choice F (Polycythemia) is defined as hematocrit >65%. This infant's hematocrit is 52-54%, well below the diagnostic threshold, ruling out this diagnosis. Educational Objective: Benign neonatal hyperbilirubinemia (physiologic jaundice) is caused by increased RBC breakdown generating bilirubin, immature hepatic bilirubin metabolism, and increased enterohepatic circulation. Jaundice within the first 24 hours of life with rapid rise (>0.5 mg/dl per hour) and predominance of direct bilirubin suggests pathologic causes requiring investigation. Physiologic jaundice requires monitoring to prevent kernicterus (bilirubin deposition in basal ganglia, pons, and cerebellum at concentrations >25-30 mg/dl), managed with phototherapy or exchange transfusion as indicated.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Cardiogenic Shock 1 questions
Source: 3A #43
A 4-year-old girl is admitted to the hospital because of a 6-hour history of fever, decreased alertness, and a rash over her chest, arms, and legs. On admission, the patient is obtunded. Her temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 30/min and shallow, and blood pressure is 70/30 mm Hg. Examination shows a purple macular rash over the trunk and extremities. The face and extremities are edematous. Fluid is administered by intravenous bolus, and intravenous administration of ceftriaxone and vancomycin is started. Fifteen minutes after admission, the patient becomes apneic. She is intubated, and mechanical ventilation is started. Serum studies show: Na+ 135 mEq/L, K+ 4 mEq/L, HCO3- 15 mEq/L, Urea nitrogen 35 mg/dL, Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis on 40% oxygen shows pH 7.2, PaCO2 35 mm Hg, PaO2 100 mm Hg. Her urine output is 1.5 mL/kg/h initially. One hour later, her urine output decreases to less than 0.5 mL/kg/h. A chest x-ray shows hazy lung fields bilaterally and cardiomegaly. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Intravenous administration of an isotonic fluid bolus B) Intravenous administration of dopamine C) Intravenous administration of furosemide D) Intravenous administration of nitroprusside E) Increased inhaled oxygen concentration
Correct Answer: B) Intravenous administration of dopamine
This clinical presentation is consistent with myocarditis and cardiogenic shock. Cardiogenic shock occurs when decreased cardiac output leads to organ hypoperfusion. In cardiogenic shock, dysfunction of cardiac myocytes results in decreased chronotropy, lusitropy, or inotropy. Decreased cardiac output and increased pulmonary capillary wedge pressure result from such dysfunction. Systemic vascular resistance increases as a physiologic attempt to maintain mean arterial pressure in the setting of decreased cardiac output and peripheral perfusion. Physical examination findings include tachycardia, tachypnea, crackles on lung auscultation, and S3 or S4 gallop. Dopamine is a vasopressor and inotrope at increased doses and is appropriate for cardiogenic shock or refractory hypotension. Choice A (isotonic fluid bolus) is typically used for distributive or hypovolemic shock. It would be harmful in cardiogenic shock due to impaired cardiac output and exacerbation of pulmonary edema, and was already empirically attempted without improvement. Choice C (furosemide) is not an initial step in cardiogenic shock management. Although total body fluid volume is increased (pulmonary edema and extremity edema), cardiac output to the kidneys is decreased. Restoration of cardiac output and mean arterial pressure to prevent organ damage is the first priority. Choice D (nitroprusside) would be detrimental to a hypotensive patient. Nitroprusside is an intravenous titratable vasodilator used for hypertensive emergencies that causes vascular smooth muscle relaxation through nitric oxide activation of guanylate cyclase. Choice E (increased oxygen) would not be beneficial; arterial blood gas analysis shows adequate partial pressure of oxygen at 100 mm Hg on 40% FiO2. Educational Objective: Cardiogenic shock manifests with hypotension, edema, cardiomegaly, oliguria, pulmonary edema, and respiratory distress. Dopamine administration is indicated in cardiogenic shock or refractory hypotension as it provides both vasopressor and inotropic support at higher doses.
▶ Immune System C1 Esterase Inhibitor Deficiency, Hereditary Angioedema 1 questions
Source: 3A #44
A 17-year-old boy comes to the physician because of swelling of his lower lip that has slowly resolved during the past 2 days. He has a 12-month history of intermittent asymmetric swelling of his face, chest, and arms. During three of the episodes, he also had abdominal pain and diarrhea. There is no history of travel outside the USA. He takes no medications. He does not use illicit drugs. He is not sexually active. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Skin testing for environmental allergies B) Measurement of serum angiotensin-converting enzyme activity C) Measurement of serum C1 esterase inhibitor concentration D) Radioallergosorbent test (RAST) E) Serum protein electrophoresis
Correct Answer: C) Measurement of serum C1 esterase inhibitor concentration
Hereditary angioedema presents with intermittent episodes of swelling of the skin, face, and lips, as well as the mucosal lining of the respiratory and gastrointestinal system. It is caused by an autosomal dominant-inherited or de novo deficiency in C1 esterase inhibitor, which leads to overactivation of the complement system and overproduction of bradykinin. Bradykinin is a vasodilator that leads to the symptoms associated with hereditary angioedema. Episodes can be caused by trauma, medications, and infections. They are not improved by antihistamines but commonly self-resolve. Further evaluation would demonstrate a decreased C4 complement concentration in addition to the decreased concentration or activity of serum C1 esterase inhibitor. Skin testing for environmental allergies (Choice A) may be useful in evaluating allergic reactions or anaphylaxis, which may also present with angioedema. However, anaphylaxis also causes wheezing from laryngeal edema, urticaria, emesis, and hypotension, and is generally acute in onset following specific exposure. Measurement of serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) activity (Choice B) would not be useful in evaluating hereditary angioedema. However, decreased ACE activity from ACE inhibitor medications can lead to angioedema from decreased bradykinin degradation, making ACE inhibitors contraindicated in hereditary angioedema. Radioallergosorbent test (RAST) (Choice D) is used to identify antibodies against particular antigens, though no longer commonly used. Since hereditary angioedema is not allergic in nature, RAST would not be useful beyond ruling out an allergic contributor, which is unlikely given the absence of specific exposure history. Serum protein electrophoresis (Choice E) is used to evaluate malignancy, kidney, and immunological disorders but is not frequently used to evaluate the complement system and would have no role in diagnosing hereditary angioedema. Educational Objective: Hereditary angioedema presents with recurrent episodes of swelling of the skin, face, lips, respiratory tract, and gastrointestinal tract caused by a deficiency in C1 esterase inhibitor, leading to overproduction of bradykinin, a vasodilator.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Inflicted Head Trauma 1 questions
Source: 3A #46
A previously healthy 5-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her mother's boyfriend 30 minutes after she stopped breathing. He says that prior to giving her a bath, she suddenly cried, became limp, and stopped breathing. She is unresponsive, flaccid, and cyanotic. Her temperature is 37.6°C (99.7°F), pulse is 160/min, respirations are 5/min, and palpable systolic blood pressure is 45 mm Hg. The pupils are fixed and dilated. Fundoscopic examination shows bilateral retinal hemorrhages. After securing an airway, a CT scan of the head shows bilateral cerebral edema and acute interhemispheric subdural hemorrhage. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Acceleration-deceleration head injury B) Apparent life-threatening event C) Aspiration D) Blunt trauma head injury E) Near drowning F) Suffocation
Correct Answer: A) Acceleration-deceleration head injury
The clinical presentation is classic for abusive head trauma (nonaccidental trauma). The key findings include: bilateral retinal hemorrhages, bilateral cerebral edema, interhemispheric subdural hemorrhage, encephalopathy with apnea, and a history inconsistent with the severity of injuries. The vague explanation from the caregiver (sudden onset while bathing) combined with severe intracranial findings raises suspicion for abusive head trauma. The mechanism of abusive head trauma is typically inflicted by blunt force trauma or shaking, resulting in acceleration-deceleration forces on the infant. Infants are particularly vulnerable because of their large head-to-body ratio, weak neck musculature (allowing greater brain movement within the cranial vault), thin skull, and immature brain parenchyma. CT findings associated with nonaccidental head trauma include subdural hemorrhage (especially multiple, interhemispheric, or posterior fossa locations), hypoxic-ischemic injury, and cerebral edema. Apparent life-threatening event (Choice B) is a transient, unexpected change in breathing, appearance, or behavior that resolves by presentation and would not cause acute encephalopathy or intracranial hemorrhage. Aspiration (Choice C) presents with choking or coughing during feeding and feeding difficulties, but would be unlikely to cause acute encephalopathy and intracranial injury. Blunt trauma head injury (Choice D) can cause altered consciousness and behavioral changes, but unintentional head trauma would have a consistent history. Retinal hemorrhages and subdural hemorrhage are more significantly associated with abusive head trauma than with unintentional injury. Near drowning (Choice E) results in aspiration, hypoxemia, respiratory distress, and cerebral edema from ischemic damage, but retinal hemorrhages and subdural hemorrhage are more characteristic of abusive head trauma. Suffocation (Choice F) causes hypoxia and neurologic injury but typically presents with petechiae on eyelids and neck bruising rather than the retinal hemorrhages and interhemispheric subdural hemorrhage seen here. Educational Objective: Recognize the clinical presentation of abusive head trauma, including encephalopathy, apnea, seizures, retinal hemorrhages, and characteristic CT findings (bilateral subdural hemorrhages, cerebral edema). Understand that acceleration-deceleration forces from shaking are the typical mechanism in infants, whose anatomy (large head, weak neck muscles, thin skull) makes them particularly vulnerable to such injury.
▶ Social Sciences Patient interviewing and consultation skills 1 questions
Source: 9A #6
A 5-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child visit. Examination shows no abnormalities, and he is about to receive an immunization and a blood test. While the physician is preparing the syringe, the mother tells her son not to worry because the procedure will not hurt at all. Which of the following is the most appropriate response? A. Ask the mother to leave the room B. First demonstrate the procedure on the mother C. Inform the boy that he will experience some discomfort during the procedure D. Inform the boy that he will experience no discomfort E. Say nothing and quickly give the immunization and obtain the specimen
Correct Answer: C. Inform the boy that he will experience some discomfort during the procedure
The most appropriate response is to inform the boy that he will experience some discomfort during the procedure. Truth-telling is a core value that underlies the physician's role as a healer and patient advocate. Gently setting expectations before a frightening or painful experience can decrease patient distress, preserve their autonomy, and strengthen the physician-patient relationship. While children cannot provide informed consent, the physician is still obligated to uphold medical ethics. Obtaining informed assent and telling the truth can help preserve the child's sense of autonomy, decrease patient distress, and strengthen the physician-patient relationship. Informing the boy that he will feel some discomfort during the procedure will prompt the child and his mother to mentally prepare for this experience. This will set appropriate expectations without overemphasizing negative aspects and unnecessarily frightening the child. Choice A (Ask the mother to leave the room) and Choice E (Say nothing and quickly give the immunization and obtain the specimen) are incorrect because both approaches would likely be perceived as confrontational and paternalistic. They may cause undue stress for the child and his mother and harm the physician-patient/family relationship. Choice B (First demonstrate the procedure on the mother) is incorrect because it is inappropriate to perform an unnecessary and uncomfortable procedure on a parent for the sake of demonstration. Truthful communication will more directly and effectively establish expectations for the child and his mother. Choice D (Inform the boy that he will experience no discomfort) is incorrect because while overemphasizing anticipated pain can make the perception of pain worse (e.g., nocebo effect), the opposite approach will not eliminate discomfort and may set false expectations for the procedure. This may undermine trust between the child and medical providers. Autonomy is one of the four core principles of medical ethics, in addition to beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice. Lying is viewed negatively in most philosophical systems because it exerts a morally negative effect on the liar, violates the autonomy of the person who is lied to, and undermines trust.
▶ Behavioral Health Separation Anxiety Disorder 1 questions
Source: 9A #9
A previously healthy 20-month-old girl is brought to the physician because her mother is concerned that she has become increasingly anxious during the past 2 months. During this period, she has had difficulty being separated from her mother and has had tantrums nightly when her mother tries to leave the room after putting her to bed. There have been no changes in her family or care arrangements. Her diet consists of a variety of foods and a snack of crackers and milk before bedtime. She is at the 50th percentile for length, weight, and head circumference. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A. Reassure the mother that this is normal behavior B. Recommend that the child does not snack after dinner C. Recommend that the child sleep with her parents for 3 weeks D. Recommend that one parent stay in the child's room until she falls asleep E. Recommend diphenhydramine therapy
Correct Answer: A. Reassure the mother that this is normal behavior
Separation anxiety is a normal aspect of childhood development that may occur at various times, including around 9 months in infancy, around 18 months during the toddler years, and during the preschool years. It presents with crying, stress, and anxiety when a caregiver leaves the sight of a child. In this case, the patient is experiencing increased separation anxiety at 20 months (consistent with the toddler years), which is developmentally appropriate. Physical examination reveals no abnormalities, and there have been no changes in family or care arrangements. Therefore, the most appropriate next step is to reassure the mother that this is normal behavior. Treatment when needed may include establishing consistent routines and goodbye rituals to help the child cope with separation from caregivers. There is no known way to prevent separation anxiety as it is a normal aspect of development. Choice B (dietary changes) would be inappropriate as snacking is unrelated to separation anxiety. Choice C (co-sleeping for 3 weeks) is incorrect because the child's presentation is normal development, not pathology requiring intervention. Choice D (parent staying in room until sleep) reinforces the separation anxiety rather than addressing the normal developmental process. Choice E (diphenhydramine) is inappropriate because medication is not indicated for normal developmental separation anxiety, and reassuring the parent is more appropriate management.
▶ Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Lice 1 questions
Source: 9A #10
A patient presents with exposure to individuals infested with head lice but has no visible signs or symptoms of head lice infestation. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
Correct Answer: E) No further treatment is indicated
Head lice is caused by Pediculus humanus capitis and presents with visible lice on the scalp, nits attached to hair shafts, and excoriations from intense pruritus. Diagnosis is made by direct visualization of nits or lice. For patients with exposure to infested individuals but no evidence of active infestation, no treatment is recommended. Treatment is only indicated for patients with confirmed head lice infestation. First-line treatment for active infestation includes topical permethrin applied to hair and scalp for several minutes before rinsing, with mechanical removal of remaining nits using a wet comb or lice comb. A second application may be given 1 week later if nits persist. Patients in close contact with affected individuals should be examined and treated only if infested. Alternative treatments for permethrin-resistant cases include topical malathion and ivermectin. Choice A (hydrocortisone) is incorrect as corticosteroids are not indicated for head lice exposure. Choice B (cutting hair and applying malathion) is incorrect because haircuts are not routinely recommended and malathion should not be used in unaffected individuals. Choice C (dry-cleaning bedding) is incorrect because environmental cleaning is unnecessary for patients without active infestation. Choice D (lice comb and permethrin shampoo) is incorrect because preventive treatment is not recommended for asymptomatic, uninfested individuals. Prevention relies on avoidance of direct contact with affected individuals. The key educational objective is recognizing that asymptomatic individuals with mere exposure do not require treatment.
▶ Gastrointestinal System Lactose intolerance 1 questions
Source: 9A #11
An 8-month-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of a 2-day history of three to four loose watery stools daily. Her mother reports that her daughter had an illness 1 week ago characterized by nasal congestion and discharge, cough, and diarrhea that lasted for 2 days. Her mother switched her from a milk-based formula to a soy-based formula during the illness. Her diarrhea resumed when she switched back to milk-based formula 3 days ago. She has not had blood in her stools, and her appetite has been normal. She has been otherwise healthy, and her immunizations are up-to-date. The child displays normal activity in the examination room. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). Examination shows no abnormalities. A stool sample tests positive for reducing substances and negative for leukocytes and blood. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings? A. Intestinal mucosal damage due to autoimmune reaction B. Intestinal mucosal damage due to dietary gluten C. Intestinal mucosal damage due to Giardia lamblia D. Transient lactase deficiency due to brush border inflammation E. Intestinal mucosal inflammation due to Shigella dysenteriae
Correct Answer: D. Transient lactase deficiency due to brush border inflammation
The most likely explanation for this patient's loose, watery stools following diarrheal illness and dairy milk reintroduction is transient lactase deficiency, a type of intestinal mucosal disaccharidase deficiency, due to intestinal brush border mucosal inflammation. Key Concept: Intestinal infections can cause inflammation and destruction of the intestinal brush border, which is the site of lactase activity. Preceding infection can be followed by transient lactose intolerance, which is usually self-resolving as the inflammation subsides and the brush border regenerates. Lactase catalyzes the breakdown of lactose, a disaccharide, to galactose and glucose, both monosaccharides, at the brush border of the enterocytes. Deficiency of lactase may be induced by several mechanisms. Primary lactase deficiency occurs after early childhood in children of ethnic groups that evolutionarily received little nutrition from dairy milk (Asian, African, or Native American descent). Gastroenteritis (as in this case) or autoimmune disease may also damage the brush border and lead to effective lactase deficiency. This patient's loose stools after reintroducing dairy products following illness is consistent with lactase deficiency acquired from infection. This pattern is most often temporary and self-resolving over time. Treatment includes gradual reintroduction of lactose-containing products. The positive reducing substances test (indicating unabsorbed disaccharides) and negative leukocytes and blood support this diagnosis, ruling out infectious colitis. Choice A (autoimmune reaction): While mucosal damage from autoimmune disease can occur and is a known pathophysiology of lactose intolerance, it is not the most likely explanation for the findings in this case. This patient is otherwise healthy, without signs of autoimmune disease, and is recovering from a self-limited viral gastroenteritis. The most likely explanation in this case is transient brush border injury. Choice B (dietary gluten): Mucosal damage due to dietary gluten defines the pathophysiology of celiac disease, which is marked by gastrointestinal inflammation from hypersensitivity to gluten. Patients present with recurrent, subacute to chronic diarrhea and weight loss, not an acute presentation following a viral infection. Choice C (Giardia lamblia): Intestinal mucosal damage due to G. lamblia describes the pathophysiology of giardiasis. Giardiasis presents with multiple episodes of foul-smelling, often oily diarrhea occurring due to malabsorption and inflammation. G. lamblia is acquired through drinking contaminated water, often when traveling or camping, features not present in this case. Choice E (Shigella dysenteriae): Shigella infection presents with watery, often bloody, diarrhea, along with abdominal pain, fever, chills, nausea, and vomiting. This patient's stool is watery and loose, not bloody, and infectious symptoms have resolved.
▶ Male Reproductive Neonatal Hydrocele 1 questions
Source: 9A #13
A 2-week-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother for a well-child examination. His mother is concerned that his scrotum appears large. He was born at 38 weeks' gestation following an uncomplicated pregnancy and vaginal delivery. He is alert and is not in distress. He is at the 25th percentile for length and weight and 50th percentile for head circumference. Examination shows moderate fullness of the scrotum. The scrotum transilluminates, and the contents are nonreducible. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A. Reexamination at 2 months of age B. Ultrasonography of the scrotum C. CT scan of the scrotum D. Needle aspiration of the scrotum E. Surgical exploration of the scrotum
Correct Answer: A. Reexamination at 2 months of age
This patient's large scrotum that transilluminates is consistent with congenital hydrocele. Hydroceles result from a patent processus vaginalis that fails to obliterate following testicular descent, allowing peritoneal fluid to collect in the scrotal space. While typically unilateral, bilateral cases can occur. Most congenital hydroceles resolve spontaneously prior to birth or in the early postnatal period. Given the 2-week-old age and classic clinical presentation (transilluminating scrotal mass with nonreducible contents), routine reexamination at 2 months of age is the most appropriate next step to observe for spontaneous resolution. There is no prevention strategy for hydrocele as most cases are physiologic and self-resolving. Small hydroceles may self-resolve and only require supportive care; lesions that do not self-resolve may require surgical resection if large or symptomatic. Choice B (Ultrasonography of the scrotum) would be appropriate if the lesion were inconsistent with hydrocele or if it persists despite reexamination. Ultrasonography would confirm the diagnosis and exclude competing structural causes such as inguinal hernia and varicocele, but is not necessary as the first step in a clinically classic presentation in a neonate expected to have spontaneous resolution. Choice C (CT scan of the scrotum) is incorrect as it is unnecessary and inappropriate. Newborns are at higher risk for radiation-induced malignancy, and diagnostic modalities should avoid radiation exposure if possible in this age group. Additionally, ultrasonography is appropriately sensitive and specific for scrotal lesions and would be preferred over CT imaging. Choice D (Needle aspiration of the scrotum) is an invasive procedure with no diagnostic or therapeutic benefit for a suspected hydrocele and risks infection and tissue damage. Choice E (Surgical exploration of the scrotum) is premature. Surgery is only indicated if the hydrocele persists beyond 12-18 months of age or if it becomes large or symptomatic. Early surgical intervention is not appropriate for a congenital hydrocele expected to resolve spontaneously.
▶ Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Herpes Simplex Type 1 1 questions
Source: 9A #14
A 17-year-old girl comes to the emergency department because of severe perineal pain and a 2-day history of a rash on her vulva. She has no history of serious illness. She is sexually active with her boyfriend and uses an oral contraceptive. On arrival, she is anxious and restless. She is 180 cm (5 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 59 kg (130 lb); BMI is 19 kg/m². Her temperature is 37.7°C, heart rate is 98/min, and blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. Pelvic examination shows a tender, midline, firm mass 10 cm above the pubic symphysis. There are vesicles and ulcers over the vulva. The remainder of the pelvic examination cannot be performed because of tenderness in that area. Bladder catheterization yields 1400 mL of urine. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Herpes simplex virus infection B) Impetigo C) Lyme disease D) Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection E) Secondary syphilis
Correct Answer: A) Herpes simplex virus infection
HSV is the most likely diagnosis in this sexually active teenage patient presenting with numerous confluent ulcers of the vulva and associated tenderness. HSV is associated with the development of clusters of painful vesicles 3 to 7 days following exposure to the virus. Patients who develop HSV may experience prodromal symptoms including tenderness, burning sensation, lymphadenopathy, fever, or malaise prior to the development of vesicles. Herpesvirus is transmitted by direct contact with an affected individual, with initial presentations commonly more severe than recurrences. HSV-2 is more often associated with genital herpes, while HSV-1 is more often associated with cold sores. Treatment includes oral acyclovir or valacyclovir, and daily viral suppression may be considered in patients with multiple flares per year. Choice B (Impetigo) is incorrect. Impetigo is a contagious, superficial bacterial infection often caused by Staphylococcus aureus common in children. It begins as focal superficial vesicles or pustules that spread locally and rupture, leaving an erythematous base with an overlying honey-colored crust. This presentation does not match the clustered, painful ulcerations seen in this patient. Choice C (Lyme disease) is incorrect. Lyme disease results from Borrelia burgdorferi infection transmitted via tick bite and presents with a targetoid rash surrounding the tick bite site. This patient's rash and symptoms are more consistent with genital herpes. Choice D (Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection) is incorrect. Although MRSA may cause cellulitis and soft-tissue infections with skin breakdown, it is unlikely to cause clustered, painful ulcerations in the genital region. Choice E (Secondary syphilis) is incorrect. Secondary syphilis presents with a generalized rash involving the trunk, extremities, and characteristically the palms and soles. Syphilis classically begins as a painless chancre in the genital region, and patients may develop a disseminated rash with fevers, malaise, and flu-like symptoms approximately 3 to 10 weeks after chancre development. This does not match the acute presentation of painful vesicles and ulcers in this patient.
▶ Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Cellulitis 1 questions
Source: 9A #16
A previously healthy 6-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents 2 days after a neighbor's cat bit her on the right arm. She has had pain and progressive redness around the wound for the past 24 hours. She appears alert. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 102/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg. Examination shows moderate tenderness over the bite wound and serosanguineous discharge. A photograph of the affected area is shown. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. A culture of the discharge grows gram-negative coccobacilli. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism? A) Bartonella henselae B) Haemophilus influenzae C) Pasteurella multocida D) Staphylococcus aureus E) Streptococcus pyogenes F) Vibrio vulnificus
Correct Answer: C) Pasteurella multocida
Pasteurella multocida is the most likely pathogen causing infection in this patient's cellulitis following a cat bite. P. multocida is a gram-negative coccobacillus and commensal organism of the oropharynx of cats and dogs. Following a bite, the organism is inoculated into the skin and soft tissue, where it causes cellulitis and, in severe cases, necrotizing soft-tissue infection. Cellulitis presents clinically with pain, redness, and tender skin from a source of inoculation such as a bite, scratch, abrasion, or crack in the skin. Diagnosis is confirmed by culture and Gram stain of wound discharge. Treatment includes oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for mild cases or intravenous antibiotics and operative source control for severe cases. While streptococcal and staphylococcal cellulitis are the most common causes of cellulitis overall, they are not the primary organisms inoculated during animal bites. Choice A (Bartonella henselae) is incorrect. B. henselae is associated with cat-scratch disease, which presents with cellulitis and lymphangitis/lymphadenitis following a cat scratch, not a bite. Choice B (Haemophilus influenzae) is not the best choice. H. influenzae is a common cause of upper respiratory infections in children such as acute otitis media, pharyngitis, and sinusitis, not animal bite wounds. Choice D (Staphylococcus aureus) is not the best choice. S. aureus is the most common cause of purulent cellulitis and abscess due to inoculation from cutaneous bacteria, but cat bites are specifically associated with P. multocida inoculation. Choice E (Streptococcus pyogenes, group A) is not the best choice. S. pyogenes is a common cause of nonpurulent cellulitis and is associated with pharyngitis, sinusitis, and otitis in children, but it is not specifically associated with cat bites. Choice F (Vibrio vulnificus) is not the best choice. V. vulnificus causes cellulitis, though it more commonly results from aquatic exposures rather than animal bites.
▶ Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Scabies 1 questions
Source: 9A #18
An 18-month-old boy is brought to the office because of a 1-week history of an itchy red rash over the skin. He has not had fever, sore throat, or exposure to ticks or contact with infected individuals. Family history is noncontributory, and he has no prior history of rashes. Immunizations are up-to-date. His pulse is 120/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 80/58 mm Hg. Examination shows a scaly, erythematous rash with raised 2-mm to 4-mm discrete lesions that do not blanch on light touch. The rash involves the flexor surfaces of both wrists, the web space of the hands and feet, the abdomen, and both lower extremities. Several of the lesions are excoriated. Several small, nontender inguinal lymph nodes are palpated bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A. Contact dermatitis B. Eczema C. Erythema multiforme D. Impetigo E. Pityriasis rosea F. Scabies
Correct Answer: F) Scabies
Scabies is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with a pruritic rash involving the flexural areas and interdigital spaces, excoriations, lymphadenopathy, and evidence of close contact transmission. Definition: Scabies is a cutaneous parasitic infection caused by the Sarcoptes scabiei mite. It may be diagnosed clinically or after observing mites on skin scrapings of affected areas using mineral oil preparation. Evaluation: Scabies classically presents with pruritic, superficial burrows and papules of the web spaces of the fingers, flexural wrists, axillary folds, periumbilical area, waist, and genitalia. Mites may be visualized with mineral oil preparation following superficial skin scraping of burrows or pruritic papules. Scabies mites are transmitted via direct skin-to-skin contact from affected individuals. Treatment: Scabies is most commonly treated with topical permethrin applied from the neck down in two applications 1 week apart. All previously worn clothing and bedding should be washed in hot water and dried on a hot dryer setting. Close contacts should also be treated with permethrin. Following treatment, pruritus may persist for several weeks and is often responsive to oral antihistamines and topical corticosteroids. In more severe cases, oral ivermectin may be used in addition to topical permethrin. Prevention: Avoidance of direct contact with affected individuals is recommended to prevent transmission. Incorrect Answers: Choice A (Contact dermatitis): Contact dermatitis is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction causing well-demarcated eczematous dermatitis in areas of exposure. It is unlikely to cause linear burrows or lymphadenopathy. Choice B (Eczema): Atopic dermatitis is characterized by pruritus and recurrent dermatitis on extensor surfaces in infants and flexural surfaces in children. While it affects flexural areas, it is not commonly associated with lymphadenopathy, is not contagious, and is typically managed with emollients and topical corticosteroids. Choice C (Erythema multiforme): Characterized by a targetoid rash triggered by herpes simplex virus or Mycoplasma pneumoniae, often with systemic symptoms. It is not associated with involvement of interdigital spaces and is not contagious. Choice D (Impetigo): A contagious, superficial bacterial infection caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Impetigo begins as focal superficial vesicles or pustules that rupture leaving honey-colored crusts. It is not typically associated with burrows in interdigital spaces or the characteristic flexural distribution seen here. Choice E (Pityriasis rosea): Characterized by acute onset of a pruritic patch followed by innumerous smaller ovoid, scaly macules and patches. Associated with viral illness and human herpesvirus 6 or 7. It self-resolves in 6-8 weeks and does not typically involve interdigital spaces or present with lymphadenopathy.
▶ Blood Lymphoreticular System Disseminated intravascular coagulation 1 questions
Source: 9A #19
A previously healthy 13-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 24-hour history of fever and headache. His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 108/56 mm Hg. Examination shows stiffness of the neck. A lumbar puncture confirms the diagnosis of meningitis and the patient is admitted to the hospital. Treatment with ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and ibuprofen is begun. During the next 8 hours, he continues to have a fever, and purpuric lesions develop over the lower extremities. Laboratory studies show: On Admission: Hematocrit 34%, Leukocyte count 14,600/mm³, Platelet count 346,000/mm³, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 54 mm/h, Prothrombin time 14 sec (INR=1.2), Partial thromboplastin time 33 sec, Serum urea nitrogen 10 mg/dL, Creatinine 0.6 mg/dL 12 Hours After Admission: Hematocrit 34%, Leukocyte count 23,400/mm³, Platelet count 60,000/mm³, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 15 mm/h, Prothrombin time 19.5 sec (INR=1.6), Partial thromboplastin time 45 sec, Serum urea nitrogen 23 mg/dL, Creatinine 1 mg/dL Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the change in this patient's erythrocyte sedimentation rate? A) Consumption of fibrinogen as a result of disseminated intravascular coagulopathy B) Hemoconcentration as a result of progressive dehydration C) Improvement in the patient as he recovers from meningitis D) Laboratory error E) Suppression of inflammation by ibuprofen
Correct Answer: A) Consumption of fibrinogen as a result of disseminated intravascular coagulopathy
The patient developed disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) as a complication of meningococcal meningitis. DIC is characterized by consumption of fibrinogen and platelets, resulting in thrombocytopenia, decreased fibrinogen, and increased D-dimer concentrations. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) depends on fibrinogen concentration as a major determinant of blood viscosity and RBC aggregation. With consumption of fibrinogen due to DIC, the ESR dramatically decreased from 54 to 15 mm/h over 8 hours, despite active infection. The patient presented with classic findings of meningitis (fever, nuchal rigidity) and developed purpuric lesions consistent with meningococcemia and DIC. Laboratory findings support DIC: platelet count dropped from 346,000 to 60,000/mm³, prothrombin time increased from 14 to 19.5 seconds (INR 1.2 to 1.6), and partial thromboplastin time prolonged from 33 to 45 seconds. Choice B is incorrect because hemoconcentration would increase hematocrit and blood viscosity, raising ESR, not lowering it. This patient had a decreased hematocrit and platelet count, which is opposite to hemoconcentration. Choice C is incorrect because the patient was only 8 hours into treatment and continued to have fever and new purpuric lesions, indicating ongoing infection and worsening clinical status. Significant ESR improvement would not be expected this early in recovery. Choice D is incorrect because the dramatic change in ESR correlates with other objective findings of DIC (thrombocytopenia, coagulation abnormalities, elevated serum creatinine from organ dysfunction), making laboratory error unlikely. Choice E is incorrect because ibuprofen would not cause a rapid and significant decrease in ESR. While NSAIDs have anti-inflammatory properties, they do not directly affect fibrinogen consumption or dramatically lower ESR. DIC explains the findings better. Educational Objective: Meningococcal meningitis (Neisseria meningitidis) is a common cause of bacterial meningitis in teenagers and young adults and carries significant morbidity and mortality. DIC is a known severe complication of bacterial meningitis and sepsis. Understanding the pathophysiology of DIC and its effect on laboratory values (particularly fibrinogen's role in ESR) is essential for clinical practice. Fibrinogen is a key acute phase reactant that determines ESR; consumption of fibrinogen in DIC results in paradoxical decrease in ESR despite ongoing inflammation.
▶ Respiratory System Vocal Cord Polyps 1 questions
Source: 9A #23
A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents because of a 6-month history of intermittent episodes of "wheezing." The episodes occur only when she is awake and last several minutes to an hour. Her parents report that she makes a high-pitched noise when she tries to catch her breath during the episodes; between episodes, her voice is normal. She has not had "heartburn" or a sour taste in her mouth. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. There is no family history of asthma. She appears well. She is at the 50th percentile for height and 60th percentile for weight. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 112/65 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 99%. Examination shows a normal voice and midline trachea. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. During the examination, the patient has an acute wheezing episode that lasts 12 minutes. During this episode, her respirations are 24/min, oxygen saturation is unchanged, and there are intercostal retractions. Pulmonary examination shows no wheezes are heard. Administration of inhaled albuterol does not improve the patient's symptoms. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the diagnosis? A) Pulmonary function testing before and after administration of albuterol B) Barium swallow C) CT scan of the chest D) Laryngoscopy during a symptomatic episode E) Esophageal pH monitoring
Correct Answer: D) Laryngoscopy during a symptomatic episode
This patient presents with vocal cord dysfunction (VCD), also known as paradoxical vocal cord motion (PVCM), which is most likely confirmed by laryngoscopy during a symptomatic episode showing inappropriate movement of one or both vocal cords. Key diagnostic features of PVCM in this case: The patient has unexplained, paroxysmal stridor (high-pitched whistling/wheezing sound) that occurs only when awake, does not improve with albuterol, lacks a family history of asthma, and lacks typical asthma features such as wheezing on examination. The stridor results from air passing between inappropriately adducted vocal cords. During breathing, the vocal cords should be held in abduction to permit air passage; during talking, cords should move according to speech pattern. In PVCM, the cords show abnormal abduction or adduction during breathing or talking. Choice A is incorrect because pulmonary function testing with bronchoconstrictors or bronchodilators is appropriate for asthma diagnosis. This patient already had a trial of albuterol with no improvement, and she has stridor rather than wheezing, which is pathognomonic for PVCM, not asthma. Choice B is incorrect because barium swallow evaluates esophageal pathology such as strictures, diverticula, achalasia, and webs. It is not used in the evaluation of vocal cord dysfunction. Choice C is incorrect because CT scan of the chest cannot adequately visualize the larynx and vocal cords, and functional abnormalities of the vocal cords would not be detected on a static CT image. Direct visualization during a symptomatic episode is required to diagnose PVCM. Choice E is incorrect because esophageal pH monitoring evaluates lower esophageal sphincter incompetence and gastroesophageal reflux disease. This patient lacks typical GERD symptoms such as heartburn or sour taste in mouth. While laryngopharyngeal reflux (a subtype of GERD) may be associated with PVCM, it is not the diagnostic test of choice. Treatment of PVCM involves identifying reversible causes (scar tissue, nodules), speech therapy, respiratory retraining, management of triggering conditions, and treatment of anxiety if psychogenic in nature. Prevention focuses on avoiding known triggers and surgical caution near the recurrent laryngeal nerves.
▶ Nervous System Special Senses Sleep Terror Disorder and Sleepwalking 1 questions
Source: 9A #24
A 22-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of difficulty sleeping. His parents say that each night he awakens screaming 1 to 2 hours after falling asleep and cannot be consoled. During these episodes, he sits or stands in the crib with his eyes open but does not focus on parents. After 10 minutes, the episode resolves, and he falls asleep. He has asthma treated with nebulized albuterol. His maternal cousin has benign familial macrocephaly. The patient is above the 95th percentile for head circumference. Examination shows a prominent forehead. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A. Addition of acetazolamide to the medication regimen B. Addition of carbamazepine to the medication regimen C. Addition of propranolol to the medication regimen D. Discontinuation of albuterol therapy E. Reassurance and sleep hygiene optimization
Correct Answer: E. Reassurance and sleep hygiene optimization
This patient is most likely experiencing sleep terrors. Sleep terror disorder is characterized by episodes of sympathetic hyperactivity and vocalizations during non-REM (stage N3) sleep. Episodes typically last minutes and occur during the first third of the night. During episodes, patients are typically partially awake and in a dissociative state, with features of sleep and wakefulness co-occurring on EEG and clinical assessment. Patients are commonly amnestic to the episode. Management involves reassurance, creating a safe sleep environment, and supporting sleep hygiene. Many children outgrow sleep terror disorder by adolescence. Choice A (acetazolamide) is incorrect because acetazolamide is used for idiopathic intracranial hypertension, and this patient lacks symptoms/signs of increased intracranial pressure such as nausea, vomiting, or sixth nerve palsy. His increased head circumference in the absence of other neurologic signs is likely idiopathic benign familial macrocephaly. Choice B (carbamazepine) is incorrect because while carbamazepine is an antiepileptic, this patient's episodes are too long in duration and lack the tonic, dystonic, or hyperkinetic movements characteristic of seizures. Choice C (propranolol) is incorrect because propranolol is a beta-adrenergic blocker used for performance anxiety and akathisia, and is unhelpful in sleep terror disorder. Choice D (discontinuation of albuterol) is incorrect because while albuterol can cause CNS stimulation, the nighttime incidence of sympathetic hyperarousal is more consistent with sleep terror disorder as a primary diagnosis. The differential diagnosis includes nightmare disorder, in which patients recall their episodes and experience nightmares during REM sleep in 90-minute intervals throughout the night.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Laryngomalacia 1 questions
Source: 9A #28
A 4-week-old female newborn is brought to the office by her parents because of stridor. She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and spontaneous vaginal delivery. On initial examination after delivery, the hospital physician attributed the symptom to nasal inflammation from amniotic fluid and said that it would resolve without treatment. The parents are concerned because the noise is getting louder. They say it is worse with feedings or when the patient is on her back. If she is placed on her stomach, the noise decreases. The parents have not noted bluish discoloration of her skin. She does not choke during feedings and is not hoarse. On examination, she is active, has a loud cry, and does not appear to be in distress. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows an inspiratory vibratory sound that increases in intensity when the patient is supine. There are no neck masses or nevi. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A. Inspiratory airway narrowing because of pharyngeal hypotonia B. Inspiratory airway narrowing because of subglottic edema C. Turbulent airflow because of nasal turbinate hypertrophy D. Variable airflow interruption at the level of the cervical trachea
Correct Answer: A. Inspiratory airway narrowing because of pharyngeal hypotonia
Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of stridor in infants and young children, resulting from inspiratory airway narrowing due to pharyngeal hypotonia. The clinical presentation in this case is classic: a 4-week-old with inspiratory stridor (described as a vibratory sound) that is positional—worse when supine and better when prone. This positional relationship is pathognomonic for laryngomalacia, as gravity helps maintain airway patency in the prone position. The stridor worsens with agitation and feeding, consistent with increased respiratory demand and decreased airway stability. The absence of cyanosis, feeding difficulty, and hoarseness indicates this is a benign condition without significant airway obstruction at rest. Laryngomalacia occurs due to abnormal supraglottic structures (arytenoid cartilages and epiglottis) that collapse inward during inspiration due to decreased muscle tone and abnormal dynamics of the pharynx, rather than a fixed anatomic obstruction. The condition typically presents within the first 2 weeks of life and is self-limiting, though symptoms may persist for weeks to months. Subglottic edema would not produce the characteristic positional variation seen here. Nasal turbinate hypertrophy would cause nasal obstruction rather than true inspiratory stridor. Tracheal pathology would present differently and would not show the dramatic positional improvement with prone positioning.
▶ Renal Urinary System Cystitis 1 questions
Source: 9A #31
A 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 3-day history of urinary frequency and urgency, burning with urination, and pain in her lower abdomen. She reports that her urine has had a strong smell and cloudy appearance during this time. She has never had these symptoms before. She has not had fever, pain in other areas of her abdomen, or vaginal discharge or itching. Menarche was at the age of 12 years; menses occur at regular 30-day intervals. Her last menstrual period ended 2 weeks ago. When interviewed alone, she states that she recently had sexual intercourse for the first time and that they did not use condoms. Examination shows no abnormalities. She refuses a pelvic examination at this time. Urinalysis by dipstick shows: Blood small, Glucose normal, Protein negative, Nitrites positive, Leukocyte esterase moderate. Results of urine culture are pending. Antibiotic therapy is prescribed. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient to avoid recurrence of her symptoms? A. Consistently using condoms B. Douching after intercourse C. Drinking cranberry juice daily D. Taking showers instead of baths E. Voiding before and after intercourse
Correct Answer: E. Voiding before and after intercourse
