This 15-year-old girl presenting with urinary frequency and urgency, burning with urination, and lower abdominal pain, along with positive nitrites and leukocyte esterase on urinalysis, has acute cystitis (lower urinary tract infection). The positive nitrites and leukocyte esterase indicate bacterial infection, most commonly caused by Escherichia coli (75-95% of cases), though Proteus mirabilis and other Enterobacteriaceae species are also common pathogens. Cystitis is more common in women due to their shorter urethra and proximity of the urethra to the rectum. In this patient with postcoital cystitis, the most appropriate recommendation is voiding before and after intercourse to help decrease her risk for recurrent UTIs. This prevents bacterial colonization of the female urethra by reducing urinary stasis and flushing potential pathogens. Choice A (Consistently using condoms) is incorrect. While condoms reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections, postcoital UTIs are related to perineal contact and bacterial colonization from structures near the anus and rectum, not to sexual transmission of infection. Choice B (Douching after intercourse) is incorrect. Douching increases the risk of vaginal infections rather than decreasing UTI risk, and can disrupt normal vaginal flora. Choice C (Drinking cranberry juice daily) is not the best answer. Although cranberry juice has been shown to decrease UTI development over time due to proanthocyanidins that prevent bacterial adherence to uroepithelial cells, voiding before and after intercourse is the most effective preventive measure for postcoital cystitis. Choice D (Taking showers instead of baths) is incorrect. While baths may increase vaginitis risk with certain bath products, this does not address the mechanism of postcoital UTI development and would not effectively prevent cystitis. The educational objective emphasizes that personal hygiene and proper voiding techniques are critical for UTI prevention. For recurrent UTIs, prophylactic antibiotics may be considered, but patients should first attempt strict adherence to voiding before and after intercourse. Treatment of acute uncomplicated cystitis includes empiric antibiotics such as nitrofurantoin, cephalexin, ciprofloxacin, or sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim, pending culture and sensitivity results.
▶ Respiratory System Streptococcus Pneumonia 1 questions
Source: 9A #32
An 8-year-old boy with sickle cell disease is brought to the emergency department in acute respiratory distress. He has had a viral upper respiratory tract infection for the past week. Immunizations were up-to-date at the age of 5 years; he has received no immunizations since that time. He takes no medications. His temperature is 40°C. An x-ray of the chest shows a left lower lobe infiltrate. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism? A) Haemophilus influenzae type b B) Mycobacterium tuberculosis C) Pseudomonas aeruginosa D) Salmonella enteritidis E) Staphylococcus aureus F) Streptococcus pneumoniae
Correct Answer: F) Streptococcus pneumoniae
Patients with sickle cell disease develop functional asplenia due to splenic infarction, making them uniquely susceptible to infection by encapsulated bacteria. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common bacterial cause of community-acquired pneumonia overall and has markedly increased prevalence in patients with asplenia or functional asplenia from sickle cell disease. S. pneumoniae is a gram-positive diplococcus that commonly presents with fever, chills, productive cough, shortness of breath, and pleuritic chest pain. Physical examination may reveal rhonchi, crackles, decreased breath sounds, and increased tactile fremitus. Chest x-ray typically shows lobar pneumonia, as seen in this patient with a left lower lobe infiltrate. The preceding viral upper respiratory infection likely provided a portal of entry or impaired local defenses, allowing superimposed bacterial pneumonia to develop. Treatment involves antibiotics (β-lactams, doxycycline, or fluoroquinolones as first-line agents), and in cases of acute chest syndrome, exchange transfusion may be required. Haemophilus influenzae type b (Choice A) is an encapsulated organism that can cause pneumonia and upper respiratory infections such as bacterial sinusitis or epiglottitis in unvaccinated patients, but it is not the most likely cause of community-acquired pneumonia in this setting. Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Choice B) presents in primary infection with fever, cough, hemoptysis, night sweats, and weight loss, and is rare outside of endemic areas such as South and Central America, Africa, India, and Southeast Asia. Tuberculosis typically shows apical disease with lymphadenopathy on x-ray, not lobar infiltrates in the lower lobe. Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Choice C) causes various infections including skin and soft-tissue infections and pneumonia, but classically affects patients with diabetes mellitus and cystic fibrosis. It is not an encapsulated organism and is not the most likely community-acquired pathogen. Salmonella enteritidis (Choice D), while some Salmonella species may have a protective capsule, generally causes gastrointestinal infections rather than respiratory infections. Staphylococcus aureus (Choice E) is not an encapsulated organism. While it can cause pneumonia and is notably associated with postviral pneumonia following influenza and health care-associated pneumonia, it is not the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia. Vaccination against encapsulated bacteria when appropriate may decrease the risk for infection in patients with functional asplenia.
▶ Behavioral Health Major Depressive Disorder Without Psychotic Features 1 questions
Source: 9A #33
A 14-year-old girl is brought to the office by her parents because she has become increasingly withdrawn, irritable, and argumentative during the past 2 months. She refuses to talk with her parents about her mood change and insists that she is fine. She has been more picky in her eating habits but does not seem to have lost weight. She stays up late on the weekends and sleeps for most of the day. Sometimes she calls herself stupid when she has trouble with homework. She quit the school basketball team even though she is an outstanding player. She spends less time on the telephone and computer because she is no longer interested in what they want to talk about and does not want to waste her time. Her best friend moved away, and her grandmother, with whom she was close, died after a long illness. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, she has a sad mood and is easily tearful. Her thought process is coherent. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's symptoms? A. Bereavement B. Major depressive disorder C. Oppositional defiant disorder D. Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) E. Age-appropriate behavior
Correct Answer: B. Major depressive disorder
The most likely explanation for this patient's symptoms is major depressive disorder (MDD). MDD in adolescents commonly presents with irritable mood (though may present with depressed mood) and involves other depressive symptoms such as anhedonia, guilt or worthlessness, difficulty concentrating, suicidal thoughts, and/or neurovegetative symptoms (decreased energy, sleep disturbance, appetite disturbance). MDD is diagnosed when patients demonstrate 2 weeks of five or more depressive symptoms. Depressive symptoms include depressed mood (or in children and adolescents, irritable mood), anhedonia, guilt or worthlessness (this patient labeling herself "stupid"), difficulty concentrating, suicidal thoughts, and/or neurovegetative symptoms (decreased energy, sleep disturbance, appetite disturbance). Anhedonia commonly presents as social withdrawal. Depression in adolescents is more commonly missed than in adults because of the prominence of irritability and fluctuation of mood symptoms. MDD is typically treated with a combination of antidepressant medications and psychotherapy. Choice A (Bereavement) is incorrect. Bereavement, or uncomplicated grief reaction, refers to a person's emotional response after a loved one dies and can include sadness, shock, anguish, guilt, regret, difficulty concentrating, decreased interest in usual activities, preoccupation with thoughts and memories of the deceased, and neurovegetative symptoms such as sleep, appetite, and energy disturbances. This patient's symptoms are numerous enough to qualify her for MDD rather than an uncomplicated grief reaction. Choice C (Oppositional defiant disorder) is incorrect. Oppositional defiant disorder manifests as a persistent pattern of angry mood, defiant behavior, and vindictiveness that causes distress and impaired functioning in the child or their caretakers. However, oppositional defiant disorder typically features chronic and persistent irritability and defiance rather than a discrete episode as in this patient. Choice D (Persistent depressive disorder/dysthymia) is incorrect. Persistent depressive disorder refers to at least three depression symptoms (including depressed mood during more days than not) that have endured for at least 2 years. Other symptoms include neurovegetative symptoms (decreased energy, sleep disturbances, appetite disturbances), impaired concentration, decreased self-esteem, and hopelessness. This patient's symptoms are numerous enough to qualify her for MDD, a more severe condition than persistent depressive disorder. Choice E (Age-appropriate behavior) is incorrect. This patient demonstrates an acute change in affect and behavior that is impairing her function in school, consistent with MDD. Irritability of MDD should be differentiated from bipolar disorder and oppositional defiant disorder. Bipolar disorder involves increased activity rather than decreased activity.
▶ Nervous System Special Senses Generalized Tonic-Clonic Seizure 1 questions
Source: 9A #36
A 2.5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents because of a 45-minute history of rhythmic shaking in both of his arms and legs. The parents say that the patient was napping in his room when they heard a loud thump and then discovered him shaking. He has no history of serious illness and receives no medications. Temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 130/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 83/56 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on 100% oxygen via nonrebreather mask shows an oxygen saturation of 100%. The patient continues to have abnormal movements in the emergency department during physical examination. Fingerstick blood glucose is 115 mg/dL (N=60-100). Intravenous administration of which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy for this patient? A) Carbamazepine B) Fosphenytoin C) Levetiracetam D) Lorazepam E) Phenobarbital
Correct Answer: D) Lorazepam
This 2.5-year-old presenting with a 45-minute history of rhythmic shaking in both arms and legs is experiencing status epilepticus, defined as continuous epileptic activity for at least 5 minutes or at least two discrete seizures with incomplete interval recovery of consciousness. Status epilepticus is a neurologic emergency requiring prompt evaluation and treatment. The first-line treatment for convulsive status epilepticus involves parenteral benzodiazepines such as lorazepam, midazolam, or diazepam, which have been shown to control seizures rapidly. Benzodiazepines bind to the gamma-aminobutyric acid type A (GABA-A) receptor, a chloride channel, and increase the frequency of channel opening. GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter that counterbalances neuronal excitation, making benzodiazepines an effective treatment for rapid seizure cessation. Choice A (Carbamazepine) is incorrect. Carbamazepine is a voltage-gated sodium channel blocker used as a mood stabilizer in bipolar disorder or as an antiepileptic for focal seizures. As a narrow-spectrum antiseizure medication, it is not useful for generalized seizures. Choice B (Fosphenytoin) is incorrect. Although fosphenytoin is a broad-spectrum antiseizure medication that blocks sodium channels, it is a second-line choice in the treatment of status epilepticus, not first-line. Choice C (Levetiracetam) is incorrect. Levetiracetam is a broad-spectrum antiepileptic medication thought to act by binding to synaptic vesicle protein 2A, resulting in neuronal inhibition and increased GABA signaling. However, it is used for benzodiazepine-refractory status epilepticus, not as initial therapy. Choice E (Phenobarbital) is incorrect. While phenobarbital can be effective for controlling seizures, it is not first-line pharmacotherapy due to slow administration rate and adverse effects including prolonged sedation and hypotension. For benzodiazepine-refractory status epilepticus, second-line treatments include intravenous levetiracetam, intravenous fosphenytoin, or intravenous valproic acid.
▶ Cardiovascular System Aortic Valve Stenosis 1 questions
Source: 9A #37
A 12-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 6-month history of chest pain with exertion. He has had a cardiac murmur since birth. He is at the 90th percentile for height and 75th percentile for weight. His pulse is 72/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 112/72 mm Hg. A suprasternal notch thrill and a grade 4/6 ejection murmur are heard over the midsternum and beneath the right clavicle; a click is heard at the apex. An ECG is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A. Aortic stenosis B. Atrial septal defect C. Patent ductus arteriosus D. Pulmonary stenosis E. Ventricular septal defect
Correct Answer: A. Aortic stenosis
This patient with exertional angina, systolic murmur heard beneath the right clavicle, and signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on ECG likely has congenital aortic stenosis. Aortic stenosis should be suspected in patients with systolic murmurs of crescendo-decrescendo pattern with radiation to the carotids in the upper right sternal border. Symptoms include exertional angina and/or syncope and dyspnea. Evaluation is through echocardiography, which will show a narrowed aortic valve that may be uni- or bicuspid in congenital cases. Aortic valve stenosis regardless of cause results in impaired cardiac output once the condition is significant enough to limit blood flow. Resultant decreased cardiac output causes symptoms of angina, dyspnea, and syncope, often with exertion, until the stenosis is critical, at which time symptoms can occur with rest. Early-onset aortic stenosis (before age 40 to 60 years) can occur in the setting of congenital valve anomalies or chronic rheumatic heart disease. Examination findings include a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur best heard at the upper right sternal border, and pulsus parvus et tardus (weak and delayed) may be noted on examination of peripheral pulses. Severe aortic stenosis can lead to left ventricular hypertrophy as seen in this patient's ECG with voltage greater than 35 mm when summing the QRS height in specific leads. Echocardiography confirms the diagnosis and will show a decreased cross-sectional valve area, increased transvalvular pressure gradient, and increased blood flow velocity. Choice B (Atrial septal defect) is incorrect. Atrial septal defect presents with a wide, fixed split-second heart sound, without a systolic murmur or signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on ECG. Right ventricular hypertrophy may be present due to increased left-to-right shunt, though such a finding is variable. Echocardiography would show a shunt on an agitated saline study. Choice C (Patent ductus arteriosus) is incorrect. Patent ductus arteriosus presents with a continuous, machine-like murmur heard radiating to the scapula, not a systolic murmur at the right sternal border. Patent ductus arteriosus also does not cause left ventricular hypertrophy. Rather, increased right-sided pressures may be present due to the shunt of high-pressure aortic blood into the pulmonary circulation. Choice D (Pulmonary stenosis) is incorrect. Pulmonary (pulmonic valve) stenosis presents with right ventricular hypertrophy and a systolic murmur at the upper left sternal border. Pulmonary stenosis is common in tetralogy of Fallot, which also presents with a ventricular septal defect, right ventricular hypertrophy, and overriding aorta. Choice E (Ventricular septal defect) is incorrect. Ventricular septal defect results in a left-to-right shunt from the left to right ventricle and presents with a midsternal holosystolic murmur. Right ventricular hypertrophy may be present.
▶ Uncategorized Duodenal Atresia 1 questions
Source: 9A #38
A newborn with Down syndrome presents with bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. The mother reports polyhydramnios during pregnancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis? A) Air-contrast enema B) Meckel scan C) Rectal biopsy D) Rectosigmoidoscopy E) X-ray of the chest and abdomen
Correct Answer: E) X-ray of the chest and abdomen
Duodenal atresia is a failure of recanalization of the duodenal lumen and is a known gastrointestinal complication of Down syndrome. The combination of Down syndrome, prenatal polyhydramnios, and neonatal bilious vomiting with abdominal distension is highly suggestive of duodenal atresia. The most appropriate confirmatory test is an x-ray of the chest and abdomen, which will demonstrate an abnormal bowel gas pattern with gastric distention and paucity of distal bowel gas suggestive of downstream obstruction. Pathophysiology: In utero, the fetus cannot recycle amniotic fluid past the atretic duodenal segment, leading to polyhydramnios as a prenatal clue. At birth, ingested milk or formula cannot pass the narrowed or absent duodenal lumen, causing vomiting (bilious if atresia is distal to the sphincter of Oddi). This leads to dehydration, decreased urine output, dry mucous membranes, hypoglycemia, and failure to thrive. Choice A (Air-contrast enema) is incorrect. Air-contrast enema is used to diagnose and treat intussusception, which presents with colicky abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and bloody mucoid stools—features not present in this case. Choice B (Meckel scan) is incorrect. A Meckel scan (technetium-99m pertechnetate gastric-mucosa scan) is used to diagnose Meckel diverticulum, which results from persistence of the vitelline duct. Meckel diverticulum presents with acute or chronic hematochezia or melena, often painless, potentially leading to iron deficiency anemia. Choice C (Rectal biopsy) is incorrect. Rectal biopsy is used to diagnose Hirschsprung disease (congenital megacolon), which presents with colonic distention and failure to pass meconium, not bilious vomiting. Choice D (Rectosigmoidoscopy) is incorrect. Rectosigmoidoscopy is used to diagnose lower gastrointestinal conditions such as polyps, malignancy, and volvulus. This patient presents with vomiting suggestive of an upper gastrointestinal cause. Treatment involves correction of fluid and electrolyte abnormalities followed by surgical correction such as gastrojejunostomy or duodenoduodenostomy to bypass the atretic segment.
▶ Immune System Adenosine Deaminase Deficiency 1 questions
Source: 9A #40
A 3-month-old boy is admitted to the hospital because of a 4-day history of diarrhea. He has had three similar episodes during the past 6 weeks; each episode lasted approximately 7 days. During each episode, oral hydration provided little relief for only 1 or 2 days. He also has had a 0.3-kg weight loss during the past week. He has a 10-day history of diaper rash that has not responded to topical nystatin. No one else in his household has been ill. The patient's 3-year-old female cousin is hospitalized and receiving mechanical ventilation because of pneumonia. The patient's family lives in an isolated religious commune; his parents are second cousins. Several individuals in the mother's family have died in childhood from infection. The patient is exclusively breastfed. He is at the 50th percentile for length and weight. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows a mild diaper rash with erythema. Diagnostic studies are most likely to show which of the following findings? A. Decreased adenosine deaminase (ADA) activity B. Decreased neutrophil oxidative burst activity C. Increased serum IgE concentration D. Increased T-lymphocyte count E. Neutrophil elastase (ELANE) gene mutation F. Wiskott-Aldrich protein (WASP) gene mutation
Correct Answer: A. Decreased adenosine deaminase (ADA) activity
This patient most likely has severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), and diagnostic studies would most likely show adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency, one of the most common causes of SCID. SCID is a syndrome of failed B and T lymphocyte activity leading to impaired cellular and humoral immunity. Patients with SCID typically present with numerous infections in early life, including a characteristic combination of viral, bacterial, and fungal infections such as otitis media, oral thrush, pneumonia, gastroenteritis, and cutaneous fungal infections. This patient's presentation of recurrent diarrhea, fungal diaper rash unresponsive to nystatin, and a family history of childhood deaths from infection with consanguineous parents are classic features suggesting SCID. ADA deficiency is a frequent underlying cause of SCID. ADA deficiency results in the accumulation of a purine derivative called deoxyadenosine within the purine salvage pathway, which is converted to 5'-deoxyadenosine triphosphate and inhibits the action of ribonucleotide reductase, thereby preventing DNA synthesis in B and T lymphocytes. The diagnosis is established through immune cell counts, mitogen assay, genetic testing, and chest x-ray findings which may show the absence of a thymic shadow. Treatment is aimed at appropriately preventing and treating infections; currently the only definitive treatment is bone marrow transplant, although genetic therapies are under development. Choice B is incorrect because decreased neutrophil oxidative burst activity is associated with myeloperoxidase deficiency, which is typically a mild disorder caused by mutations in the MPO gene and presents with recurrent Candida albicans infections. Choice C is incorrect because increased serum IgE concentration is associated with Hyperimmunoglobulin E recurrent infection syndrome, which presents with eczema and recurrent pulmonary and skin infections along with findings such as scoliosis, recurrent fractures, and coarse facial features. Choice D is incorrect because T-lymphocyte counts are typically decreased in immunodeficiency, not increased. Choice E is incorrect because neutrophil elastase (ELANE) gene mutations are associated with cyclic neutropenia, characterized by recurrent episodes of neutropenia occurring every 14 to 35 days. Choice F is incorrect because Wiskott-Aldrich protein (WASP) gene mutations cause Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, an X-linked disorder affecting actin cytoskeleton rearrangement and typically presenting with thrombocytopenia, eczema, and recurrent infections, with a different clinical presentation than this patient.
▶ Nervous System Special Senses Adenovirus Conjunctivitis and Keratoconjunctivitis 1 questions
Source: 9A #41
A 5-year-old girl is brought to the office because of a 3-day history of photophobia and crusted discharge in the eyes when she wakes in the morning. Examination shows diffuse erythema of the bulbar and palpebral conjunctivae, and mucopurulent discharge in both eyes. There is no change in visual acuity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Allergic conjunctivitis B) Anterior uveitis C) Bacterial conjunctivitis D) Blepharitis E) Endophthalmitis
Correct Answer: C) Bacterial conjunctivitis
This 5-year-old patient presents with photophobia, mucopurulent discharge from the eyes, and erythema of the conjunctivae, which is most consistent with bacterial conjunctivitis. The most common causative organisms are Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Moraxella (Branhamella) catarrhalis. Bacterial conjunctivitis occurs commonly in the pediatric population, particularly in children with exposure risks such as attending school or daycare. Transmission occurs through hand-to-eye contact, respiratory droplets, or contact with fomites. Patients typically present with acute-onset erythema of the conjunctivae combined with mucopurulent discharge, which differentiates it from other causes of conjunctivitis. Treatment requires topical antibiotics (aminoglycosides, macrolides, or fluoroquinolones) for 5 to 7 days, with broader-spectrum agents if risk factors for resistant organisms like Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Staphylococcus aureus are present. Prevention is achieved through avoiding hand-to-eye contact, handwashing, and good hand hygiene. Choice A (Allergic conjunctivitis) is incorrect because it typically presents with watery discharge following allergen exposure, not mucopurulent discharge. This patient has no known allergen exposure. Choice B (Anterior uveitis) is incorrect because it refers to inflammation of the uvea (iris, ciliary body, choroid) rather than conjunctival infection. Anterior uveitis can result from systemic inflammatory disorders (sarcoidosis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis) or infectious causes (herpes simplex virus, syphilis, Lyme disease), but this patient's presentation is more suggestive of conjunctival rather than uveal involvement. Choice D (Blepharitis) is incorrect because it is a chronic inflammatory condition affecting the eyelid margins, presenting with discomfort, redness, and irritation of the eyelid borders themselves, not diffuse erythema of the conjunctivae as seen in this patient. Choice E (Endophthalmitis) is incorrect because it refers to inflammation of the inner surface of the eye with exudative colonization of the vitreous and aqueous fluids. It can occur endogenously from hematogenous seeding or exogenously from trauma. Patients typically present with decreased vision and pain rather than erythematous conjunctivae.
▶ Musculoskeletal System Chondromalacia 1 questions
Source: 9A #44
A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 6-month history of intermittent, bilateral knee pain. The pain is worse after prolonged sitting. She has not had fever or "locking" or swelling of her knees. Occasionally her knees feel as though they will "give way." She is not sexually active. She does not play sports. She has no history of serious illness, and her only medication is occasional ibuprofen for knee pain. The patient is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 91 kg (200 lb); BMI is 34 kg/m2. Her blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg; other vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows truncal obesity. Examination of the lower extremities shows flat feet. When asked to stand, the medial aspects of the patient's knees touch. Sexual maturity rating is 5 for breast and pubic hair development. Range of motion of the hips and knees is full; there is no knee effusion. Muscle strength is 5/5 in the lower extremities bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's knee pain? A) Anterior cruciate ligament insufficiency B) Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease C) Osgood-Schlatter disease D) Patellofemoral pain syndrome E) Reactive arthritis F) Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
Correct Answer: D) Patellofemoral pain syndrome
This patient presents with intermittent bilateral knee pain that is worse after prolonged sitting without a history of trauma to the knees. The most likely cause of her knee pain is patellofemoral pain syndrome. Patellofemoral pain syndrome is a common overuse disorder that classically presents with anterior knee pain that is worsened with prolonged sitting, running, squatting, or when navigating stairs. The cause is thought to be due to deviation of patellar tracking as a result of abnormal force generation and distribution as the patella tracks within the femoral trochlea. This patient's examination findings of flat feet and knee malalignment (genu valgum - medial aspects of knees touching when standing) are consistent with biomechanical factors that contribute to patellofemoral pain syndrome. The diagnosis is clinical, as x-ray findings often do not correlate well with reported symptoms. Risk factors include overuse, malalignment, and history of trauma. Treatment is conservative with activity modification and NSAIDs for pain relief, along with physical therapy focusing on strengthening the lower body kinetic chain. Choice A (Anterior cruciate ligament insufficiency) is incorrect because ligamentous injuries typically occur as acute sports injuries with abrupt knee pain and severe swelling, often from sudden deceleration, direction changes, or direct blow causing hyperextension or valgus deformation. This patient has no trauma history. Choice B (Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease) is incorrect because this condition involves idiopathic avascular necrosis of the hip (not knee), most commonly occurs in children aged 3-12 years, and presents with limp and hip pain, not bilateral knee pain in a 16-year-old. Choice C (Osgood-Schlatter disease) is not the most likely cause because while it occurs in adolescents, it is primarily an osteochondrosis/traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle that typically presents with pain along the anterior proximal tibia exacerbated by kneeling or knee extension. This patient is sedentary and not athletic, and has bilateral diffuse symptoms worse with sitting. Choice E (Reactive arthritis) is incorrect because this spondylarthritis presents with joint pain developing after infection elsewhere in the body, classically with arthritis, enthesitis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis. No such systemic findings are present in this patient. Choice F (Slipped capital femoral epiphysis) is incorrect because while it occurs in overweight children aged 10-15 years, it results in hip pain and impaired gait from displacement of the femoral epiphysis relative to the femoral neck. This patient presents with knee pain, not hip pain.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Phenylketonuria 1 questions
Source: 9A #47
A male infant undergoes initial examination following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery at term. The mother received routine prenatal care. Maternal prenatal screening at 8 weeks' gestation suggested PKU; the mother received nutritional counseling. The newborn is at the 50th percentile for length and weight and at the 40th percentile for head circumference. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Which of the following measures is most likely to decrease this patient's risk for abnormal neurologic development? A. Limited exposure to sunlight B. Low-protein diet C. Carbidopa-levodopa therapy D. Tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy E. No specific measures are indicated
Correct Answer: B. Low-protein diet
PKU refers to an inborn error of metabolism in the PAH gene, which encodes phenylalanine hydroxylase. This enzyme deficiency results in accumulation of phenylalanine, which can cause musty odor of skin and urine, eczema, seizures, tremors, and intellectual disability if left untreated. A low-protein diet decreases the patient's risk for these neurologic consequences by limiting phenylalanine intake. Key Concept: PKU is an autosomal recessive disorder with approximately 1000 different mutations that can cause the condition. The overall incidence is 1 in 15,000 patients in the United States, with increased incidence in White and Native American populations. Treatment requires lifelong dietary therapy maintaining decreased phenylalanine and adequate tyrosine intake. Other compounds such as aspartame should also be avoided. PKU is typically detected by newborn screening. Often newborns appear normal at birth, although increased phenylalanine concentrations can be present depending on the mutation type. The diagnosis is confirmed during newborn screening with evaluation of phenylalanine hydroxylase function. Choice A: Limited exposure to sunlight is incorrect. This measure is critical in xeroderma pigmentosum (extreme UV sensitivity) and photosensitivity conditions such as porphyrias or following tetracycline therapy, not PKU. Choice C: Carbidopa-levodopa therapy is incorrect. This is the mainstay treatment for Parkinson disease, which typically develops in older individuals with parkinsonism, slow movements, tremors, and muscle rigidity. It is not indicated for PKU. Choice D: Tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy is incorrect. These agents are used primarily in targeted cancer treatment and would be inappropriate and unhelpful in the management of PKU. Choice E: No specific measures are indicated is incorrect. This patient with likely PKU requires dietary therapy throughout life to avoid inappropriate accumulation of phenylalanine and prevent neurologic sequelae.
▶ Blood Lymphoreticular System ABO incompatibility 1 questions
Source: 9A #49
A 2-day-old female newborn is brought to the emergency department by her parents because they think she appears "more yellow" than on discharge from the hospital 12 hours ago. She was born at 38 weeks' gestation to a 29-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, who received routine prenatal care. The patient weighed 3345 g (7 lb 6 oz) at birth. Examination at the age of 36 hours showed mild jaundice but no other abnormalities. The parents report that since discharge their daughter has been breast-feeding well every 2 to 3 hours. She has passed five stools and has started making transitional stools. She has not had fever and has no ill contacts. Today, she weighs 3232 g (7 lb 2 oz). Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 144/min, and respirations are 28/min. On examination, she is vigorous. There is jaundice of the face and chest but not of the abdomen. No ecchymoses are noted. There is no hepatosplenomegaly. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Her serum total bilirubin concentration is 19 mg/dL, with direct component of 0.6 mg/dL. The infant's blood group is B, Rh-positive. The mother's blood group is O, Rh-positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A. Restrict breast feeding B. Fasting hepatic ultrasonography C. Phototherapy D. Exchange transfusion E. Intravenous administration of fluids
Correct Answer: C) Phototherapy
Hemolytic disease of the newborn refers to a condition where fetal red blood cells are destroyed due to blood group incompatibility with the mother. This patient presents with jaundice, hyperbilirubinemia, and likely has a positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test consistent with ABO incompatibility hemolytic disease of the newborn. In assessing newborn jaundice, the initial step is to differentiate between indirect versus direct hyperbilirubinemia through serum bilirubin assessment. This patient has predominantly indirect hyperbilirubinemia (total 19 mg/dL, direct 0.6 mg/dL) consistent with hemolysis. A direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is necessary in patients with known ABO blood group incompatibility between infant and mother (infant B, Rh-positive; mother O, Rh-positive). While ABO incompatibility is often milder than Rh incompatibility, it can result in clinically significant hyperbilirubinemia requiring intervention. With a serum total bilirubin concentration of 19 mg/dL in a 2-day-old term infant (38 weeks gestation), this exceeds the phototherapy threshold and phototherapy should be initiated to prevent neurotoxicity (kernicterus). Choice A (Restrict breast feeding) is incorrect because this patient's increased bilirubin concentration is related to ABO incompatibility hemolysis, not breast-feeding or breast milk jaundice. Continued breast-feeding provides important nutritional and immunologic benefits and should be encouraged. Choice B (Fasting hepatic ultrasonography) is incorrect. While hepatic ultrasonography can evaluate liver parenchyma, blood vessels, and biliary system abnormalities, this patient's hyperbilirubinemia is related to ABO incompatibility, not a hepatobiliary abnormality. Choice D (Exchange transfusion) is not the best answer. Exchange transfusion is reserved for severe cases of hyperbilirubinemia typically greater than 20 mg/dL. This patient's bilirubin concentration of 19 mg/dL in a term infant does not yet require this therapy. The patient would benefit most from phototherapy as the initial management. Choice E (Intravenous administration of fluids) is incorrect. This patient shows no signs or symptoms of hypovolemia but rather the sequelae of increased bilirubin concentrations. Intravenous fluids are not necessary. The patient should continue receiving adequate nutrition through continued breast-feeding.
▶ Behavioral Health Language Disorder 1 questions
Source: 5A #4
A 2½-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because she is concerned about his language development. He uses fewer words than his two older siblings did at the same age. He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He began walking at the age of 11 months. He feeds himself, plays well with his siblings, and does well in day care. Motor development is appropriate for age. He knows 100 words but does not use them in phrases. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluating this child's language development? A) Intelligence testing B) Speech evaluation C) Audiometry D) MRI of the inner ears E) No further evaluation is indicated at this time
Correct Answer: C) Audiometry
Children with developmental delay should undergo audiometry to evaluate for hearing loss. Failure to detect hearing loss can cause preventable delays in a child's language, social, and educational development. This 2½-year-old presents with isolated language delay (knows 100 words but does not use them in phrases) with otherwise normal developmental milestones (walking at 11 months, normal motor development, normal play and social interaction), which is highly concerning for hearing loss as the underlying etiology. Hearing loss in children may occur because of either conductive or sensorineural etiologies. A careful history and general physical examination should be performed to evaluate for possible syndromic features. Weber and Rinne tests can distinguish between conductive and sensorineural hearing loss. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends routine audiometry screening for all school-aged children. Choice A (Intelligence testing) is not an appropriate initial test for isolated delay in language development. The pattern of selective language delay with normal other developmental milestones makes hearing loss more likely than global developmental delay. Choice B (Speech evaluation) may be useful for identifying abnormalities of speech production and may be warranted eventually given the low-normal vocabulary for age. However, audiometry should be performed first to rule out hearing loss as the primary cause before pursuing speech evaluation. Choice D (MRI of the inner ears) may be indicated based on the results of audiometry and a careful physical examination but is not an appropriate initial test. MRI is not a first-line diagnostic tool for suspected hearing loss. Choice E (No further evaluation is indicated at this time) is incorrect because failure to detect hearing loss can result in preventable delays in language, social, and educational development. Early detection and intervention are critical in pediatric hearing loss.
▶ Behavioral Health Autism Spectrum Disorder 1 questions
Source: 8A #42
An 8-year-old girl is brought to the physician because her parents are concerned that she is different from their older child and prefers to be alone instead of socializing with peers or family. She carries a doll that she found at a yard sale wherever she goes but never plays with it. Whenever she is without the doll, she becomes distraught and has a tantrum. The parents once invited a girl from their daughter's class to their home, but the patient appeared disinterested and would not play with the other girl. The patient's teachers report that she is often off task and distracted in her second-grade class but that she answers direct questions. She does not participate in games at recess, and she tends to drift off by herself and wander about the playground. She is at the 50th percentile for height, 30th percentile for weight, and 90th percentile for head circumference. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. During the examination, the patient holds an undressed doll by its feet. She makes little eye contact. She occasionally repeats the physician's words instead of answering questions. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Learning disorder B) Mild intellectual developmental disorder C) Oppositional defiant disorder D) Parent-child relational problem E) Pervasive developmental disorder
Correct Answer: E) Pervasive developmental disorder
Pervasive developmental disorder, which has been reclassified as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), includes a group of neurodevelopmental/neurodivergent syndromes that are characterized by atypical forms of social communication and interaction. ASD includes autism, Asperger syndrome, childhood disintegrative disorder, and pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified. ASD is characterized by a broad range of signs and symptoms involving restricted and repetitive patterns of behavior or activities. Children with autism often display decreased interest in socializing and may have challenging behaviors conflicting with established societal norms. Children may also display a narrow and focused range of interests, an increased reliance on routine, and apprehension to change or unexpected circumstances. The clinical manifestations of ASD typically present within the first 2 years of life with an observed delay or regression of communication and/or social skills. This typically includes decreased nonverbal communication, such as eye contact and facial expressions. Management of ASD is individualized depending on the clinical manifestations and degree of social distress for the patient. Therapy involves behavioral, developmental, social, and educational interventions to improve social functioning, communication skills, and academic functioning. This patient demonstrates classic features of ASD: persistent preference for solitude over peer interaction, restricted interests (carrying a specific doll without true play), repetitive behaviors (reliance on the doll as a comfort object), decreased eye contact, echolalia (repeating the physician's words), and difficulty with social reciprocity. The relatively normal cognitive responses to direct questions help differentiate this from intellectual developmental disorder. Incorrect Answers: Choice A - Learning disorder is not likely for this patient. Learning disorders are characterized by a persistent impairment in reading, written expression, or mathematical ability. Patients may have difficulty with specific skills relating to these subjects. Learning disorders may coexist with ASD but do not explain the social and communication deficits observed. Choice B - Mild intellectual developmental disorder refers to mild impairment related to abstract or theoretical thinking, and patients may also have decreased social and daily functional skills. They are typically able to adapt to living in society with life-skills training in specific areas. However, this patient answers direct questions appropriately, suggesting adequate cognitive functioning. Choice C - Oppositional defiant disorder manifests as a persistent pattern of angry mood, defiant behavior, and vindictiveness that can cause impaired functioning in the child and distress to their caretakers. The patient's withdrawal and social avoidance do not fit the defiant behavioral pattern of ODD. Choice D - Parent-child relational problem is diagnosed by the presence of pervasive dissatisfaction with the relationship, persistent thoughts of running away, and a perception that professional help is needed for maintaining the relationship. It often manifests as difficulties with conflict resolution that may escalate quickly or be marked by withdrawal that prevents resolution. There are frequent feelings of anger, contempt, apathy, and sadness. This diagnosis does not address the core social communication deficits and restricted interests observed. Educational Objective: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD), formerly classified as pervasive developmental disorder, includes a group of syndromes including autism, Asperger syndrome, childhood disintegrative disorder, and pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified. ASD refers to a range of neurodevelopmental/neurodivergent syndromes that are characterized by atypical forms of social communication and interaction. External manifestations include avoidance of eye contact, narrow and focused interests, disinterest in typical forms of socialization and play, and a reliance on predictable routine.
▶ Male Reproductive Testicular Rupture 1 questions
Source: 5A #6
A previously healthy 9-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of moderate groin pain since he participated in a hockey game 24 hours ago. He recalls no trauma or injury to this area. He reports a decreased appetite today. He has not had fever. He appears well. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows edema of the left aspect of the scrotum. There is marked tenderness to palpation of the superior aspect of the left testicle; the pain does not improve with elevation of the testicle. A 3-mm area of bluish discoloration overlays the point of maximal tenderness; there is no erythema. Cremasteric reflex is intact. Genital and pubic hair development are Tanner stage 2. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Epididymitis B) Incarcerated hernia C) Orchitis D) Testicular hematoma E) Torsion of the appendix testis
Correct Answer: E) Torsion of the appendix testis
The correct diagnosis is torsion of the appendix testis. The appendix testis is a vestigial structure typically located on the anterior and superior aspect of the testis with a pedunculated shape that predisposes it to torsion. When torsed, it may appear as a small blue or black mass in the scrotum. Patients with torsion of the appendix testis present with groin pain, a nontender testicle, a tender palpable localized mass adjacent to one pole of the testicle, and an intact cremasteric reflex. The diagnosis may be made clinically or with ultrasound when testicular torsion cannot be excluded. Management is generally supportive with analgesics and scrotal support. Choice A (Epididymitis) is a common cause of painful scrotal swelling from acute infection and inflammation of the epididymis, commonly secondary to sexually transmitted infections such as Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae in younger males. Patients with epididymitis may have moderate pain relief with elevation of the testis, which is not seen in this patient. Choice B (Incarcerated hernia) refers to hernia contents becoming trapped in the defect, potentially resulting in obstruction if bowel is involved. An inguinal hernia becoming incarcerated would typically present with severe tenderness and a larger mass with swelling in the inguinal area, not the localized findings described. Choice C (Orchitis) is inflammation of the testes from infection, sometimes from the paramyxovirus causing mumps. Clinical manifestations include fever, myalgias, and fatigue. This patient has no fever and does not have the systemic symptoms associated with orchitis. Choice D (Testicular hematoma) can occur from blunt scrotal trauma and presents with testicular swelling, warmth, and pain. A 3-mm area of bluish discoloration is more likely caused by torsion of an appendix testis, not testicular hematoma, especially with no history of trauma. This case demonstrates the classic presentation of torsion of the appendix testis with localized tenderness at the superior aspect of the testicle, a characteristic small blue mass, an intact cremasteric reflex (which differentiates it from true testicular torsion), and lack of improvement with elevation.
▶ Immune System Hypogammaglobulinemia/Agammaglobulinemia, X-linked (Bruton) 1 questions
Source: 5A #7
A 1-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination. He completed a 1-week course of intravenous ceftriaxone followed by a 5-day course of amoxicillin for pneumococcal pneumonia 2 weeks ago and has been asymptomatic since then. He has had six episodes of acute otitis media during the past 6 months. Immunizations are up-to-date. He is at the 50th percentile for length and weight. Tympanic membranes are dull with clear effusions. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 12 g/dL, Leukocyte count 8500/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 40%, Lymphocytes 50%, Monocytes 10%, Platelet count 420,000/mm³, Serum IgA 10 mg/dL, IgE 10 IU/mL, IgG 100 mg/dL, IgM 20 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment of this patient's underlying condition? A) Amoxicillin prophylaxis B) Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor therapy C) Oral prednisone therapy D) Monthly infusion of immune globulin E) Splenectomy
Correct Answer: D) Monthly infusion of immune globulin
This patient has X-linked agammaglobulinemia, defined by defects in the Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) gene, which is necessary for all stages of B lymphocyte development and proliferation. Deficiency of this enzyme results in failed B lymphocyte development. As B lymphocytes are responsible for secreting immunoglobulins once they differentiate into plasma cells, a defect in B lymphocyte maturation leads to a dearth of plasma cells and severely decreased immunoglobulin concentrations of every class, including IgM, IgG, IgE, and IgA—all of which are markedly low in this patient. The recurrent episodes of pneumococcal pneumonia and acute otitis media reflect the impaired humoral immunity characteristic of this condition. Monthly infusions of immune globulin (intravenous immunoglobulin concentrates) are the appropriate treatment to provide passive immunity and prevent recurrent infections. Amoxicillin prophylaxis (Choice A) is given to patients with congenital heart disease or those with a history of endocarditis undergoing certain procedures. While amoxicillin would treat recurrent episodes of otitis media, it does not correct the underlying immunodeficiency. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor therapy (Choice B) is used to stimulate production of granulocytes in patients receiving cytotoxic chemotherapy. It is not the treatment for agammaglobulinemia, which involves defective B lymphocytes, not granulocytes. Oral prednisone therapy (Choice C) results in immunosuppression and increased risk for infections, making it inappropriate for a patient with an already compromised immune system. Splenectomy (Choice E) is employed for patients with refractory hereditary spherocytosis. Moreover, splenectomy increases the risk for infection with encapsulated organisms such as Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Streptococcus pneumoniae—this patient already has increased susceptibility to these organisms due to his immunodeficiency. Educational Objective: Patients with X-linked agammaglobulinemia have mutations in the BTK gene, which encodes a tyrosine kinase essential for all stages of B lymphocyte development and proliferation. They present with recurrent infections caused by impaired humoral immunity and have decreased or absent concentrations of all immunoglobulin subclasses. Treatment is with intravenous immune globulin infusions.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Acute Rheumatic Fever 2 questions
Source: 5A #9
A 6-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her father because of a 36-hour history of fever and a 1-day history of pain and swelling of her joints. The pain and swelling began in her right knee, then increased to involve both knees, and has now migrated to her left ankle and left elbow. She is currently unable to walk because of the pain. Two weeks ago, she had a sore throat that resolved after 2 days without treatment. She has no known drug allergies. She appears uncomfortable when she moves. She is at the 50th percentile for height and weight. Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 136/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Examination shows no rash. There is a grade 2/6, pansystolic, high-pitched murmur that is heard best at the apex and accentuated when she makes a fist. There is mild swelling of the left elbow and both knees; the left elbow and left knee are warm. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 110 mm/h. An antistreptolysin O titer is 800 Todd/U (N<240). Salicylate therapy is begun and results in marked improvement of the patient's symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to prevent a recurrence of this patient's disorder? A) Clindamycin B) Erythromycin C) Penicillin D) Prednisone E) No pharmacotherapy is indicated
Correct Answer: C) Penicillin
This patient presents with acute rheumatic fever (ARF), a sequela of untreated group A Streptococcus pharyngitis that occurs 2-3 weeks after the initial infection. The diagnosis is supported by the clinical presentation including polyarthritis (migratory arthritis affecting multiple joints), carditis (apical pansystolic murmur consistent with mitral regurgitation), elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (110 mm/h), and elevated antistreptolysin O titer (800 Todd/U), which all meet Jones criteria. The pathophysiology involves a type II hypersensitivity reaction where streptococcal M protein molecularly mimics cardiac myosin and other cardiac self-antigens, leading to autoimmune-mediated cardiac inflammation and damage. Per American Heart Association (AHA) guidelines, secondary prevention of ARF recurrence requires prolonged penicillin therapy (typically monthly intramuscular penicillin G or daily oral penicillin V) to prevent subsequent group A Streptococcus infections and further valvular damage. Choice A (Clindamycin) and Choice B (Erythromycin) are appropriate alternatives only for primary prevention in patients with penicillin allergies but are not first-line agents for secondary prevention in non-allergic patients. Choice D (Prednisone) may reduce acute inflammation but does not prevent disease recurrence. Choice E (No pharmacotherapy) is incorrect because failure to administer prolonged penicillin prophylaxis significantly increases the risk of ARF recurrence and progressive, irreversible mitral valve damage (regurgitation, stenosis, or prolapse). Penicillin is the gold standard for both preventing the initial development of ARF after streptococcal infection and for preventing recurrent episodes in patients with established disease.
Source: 8A #43
A 10-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother 3 hours after she refused to get out of bed this morning. Over the past 4 days, she has had fever, malaise, and severe pain in her elbows, wrists, and knees. The family recently lived in a refugee camp. She appears flushed and acutely ill. Her pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 100/40 mm Hg. The knee and ankle joints are warm and swollen. A grade 4/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex and radiates to the left axilla. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Dengue fever B) Lyme disease C) Malaria D) Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease) E) Rheumatic fever F) Typhoid fever
Correct Answer: E) Rheumatic fever
The most likely diagnosis is rheumatic fever, characterized by arthritis and a murmur suggestive of mitral regurgitation. Rheumatic fever is a sequela of untreated Streptococcus (group A) infection, commonly pharyngitis, in which there is a type II hypersensitivity reaction to self-antigens having a similar structure to, and thus molecularly mimicking, streptococcal M protein. The cause is related to immune cross-reactivity between streptococcal M protein and human cardiac myosin proteins. Diagnosis is made by the Jones criteria, which describe many of the core clinical features of rheumatic fever, including the major criteria of polyarthritis, carditis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, and Sydenham chorea, as well as minor criteria of fever, leukocytosis, arthralgia, and PR interval prolongation. Patients often have an increased antistreptolysin O titer. Complications of rheumatic fever include mitral valve inflammation leading to long-term sequelae of chronic mitral valve regurgitation, prolapse, or stenosis. Treatment of the initial streptococcal infection is effective for reducing the risk for developing rheumatic fever. Per American Heart Association guidelines, once rheumatic fever has developed, treatment includes salicylates and a prolonged course of monthly penicillin treatments to reduce the risk for recurrence and further valvular damage. Dengue fever (Choice A) is caused by a flavivirus transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes in endemic tropical and subtropical regions. Primary infection is typically benign, but a second exposure can result in dengue fever, which typically presents with a high fever, headache, myalgias, and arthralgias. Severe cases may be complicated by diffuse hemorrhagic disease and/or distributive shock. Lyme disease (Choice B) is a tick-borne disease caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi and characteristically causes erythema chronicum migrans, an expanding rash that may have a central ring-like clearing. Later stages can be characterized by carditis, atrioventricular heart block, facial nerve palsy (which may be bilateral), migratory arthralgias, and, if left untreated, encephalopathy and chronic arthritis. Malaria (Choice C) typically presents with fatigue, fever, chills, and anemia in a patient with recent exposure to an endemic region, particularly within the tropical latitudes of Africa or Central/South America. Plasmodium falciparum infection can be complicated by severe disease, including cerebral malaria and acute kidney injury. Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease) (Choice D) is a multisystemic vasculitis resulting in acute arteritis with a risk for the development of coronary artery aneurysms. In children, the disease is characterized by fever for at least 5 days, bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, a polymorphous rash, lymphadenopathy, erythema and edema of the hands and feet, and erythema affecting the mucous membranes with dry, cracked lips. Typhoid fever (Choice F) is caused by the gram-negative bacillus Salmonella typhi and typically presents with fever, abdominal pain, and nonbloody diarrhea. Physical examination may show a characteristic rash of small red macules (called rose spots) that spreads from the trunk to the extremities.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Congenital Hepatitis B Infection 1 questions
Source: 5A #10
A 3977-g (8-lb 12-oz) male newborn is delivered at term to a 30-year-old primigravid woman. Apgar scores are 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. The mother's hepatitis B status is unknown because she received no prenatal care. Maternal hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) assay is ordered. Examination of the newborn shows no abnormalities. In addition to administration of hepatitis B vaccine (HBV) now, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment regimen for the newborn? A) Observation only B) Hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) only now C) HBIG at 2 and 6 months of age D) HBV at 2 and 6 months of age E) HBIG only if maternal HBsAg is positive and HBV at 2 and 6 months of age
Correct Answer: E) HBIG only if maternal HBsAg is positive and HBV at 2 and 6 months of age
The recommended schedule of hepatitis B immunization and immunoprophylaxis in newborns is dependent on the maternal HBsAg status. If maternal HBsAg is positive or there are signs of active maternal hepatitis B infection, the newborn should receive the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine (HBV) intramuscularly and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) as early as possible, with additional doses of HBV at 2 and 6 months of age. In a HBsAg negative mother, only HBV is needed at birth, 2 months, and 6 months. When maternal HBsAg status is unknown but there is no evidence of active infection, the newborn should receive HBV within 12 hours and HBIG can be delayed until maternal serologies return. If serology returns positive for HBsAg, the infant should receive HBIG within 1 week. If serology returns negative for HBsAg, the newborn does not require HBIG. In either case, the newborn requires the second and third doses of HBV at 2 and 6 months. Choice A (Observation only) is inappropriate without follow-up of maternal HBsAg status; if positive or unknown, HBIG must be given. Choice B (HBIG only now) is unnecessary because there is adequate time (up to 1 week) for maternal HBsAg assay to return before HBIG administration is required. Choice C (HBIG at 2 and 6 months) is incorrect because HBIG is only needed at birth if maternal HBsAg is positive; HBV (not HBIG) is given at 2 and 6 months. Choice D (HBV at 2 and 6 months only) is inadequate if maternal HBsAg titer is positive, as the newborn would miss critical HBIG prophylaxis at birth. Choice E correctly states that HBV should be given now and at 2 and 6 months, with HBIG administered only if maternal HBsAg testing returns positive. Educational Objective: In a mother without prenatal care and unknown HBsAg status, the newborn should receive the first dose of HBV immediately. HBIG should be given if the maternal HBsAg assay returns positive or remains unknown, but not if it returns negative. Regardless of maternal status, the newborn should receive the complete HBV series with additional doses at ages 2 and 6 months.
▶ Endocrine System Diabetes insipidus 1 questions
Source: 5A #11
A 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of a 5-day history of increased thirst and urination and a 2-day history of decreased activity. Although she had been previously toilet trained and dry at night, she has had several episodes of nocturnal wetting over the past week. She has not had fever, vomiting, or diarrhea. Two weeks ago, she fell off her tricycle, but no injuries were apparent. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 160/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 80/60 mm Hg. Examination shows sunken eyes and dry mucous membranes. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Serum Na+ 159 mEq/L, Cl- 125 mEq/L, K+ 4.5 mEq/L, HCO3- 15 mEq/L, Urea nitrogen 43 mg/dL, Glucose 122 mg/dL, Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. Urine pH 6, Specific gravity 1.001, Blood Glucose negative, Protein negative, Osmolality 125 mOsmol/kg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Chronic renal failure B) Diabetes insipidus C) Diabetes mellitus D) Inappropriate secretion of ADH (vasopressin) E) Psychogenic polydipsia F) Urinary tract infection
Correct Answer: B) Diabetes insipidus
Central diabetes insipidus may result from head trauma and is characterized by the inadequate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (ADH, also known as vasopressin) from the posterior pituitary. In this patient, the recent head trauma from falling off a tricycle 2 weeks ago is a significant risk factor. ADH binds V2 receptors of the late distal convoluted tubule and the collecting tubule principal cells, which results in the insertion of aquaporin channels in the luminal surface. This results in increased free water absorption and maintains tight regulation of serum osmolality. When ADH production is inadequate, there is a decreased concentration of aquaporin channels inserted within the principal cells of the collecting tubule, leading to an inability to absorb adequate amounts of free water. This causes dilute urine (low specific gravity of 1.001 and low urine osmolality of 125 mOsmol/kg), dehydration (evidenced by sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, tachycardia, and hypotension), hypernatremia (Na+ 159 mEq/L), and increased serum osmolality. The hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect this increased serum osmolality, which causes the patient to report extreme thirst and polydipsia. Patients typically present with production of large volumes of dilute urine, dehydration, and altered mental status. Treatment is with desmopressin, an analog of vasopressin, which results in recovery of free water via aquaporin insertion in the collecting tubule. Choice A (Chronic renal failure) would be unlikely in this patient with normal creatinine and no history of kidney impairment. Choice C (Diabetes mellitus) can occur in children due to autoimmune destruction of pancreatic islet cells, but this patient has normal glucose concentrations and the laboratory pattern of imbalanced serum and urine osmolality is inconsistent with diabetes mellitus. Choice D (Inappropriate secretion of ADH) can occur secondary to head trauma, but involves excess ADH production, which leads to euvolemic hyponatremia. This patient has hypernatremia and increased serum osmolality, which is opposite to what occurs with SIADH. Choice E (Psychogenic polydipsia) refers to excess intake of free water. Excess free water consumption dilutes urea and sodium which are lost in diuresis; the resultant lack of concentration of sodium and urea within the renal interstitium results in loss of ability to concentrate urine. This results in hyponatremia and decreased serum osmolality, not the hypernatremia and increased serum osmolality seen in this patient. Choice F (Urinary tract infection) can present with dysuria, urinary frequency, foul-smelling urine, suprapubic discomfort, and fever. In pediatric patients, it can also cause nocturia, but this patient does not have fever or other signs of a urinary tract infection. It would not cause hypernatremia and increased serum osmolality. Educational Objective: Central diabetes insipidus may result from head trauma and is characterized by the inadequate secretion of ADH from the posterior pituitary. Patients typically present with large volumes of dilute urine, dehydration, thirst, and increased serum osmolality.
▶ Nervous System Special Senses Retinoblastoma 1 questions
Source: 5A #13
A previously healthy 14-month-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because of a 2-month history of the left eye wandering. She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. Examination of the eye shows left eye wandering and leukocoria (white pupillary reflex). The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Acquired exotropia B) Chronic endophthalmitis C) Congenital glaucoma D) Familial cataract E) Retinoblastoma
Correct Answer: E) Retinoblastoma
This child presents with leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) and sensory exotropia, which is highly suggestive of retinoblastoma. Retinoblastoma is a malignant proliferation of retinal neuroendocrine cells and is the most common ophthalmic malignancy in children. It results from biallelic inactivating mutations of the RB1 gene, which functions as a tumor suppressor by halting cell cycle progression at the G1 checkpoint. RB1 mutations may be either acquired or inherited. In germline mutations, a single mutated allele is inherited, and the second allele acquires a subsequent mutation during development. Infants carrying germline mutations are more likely to have bilateral retinoblastoma with multiple tumor foci, while those with two acquired mutations typically have unilateral disease. Ultrasound of the eye helps define lesion size and detect characteristic intralesional calcifications. Poor prognostic factors include large tumor size, vitreous seeding, iris involvement, and anterior chamber involvement. If undetected, the tumor may invade the optic nerve, increasing metastasis risk to the brain. Most cases are successfully managed with chemotherapy, though advanced cases may require enucleation with careful attention to achieving negative margins at the optic nerve. Acquired exotropia (Choice A) may result from visual sensory deprivation in a non-seeing eye but does not cause leukocoria. Chronic endophthalmitis (Choice B) typically results from hematogenous spread of bacteria or fungus or following ocular surgery. This infant appears well without a suggestive history; endophthalmitis typically presents with pain and conjunctival injection. Congenital glaucoma (Choice C) presents with buphthalmos (enlarged eye), large cornea with potential edema and opacification, increased intraocular pressure, epiphora, photophobia, and blepharospasm or eye rubbing—it does not cause leukocoria. Familial cataract (Choice D) may be unilateral or bilateral and associated with chromosomal abnormalities or inherited mutations. Congenital cataracts are present at birth; this child developed symptoms after normal development for several months, which is more consistent with retinoblastoma. Educational Objective: Leukocoria in an infant raises concern for retinoblastoma. Retinoblastoma is the most common ophthalmic malignancy in children, resulting from biallelic inherited or acquired inactivating mutations of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene. Treatment is with chemotherapy or enucleation.
▶ Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Psoriasis 1 questions
Source: 5A #14
A 10-year-old boy develops a rash on the chest 2 days after returning from a beach vacation. Over the next 2 weeks, the lesions spread to the back, abdomen, and extremities. There are multiple well-demarcated papules and small, thin, round plaques covered with fine white scales over the torso and extremities. Removal of a scale causes minor bleeding at the site. There is pitting of the fingernails. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Cellulitis B) Nummular eczema C) Pityriasis rosea D) Psoriasis E) Tinea corporis
Correct Answer: D) Psoriasis
Guttate psoriasis is characterized by numerous papules and small plaques scattered diffusely over the trunk and extremities. Each individual papule or plaque is covered with a small amount of white scale. Like psoriasis vulgaris, removal of the white scale causes pinpoint bleeding, known as the Auspitz sign, because of thinning of the epidermis over dilated dermal capillaries. Removal of scales can also cause the Koebner phenomenon, the development of new lesions at sites of trauma. All forms of psoriasis, including guttate psoriasis, may be accompanied by nail changes. The most common nail change is pitting, as seen in this patient, though onycholysis (splitting of the nail plate from the nail bed) also occurs. Guttate psoriasis is often triggered by streptococcal infection or medications. Treatment includes topical corticosteroids and vitamin D analogs, with phototherapy, methotrexate, or biologic medications reserved for refractory cases. Cellulitis (Choice A) presents with cutaneous pain, erythema, and induration spreading outward from a source of infection, often an initial abrasion. The numerous papules and small plaques seen here are characteristic of guttate psoriasis, not cellulitis, though streptococcal cellulitis could potentially trigger guttate psoriasis. Nummular eczema (Choice B) describes eczematous patches that are round or coin-shaped. Like other forms of eczema/dermatitis, the rash is initially characterized by erythematous papules and vesicles with exudates and crusting. With chronic scratching, areas become dry, scaly, and excoriated through lichenification. Pityriasis rosea (Choice C) is characterized by acute onset of a pruritic patch followed by numerous smaller macules and patches, commonly involving the trunk and proximal extremities. It is usually induced by viral infection (human herpesvirus 6 and 7). The absence of an initial pruritic patch makes guttate psoriasis more likely in this case. Tinea corporis (Choice E) is caused by superficial dermatophyte infection, most often Trichophyton tonsurans. The classic appearance is a round, annular patch with a scaly border. Potassium hydroxide preparation shows hyphae. Numerous small papules and plaques are not typical. Educational Objective: Guttate psoriasis is a form of psoriasis characterized by small, scaly papules and plaques developing diffusely over the trunk and extremities. It is often triggered by streptococcal infection. Nail pitting and onycholysis may be seen in all types of psoriasis, including guttate.
▶ Uncategorized Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease 1 questions
Source: 5A #16
A 5-year-old boy has had pain in the groin and thigh for 2 weeks; 1 week ago, he began limping. There is no history of recent febrile illness. X-rays of the hips show normal findings. A bone scan shows decreased uptake in the right hip. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Ankylosing spondylitis B) Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease C) Pauciarticular juvenile rheumatoid arthritis D) Septic arthritis E) Slipped capital femoral epiphysis F) Systemic lupus erythematosus G) Toxic synovitis
Correct Answer: B) Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease
Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease refers to idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head that most commonly occurs in younger boys aged 4 to 9 years. The classic presentation includes slow onset of hip pain worsened by activity and associated with a limp. Pain may or may not be relieved with rest. X-rays often show no abnormalities initially, but bone scan characteristically shows decreased perfusion of the femoral head, as demonstrated in this case. MRI may also be used for diagnosis and shows bone marrow changes. Treatment includes preventing weight-bearing on the affected leg and occasionally requires operative intervention or hip arthroplasty. Inadequate treatment results in fragmentation and subsequent deformity of the femoral head. Ankylosing spondylitis (Choice A) is a rheumatologic inflammatory condition involving the vertebrae presenting with subacute to chronic back pain and limited range of motion improved with exercise. It would be unlikely without back pain or systemic inflammatory manifestations. Pauciarticular juvenile rheumatoid arthritis/oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis (Choice C) is most common in girls aged 2 to 3 years, presenting with swelling of a single joint (often the knee) and limping but typically no pain. Involved joints are swollen and tender without erythema, and systemic manifestations are characteristically absent. Septic arthritis (Choice D) results from bacterial infection (most commonly Staphylococcus aureus) of the synovial joint space. The affected joint demonstrates pain, swelling, and erythema. Arthrocentesis shows purulent synovial fluid with greater than 50,000 leukocytes per mm³. This presentation lacks the inflammatory signs typical of septic arthritis. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (Choice E) most commonly occurs in overweight children between ages 10 to 15 years, resulting from displacement of the femoral epiphysis relative to the femoral neck. The age of this patient (5 years) is much younger than typical. Systemic lupus erythematosus (Choice F) is an autoimmune disease presenting with fever, rash, photosensitivity, renal disease, and nonerosive arthritis. It is more common in females and isolated monoarticular joint involvement is insufficient for diagnosis. Toxic synovitis/transient synovitis (Choice G) is a non-infectious arthropathy presenting with joint pain (often hip) frequently following viral infection in children. This patient has no history of recent illness, and the decreased uptake on bone scan is inconsistent with this diagnosis. Educational Objective: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease is idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head typically presenting in young boys with a limp and hip pain. It requires early recognition and intervention to prevent long-term deformity. The characteristic finding of normal X-rays with decreased bone scan uptake is a key diagnostic clue.
▶ Blood Lymphoreticular System Aplastic anemia 1 questions
Source: 5A #18
A 4-year-old African American girl has pallor and progressive malaise 6 weeks after being diagnosed with severe hepatitis A. Examination 4 weeks after diagnosis showed improvement in symptoms. She now has scattered petechiae and ecchymoses. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 6.5 g/dL, Mean corpuscular volume 82 µm³, Leukocyte count 2100/mm³, Reticulocyte count 1.0%, Platelet count 21,000/mm³, Serum iron 250 µg/dL. A blood smear shows normochromic, normocytic cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Anemia, acute hemorrhagic B) Anemia, aplastic C) Anemia, autoimmune hemolytic D) Anemia, chronic disease E) Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency F) Hereditary spherocytosis G) Sickle cell disease H) Sickle cell trait I) Thalassemia minor
Correct Answer: B) Anemia, aplastic
Aplastic anemia (AA) is the most likely cause of this patient's normocytic anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia with normal serum iron following infection with hepatitis A. AA can either be inherited or acquired. Acquired AA may follow exposure to certain types of viruses (hepatitis, Epstein-Barr virus, or HIV), chemicals (benzene), or medications (methimazole, sulfa antibiotics, or chloramphenicol), or it may be idiopathic. The method of bone marrow progenitor destruction is thought to be autoimmune. Patients who develop AA after a viral infection usually present with pancytopenia within 6 months after diagnosis, but symptoms related to pancytopenia such as fatigue, exercise intolerance, pallor, and petechiae often appear sooner. Diagnosis includes bone marrow biopsy and aspiration, which will show a profoundly hypocellular bone marrow with a paucity of progenitor cells of all lineages with replacement by fat and stroma. Importantly, malignant cells and fibrosis will be absent. Treatment is either with immunosuppressive medications or hematopoietic stem cell transplant from a matched sibling if available. Choice A (Anemia, acute hemorrhagic) describes massive blood loss that leads to anemia, common in trauma, and presents with anemia in the absence of leukopenia or thrombocytopenia. Choice C (Anemia, autoimmune hemolytic) results from binding of autoantibody to red blood cell surface antigens, leading to removal via the reticuloendothelial system or intravascular hemolysis. Diagnosis is made by positive Coombs test, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, decreased haptoglobin, and presence of spherocytes and reticulocytes on peripheral smear. Choice D (Anemia, chronic disease) is common in autoimmune and inflammatory disease, chronic infections, and malignancy. Increased hepcidin concentrations decrease iron absorption and increase iron storage in the bone marrow, preventing use of iron by erythrocyte precursors. Choice E (Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency) results in hemolysis upon exposure to medications such as sulfa drugs and oxidants but does not cause marked leukopenia or thrombocytopenia. Choice F (Hereditary spherocytosis) is caused by autosomal dominant mutations in ankyrin, spectrin, and band erythrocyte membrane proteins that lead to loss of normal connection between inner membrane skeleton and outer lipid bilayer. Clinical symptoms include jaundice, splenomegaly, and anemia, with spherocytes on peripheral smear.
