Choice G (Sickle cell disease) is caused by mutations in both β-globin alleles resulting in abnormal hemoglobin S, which polymerizes in hypoxia and causes sickling of erythrocytes. Patients have anemia and sickle forms on peripheral blood smear. Choice H (Sickle cell trait) is caused by mutation in one β-globin allele and infrequently causes symptoms associated with sickle cell disease. Anemia, if present, is mild, and other cell lines show no abnormalities. Choice I (Thalassemia minor) results from mutations or deletions in one β-globin allele or one or more α-globin alleles, leading to impaired production of hemoglobin A. Patients have mild microcytic anemia and normal concentrations of leukocytes and platelets. Educational Objective: Aplastic anemia can be acquired following a viral infection and presents with normocytic, normochromic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and leukopenia. Bone marrow biopsy and aspirate is required for diagnosis and will show a paucity of progenitor cells with marrow replacement by fat in the absence of fibrosis or malignant infiltration.
▶ Respiratory System Pulmonary Tuberculosis 1 questions
Source: 5A #19
A previously healthy 17-year-old girl comes to the physician for a follow-up examination after a PPD skin test produced 17 mm of induration at 48 hours. She takes no medications. She drinks alcohol and smokes cigarettes and marijuana occasionally. She is sexually active and uses condoms inconsistently for contraception. She lives in a rural community and raises chickens and cows. She participates in the student government and volunteers at a skilled nursing care facility. She traveled to Ireland for 10 days last summer with her high school. Examination shows no additional abnormalities. Which of the following activities is the strongest predisposing factor for this patient's positive PPD skin test? A) Overseas travel B) Participation in high school events C) Raising livestock D) Sexual activity E) Smoking marijuana F) Volunteering at a skilled nursing care facility
Correct Answer: F) Volunteering at a skilled nursing care facility
Induration exceeding 15 mm is considered a positive PPD skin test result and is suggestive of latent tuberculosis infection. Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a slow-growing mycobacterial organism transmitted via respiratory secretions and presents in primary, latent, and reactivation patterns. Primary disease presents with subacute fevers, weight loss, night sweats, cough, and malaise. Latent tuberculosis occurs when the organism proliferates within macrophages and is maintained within caseating granulomas. PPD skin testing stimulates a T-lymphocyte driven type IV hypersensitivity reaction against subdermal tuberculin antigen. False positive PPD testing can occur after prior BCG vaccination. This patient's positive test likely represents a true positive. The strongest risk factor for tuberculosis in this patient is volunteering at a skilled nursing care facility because tuberculosis is more common and spreads more easily in crowded populations such as nursing facilities and prisons. Choice A (Overseas travel) is incorrect because while travel to endemic areas is a significant risk factor for tuberculosis, Ireland and western Europe are not endemic areas; endemic regions include sub-Saharan Africa, the Indian subcontinent, and eastern and southeastern Asia. Choice B (Participation in high school events) is incorrect because single large events do not confer significant risk in non-endemic areas; prolonged crowding is more significant. Choice C (Raising livestock) is incorrect because M. tuberculosis is not zoonotic and is not acquired from animals; raising livestock increases risk for organisms like Bacillus anthracis, Coxiella burnetii, and Francisella tularensis. Choice D (Sexual activity) is incorrect because M. tuberculosis is not sexually transmitted and spreads via respiratory secretions. Choice E (Smoking marijuana) is incorrect because occasional marijuana use does not increase tuberculosis risk; only chronic pulmonary disease such as silicosis significantly increases risk, which is unlikely in a teenage patient with occasional use. Educational Objective: Induration exceeding 15 mm on PPD skin test indicates positive result. Risk factors for tuberculosis include exposure to crowded conditions (skilled nursing facilities, prisons), residence or travel in endemic areas, and immunocompromising conditions (diabetes mellitus, alcoholism, HIV infection). Latent tuberculosis is treated with prolonged courses of isoniazid or rifampin.
▶ Immune System AIDS 1 questions
Source: 5A #20
A 7-year-old girl is brought for a follow-up examination 2 days after completing a 10-day course of antibiotics for her second episode of pneumococcal pneumonia during the past year; during this time, she has also had two episodes of otitis media and one episode of herpes zoster. She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery and was healthy until 1 year ago when she began to have frequent upper and lower respiratory tract infections. Her mother was recently hospitalized for treatment of nontuberculous mycobacterial bacteremia. Examination of the patient shows 2-cm nontender lymph nodes in the axillae. There is fluid behind both tympanic membranes. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Chronic granulomatous disease B) HIV infection C) Hyperimmunoglobulinemia E syndrome D) Thymic-parathyroid dysplasia (DiGeorge syndrome) E) X-linked agammaglobulinemia
Correct Answer: B) HIV infection
HIV infection, acquired via vertical transmission from the patient's mother, is the most likely cause of the patient's recurrent pneumococcal pneumonia, otitis media, and herpes zoster infection with axillary lymphadenopathy. HIV transmission may occur at any time during gestation but is most commonly acquired at or around the time of delivery and in the immediate postpartum period during breastfeeding. Transmission is uncommon if the mother is taking antiretroviral therapy and has a decreased HIV viral load. As a result of screening for HIV in most developed countries, the incidence of perinatal and pediatric HIV infection has decreased, although this is not true around the world. While many pediatric patients with perinatally acquired HIV infection will manifest symptoms within the first few months to years, a subpopulation of patients will not develop symptoms or AIDS-defining conditions until many years later, as in this case. Symptoms in children are non-specific, and AIDS-defining conditions in children younger than six vary slightly from those in older children and adults. A crucial clue to the diagnosis is the presence of nontuberculous mycobacterial infection in the patient's mother, which is an AIDS-defining illness and should prompt evaluation for HIV infection in this patient. Choice A (Chronic granulomatous disease) is caused by NADPH oxidase deficiency and results in impaired intracellular killing of catalase-positive pathogens. Streptococcus pneumoniae is catalase-negative, making this diagnosis unlikely. Patients with CGD present with recurrent pyogenic infections with organisms such as S. aureus. Choice C (Hyperimmunoglobulinemia E syndrome) is caused by mutations in the JAK-STAT signaling cascade, which impairs the development and function of T helper 17 (Th17) cells. Th17 cells secrete interleukin-17 (IL-17), a potent neutrophil chemotaxis agent, so deficiency results in poor neutrophil migration to sites of infection. Patients typically have recurrent skin infections with non-inflamed abscesses (cold abscesses) and diffuse atopic dermatitis, not the systemic infections seen in this patient. Choice D (Thymic-parathyroid dysplasia/DiGeorge syndrome) is caused by a 22q11 deletion that leads to failure of the third and fourth branchial pouches to develop. These structures give rise to the thymus and parathyroid glands, and their absence leads to thymic aplasia and hypocalcemia along with cardiac and craniofacial defects. Patients are susceptible to viral and fungal infections but would typically present earlier with more obvious anatomic abnormalities. Choice E (X-linked agammaglobulinemia) occurs as a result of mutations in the BTK gene that encodes a tyrosine kinase essential for all stages of B-lymphocyte development and proliferation. Patients lack functioning B lymphocytes and therefore lack normal concentrations of immunoglobulins. It nearly always presents within the first eighteen months of life with recurrent infections and is more common in male patients given X-linked inheritance. Educational Objective: Pediatric HIV/AIDS infection should be suspected in patients who present with recurrent bacterial pneumonia or AIDS-defining illnesses such as disseminated mycobacterial and non-mycobacterial infection or Pneumocystis jiroveci infection. The presence of maternal AIDS-defining illness, particularly nontuberculous mycobacterial infection, should raise suspicion for vertical transmission of HIV to the child.
▶ Gastrointestinal System Entamoeba histolytica infection 1 questions
Source: 5A #21
A previously healthy 8-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of fever, abdominal pain, and bloody diarrhea for 6 hours. He and his family recently immigrated to the USA from Mexico. Abdominal examination shows pain and tenderness in the right upper quadrant. There is mild hepatomegaly. Sigmoidoscopy with mucosal biopsy shows flask-shaped ulcers with healthy intervening mucosa. Which of the following is the most likely pathogen? A) Entamoeba histolytica B) Giardia lamblia C) Rotavirus D) Salmonella typhi E) Shigella sonnei
Correct Answer: A) Entamoeba histolytica
Entamoeba histolytica is an amoebic parasite that causes amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery), which is much more common in the developing world. E. histolytica forms cysts transmitted through the fecal-oral route and contaminated water. Amoebic cysts mature to trophozoites in the large bowel. Trophozoites invade the colonic mucosa and interstitium, causing abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. Invasive infections can lead to colonic perforation and sepsis. When trophozoites enter the bloodstream, they travel to the liver and cause hepatic amoebic abscesses, presenting with fever and right upper quadrant pain with hepatomegaly. Sigmoidoscopy characteristically shows flask-shaped mucosal ulcers with healthy intervening mucosa. Diagnosis is made through identification of cysts on stool microscopy, trophozoites with endosomes containing red blood cells on peripheral smear, antibody assay, or PCR testing. Treatment requires combination therapy with metronidazole or tinidazole plus an anti-luminal agent such as paromomycin or iodoquinol. Giardia lamblia (Choice B) causes giardiasis presenting with malabsorption and watery diarrhea; bloody diarrhea is less common and it does not cause right upper quadrant pain or hepatomegaly. Rotavirus (Choice C) is a double-stranded RNA virus causing watery, profuse, foul-smelling diarrhea in children, but not bloody diarrhea or right upper quadrant pain. Salmonella typhi (Choice D) causes typhoid fever with fever, abdominal pain, rash, and diarrhea, but does not typically present with focal right upper quadrant pain, hepatomegaly, or bloody diarrhea. Shigella sonnei (Choice E) causes shigellosis with bloody diarrhea and may cause hemolytic uremic syndrome, but does not cause focal right upper quadrant pain suggesting hepatic abscess. The clinical presentation of fever, bloody diarrhea, right upper quadrant pain with hepatomegaly, flask-shaped ulcers on sigmoidoscopy, and recent immigration from Mexico are classic for E. histolytica with hepatic abscess formation.
▶ Renal Urinary System Renal Laceration 1 questions
Source: 5A #22
A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after he fell approximately 8 feet from a backyard porch onto a firm dirt surface, landing on his back. On arrival, he appears mildly uncomfortable. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 85/55 mm Hg. Examination shows moderate right-sided flank tenderness. The most appropriate next step in diagnosis is measurement of which of the following? A) Serum creatinine B) Serum urea nitrogen C) Urine blood D) Urine protein E) Urine volume
Correct Answer: C) Urine blood
This patient's fall from a height with subsequent flank tenderness raises concern for blunt kidney trauma. Motor vehicle collisions, falls, and sports injuries are common causes of this type of injury. A rapid deceleration injury, such as caused by a fall, can cause the kidney to be crushed against the paravertebral muscles, avulsed from the ureteropelvic junction or the renal vessels, or thrombosed. In any of these cases, blood supply to the kidney is interrupted. Flank tenderness, flank bruising, or lower rib fractures should all raise concern for blunt kidney injury. Hematuria is a common presenting symptom seen in over two-thirds of patients with blunt renal injury. It should be investigated quickly with measurement of urine blood as part of the initial trauma assessment, as intravenous fluid administration can dilute hematuria and preclude detection. Choice A (Serum creatinine) and Choice B (Serum urea nitrogen) are not helpful in diagnosing acute blunt kidney trauma. Any abnormality in renal function caused by trauma is masked by the contralateral functioning kidney. Therefore, neither creatinine nor urea nitrogen may be used as an indicator of renal trauma. Choice D (Urine protein) and Choice E (Urine volume) may also be normal after blunt kidney trauma and are not helpful in identifying the presence or absence of traumatic kidney injury. These values may later change if the filtering capacity of the kidney is impaired, but they are not useful in the initial trauma assessment. Educational Objective: Blunt kidney trauma is caused by rapid deceleration, such as a fall from a height. Evaluating for hematuria should be included in the initial trauma assessment and is the best indicator of kidney trauma.
▶ Musculoskeletal System Fractures 1 questions
Source: 5A #24
An 11-year-old girl with spina bifida is brought to the physician because of right thigh pain for 2 days. She is paraplegic and has limited sensation below the waist. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 95/min, and respirations are 16/min. Examination shows swelling of the right distal thigh without redness. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Reassurance B) Application of local heat C) X-ray of the lower extremity D) Range of motion exercises E) Acetaminophen therapy
Correct Answer: C) X-ray of the lower extremity
The patient's presentation with distal thigh swelling in the context of a pediatric patient is concerning for a femoral shaft fracture. Femoral fractures are a common long bone fracture in children, with peaks of incidence in toddlers due to accidental trauma and adolescents due to motor vehicle collisions. A femoral shaft fracture may be complicated by shortening of the muscles of the knee and hip, which causes the fractured femur to displace, necessitating early recognition and intervention to prevent permanent limb length discrepancy. Most femoral shaft fractures demonstrate obvious deformity, swelling, shortening, or crepitus on examination. A neurovascular examination distal to the site of swelling should be performed to ensure the fracture has not caused damage to nerves or arteries. The next step in management of a suspected femoral fracture is radiographic assessment using standard anterior-posterior and lateral plain x-rays of the affected area and the joints above and below the suspected fracture. This ensures correct diagnosis and assists in management planning. Reasssurance (Choice A) and application of local heat (Choice B) are not appropriate as a suspected femoral fracture requires immobilization and may require operative intervention. In cases of mild musculoskeletal injuries not requiring medical evaluation, application of ice is more effective than heat. Range of motion exercises (Choice D) may be needed following complete healing but would worsen the fracture if performed without adequate treatment; immobilization is essential. Acetaminophen therapy (Choice E), while safe for pediatric use, is inappropriate as it treats pain without addressing the underlying fracture. Educational Objective: When a fracture is suspected, the next step in management is radiographic assessment of the affected area and the joints above and below it.
▶ Nervous System Special Senses Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy 1 questions
Source: 5A #27
A 5-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of clumsiness and frequent falls over the past 6 months. He did not walk independently until 17 months of age and has always had poor motor skills. There is enlargement of the calf muscles and a positive Gowers sign. Which of the following is the most likely inheritance pattern? A) Autosomal dominant B) Autosomal recessive C) X-linked dominant D) X-linked recessive E) No known mendelian pattern
Correct Answer: D) X-linked recessive
Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern. This case presents classic features of DMD: delayed motor milestones (didn't walk until 17 months), progressive proximal muscle weakness manifesting as clumsiness and frequent falls in early childhood, calf pseudohypertrophy (enlargement of calf muscles), and a positive Gowers sign (characteristic maneuver of using hands to "climb" up the lower extremities when rising from the floor, indicating proximal hip and thigh weakness). Children typically have unremarkable birth histories but develop signs of proximal muscle weakness early in childhood. Proximal muscles affected include those of the shoulder and hip girdles (adductors and flexors of hip and thigh). Diagnosis is confirmed through genetic testing, which has largely replaced muscle biopsy. Most affected males require wheelchair use by early adolescence, with late complications including dilated cardiomyopathy and respiratory failure. Autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive patterns are seen in Limb-Girdle muscular dystrophy, which presents with shoulder and pelvic girdle weakness but normal distal muscle strength. X-linked dominant inheritance (seen in scapuloperoneal myopathy) requires only a single copy for disease expression in both males and females, and presents with distal leg and scapular weakness with occasional facial involvement. No known mendelian pattern applies to inflammatory and infectious myopathies, which occur sporadically and are not genetically determined. Many muscular dystrophies do follow mendelian inheritance patterns. Educational Objective: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked recessive condition resulting in progressive proximal muscle weakness after initial normal development. Key clinical features include difficulty rising from squatting position, lower limb girdle weakness, calf pseudohypertrophy, and positive Gowers sign. Late complications include dilated cardiomyopathy and respiratory insufficiency.
▶ Cardiovascular System Aortic Valve Regurgitation 1 questions
Source: 5A #33
A 14-year-old boy with a cardiac murmur is brought to the physician for a school physical examination. He reports that during this past soccer season, he easily became short of breath at times but did not seek medical attention. He has no symptoms of chest pain, palpitations, or syncope, and he appears healthy. His pulse is 72/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 126/42 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows a blowing diastolic murmur at the upper right sternal border; there is no systolic murmur. Radial and pedal pulses are 3+ bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Increased pulmonary vascular resistance B) Increased systemic cardiac output C) Increased systemic vascular resistance D) Left ventricular pressure overload E) Left ventricular volume overload
Correct Answer: E) Left ventricular volume overload
Left ventricular volume overload as a result of aortic insufficiency (AI), also called aortic regurgitation, explains this patient's clinical presentation. AI results from an incompetent aortic valve that allows retrograde blood flow from the aortic root to the left ventricle during diastole. This produces the characteristic blowing diastolic murmur at the upper right sternal border. The increased LV end-diastolic volume occurs because both blood from the aorta and the left atrium fill the LV. This increased volume stretches the compliant ventricle, thereby increasing myocardial contractility, which is reflected as an increased stroke volume and cardiac output. The widened pulse pressure (systolic 126, diastolic 42 mm Hg) results from the large volume ejected during systole, which transiently increases systolic pressure, while the regurgitant volume back into the LV leads to a lower diastolic pressure. The bounding radial and pedal pulses (3+ bilaterally) reflect this increased stroke volume. Over time, eccentric hypertrophy of the LV leads to loss of normal compliance and progressive LV systolic dysfunction. Common causes of AI include bicuspid aortic valve, aortic root dilation, rheumatic heart disease, and syndromes such as Marfan and Turner syndrome. Increased pulmonary vascular resistance (Choice A) is not a feature of isolated AI. Increased PVR occurs in conditions such as pulmonary hypertension or pulmonic stenosis, and while left-sided heart failure can eventually lead to increased PVR, this patient shows no symptoms of pulmonary hypertension or cor pulmonale. Increased systemic cardiac output (Choice B) is incorrect. In compensated AI, the cardiac output is maintained, but over time the progressive hypertrophy of the LV in combination with ongoing aortic regurgitation leads to systolic dysfunction and decreased cardiac output. Increased systemic vascular resistance (Choice C) is incorrect. SVR tends to be relatively normal in individuals with chronic compensated AI, although they tend to have a greater disparity between systolic and diastolic pressures. Left ventricular pressure overload (Choice D) is incorrect. In young patients with chronic AI and no evidence of heart failure, the LV is able to compensate for increased end-diastolic volume by distending, thereby maintaining a normal LV end-diastolic pressure. Over time, however, eccentric hypertrophy can cause diastolic dysfunction and increased LV pressure. Educational Objective: AI results in an increased LV end-diastolic volume as regurgitant blood from the aorta enters the LV during diastole, which can be auscultated as a diastolic murmur. The retrograde flow of blood during diastole results in a lower diastolic pressure, which is reflected as an increased pulse pressure.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Failure to Thrive 1 questions
Source: 5A #34
A 15-month-old boy is brought to the physician for an initial examination. According to his mother and previous medical records, he has been healthy, and developmental milestones are appropriate for age. At his last examination 3 months ago, he was at the 25th percentile for length and weight. Today, he is at the 25th percentile for length and the 10th percentile for weight. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation of his poor weight gain? A) Recommend a diet diary with calorie counts B) Reevaluate weight in 1 week C) Test the stool for reducing substances and fecal fat D) Admit to the hospital for observation E) Obtain an x-ray of the abdomen
Correct Answer: A) Recommend a diet diary with calorie counts
This child demonstrates a decreased velocity of weight gain compared to his growth in length, raising concern for poor weight gain and malnutrition. Poor weight gain is a common diagnosis in approximately 5% of pediatric patients and can result from inadequate intake, absorption, or metabolism of nutrients. Risk factors include prematurity, developmental delay, congenital abnormalities, poverty, social isolation, nutritional beliefs, poor parenting skills, substance abuse, violence, or other abuse. The first step in evaluation of poor weight gain is to take a thorough history of dietary practices and review of systems. If no suspected underlying organic cause is found, management of mild malnutrition should involve parental education, dietary advice, changes to dietary practices, home-based support, and referral to community or governmental programs to increase access to food. Recommending a diet diary with calorie counts both investigates whether inadequate caloric intake is the cause of the child's poor weight gain and assists caregivers in creating a personalized feeding plan. Choice B (Reevaluate weight in 1 week) without an associated intervention will not likely improve the patient's weight gain. While close follow-up is warranted after initiating a dietary plan, this alone is insufficient. Choice C (Test the stool for reducing substances and fecal fat) may be performed in children whose poor weight gain has not resolved with appropriate dietary intervention to investigate malabsorption as a potential cause. It is not warranted prior to attempting dietary intervention in an otherwise asymptomatic child. Choice D (Admit to the hospital for observation) is not necessary at this time as conservative measures including dietary changes have not yet been tried. There is no reason to suspect weight loss is caused by caregiver neglect or non-accidental trauma, which would warrant admission. Choice E (Obtain an x-ray of the abdomen) is not necessary as the patient has no symptoms such as vomiting, abdominal pain, decreased appetite, or diarrhea suggestive of abdominal pathology. Educational Objective: A decreased velocity of weight gain compared to growth in length raises concern for poor weight gain and malnutrition. A diet diary with calorie counts investigates whether inadequate caloric intake is the cause of the child's poor weight gain and is the appropriate initial intervention in an otherwise healthy child with failure to thrive.
▶ Gastrointestinal System Hirschsprung disease 1 questions
Source: 5A #36
A 3-day-old girl with Down syndrome has not had a bowel movement since birth. She feeds poorly but has not vomited. She has not had any other symptoms. She was born at term to a 39-year-old primigravid woman following an uncomplicated pregnancy and spontaneous vaginal delivery. Rupture of the membranes occurred 6 hours prior to delivery; there was no meconium staining of fluid. Apgar scores were 6 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. The patient's temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 40/min, and blood pressure is 90/55 mm Hg. Examination shows epicanthal folds, white stellate spots on the irides, single palmar creases, and wide spaces between the great and second toes. The abdomen is soft and nontender; there is no organomegaly. Muscle tone is decreased in the trunk. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's failure to pass stool? A) Absence of ganglion cells in the bowel wall B) Dilation of lymphatic vessels of the bowel C) Duodenal atresia D) Pancreatic enzyme insufficiency E) Villous atrophy
Correct Answer: A) Absence of ganglion cells in the bowel wall
Congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung disease or intestinal aganglionosis) is caused by the congenital absence of the distal portion of the myenteric plexus, a part of the enteric nervous system located between the inner and outer layers of the muscularis externa in the bowel wall. During development, the myenteric plexus migrates cephalad to caudal, and incomplete migration results in absence of the plexus in the distal portion of the gastrointestinal tract. This absence of ganglion cells prevents normal peristalsis and leads to inability to pass meconium within the first few days of life and eventually large bowel obstruction. An explosive expulsion of feces on rectal examination is a common clinical finding. Barium enema is the diagnostic imaging study of choice for evaluating congenital megacolon. Congenital megacolon is strongly associated with Down syndrome (as evidenced by this patient's characteristic features: epicanthal folds, white stellate spots on the irides, single palmar creases, and widely spaced toes). Choice B (Dilation of lymphatic vessels of the bowel) describes intestinal lymphangiectasia, caused by obstruction of lymphatic vessels. Loss of lymphocytes into the gut can lead to lymphopenia and immunosuppression but does not explain failure to pass meconium after birth. Choice C (Duodenal atresia) results from failure of re-canalization of the duodenal lumen and presents with vomiting, abdominal distension, and characteristic radiographic findings of dilated stomach and duodenum. While duodenal atresia is also associated with Down syndrome, this patient lacks vomiting and has a soft, nontender abdomen, making congenital megacolon more likely. Choice D (Pancreatic enzyme insufficiency) is characteristic of cystic fibrosis, where destruction of the pancreatic duct leads to absent digestive enzymes, causing malnutrition, weight loss, vitamin deficiencies, and frequent loose, foul-smelling, oily stools (steatorrhea). Cystic fibrosis may present with meconium ileus, but this patient's presentation is more consistent with congenital megacolon. Choice E (Villous atrophy) is the pathologic hallmark of celiac disease, a gluten-sensitive enteropathy. Villous atrophy in the proximal small bowel causes malabsorption presenting as chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, and nutritional deficiencies. This does not explain acute meconium passage failure in a newborn. Educational Objective: Congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung disease) is caused by the congenital absence of ganglion cells in the distal myenteric plexus, resulting in failure to pass meconium and constipation. It is strongly associated with Down syndrome. An explosive expulsion of feces on rectal examination is a characteristic clinical finding, and barium enema is used to evaluate for this condition.
▶ Blood Lymphoreticular System Hereditary spherocytosis 1 questions
Source: 5A #37
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of increasing lethargy and jaundice over the past week. At birth, he had jaundice treated with phototherapy for 5 days. His father had a splenectomy at the age of 6 years. Developmental milestones and diet are normal for age. Examination shows mild scleral icterus. A grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur is heard. The spleen tip is palpated 4 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL, Leukocyte count 6500/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 40%, Lymphocytes 55%, Monocytes 5%, Reticulocyte count 10%, Serum total bilirubin 5 mg/dL. Direct and indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) tests are negative. A blood smear is most likely to show which of the following types of erythrocytes? A) Macrocytic and hyperchromic B) Macrocytic and hypochromic C) Microcytic and hypochromic D) Normocytic and hypochromic E) Normocytic and normochromic
Correct Answer: E) Normocytic and normochromic
This patient with evidence of hemolytic anemia, increased reticulocyte count (10%), and a family history of similar symptoms requiring splenectomy at age 6 (father's splenectomy) likely has hereditary spherocytosis (HS). HS results from autosomal dominant mutations in one or more proteins that link the erythrocyte inner membrane skeleton to the outer lipid bilayer, including mutations in spectrin, ankyrin, band 3, and band 4.2. Spherocytosis results from progressive loss of the erythrocyte membrane over time, giving erythrocytes a spherical shape. The surface area decreases but the volume of the cell remains unchanged, impairing the erythrocyte's ability to conform in small vessels of the microcirculation, especially within the spleen where spherocytes accumulate. Patients present with splenomegaly, hemolytic anemia (Hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL, total bilirubin 5 mg/dL, and negative Coombs tests indicating non-autoimmune hemolysis), and pigmented gallstones. Peripheral smear shows normocytic, normochromic erythrocytes. With a high degree of hemolysis, reticulocytes appear as larger, pale blue erythrocytes. Definitive management involves splenectomy. Choice A (Macrocytic and hyperchromic) erythrocytes are seen in vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, occurring in pediatric patients with malabsorptive conditions such as celiac disease, or in older patients with gastric bypass, chronic alcohol use, and pernicious anemia. Choice B (Macrocytic and hypochromic) erythrocytes result from a combination of diseases such as vitamin B12 deficiency, folate deficiency (macrocytosis), iron deficiency, anemia of chronic disease, or thalassemia (hypochromia). Choice C (Microcytic and hypochromic) erythrocytes are seen in iron deficiency from chronic blood loss. This would be uncommon in such a young patient without evidence of chronic gastrointestinal bleeding. Choice D (Normocytic and hypochromic) erythrocytes are commonly seen in thalassemia, with additional findings of target cells on peripheral smear. Educational Objective: Autosomal dominant mutations in ankyrin, spectrin, and band erythrocyte membrane proteins cause hereditary spherocytosis through loss of the normal connection between the inner membrane skeleton and the outer lipid bilayer. Clinical symptoms include jaundice, splenomegaly, and anemia. Peripheral smear shows normocytic, normochromic anemia with the presence of spherocytes. Definitive treatment is with splenectomy.
▶ Blood Lymphoreticular System Hemophilia A 1 questions
Source: 5A #39
Twelve hours after undergoing circumcision, a 3-day-old boy has persistent bleeding at his circumcision site. He was born at 38 weeks' gestation to a 23-year-old primigravid woman following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. He was given an intramuscular injection of vitamin K immediately after delivery. His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 55/min, and blood pressure is 60/40 mm Hg. Examination shows a prominent right parietal cephalohematoma. There is an ecchymosis at the vitamin K injection site and continuous oozing of blood at the circumcision site. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 53%, Leukocyte count 10,500/mm³, Segmented neutrophils 50%, Basophils 4%, Lymphocytes 40%, Monocytes 6%, Platelet count 350,000/mm³, Prothrombin time 12 sec (INR=1.05), Partial thromboplastin time 90 sec. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these findings? A) Factor VIII deficiency B) Platelet dysfunction C) Sepsis D) Vitamin K deficiency E) von Willebrand factor deficiency
Correct Answer: A) Factor VIII deficiency
Factor VIII deficiency resulting in hemophilia A is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with uncontrolled bleeding from his circumcision site, large right cephalohematoma, abnormally prolonged partial thromboplastin time (PTT) of 90 seconds, normal prothrombin time (PT) of 12 seconds (INR=1.05), and normal platelet count of 350,000/mm³. Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive condition more commonly seen in males, with most females being silent carriers. It is caused by absence or deficiency of factor VIII, a component of the intrinsic clotting cascade. Factor VIII serves as a cofactor for activation of factor X to factor Xa, which converts prothrombin to thrombin to complete clot formation. The PTT measures intrinsic pathway activity and is prolonged in hemophilia A, while PT measures extrinsic pathway activity (factor VII), which is normal in this disease. Choice B (Platelet dysfunction) can result in prolonged bleeding but typically presents with normal PTT and increased bleeding time, not the prolonged PTT seen here. Examples include Glanzmann thrombasthenia, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, and platelet granule disorders. Choice C (Sepsis) is unlikely without fever or signs of infection. Common neonatal infections causing sepsis include meningitis and pneumonia, which are not evident here. Choice D (Vitamin K deficiency) is unlikely because this child received adequate vitamin K immediately after delivery, and vitamin K deficiency presents with prolonged PT, not isolated prolonged PTT. Choice E (von Willebrand factor deficiency) presents with quantitative or qualitative abnormality of von Willebrand factor causing impaired platelet adherence and prolonged bleeding time. It typically manifests with epistaxis, gingival bleeding, petechiae, easy bruising, and menorrhagia, not the profound factor-deficiency bleeding pattern seen here. Educational Objective: Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disease resulting in deficiency or absence of factor VIII. It presents with prolonged bleeding following tissue injury, particularly in males. Laboratory findings include prolonged PTT with normal PT and normal platelet count. Treatment is with recombinant factor VIII.
▶ Respiratory System Pulmonary Hypertension 1 questions
Source: 5A #41
A 3714-g (8-lb 3-oz) newborn is delivered at 43 weeks' gestation to a 32-year-old woman, gravida 4, para 3. Apgar scores are 3 and 5 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. The newborn's skin and nails are meconium stained, and he is cyanotic. He is immediately intubated and mechanically ventilated at an FiO2 of 100%. No meconium is noted below the vocal cords prior to insertion of the endotracheal tube. One hour later, he remains cyanotic. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Umbilical arterial blood gas analysis shows: pH 7.1, PCO2 34 mm Hg, PO2 26 mm Hg. An x-ray of the chest shows no cardiomegaly or pulmonary infiltrates. Echocardiography shows normal cardiac anatomy with a right-to-left shunt across the foramen ovale. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of these findings? A) Closure of ductus arteriosus B) Closure of foramen ovale C) Decreased pulmonary vascular resistance D) Failure of pulmonary vasodilation E) Increased peripheral vascular resistance F) Intracardiac left-to-right shunt
Correct Answer: D) Failure of pulmonary vasodilation
Failure of pulmonary vasodilation resulting in significant pulmonary hypertension is the most likely cause of this patient's right-to-left shunt across the foramen ovale and persistent hypoxemia. Normal fetal circulation involves oxygenated blood arriving from the maternal circulation via the umbilical vein, reaching the inferior vena cava, and being shunted from the right atrium to the left atrium and left ventricle to supply the systemic circulation. Oxygenated blood reaching the right ventricle and pulmonary arteries is shunted through the ductus arteriosus to the aortic arch. Before birth, the fetal lungs are filled with amniotic fluid and pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) is high. Under normal circumstances, the first breath leads to a decrease in PVR as pulmonary vessels dilate. Peripartum asphyxia, as in this case, combined with acidosis, impairs the normal transition from increased to decreased PVR. Despite adequate oxygen delivery after intubation, persistently increased PVR impairs oxygenation and causes pulmonary hypertension, explaining the patient's persistent hypoxemia. Choice A is incorrect because closure of the ductus arteriosus, a shunt between the pulmonary arteries and aortic arch, typically occurs within several days after birth. Failure to close results in an extracardiac left-to-right shunt presenting with a continuous machine-like murmur. Choice B is incorrect because closure of the foramen ovale occurs within the first 6 months of life as a normal occurrence. Persistence (patent foramen ovale) causes left-to-right shunting, which would not result in hypoxemia; if large enough, it can eventually lead to right-sided hypertrophy and shunt reversal. Choice C is incorrect because decreased pulmonary vascular resistance is the normal and expected occurrence after birth. A normal decrease in PVR improves oxygenation, not impairs it. Choice E is incorrect because increased peripheral vascular resistance causes systemic hypertension but would not affect oxygenation as it has no effect on ventilation or perfusion of the lungs. Choice F is incorrect because an intracardiac left-to-right shunt (from a patent foramen ovale or ventricular septal defect) allows oxygenated blood to re-enter the pulmonary vasculature, which would not result in hypoxemia. Educational Objective: Pulmonary vascular resistance normally decreases immediately after birth to allow deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to enter the pulmonary vasculature where it is oxygenated. In instances of perinatal asphyxia, the normal decrease in PVR is disrupted, leading to persistently increased PVR (pulmonary hypertension). This restricts blood flow through the pulmonary vasculature and causes persistent hypoxemia despite adequate oxygen delivery and ventilation.
▶ Gastrointestinal System Peutz-Jeghers syndrome 1 questions
Source: 5A #42
A previously healthy 7-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her father because of a 4-month history of episodes of bright red blood in her stool. The episodes are not associated with pain, constipation, or diarrhea. Growth and development are appropriate for age. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 110/65 mm Hg. Examination of the face shows areas of hyperpigmentation on the lips and buccal mucosa. A photograph of the mouth is shown. Examination of the anus shows no fissures or signs of trauma. Digital rectal examination shows bright red blood. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Stool culture B) Air-contrast enema C) Upper gastrointestinal series D) Meckel scan E) Colonoscopy
Correct Answer: E) Colonoscopy
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is a genetic condition inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. It is characterized by the triad of colonic polyps, mucocutaneous hyperpigmented macules, and an increased risk for gastrointestinal and non-gastrointestinal malignancy. In this syndrome, hamartomatous polyps are scattered throughout the gastrointestinal tract and are associated with an increased risk for colorectal and gastric carcinoma. Acute bleeding episodes from one of these polyps leading to bright red blood in the stool, as in this case, are common, but bleeding may also be occult and cause iron deficiency anemia. Yearly complete blood count to screen for anemia is recommended. Baseline endoscopic evaluation utilizing both upper endoscopy and colonoscopy is recommended to evaluate for malignancy. The blue-gray pigmented macules are scattered primarily in the perioral region and on the lips and are caused by increased numbers of dermal macrophages containing melanin rather than increased size of melanosomes. These cutaneous macules are not malignant. Colonoscopy (Choice E) allows direct visualization of colonic polyps and is the most appropriate next step. If a source of bleeding is identified, intervention can be made to stop it. Stool culture (Choice A) is appropriate for bloody diarrhea caused by bacterial infection such as Escherichia coli or Shigella, but this patient has had blood in her stools for 4 months with no fever or signs of infection. Air-contrast enema (Choice B) is both diagnostic and therapeutic for intussusception, which presents with recurrent episodes of severe colicky abdominal pain often punctuated by asymptomatic periods. This patient has no pain or associated symptoms. Upper gastrointestinal series (Choice C) will not be useful in evaluating colonic polyps. Direct visualization of the colon via colonoscopy is better suited for evaluation of polyps. Meckel scan (Choice D), or technetium 99m pertechnetate scan, is used to confirm a Meckel diverticulum. While Meckel diverticulum can present with painless hematochezia, the clinical presentation and findings of mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation are characteristic of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, not Meckel diverticulum. Educational Objective: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is a genetic condition characterized by the triad of colonic polyps, mucocutaneous hyperpigmented macules, and an increased risk for gastrointestinal and non-gastrointestinal malignancy. At the time of diagnosis, upper endoscopy and colonoscopy should be performed to evaluate existing polyps and screen for malignancy.
▶ Behavioral Health Alcohol Intoxication 1 questions
Source: 5A #43
A 16-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by friends after she passed out at a party. She has a history of substance abuse, and they say that she drank more than eight glasses of alcohol during the past 2 hours. On arrival, she does not respond to painful stimuli. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 61/min and shallow, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 90%. Examination shows scleral icterus. The liver edge is palpated 1 cm below the right costal margin. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management? A) Determine the exact amount and type of alcohol ingested B) Measurement of blood alcohol concentration C) Nebulized acetylcysteine therapy D) Endotracheal intubation E) Hemodialysis
Correct Answer: D) Endotracheal intubation
This patient presents with acute alcohol intoxication complicated by altered mental status (obtundation, unresponsiveness to pain), severe respiratory distress (tachypnea at 61/min with shallow breathing), and hypoxia (oxygen saturation 90% on room air). She also demonstrates signs of chronic alcohol abuse including hepatomegaly (liver 1 cm below costal margin) and scleral icterus consistent with alcoholic hepatitis. The immediate life-threatening issue is airway compromise and inadequate ventilation/oxygenation. The initial management must prioritize airway protection through endotracheal intubation to secure the airway, support ventilation, and improve oxygenation. Choice A (determining exact amount and type of alcohol ingested) and Choice B (blood alcohol concentration) may provide useful clinical information for prognosis and metabolism timeline but are not immediately necessary for emergency management of a patient with respiratory distress and hypoxia. Choice C (nebulized acetylcysteine) is a mucolytic agent used for conditions like asthma, cystic fibrosis, and diseases with mucous plugging. It is not indicated here as the respiratory distress results from alcohol intoxication and CNS depression causing hypoventilation, not airway obstruction from secretions. Choice E (hemodialysis) is not typically used for alcohol intoxication because the liver efficiently metabolizes alcohol through normal hepatic metabolism. Dialysis is reserved for toxic alcohol poisonings (ethylene glycol, methanol) causing severe metabolic acidosis. Educational Objective: In an obtunded patient presenting with respiratory distress and hypoxia, the initial management priority is airway protection through endotracheal intubation to support adequate ventilation and oxygenation, regardless of the underlying cause of altered consciousness.
▶ Respiratory System Obstructive sleep apnea 1 questions
Source: 5A #45
A 3-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of cough and nasal congestion. Her parents say that she has been tired and irritable for 6 months; during this period, she has been sleeping excessively during the day and snoring loudly. Her pulse is 126/min, respirations are 36/min, and blood pressure is 120/86 mm Hg. On examination, she has nasal congestion and breathes predominantly through her mouth. A grade 1/6 holosystolic murmur is heard in the fourth left parasternal space. There is tonsillar and adenoidal hypertrophy. An x-ray of the chest shows cardiomegaly. Echocardiography shows right ventricular hypertrophy, pulmonary hypertension, and mild tricuspid regurgitation. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term management? A) Digoxin and diuretic therapy B) Pulmonary vasodilator therapy C) Pulmonary artery banding D) Adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy E) Repair of tricuspid regurgitation
Correct Answer: D) Adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy
Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is common in the pediatric population and is characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness and snoring. Risk factors include adenotonsillar hypertrophy and obesity, both of which decrease airway size and increase risk for obstruction during sleep, leading to pulmonary hypertension. This patient demonstrates cor pulmonale (right ventricular dysfunction caused by primary pulmonary disease), evidenced by cardiomegaly, right ventricular hypertrophy, pulmonary hypertension, and tricuspid regurgitation. Other complications of untreated OSA include systemic hypertension, left ventricular dysfunction, failure to thrive, and behavioral problems. In children with adenotonsillar hypertrophy, the first-line treatment of OSA is adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy. Given this patient's significant cardiovascular complications secondary to OSA, surgical removal is necessary. Digoxin and diuretic therapy (Choice A) manages congestive heart failure by improving contractility and preventing volume overload, but these are only temporizing measures, not long-term solutions. Pulmonary vasodilator therapy (Choice B) is used for primary pulmonary hypertension to decrease pressure within the pulmonary vasculature. However, this patient's pulmonary hypertension stems from OSA; dilating the pulmonary vasculature does not address the underlying cause. Pulmonary artery banding (Choice C) is used in left transposition of the great arteries to train the left ventricle for systemic circulation. This patient requires decreased pulmonary resistance through OSA treatment, not left ventricular training. Repair of tricuspid regurgitation (Choice E) does not address the underlying cause. The tricuspid regurgitation results from right ventricular dilation and widening of the valvular opening. Surgical repair may be indicated after the underlying cause of cardiomegaly is addressed and if regurgitation persists, but not currently. Educational Objective: Obstructive sleep apnea is characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness and snoring. Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is a common cause of OSA in children. If present, adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy represent the first-line treatment of OSA.
▶ Musculoskeletal System Dermatomyositis 1 questions
Source: 5A #46
A previously healthy 10-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a rash over the eyelids and fingers for 1 week. Examination shows a violaceous erythema of the upper eyelids and an erythematous, atrophic, scaly lesion over the knuckles and dorsal surfaces of the finger joints. There is weakness of the proximal extremities and trunk. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Dermatomyositis B) Eosinophilic granuloma C) Inflammatory bowel disease D) Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis E) Mixed connective tissue disease F) Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease) G) Periarteritis nodosa H) Systemic lupus erythematosus I) Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma)
Correct Answer: A) Dermatomyositis
Dermatomyositis is an autoimmune connective tissue disease affecting the skin and proximal muscles. The clinical presentation in this case is classic for juvenile dermatomyositis with characteristic cutaneous manifestations including pink papules over the dorsal fingers (Gottron papules), pink to light purple patches over the upper eyelids (heliotrope sign), light pink to lilac colored patches with telangiectasias on the upper back and sun-exposed chest, and dilated capillaries with dropout on the proximal nail folds. Proximal muscle weakness of the extremities and trunk is a hallmark feature. Juvenile dermatomyositis commonly demonstrates calcinosis cutis, the deposition of calcium in the skin. An inflammatory infiltrate of muscle causes myocyte damage, leading to release of creatine kinase, which can be used to monitor disease progression. Dermatomyositis is characterized by several autoantibodies including positive antinuclear antibody, anti-Jo-1, anti-SRP, and anti-Mi-2 antibodies. In children, dermatomyositis is less likely to be associated with malignancy compared to adults. Treatment involves systemic steroids followed by long-term immunosuppressive therapy with methotrexate or azathioprine. Choice B (Eosinophilic granuloma): A form of Langerhans cell histiocytosis primarily involving bones with lytic lesions commonly in the skull. Does not cause muscle weakness or the characteristic skin findings described. Choice C (Inflammatory bowel disease): Comprises Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis, presenting with bloody diarrhea and abdominal pain. Does not produce muscle weakness or eyelid/finger rashes. Choice D (Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis): Characterized by fever, arthritis, evanescent pink rash, and lymphadenopathy. Lacks the specific cutaneous findings of dermatomyositis and characteristic muscle weakness pattern. Choice E (Mixed connective tissue disease): An autoimmune connective tissue disease with overlapping, non-specific features of SLE, dermatomyositis, systemic sclerosis, and rheumatoid arthritis. This patient's symptoms are specific to dermatomyositis rather than mixed features. Choice F (Kawasaki disease): A multisystemic inflammatory disease in children characterized by fever for at least 5 days, bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, polymorphous rash, lymphadenopathy, erythema and edema of hands and feet, and mucosal erythema with dry cracked lips. Does not cause proximal muscle weakness. Choice G (Polyarteritis nodosa): A medium-vessel vasculitis with characteristic symptoms including fatigue, weight loss, weakness, fever, arthralgias, and skin ulcers. Does not present with the specific cutaneous manifestations (Gottron papules and heliotrope sign) or proximal muscle pattern of dermatomyositis. Choice H (Systemic lupus erythematosus): An autoimmune disease with fever, rash, photosensitivity, renal disease, and nonerosive arthritis. The characteristic malar rash spares the nasolabial folds and eyelid involvement is not typical. Choice I (Systemic sclerosis/scleroderma): Presents with taut hardened skin, Raynaud phenomenon, renal failure, telangiectasias, cardiac fibrosis, esophageal dysmotility, and GI fibrosis. Muscle weakness is not a common characteristic. Educational Objective: Dermatomyositis is an autoimmune connective tissue disease that causes characteristic pathognomonic skin findings (Gottron papules on dorsal fingers and heliotrope sign on upper eyelids) combined with proximal muscle weakness, making it readily distinguishable from other connective tissue and systemic diseases.
▶ Gastrointestinal System Staphylococcus aureus gastrointestinal infection 1 questions
Source: 5A #48
A previously healthy 6-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of severe abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting that began 4 hours after attending a friend's birthday party. Cake and other pastries were served at the party. She appears acutely ill and mildly dehydrated. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities of the skin. Bowel sounds are hyperactive. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism? A) Campylobacter jejuni B) Clostridium botulinum C) Enteroinvasive Escherichia coli D) Salmonella enteritidis E) Shigella sonnei F) Staphylococcus aureus
Correct Answer: F) Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is a Gram-positive organism that secretes several exotoxins, including enterotoxin, exfoliatoxin, and toxic shock syndrome toxin. S. aureus enterotoxin is heat-stable and commonly contaminates cream-based foods and pastries. When foods containing S. aureus are left at room temperature, the organism multiplies and produces enterotoxin. Ingestion of S. aureus enterotoxin leads to nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramping that typically occurs within 6 hours of ingestion, which matches this patient's presentation perfectly (symptom onset 4 hours after the party with cake and pastries). Choice A (Campylobacter jejuni), Choice C (Enteroinvasive Escherichia coli), Choice D (Salmonella enteritidis), and Choice E (Shigella sonnei) all cause mucosal inflammation and invasion, typically presenting with a toxic appearance and bloody diarrhea. This patient has vomiting and abdominal cramping without bloody diarrhea, making these organisms less likely. Choice B (Clostridium botulinum) produces botulinum toxin that can cause foodborne gastroenteritis with nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, and potentially neurologic symptoms including flaccid paralysis. However, symptoms typically begin between 18 to 36 hours after toxin ingestion, which is much later than the 4-hour onset in this patient. Educational Objective: S. aureus enterotoxins commonly cause nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and intestinal cramping within 6 hours after ingestion of contaminated food, particularly cream-based foods and pastries left at room temperature.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Candidiasis 1 questions
Source: 5A #49
A 1-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 1-day history of decreased oral intake. Her mother says that the child has also had blood in her saliva. She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. Examination shows inflammation and erythema of the oral cavity with diffuse white plaques that bleed when scraped. There is a papular erythematous rash with satellite lesions over the diaper area. Which of the following is the most likely immune mechanism for these findings? A) Decreased B-lymphocyte activity B) Decreased dendritic cell activity C) Decreased segmented neutrophil function D) Decreased T-lymphocyte activity E) Increased B-lymphocyte activity F) Increased dendritic cell activity G) Increased segmented neutrophil function H) Increased T-lymphocyte activity
Correct Answer: D) Decreased T-lymphocyte activity
Decreased T-lymphocyte activity is the most likely cause of this patient's presentation consistent with Candida albicans infection. The clinical findings of white, bleeding oral lesions (oral thrush) and papular erythematous rash with satellite lesions in the diaper area are characteristic of mucocutaneous candidiasis, which indicates deficient cellular immunity. C. albicans is a dimorphic fungus that phenotypically switches from yeast to hyphae based on temperature and commonly causes infections in immunocompromised patients. T lymphocytes play a critical role in preventing fungal infections. The immune response to fungal organisms involves fungal element recognition by antigen-presenting cells (APCs) through C-lectin receptors, which interact with CD8+ T lymphocytes for cytotoxic killing and cytokine release. These activated T cells produce interleukin-17 (IL-17), promoting Th17 cell proliferation, which produces IL-17 and IL-22 to attract neutrophils that are fungicidal. Additionally, Th1 cells are induced and play a role in fungal immunity. Therefore, T-lymphocyte deficiency significantly increases susceptibility to both mucocutaneous and invasive fungal infections. Choice A (Decreased B-lymphocyte activity) causes deficient humoral immunity seen in conditions like X-linked agammaglobulinemia, predisposing to invasive bacterial infections rather than fungal infections. Choice B (Decreased dendritic cell activity) would impair antigen presentation to both T and B lymphocytes, potentially affecting multiple immune responses. Choice C (Decreased segmented neutrophil function) results in recurrent bacterial infections, not fungal infections. Choice E (Increased B-lymphocyte activity) occurs during normal immune response to bacterial and viral infections through differentiation into plasma cells and memory cells producing immunoglobulins, and does not increase fungal infection risk. Choice F (Increased dendritic cell activity) would enhance antigen presentation and activate lymphocytes without causing immunodeficiency. Choice G (Increased segmented neutrophil function) would not cause immunodeficiency or increased fungal infection risk. Choice H (Increased T-lymphocyte activity) is associated with some autoimmune conditions but does not increase susceptibility to fungal infections. Educational Objective: T lymphocytes, including cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes, Th1 cells, and Th17 cells, play essential roles in controlling fungal organisms. Deficiency in T-lymphocyte function significantly increases the risk for both mucocutaneous and invasive fungal infections such as candidiasis.
▶ Nervous System Special Senses Charcot-Marie-Tooth Disease 1 questions
Source: 5A #50
A 14-year-old boy is brought to the physician because his parents are concerned that he has had several episodes of tripping and incoordination over the past 10 months. He has high-arched feet and hammer toes. His father also has high-arched feet and a history of distal extremity weakness. His mother has type 2 diabetes mellitus and severe diabetic neuropathy. Examination of the patient shows mild weakness of the hand musculature and weakness and wasting of the anterior tibial and intrinsic foot muscles. Deep tendon reflexes are absent at the ankles and decreased elsewhere. Sensation to vibration and proprioception are mildly decreased over the distal lower extremities. Motor nerve conduction velocities are markedly decreased with prolonged distal motor latencies in the extremities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's weakness? A) Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease B) Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy C) Diabetic neuropathy D) Duchenne muscular dystrophy E) Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy
Correct Answer: A) Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT) is a heritable disease of peripheral neuropathy resulting from primarily autosomal dominant mutations in genes expressed in Schwann cells, the myelinating cells of the peripheral nervous system. This leads to progressive demyelination of peripheral sensory and motor nerves. Patients demonstrate motor weakness and decreased sensation to vibration and proprioception most prominent in the distal lower extremities. Physical examination findings include hyporeflexia or areflexia, clumsy walking, and musculoskeletal deformities such as pes cavus (high-arched feet) and hammer toes. Later in the disease course, atrophy of lower extremity muscles and intrinsic hand muscle weakness and atrophy may occur. Diagnosis is confirmed via nerve conduction studies, which show decreased conduction velocities and prolonged distal motor latencies consistent with demyelinating disease. Treatment is supportive and includes physical therapy. Choice B (Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy) is an acquired, immune-mediated disease presenting with symmetric proximal and distal motor weakness and sensory changes. The key distinguishing feature is that this patient has a clear family history suggestive of an inherited peripheral neuropathy, making CMT more likely. Choice C (Diabetic neuropathy) is an acquired, symmetric polyneuropathy that predominantly affects sensory nerves of the distal lower and upper extremities. Motor weakness typically occurs only in severe cases after years of hyperglycemia. Although the mother has diabetic neuropathy, the patient's presentation with progressive symptoms starting at age 14, family history of similar neuropathy in the father, and prominent motor findings make this unlikely. Choice D (Duchenne muscular dystrophy) is caused by an inherited mutation in the dystrophin gene and typically presents at ages 2-3 years with progressive weakness affecting proximal more than distal muscles. Cardiac conduction abnormalities are common, and sensory neuropathy would be atypical. Choice E (Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy) results in slowly progressive, asymmetric muscle weakness in facial, scapular, upper arm, lower leg, and abdominal muscles. Sensory neuropathy would be atypical. Educational Objective: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is an autosomal dominant peripheral neuropathy caused by mutations in genes expressed in Schwann cells, leading to demyelination. It presents with symmetric motor and sensory polyneuropathy beginning in the distal lower extremities and potentially progressing to upper extremities. Clinical features include progressive muscle weakness with hyporeflexia, muscle atrophy, decreased vibration and proprioceptive sensation, clumsy gait, and skeletal deformities (pes cavus and hammer toes). Nerve conduction studies show decreased velocities and prolonged distal motor latencies. Family history is often positive, and treatment is supportive.
▶ Nervous System Special Senses Otitis Media 1 questions
Source: 7A #1
A previously healthy 6-year-old boy is brought to the office because of a 2-day history of right ear pain. He went swimming in a lake 3 days ago. On examination, the right ear canal appears normal with no pain on motion of the canal or tragus; the eardrum is red, bulging, and immobile. The left ear and pharynx appear normal. The neck is supple; there is no lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Acute otitis media B) Bullous otitis C) Foreign body D) Labyrinthitis E) Otitis externa F) Otitis media with effusion
Correct Answer: A) Acute otitis media
Acute otitis media is an infection of the middle ear that classically occurs in children. The clinical presentation in this case is classic: a red, bulging, and immobile tympanic membrane with ear pain in a child following a viral upper respiratory infection risk exposure. Causative agents include viral or bacterial pathogens, commonly Streptococcus pneumoniae, Moraxella catarrhalis, or nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae. The key clinical findings that support acute otitis media are the erythematous (red), bulging tympanic membrane and immobility, which indicate retrotympanic pus or middle ear effusion with inflammation. The middle ear is bounded externally by the tympanic membrane and internally by the oval window, connected to the nasopharynx via the eustachian tubes. Infection usually spreads to the middle ear via the eustachian tubes. First-line therapy includes antibiotic treatment with amoxicillin with or without clavulanate, plus symptomatic treatment. Recurrent episodes may lead to mastoiditis, and children with recurrent acute otitis media may benefit from myringotomy and tympanostomy tube placement. Choice B (Bullous otitis) presents with severe otalgia and serous bullae or vesicles on the tympanic membrane, often with fever. While causative agents can include Streptococcus pneumoniae and Moraxella catarrhalis, bullous otitis is characterized by visible bullae/vesicles, which are not described in this case. Choice C (Foreign body) can present with earache, otorrhea, conductive hearing loss, or fullness, or be asymptomatic. Extraction requires direct visualization. However, the normal ear canal appearance and the classic appearance of an inflamed tympanic membrane make foreign body unlikely. Choice D (Labyrinthitis) is inflammation of the inner ear, usually viral, presenting with vertigo, nystagmus, tinnitus, hearing loss, balance issues, nausea, fever, and otalgia. This patient has no vertigo or balance issues reported, making labyrinthitis unlikely. Additionally, labyrinthitis would not produce the characteristic bulging, red tympanic membrane. Choice E (Otitis externa) presents with otalgia, otorrhea, pruritus, and hearing loss, with pain on ear manipulation and edema, debris, and erythema in the external auditory canal. The key distinction is that otitis externa involves the external auditory canal with pain on tragal or canal manipulation, while this patient has a normal canal and no pain on canal/tragus manipulation. The inflamed tympanic membrane is characteristic of middle ear infection, not external ear infection. Choice F (Otitis media with effusion), also called serous otitis media, is suggested by middle ear effusion without inflammatory signs of acute infection (no fever, tympanic membrane erythema, or retrotympanic pus). This patient has clear signs of acute inflammation with an erythematous, bulging tympanic membrane and acute symptoms, ruling out serous otitis media. Educational Objective: Acute otitis media is an infection of the middle ear that usually spreads to this space via the eustachian tubes from the nasopharynx. It presents with ear pain, often with fever, an erythematous tympanic membrane with retrotympanic pus or a middle ear effusion, and conductive hearing loss. Commonly implicated pathogens include Streptococcus pneumoniae, nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. Treatment is with antibiotics, typically amoxicillin.
▶ Blood Lymphoreticular System Von Willebrand disease 1 questions
Source: 7A #5
A 12-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of vaginal bleeding for 2 weeks. Pubertal development began at the age of 10 years. Her first menstrual period began 6 weeks ago and lasted for 10 days; she used 10 to 12 sanitary pads daily. Her second menstrual period began 2 weeks ago and has not stopped. She had been using 12 pads daily until 2 days ago; since then, she has used 6 daily. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 95/60 mm Hg. Examination shows no other abnormalities. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 10 g/dL Leukocyte count 10,000/mm³ with a normal differential Platelet count 180,000/mm³ Prothrombin time 12 sec (INR=1) Partial thromboplastin time 45 sec Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Acute lymphocytic leukemia B) Anovulatory menstrual cycles C) Factor XI deficiency D) Factor XIII deficiency E) Hyperthyroidism F) Von Willebrand disease
Correct Answer: F) Von Willebrand disease
Von Willebrand disease (VWD) is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with menorrhagia leading to anemia and an isolated increase in partial thromboplastin time (PTT). VWD results from impairments in the amount or function of the von Willebrand protein multimer, a plasma protein that binds platelets to subendothelial collagen. The deficiency results in impaired hemostasis, generally involving mucosal and epithelial locations, due to deficiency of platelet adhesion. VWD can be genetic (autosomal dominant) or acquired. Since the von Willebrand multimer also acts as a serum transport protein for coagulation factor VIII, factor VIII concentrations may be decreased, leading to the increase in PTT without affecting the prothrombin time (PT). Patients often present with menorrhagia, recurrent nosebleeds, easy bruising, petechiae, gastrointestinal, and gingival bleeding. Unless blood loss is substantial, laboratory studies will otherwise be normal. The platelet count is typically normal, which distinguishes VWD from other coagulopathies. Treatment, in addition to supportive care with bleeding control and transfusions, may involve the administration of desmopressin, which promotes the release of additional vWF stored in endothelial cells. Choice A (Acute lymphocytic leukemia) is most common in pediatric patients and presents with weight loss, fevers, and malaise. Anemia and thrombocytopenia can also occur, leading to easy bruising and petechiae. This patient has a clear source of bleeding leading to her anemia with a normal concentration of platelets and no systemic symptoms, making von Willebrand disease a more likely diagnosis. Choice B (Anovulatory menstrual cycles) can cause menorrhagia caused by prolonged proliferation of the endometrial lining. However, anovulatory menstrual cycles are generally associated with irregularly timed intervals between periods. This patient has had a normal cycle length and recurrence, making anovulatory cycles an unlikely cause of her menorrhagia. They would also not explain the increase in this patient's PTT. Choice C (Factor XI deficiency) is an uncommon coagulopathy caused by genetic or acquired quantitative or qualitative compromise of factor XI. It may result in bleeding, such as that seen in this patient. However, bleeding associated with factor deficiency more commonly occurs early in life and in visceral as opposed to mucosal locations. Choice D (Factor XIII deficiency) is a rare coagulopathy that leads to spontaneous bleeding, including hemarthrosis and intracranial hemorrhages. While it can cause menorrhagia, it more commonly presents early in life. Factor XIII deficiency would also cause a prolonged PT and PTT, not an isolated PTT prolongation. Choice E (Hyperthyroidism) can lead to menorrhagia via anovulatory cycles, which often cause irregular and heavy menstrual bleeding. However, other symptoms of hyperthyroidism, such as hot flashes, weight loss, tachycardia, and tremors are not present in this patient. Educational Objective: Von Willebrand disease results from impairments in the amount or function of the von Willebrand protein multimer, a plasma protein that binds platelets to subendothelial collagen. The deficiency results in impaired hemostasis, generally involving mucosal and epithelial locations, caused by deficiency of platelet adhesion. The platelet count is generally normal, and the partial thromboplastin time is increased because of the protein's role in shuttling factor VIII in plasma. Treatment includes supportive care plus supplemental desmopressin.
▶ Behavioral Health Fetal Alcohol Syndrome 1 questions
Source: 7A #6
A 2-week-old newborn is brought for a well-child examination. He was born at 38 weeks' gestation to a 27-year-old primigravid woman following an uncomplicated pregnancy. Physical examination shows short palpebral fissures, maxillary hypoplasia, micrognathia, and a thin upper lip. The lungs are clear to auscultation. A grade 1/6 systolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border with radiation to the left axilla and back. Femoral pulses are normal. Neurologic examination shows mild hypotonia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Congenital toxoplasmosis B) Down syndrome C) Fetal alcohol syndrome D) Fragile X syndrome E) Seminiferous tubule dysgenesis (Klinefelter syndrome) F) Trisomy 13 syndrome
Correct Answer: C) Fetal alcohol syndrome
Alcohol is a proven teratogen that causes fetal alcohol syndrome when used during pregnancy. Due to disruption of cell migration during development, fetal alcohol syndrome presents with a characteristic cluster of physical abnormalities including microcephaly, facial dysmorphia (small palpebral fissures, maxillary hypoplasia, thin vermilion border, cleft lip/palate, smooth philtrum), limb deformities, and congenital heart disease. The patient's presentation of short palpebral fissures, maxillary hypoplasia, micrognathia, thin upper lip, mild hypotonia, and a systolic murmur are all consistent with this diagnosis. Muscular abnormalities such as gross motor delays, hypotonia, and tremulousness are common. Patients may also demonstrate abnormal bone development and delayed bone growth. Fetal alcohol syndrome is the leading cause of intellectual disability in the United States. Congenital toxoplasmosis (Choice A) typically presents with chorioretinitis, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, convulsions, cerebral calcifications, and hydrocephalus—features not seen in this patient. Down syndrome (Choice B) is a chromosomal trisomy presenting with hypotonia, downturned (not short) palpebral fissures, prominent epicanthal folds, flat facies, single palmar creases, and intellectual developmental disorder. This patient has dysmorphic features more consistent with fetal alcohol syndrome. Fragile X syndrome (Choice D) is an X-linked dominant cause of intellectual disability presenting with intellectual developmental disorder, an elongated face with prominent jaw, high-arched palate, large ears, hyperextensible joints, and postpubertal macroorchidism. This patient has decreased jaw size and does not demonstrate hyperextensible joints. Seminiferous tubule dysgenesis/Klinefelter syndrome (Choice E) features an XXY karyotype causing testicular atrophy and decreased spermatogenesis. Dysmorphic features include eunuchoid body shape, long extremities, and gynecomastia—not present in this patient. Trisomy 13/Patau syndrome (Choice F) presents with intellectual developmental disorder and characteristic features including cleft lip and palate, holoprosencephaly, microphthalmia, cutis aplasia, abnormal feet with prominent calcaneus and convexly rounded soles, and polydactyly. This patient does not demonstrate these gross neurologic abnormalities. Educational Objective: Recognize that alcohol is a known teratogen causing fetal alcohol syndrome with characteristic facial dysmorphia (small palpebral fissures, thin vermilion border, smooth philtrum), intellectual developmental disorder, muscular deformities (hypotonia, gross motor delays), limb deformities, and congenital heart disease.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Rickets 1 questions
Source: 7A #7
A 15-month-old girl is brought to the physician because she has not begun to crawl or walk. She has been exclusively breast-fed since birth. She is at the 50th percentile for length and the 85th percentile for weight. Her language and social skills are appropriate for age. Examination shows no abnormalities except for widening of the wrists. Which of the following serum findings is most likely to be increased? A) ALT activity B) Alkaline phosphatase activity C) Calcium concentration D) Magnesium concentration E) Phosphorus concentration
Correct Answer: B) Alkaline phosphatase activity
Vitamin D deficiency in breastfed infants leads to rickets due to impaired calcium and phosphate homeostasis and bone mineralization. Alkaline phosphatase is an enzyme present in bile ductules and bone that plays a role in bone mineralization by osteoblasts. Vitamin D deficiency results in decreased intestinal calcium absorption and hypocalcemia, which is sensed by the parathyroid gland via calcium-sensing receptors, leading to increased PTH secretion. Increased PTH stimulates osteoclastic bone reabsorption and increased bone turnover, which releases both calcium and alkaline phosphatase into the bloodstream, resulting in elevated serum alkaline phosphatase. Rickets in children presents with frontal bossing, bone pain and deformities such as bowing of the legs, widening of zones of mineralization on radiography caused by unmineralized osteoid, hypoplastic teeth, bulging of costochondral junctions, and growth delay. In infants, bone pain may manifest as refusal or inability to crawl or walk, as seen in this patient. Choice A (ALT activity) increases in conditions that damage the liver, such as hepatitis and medication-induced hepatotoxicity, not in rickets. Choice C (Calcium concentration) is likely normal or decreased because intestinal calcium absorption is low in vitamin D deficiency. Hypercalcemia and bone turnover are features of primary hyperparathyroidism, not rickets. Choice D (Magnesium concentration) would not be affected in rickets as magnesium does not play a significant role in bone or vitamin D metabolism. Choice E (Phosphorus concentration) will be normal or low in this patient due to decreased vitamin D and increased PTH, which promotes kidney phosphorus excretion.
