Hyperphosphatemia is associated with hypoparathyroidism and secondary hyperparathyroidism due to chronic kidney disease, not vitamin D deficiency rickets. Educational Objective: Rickets is most commonly caused by childhood vitamin D deficiency, which impairs calcium and phosphate homeostasis and bone mineralization. This presents as frontal bossing, bone pain and deformities such as bowing of the legs, widening of zones of mineralization on radiography due to unmineralized osteoid, hypoplastic teeth, bulging of costochondral junctions, and growth delay. Breastfed infants are at risk for vitamin D deficiency and are recommended to receive oral vitamin D supplementation.
▶ Behavioral Health Elimination Disorders Incontinence 1 questions
Source: 7A #8
A 6-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his mother because of intermittent bed-wetting. He was toilet trained at the age of 4 years but has never remained dry through the night and typically wets the bed three to four times weekly. He does not wet himself during the day. He has not had pain with urination or urinary urgency, hesitancy, or dribbling. Urine stream is normal. He is a "heavy sleeper." He has not had fever, diarrhea, or constipation. He recently started first grade and has not yet made any friends. Growth and development are otherwise appropriate for age. Vital signs are within normal limits. The abdomen is soft and nontender. The penis is circumcised. The testes are descended. Urinalysis shows: pH 7.0, Specific gravity 1.020, Blood negative, Glucose negative, Protein negative, Ketones negative, Nitrites negative, Leukocyte esterase negative. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's enuresis? A) Adjustment disorder B) Detrusor muscle overactivity C) Primary enuresis D) Primary sleep disorder E) Urinary tract infection
Correct Answer: C) Primary enuresis
Primary enuresis refers to episodic urinary incontinence occurring in children older than age 5 years who have never remained dry through the night. The pathogenesis of primary enuresis most commonly involves a delay in maturation, though may alternatively be related to a small functional bladder capacity or genetic factors. This patient fits the classic presentation: he was toilet trained at age 4 but has never remained consistently dry at night, with no daytime incontinence and no symptoms of dysuria or urgency. His urinalysis is completely normal, ruling out organic causes. The episodes commonly lead to adjustment problems and low self-esteem, but the enuresis itself is not caused by these psychological factors. Management includes motivational therapy (rewarding the patient for urinating prior to bed and/or having incontinence-free nights), and for persistent cases, enuresis alarms or desmopressin may be indicated. Choice A (Adjustment disorder) refers to the onset of disproportionate distress within 3 months of an identifiable stressor. Though the patient recently started first grade and has difficulty making friends, he does not demonstrate depressive or anxiety symptoms meeting criteria for an adjustment disorder. Additionally, adjustment disorder does not cause enuresis. Choice B (Detrusor muscle overactivity) results in urge incontinence with symptoms of urinary urgency. This patient explicitly denies urinary urgency, making this diagnosis unlikely. Choice D (Primary sleep disorder) is characterized by insomnia or dysregulated sleep patterns, not heavy sleeping. While the patient is described as a "heavy sleeper," primary enuresis is not classified as a sleep disorder. The heavy sleeping may be a contributing factor (difficulty waking to sensation of full bladder), but it does not explain the enuresis itself. Choice E (Urinary tract infections) present with dysuria, frequency, urgency, and suprapubic discomfort. They occur more frequently in women than men due to anatomical factors such as a shorter urethra. This patient denies dysuria and urgency. Most importantly, his urinalysis did not demonstrate leukocyte esterase or nitrites, which are hallmark findings in urinary tract infection. The normal urinalysis effectively rules out UTI as a cause. Educational Objective: Primary enuresis refers to episodic urinary incontinence occurring in children older than 5 years who have never remained dry through the night. The pathogenesis of primary enuresis most commonly involves a delay in maturation.
▶ Blood Lymphoreticular System Immune thrombocytopenic purpura 1 questions
Source: 7A #11
A previously healthy 4-year-old boy is brought to the office because of a 3-day history of easy bruising that began on the extremities but now includes the trunk. There is no history of trauma. His parents say that he is very active. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 100/min, and respirations are 16/min. Examination shows scattered petechiae and multiple ecchymoses in various stages of healing over the trunk and extremities; they are most pronounced on the extremities. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 12 g/dL, Leukocyte count 6000/mm³, Platelet count 1000/mm³, Prothrombin time 12 sec (control 12.2) (INR=1), Partial thromboplastin time 34 sec (control 33). Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition? A) Abnormal platelet function B) Child abuse C) Decreased platelet production D) Disseminated intravascular coagulation E) Increased platelet destruction
Correct Answer: E) Increased platelet destruction
Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is caused by antiplatelet antibodies that bind platelets, leading to opsonization and destruction. Platelet destruction occurs when macrophages within the spleen phagocytose the platelet-antibody complex, resulting in thrombocytopenia. ITP is diagnosed in the setting of a low platelet count and absence of other explanatory causes for thrombocytopenia. Bone marrow biopsy will classically show an increased number of megakaryocytes indicating adequate platelet production but increased peripheral destruction of platelets. It classically presents with petechiae, purpura, and prolonged bleeding time on laboratory analysis. Acute ITP is often seen in pediatric patients, may follow an infection, generally is self-limited, and is managed conservatively in the absence of life-threatening bleeds. This patient's presentation is classic for ITP: sudden onset of petechiae and ecchymoses, severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count 1000/mm³), normal coagulation studies (normal PT and PTT), normal hemoglobin, and normal leukocyte count, all in an otherwise healthy child. The absence of other systemic findings and normal coagulation parameters help exclude other causes. Choice A (Abnormal platelet function) may be seen in genetic conditions such as Glanzmann thrombasthenia, in which patients have a defect in the GpIIb/IIIa protein, preventing both platelet aggregation and formation of a platelet plug. However, this would typically present with a normal platelet count. Choice B (Child abuse) is associated with the development of both unexplained ecchymosis and bone fractures at different stages of healing, as well as cerebral hematomas. However, the laboratory findings showing severe thrombocytopenia with normal coagulation studies are more consistent with a primary hematologic disorder than with abuse. Choice C (Decreased platelet production) may result from conditions including aplastic anemia, which typically presents with anemia, thrombocytopenia, and leukopenia. It may be associated with parvovirus B19 infection in children. However, this patient has a normal hemoglobin and normal leukocyte count, making decreased production less likely than increased destruction. Choice D (Disseminated intravascular coagulation) is a systemic disorder characterized by the widespread activation of the clotting cascade resulting in microthrombi formation, thrombocytopenia, and bleeding complications due to consumption of platelets and clotting factors. Laboratory studies show thrombocytopenia, prolonged prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time, decreased fibrinogen concentrations, and increased D-dimer concentrations. This patient's normal PT and PTT make DIC unlikely. Educational Objective: Increased platelet destruction in immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is associated with the development of antibodies that bind platelets, leading to opsonization and phagocytosis by macrophages in the spleen. ITP is diagnosed in patients with a low platelet count without alternative explanatory causes, and presents with petechiae and purpura, often in patients who appear otherwise well. Acute ITP may follow an infection in children, generally is self-limited, and requires clinical monitoring.
▶ Endocrine System Adrenal adenoma 1 questions
Source: 7A #12
A 10-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 6-month history of increased facial hair growth and facial acne. She is at the 50th percentile for height and weight. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 64/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. Examination shows mild clitoral enlargement and an early male pubic hair pattern. Laboratory studies show a serum testosterone concentration of 0.2 nmol/L (N=0.17-0.7), dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate concentration of 9 g/mL (N=0.5-5.4), and urine 17-ketosteroid excretion of 20 mg/24 h (N=6-15). Pelvic ultrasonography shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Adrenal adenoma B) Androgen insensitivity syndrome C) Ovarian adenoma D) Pituitary adenoma E) Polycystic ovarian syndrome
Correct Answer: A) Adrenal adenoma
The adrenal cortex is composed of three zones: the zona glomerulosa producing aldosterone, zona fasciculata producing cortisol, and zona reticularis producing dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate. In the zona reticularis, 17-hydroxypregnenolone is converted to dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate by 17α-hydroxylase. Patients presenting with virilization of female genitalia, hirsutism, and elevation of dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate and 17-ketosteroid excretion should be evaluated for adrenal adenoma. These patients have normal testosterone concentrations and normal pelvic ultrasound, which matches this case perfectly. Choice B (Androgen insensitivity syndrome) results from a defect in the androgen receptor. Genotypically male patients with this condition exhibit a female phenotype with female external genitalia and rudimentary vagina but internally develop normal functioning testes. This patient does not display these characteristics. Choice C (Ovarian adenoma), specifically Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor, produces androgens including testosterone, presenting with hirsutism and virilization. Patients with Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors present with increased testosterone levels, making this diagnosis unlikely. Choice D (Pituitary adenoma), including prolactinoma, presents with bilateral peripheral vision loss, headache, amenorrhea, and galactorrhea in female patients. A pituitary adenoma leading to virilization would be uncommon as most functional adenomas produce prolactin or growth hormone. Choice E (Polycystic ovarian syndrome) presents with hirsutism, increased body weight, and anovulation leading to irregular menstrual bleeding and infertility. Pelvic ultrasound shows enlarged ovaries with numerous follicular cysts. PCOS presents with increased luteinizing hormone to follicle-stimulating hormone ratio and increased testosterone, but normal pelvic ultrasound excludes this diagnosis. Educational Objective: An adrenal adenoma arising from the zona reticularis of the adrenal cortex produces high levels of dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate leading to hirsutism, virilization, and increased 17-ketosteroid concentrations. These tumors should be suspected in female patients with hirsutism and virilization who have a normal pelvic ultrasound, normal testosterone concentrations, and increased dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate concentrations.
▶ Renal Urinary System Renal Tubular Acidosis 1 questions
Source: 7A #17
An 18-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of poor linear growth. There is no history of vomiting or diarrhea. His blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show: Na+ 138 mEq/L Cl- 112 mEq/L K+ 3.1 mEq/L HCO3- 16 mEq/L Urine pH 7.6 Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows: pH 7.28 PCO2 26 mm Hg PO2 98 mm Hg Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's hypokalemia? A) Addison disease B) Congenital adrenal hyperplasia C) Hyperparathyroidism D) Juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia E) Pheochromocytoma F) Primary hyperaldosteronism G) Pseudohypoaldosteronism H) Renal artery stenosis
Correct Answer: I) Renal tubular acidosis
Renal tubular acidosis (RTA) results in a hyperchloremic, non-anion gap metabolic acidosis from dysregulation of the kidney tubules. This patient's laboratory findings are consistent with RTA: low bicarbonate concentration (16 mEq/L) with a normal anion gap (Na+ - Cl- - HCO3- = 138 - 112 - 16 = 10), indicating non-anion gap metabolic acidosis. The urine pH of 7.6 is characteristic of distal RTA (type 1), which is caused by a defect in kidney secretion of H+, resulting in lack of HCO3- generation and metabolic acidosis. The arterial blood gas shows incomplete respiratory compensation (low PCO2 of 26 mm Hg). RTA is associated with kidney potassium wasting and hypokalemia, which explains this patient's K+ of 3.1 mEq/L. Common causes include analgesic nephropathy, congenital obstructive urinary tract anomalies, drugs (amphotericin), and autoimmune diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, Sjogren syndrome). Choice A (Addison disease): Primary adrenal insufficiency causes hypotension, hyperkalemia (not hypokalemia), metabolic acidosis, and skin hyperpigmentation due to deficiency of aldosterone and cortisol. Choice B (Congenital adrenal hyperplasia): Results from defects in adrenal steroid biosynthesis. The most common form, 21-hydroxylase deficiency, presents with salt-wasting, hypotension, hyperkalemia (not hypokalemia), and virilization of XX fetuses. Choice C (Hyperparathyroidism): Leads to bone resorption and hypercalcemia through increased parathyroid hormone production. Does not explain the acid-base disturbance or hypokalemia. Choice D (Juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia): Results in increased renin and angiotensin II production, leading to hypertension, increased Na+ reabsorption, aldosterone release, and hypokalemia. However, it would not cause metabolic acidosis or the characteristic urine pH findings. Choice E (Pheochromocytoma): A tumor of the adrenal medulla presenting with episodic hypertension, headache, and palpitations. Does not cause hypokalemia, metabolic acidosis, or the observed electrolyte pattern. Choice F (Primary hyperaldosteronism): Presents with hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis (not acidosis), with increased aldosterone-to-renin ratio. Associated with adrenal adenoma or bilateral hyperplasia. Choice G (Pseudohypoaldosteronism): Characterized by problems with sodium regulation leading to hyponatremia, hyperkalemia (not hypokalemia), and hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. Choice H (Renal artery stenosis): Can lead to chronic kidney disease with electrolyte derangements and hypertension, but does not explain the specific pattern of non-anion gap metabolic acidosis with elevated urine pH and hypokalemia. Educational Objective: Renal tubular acidosis results in a hyperchloremic, non-anion gap metabolic acidosis from dysregulation of the kidney tubules and is associated with compensatory respiratory alkalosis and hypokalemia. Distal RTA (type 1) is characterized by a urine pH greater than 5.5 and results from defective renal H+ secretion.
▶ Cardiovascular System Pulmonary Valve Stenosis 1 questions
Source: 7A #18
A 3-day-old girl undergoes evaluation prior to discharge from the hospital. She was born at 39 weeks' gestation following an uncomplicated pregnancy and cesarean delivery for cephalopelvic disproportion and weighed 3256 g (7 lb 3 oz). Examination at birth showed no abnormalities. She is exclusively breast-fed. She is alert and active. Her temperature is normal and O2 saturation is normal. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 99%. A new grade 2/6, early systolic murmur is heard in the pulmonic area with radiation to the lung fields and is loudest in the right axilla. Peripheral pulses are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Aortic stenosis B) Atrial septal defect C) Patent ductus arteriosus D) Pulmonary stenosis E) Ventricular septal defect
Correct Answer: D) Pulmonary stenosis
The most likely diagnosis is pulmonary stenosis. It is often diagnosed early in life and in female patients more than males. Pulmonary stenosis is typically congenital and benign, or it may be associated with other congenital cardiac syndromes. The blockage may occur at the level of the pulmonic valve as a result of fusion of the commissures or other defects of the leaflets, subvalvular caused by narrowing of the right ventricular outflow tract, or supravalvular (also called peripheral pulmonic stenosis) caused by narrowing or impingement of the pulmonary artery. Physical examination findings depend on the severity of stenosis. Most patients will have a systolic ejection murmur with radiation to the back. Some may have an associated ejection click, split S2, or left parasternal heave. Most patients are asymptomatic, though complications can occur if the condition persists into adulthood. Surgical revision and balloon valvotomy have excellent prognosis. Choice A (Aortic stenosis) presents with a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur, best heard at the upper right sternal border, and radiates to the carotid arteries. In a newborn, it may be caused by a congenital bicuspid aortic valve or other congenital cardiac syndromes. Choice B (Atrial septal defect) is a common congenital malformation of the interatrial septum resulting in a left-to-right shunt. Examination typically shows a fixed, widely split S2 caused by increased blood flow through the pulmonic valve. Severe defects can result in pulmonary hypertension and development of Eisenmenger syndrome over time, with reversal of the left-to-right shunt. Choice C (Patent ductus arteriosus) results from failure of the normal, extracardiac embryonic shunt between the pulmonary artery and aorta to appropriately close in the neonatal period. It results in an extracardiac left-to-right shunt and classically presents with a continuous machine-like murmur. Choice E (Ventricular septal defect) represents common cardiac malformations that result in a left-to-right intracardiac shunt. They may form in isolation or in conjunction with other malformations. They are characterized by a holosystolic murmur best heard in the left lower sternal border and may have an associated palpable thrill. Educational Objective: Pulmonary stenosis is a congenital, benign cardiac malformation that may occur in isolation or as part of a congenital cardiac syndrome. The stenosis may occur at the level of the right ventricular outflow tract, pulmonic valve, or pulmonary artery. A systolic ejection murmur with radiation to the back may be heard. Prognosis is excellent with corrective intervention.
▶ Respiratory System Mycoplasma pneumoniae Pneumonia 1 questions
Source: 7A #23
A previously healthy 10-year-old boy has a 10-day history of progressive cough, low-grade fever, and slight dyspnea on exertion. Examination shows diffuse crackles bilaterally. An x-ray of the chest shows a diffuse perihilar infiltrate. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Pneumonia due to respiratory syncytial virus B) Pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae C) Pneumonia due to Mycoplasma pneumoniae D) Congestive heart failure E) Tuberculosis
Correct Answer: C) Pneumonia due to Mycoplasma pneumoniae
Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a pleomorphic organism lacking a cell wall that typically causes atypical pneumonia in young patients and is transmitted by respiratory droplets. The most common symptoms include mild fever, headache, and non-productive cough. Physical examination may reveal bilateral crackles and/or wheezing and a vesicular rash. A characteristic finding is that the chest x-ray appearance is more severe than the patient's clinical presentation, showing patchy or diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates, which matches this patient's presentation. Mycoplasma is fastidious and can be grown on Eaton agar though this takes weeks, and it does not appear on Gram stain due to lacking a cell wall. Diagnosis is usually based on clinical presentation. Laboratory support includes high titer serum cold agglutinins (IgM antibodies). Treatment consists of macrolide antibiotics, doxycycline, or fluoroquinolones. Other atypical pneumonia causes include respiratory viruses, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, and Legionella. Choice A (RSV pneumonia) is less common than bronchiolitis in children and typically presents with fever, tachypnea, rhinorrhea, and wheezing with possible apneic episodes; bronchiolitis is less common beyond infancy. Choice B (Streptococcus pneumoniae) classically presents with fever, dyspnea, productive cough, and pleuritic chest pain. Bacterial pneumonia is typically lobar and involves a single lobe rather than being widely distributed. Choice D (Congestive heart failure) in children presents with shortness of breath, weight gain, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and peripheral edema. In children it is most commonly associated with congenital cardiac malformations, arteriovenous fistula, and severe malnutrition, making it unusual in a previously healthy 10-year-old. Choice E (Tuberculosis) presents with subacute fever, weight loss, night sweats, cough, and malaise in primary disease. Latent tuberculosis is commonly asymptomatic. Reactivation presents similarly to primary disease but occurs after latency, typically affecting lung apices or resulting in miliary disease. Educational Objective: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a pleomorphic organism associated with causing atypical pneumonia in young patients. The chest x-ray characteristically appears more severe than the patient's clinical presentation, with patchy or diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates.
▶ Renal Urinary System Polycystic Kidney Disease 1 questions
Source: 7A #24
A 3200-g (7-lb 1-oz) male newborn is delivered at 38 weeks' gestation. Pregnancy, labor, and delivery were uncomplicated. Apgar scores are 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. Examination shows no abnormalities except lateral flank masses. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit 50%, pH 6.8, Specific gravity 1.009, Blood moderate, Protein trace. Ultrasonography shows bilateral enlargement of the kidneys with mixed echogenicity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor) B) Neuroblastoma C) Polycystic kidney disease D) Renal cell carcinoma E) Renal vein thrombosis
Correct Answer: C) Polycystic kidney disease
Polycystic kidney disease is caused by genetic mutations resulting in the development of multiple cysts in the kidney due to structural abnormalities of the renal tubules. Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) results from a mutation in PKHD1 and is a form of infantile cystic kidney disease manifesting with numerous small kidney cysts that replace normal kidney parenchyma. The clinical presentation of bilateral kidney enlargement with mixed echogenicity on ultrasound in a newborn with lateral flank masses is characteristic of ARPKD. ARPKD is associated with hepatic fibrosis and Caroli disease, and can cause oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia (Potter sequence) if it develops in utero. Choice A (Nephroblastoma/Wilms tumor) is the most common kidney malignancy in childhood caused by mutations in WT1 or WT2. It typically presents as a unilateral flank mass that is smooth rather than nodular and does not cross the midline, characterized by hematuria. Choice B (Neuroblastoma) is a malignancy of sympathetic nervous system neuroendocrine cells commonly affecting the adrenal glands. It is distinguished by its tendency to cross the midline with nodular texture and association with opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome and elevated catecholamine metabolites. Choice D (Renal cell carcinoma) is an adenocarcinoma of tubular epithelial cells presenting with gross hematuria without RBC casts, flank pain, and possible palpable mass. Diagnosis is confirmed by contrast-enhanced CT/MRI and biopsy. Choice E (Renal vein thrombosis) occurs in patients with thrombophilic conditions and presents with flank pain, hematuria, acute kidney injury, or may be asymptomatic. It would not distort intrarenal architecture as seen in polycystic kidney disease.
▶ Nervous System Special Senses Hordeolum 1 questions
Source: 7A #25
A 10-year-old boy is brought to the office because of a 2-day history of redness and mild pain in his left eye. He is afebrile. Examination of the left eye shows a mildly erythematous conjunctiva. There is conjunctival edema and tenderness and a 3-mm nodule at the lower lateral lid margin. Examination of the right eye shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment? A) Nasolacrimal massage B) Oral amoxicillin C) Topical prednisolone D) Topical tetrahydrozoline E) Warm compresses and gentle massage
Correct Answer: E) Warm compresses and gentle massage
A hordeolum, or stye, is a common, acute infection of the oil glands of the eyelid caused by obstruction of the oil gland orifice with subsequent accumulation of sebaceous material and overgrowth of skin flora, most commonly Staphylococcal species. Patients present with a focal, well-defined subcutaneous nodule at the eyelid margin with associated skin erythema. A blocked glandular orifice may be visible as a focal white point with associated discharge, which may cause ocular surface irritation and conjunctival injection and chemosis. Initial treatment is with warm compresses and gentle massage of the lesion, which help to dissolve inspissated glandular material and promote drainage of the gland. Topical antibiotic ointment is helpful, although systemic antibiotics are not usually necessary. Incision and drainage may be considered for hordeola that do not improve within several weeks. Choice A (Nasolacrimal massage) is useful for dacryocystitis, which presents with pain, erythema, and swelling beneath the medial aspect of the lower eyelid with purulent discharge from the lower punctum, not the focal nodule at the lid margin seen here. Choice B (Oral amoxicillin) is useful for mild preseptal cellulitis but not for hordeolum. Preseptal cellulitis presents with diffuse erythema, warmth, and edema of preseptal soft tissues, which is absent in this patient. While preseptal cellulitis may originate from a hordeolum, the absence of diffuse soft tissue erythema argues against this diagnosis. Choice C (Topical prednisolone) is a glucocorticoid useful for reducing intraocular inflammation in anterior uveitis. It is not helpful for hordeolum management and is typically avoided in suspected infectious conditions. Choice D (Topical tetrahydrozoline), an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist, reduces conjunctival injection and is available over-the-counter for cosmetic improvement. However, it does not address the underlying cause of hordeolum and may increase ocular surface irritation. A hordeolum should be distinguished from a chalazion, which is a sterile, noninfectious, chronic, granulomatous inflammation of obstructed meibomian gland material on the eyelid margin.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency 1 questions
Source: 7A #26
A 16-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of cough productive of thick yellowish sputum and a 1-day history of shortness of breath. She has not had fever. She has a history of asthma treated with albuterol and inhaled corticosteroids for which she required hospitalization on 10 occasions between the ages of 8 and 10 years. She has smoked one and one-half packs of cigarettes daily for 4 years. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 102/min, respirations are 42/min, and blood pressure is 108/80 mm Hg. Examination shows mild clubbing of the digits and increased anteroposterior chest diameter. Occasional end-expiratory wheezes are heard on auscultation. A chest x-ray shows no abnormalities other than severe bilateral hyperinflation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Alpha-1-Antitrypsin deficiency B) Congenital lobar emphysema C) Kartagener syndrome D) Pulmonary sequestration E) Sarcoidosis
Correct Answer: A) Alpha-1-Antitrypsin deficiency
Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency is an inherited protease inhibitor deficiency caused by mutations in the SERPINA1 gene, which encodes alpha-1-antitrypsin. Alpha-1-antitrypsin normally regulates neutrophil elastase, a serine protease secreted by neutrophils and macrophages as part of localized inflammatory response. Reduced activity of alpha-1-antitrypsin results in host tissue damage from neutrophil elastase, especially in the lungs. Pulmonary manifestations classically include panlobular emphysema, especially in the lung bases, as evidenced by this patient's bilateral hyperinflation on chest x-ray. The diagnosis should be suspected in a young patient presenting with chronic lung disease and bibasilar emphysematous changes. Patients are also at risk for chronic liver inflammation and cirrhosis due to accumulation of misfolded alpha-1-antitrypsin polymers in hepatocytes. This patient's presentation with early-onset emphysema in a young smoker with a history of asthma requiring hospitalization, clubbing, increased anteroposterior diameter, and bilateral hyperinflation is classic for this condition. Congenital lobar emphysema (Choice B) is a rare pulmonary disorder caused by disrupted embryonic bronchopulmonary development characterized by air trapping and lung hyperinflation visible on chest imaging. Disease severity varies widely and may be asymptomatic until adulthood or present in the newborn with respiratory distress. Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency is more common and better explains this patient's clinical picture. Kartagener syndrome (Choice C) is an inherited disorder of ciliary function that typically presents in early childhood with situs inversus, impaired mucociliary clearance with recurrent pneumonia and bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis, and infertility disorders. This patient lacks these characteristic features. Pulmonary sequestration (Choice D) is a congenital lung malformation with dysplastic, nonfunctional lung tissue that does not communicate with the airway. Patients typically present with recurrent pneumonia in the same localized lung region, along with persistent cough, hemoptysis, exertional dyspnea, and back pain. This does not fit this patient's bilateral presentation. Sarcoidosis (Choice E) is a chronic granulomatous inflammatory condition affecting multiple organ systems. It typically presents with cough, dyspnea, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, potentially with anterior uveitis, erythema nodosum, and arthralgias. Characteristic imaging shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with or without bilateral upper lobe predominant interstitial infiltrates. This patient's imaging shows only hyperinflation without lymphadenopathy. Educational Objective: Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency should be suspected in young patients who present with emphysematous lung changes. Alpha-1-antitrypsin is a protease inhibitor responsible for regulating neutrophil elastase. Patients are also at risk for chronic liver inflammation and cirrhosis due to accumulation of misfolded alpha-1-antitrypsin polymers in hepatocytes.
▶ Immune System Chronic Granulomatous Disease 1 questions
Source: 7A #27
A 5-year-old boy is brought to the office because of a 3-day history of a rash on his left leg. He has had five previous skin abscesses that have required prolonged treatment. He was admitted to the hospital for osteomyelitis at the ages of 2 and 4 years and pneumonia at the age of 3 years. The patient's temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F). Examination shows several enlarged, tender left inguinal lymph nodes. There is a 2 x 3-cm warm, erythematous macular rash over the left lower extremity. Which of the following mechanisms of disease is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms? A) Abnormal leukocyte adhesion B) Abnormal leukocyte degranulation C) Bone marrow infiltration D) Impaired leukocyte chemotaxis E) Impaired leukocyte microbicidal activity
Correct Answer: E) Impaired leukocyte microbicidal activity
Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is a rare primary immunodeficiency syndrome caused by mutations in the gene coding for NADPH oxidase, inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern. The condition results in defective intracellular killing of catalase-positive pathogens because NADPH oxidase is necessary for producing the respiratory/oxidative burst. The impaired leukocyte microbicidal activity makes patients susceptible to recurrent pyogenic bacterial and fungal infections with organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, Serratia marcescens, Aspergillus species, and Candida species. Symptoms typically appear within the first few years of life with recurrent pneumonia, lung abscesses, aspergillosis infection, skin abscesses, osteomyelitis, and chronic diarrhea. Physical examination may reveal hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis is made by an abnormal dihydrorhodamine test or nitroblue tetrazolium reduction test; in the latter, normal phagocytes reduce nitroblue (yellow to blue color change), while CGD patients show no color change. Choice A (Abnormal leukocyte adhesion) and Choice D (Impaired leukocyte chemotaxis) are implicated in leukocyte adhesion deficiency, which presents with recurrent bacterial infections, impaired wound healing, delayed umbilical cord detachment, and absence of neutrophils at infection sites with no pus formation. Choice B (Abnormal leukocyte degranulation) occurs in Chediak-Higashi syndrome, characterized by frequent bacterial infections, oculocutaneous albinism, peripheral neuropathy, and progressive neurologic dysfunction; leukocyte degranulation is normal in CGD. Choice C (Bone marrow infiltration) occurs in leukemia, lymphomas, and myelodysplastic syndromes, resulting in anemia, leukopenia, and/or thrombocytopenia, which does not match this patient's presentation. The educational objective is that NADPH oxidase is necessary for reactive oxygen species formation in phagocytes, enabling bactericidal activity; mutations in NADPH oxidase complex proteins result in chronic granulomatous disease, characterized by recurrent pyogenic bacterial and fungal infections.
▶ Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Wounds affecting the Skin or Subcutaneous Tissue 1 questions
Source: 7A #34
A 17-year-old boy comes to the physician because of a 1-day history of swelling of his right hand. The swelling began 6 hours after he was involved in a fistfight at school the previous day. On questioning, he says he hit his opponent in the mouth and abdomen. Examination shows an erythematous, tender dorsum of the right hand. There is a small laceration over the fourth metacarpal head. Which of the following organisms are the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms? A) Aerobic gram-positive cocci B) Anaerobic gram-positive cocci C) Gram-negative bacilli D) Gram-positive bacilli E) Mixed oral and skin flora
Correct Answer: E) Mixed oral and skin flora
Human bites are associated with mixed oral flora and skin flora including Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, Eikenella corrodens, and various anaerobes. This patient's clenched-fist injury (hitting an opponent in the mouth) with interrupted skin barrier at the fourth metacarpal head puts him at high risk for polymicrobial infection. When the skin barrier is interrupted, these injuries are at high risk for infection with multiple organisms. Signs of superficial skin infection include tenderness at the affected site, erythema, swelling, purulent drainage, and potentially fever. Choice A (Aerobic gram-positive cocci) including Staphylococcus and Streptococcus spp. are commensal organisms that may be present as part of the mixed flora but are not the sole or primary cause. Choice B (Anaerobic gram-positive cocci) including Peptostreptococcus are also commensal organisms present in oral flora but represent only part of the mixed infection. Choice C (Gram-negative bacilli) such as Escherichia coli, Klebsiella spp., and Pseudomonas spp., although implicated in pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and bloodstream infections, are not commonly associated with secondary infection of human bites. Choice D (Gram-positive bacilli) such as Clostridium perfringens are associated with puncture wound injuries and gas gangrene rather than typical human bite infections. Affected patients should be evaluated for infection development at the injury site. These wounds should be irrigated, debrided if necessary, and left open due to high risk for infection. The first-line antibiotic of choice for infected human bites is amoxicillin-clavulanate acid.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Child Abuse 1 questions
Source: 7A #35
A 9-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his mother who reports that he injured his right thigh 2 hours ago when he slipped on a wet floor. Examination of the right thigh shows tenderness and swelling. Range of motion of the right hip is limited. An x-ray of the right lower extremity shows a spiral fracture of the femur. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Notification of child protective services B) Measurement of serum calcium concentration C) Complete blood count D) Bone scan of the right femur E) CT scan of the hip
Correct Answer: A) Notification of child protective services
This infant with a spiral femur fracture after slipping on a wet floor has a presentation concerning for child abuse. Several "red flags" should alert medical providers to potential child abuse, including a history inconsistent with the type of injury present, a mechanism of injury inconsistent with the child's physical ability (e.g., a 3-week-old infant rolling off the bed), and delay in presentation. Certain physical examination findings, such as retinal hemorrhages, bruises on the ears, trunk, neck, and certain burn patterns (e.g., circumferential hand or foot distribution, cigarette burns) should also alert the provider to potential abuse. Fractures of posterior ribs, metaphyseal corner fractures, and subdural hematomas in an infant are all suspicious imaging findings. Spiral fractures typically occur when a rotational force is applied, such as twisting of a limb. This infant's injury is inconsistent with the history that was given, and child protective services (CPS) should be notified immediately. Choice B (Measurement of serum calcium concentration) may be useful if hypocalcemia was thought to contribute to this patient's fracture. Vitamin D deficiency can lead to hypocalcemia and rickets in children and may increase the risk for fractures. However, this child does not have any examination findings consistent with rickets. Choices C (Complete blood count), D (Bone scan of the right femur), and E (CT scan of the hip) are unlikely to be useful for this patient. Furthermore, anytime child abuse is suspected, CPS should be notified right away, and any additional testing can be performed after. Educational Objective: A history inconsistent with the type of injury present, a mechanism of injury inconsistent with the child's physical ability, and delay in presentation are all historical factors that should raise suspicion for potential child abuse. If a physician suspects child abuse, child protective services should be notified immediately.
▶ Uncategorized Neonatal Sepsis 1 questions
Source: 7A #36
A 2000-g (4-lb 7-oz) female newborn is jittery. She was born at 35 weeks' gestation to a 16-year-old primigravid patient. The membranes ruptured 6 hours before delivery. Her rectal temperature is 35.6°C (96°F). Examination shows no abnormalities except increased irritability. A heel-stick blood glucose concentration is 35 mg/dL. After administration of glucose water, a repeat heel-stick blood glucose concentration is 40 mg/dL. Blood is drawn for a complete blood count and culture. Urinalysis and cerebrospinal fluid analysis are ordered. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this newborn? A) Ampicillin and gentamicin B) Ceftriaxone C) Cilastatin-imipenem D) Erythromycin E) Penicillin G and tobramycin
Correct Answer: A) Ampicillin and gentamicin
This preterm newborn presents with hypothermia and hypoglycemia, indicating neonatal sepsis. Neonatal sepsis is most commonly caused by a bacterial infection and presents with fever or hypothermia, hypoglycemia, lethargy, irritability, and poor feeding. Evaluation should include a complete blood count, blood culture, urine culture, as well as testing and culture of the cerebrospinal fluid. Common microbiological causes of neonatal sepsis include Escherichia coli, Streptococcus agalactiae (group B), and Listeria monocytogenes. Risk factors for the development of neonatal sepsis include preterm birth, low birth weight, premature rupture of membranes, and maternal infection. The most common pathogen associated with early-onset neonatal sepsis is considered to be Streptococcus (group B), but the frequency of sepsis from this has decreased through the routine use of intrapartum antibiotic therapy for mothers that test positive for it in the antepartum period. Neonatal sepsis is treated with ampicillin and gentamicin for appropriate broad-spectrum coverage. Choice B (Ceftriaxone) would cover gram-negative rods but would be insufficient to cover Listeria monocytogenes. Choice C (Cilastatin-imipenem) is a broad-spectrum antibiotic that treats a variety of organisms. However, ampicillin and gentamicin are sufficient and effective against neonatal sepsis. Choice D (Erythromycin) is typically used for topical prophylaxis against bacterial conjunctivitis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. Erythromycin is the most used prophylactic agent and functions by binding to the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit and preventing bacterial protein synthesis. Choice E (Penicillin G and tobramycin) consists of penicillin G, which is commonly used to treat syphilis, and tobramycin, which is an aminoglycoside antibiotic like gentamicin. However, penicillin G and tobramycin are not first-line treatment for neonatal sepsis. Educational Objective: Neonatal sepsis is most commonly caused by a bacterial infection and presents with fever or hypothermia, hypoglycemia, lethargy, irritability, and poor feeding. Neonatal sepsis is commonly treated with ampicillin and gentamicin for appropriate broad-spectrum coverage.
▶ Endocrine System Hypoglycemic shock 1 questions
Source: 7A #40
A 12-year-old girl with a 5-year history of type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought for a follow-up examination. Over the past 4 weeks, she has had persistent sweating, shakiness, and pallor. Her glucose concentrations continue to range between 40 and 59 mg/dL throughout the day. Her exercise regimen and dietary intake have not changed. Examination shows no abnormalities. Serum studies show: Na+ 137 mEq/L Cl- 102 mEq/L K+ 4.2 mEq/L HCO3- 24 mEq/L Glucose 45 mg/dL Insulin increased C-peptide not detectable Glucagon increased Cortisol increased Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Decreased growth hormone production B) Increased exogenous insulin administration C) Increased endogenous insulin production D) Increased epinephrine production E) Insulin resistance
Correct Answer: B) Increased exogenous insulin administration
This patient presents with symptoms of hypoglycemia (sweating, shakiness, pallor) with persistent glucose concentrations between 40-59 mg/dL. The critical laboratory finding is the combination of increased insulin concentrations with undetectable C-peptide concentrations, which most likely indicates exogenous insulin administration as the cause of hypoglycemia. Insulin synthesis occurs in the pancreatic beta cells. Preproinsulin is synthesized in the rough endoplasmic reticulum and cleaved into proinsulin, which is stored in cytoplasmic granules. Prior to secretion, proinsulin is cleaved, releasing equal amounts of insulin and C-peptide into circulation. Therefore, hyperinsulinemia due to endogenous secretion is associated with increased C-peptide concentrations, whereas hyperinsulinemia from exogenous insulin administration is not accompanied by elevated C-peptide. The patient's undetectable C-peptide suggests suppressed endogenous insulin production, yet her hypoglycemic episodes persist despite apparent lack of another clear cause, raising the likelihood of excess exogenous insulin administration. Choice A (Decreased growth hormone production): May be associated with fasting hypoglycemia due to increased insulin sensitivity, but these patients would have decreased insulin concentrations in response to hypoglycemia. Additionally, growth hormone deficiency presents with short stature, increased central adiposity, muscle weakness, and prominent forehead—not present here. Choice C (Increased endogenous insulin production): Would lead to hypoglycemia with increased C-peptide concentrations, not the undetectable C-peptide seen in this patient. Choice D (Increased epinephrine production): Leads to increased glycogen phosphorylase activity and hepatic glycogen breakdown, resulting in hyperglycemia rather than hypoglycemia. Choice E (Insulin resistance): Would lead to decreased glucose uptake and hyperglycemia, opposite of this patient's presentation. Educational Objective: Hypoglycemia with increased insulin concentrations and undetectable C-peptide concentrations is consistent with exogenous insulin administration. In contrast, hypoglycemia from increased endogenous insulin release will show both elevated insulin and C-peptide concentrations. The C-peptide level is the key diagnostic discriminator between endogenous and exogenous insulin as the cause of hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.
▶ Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Stevens-Johnson Syndrome 1 questions
Source: 7A #43
A 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of fever, nausea, vomiting, pain during urination, and a widespread, red, bumpy rash. Three days ago, he began amoxicillin therapy for exudative pharyngitis. He appears ill. His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 95/48 mm Hg. A photograph of the rash is shown. There is anterior cervical lymphadenopathy bilaterally. Examination shows bilateral conjunctival erythema and photophobia. There are several 3- to 5-mm oral ulcers. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease) B) Scarlet fever C) Serum sickness D) Staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome E) Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Correct Answer: E) Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) is a severe mucocutaneous drug reaction that may progress to toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) with an accompanying high mortality rate. SJS and TEN are distinguished from each other based on the amount of body surface area involvement (<10% for SJS and >30% for TEN) and are driven by the same underlying pathophysiology. Common drugs implicated in the development of SJS or TEN include beta-lactam antibiotics (such as amoxicillin in this case), antiepileptics, sulfa-containing medications including trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and allopurinol. SJS and TEN are characterized by confluent areas of dusky erythema with desquamation of the epidermis. It can be distinguished from a morbilliform drug eruption by the presence of skin pain, desquamation, and mucosal involvement. SJS and TEN are often complicated by infection of the denuded areas of skin, thus meticulous wound care, preferably in a burn unit, is critical. The first step in treatment is to identify and discontinue the offending agents. Supportive care in a burn intensive care unit setting has been shown to improve mortality, but the role of other agents including systemic steroids, cyclosporine, and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) are controversial. This patient's presentation of fever, widespread rash, oral ulcers, conjunctival erythema, and photophobia beginning shortly after initiation of amoxicillin is classic for SJS. Choice A (Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome/Kawasaki disease) is a multisystemic vasculitic disease in children, characterized by fever for at least 5 days, bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, a polymorphous rash, lymphadenopathy, erythema and edema of the hands and feet, and erythema affecting the mucous membranes with dry, cracked lips. Complications include coronary artery aneurysm, and patients are managed with IVIG and aspirin therapy. However, Kawasaki disease is not typically associated with medication exposure and has a different clinical presentation. Choice B (Scarlet fever) is associated with group A streptococcus pharyngitis infection and may present with an erythematous tongue, an erythematous rough, papular, sandpaper-like rash, and desquamation of hands and feet. While this patient had preceding pharyngitis, the temporal relationship to amoxicillin initiation and the presence of oral ulcers and mucosal involvement make SJS more likely. Choice C (Serum sickness) is a type III hypersensitivity reaction defined by the presence of circulating antigen-antibody complexes that deposit in tissues. Deposition of these complexes triggers complement activation and subsequent inflammation. Clinical features include fever, malaise, urticarial rash, and arthralgias or arthritis. Serum sickness occurs after inoculation to a protein antigen from a nonhuman species, such as equine botulism antitoxin, equine anti-thymocyte globulin, or murine monoclonal antibodies (e.g., rituximab, infliximab). While amoxicillin can cause serum sickness, the presence of mucosal ulceration and skin desquamation is more characteristic of SJS. Choice D (Staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome) occurs due to the release of exfoliative toxin from Staphylococcus aureus infection. It most commonly presents in children and immunosuppressed adults with a diffuse erythematous rash that starts in the skin folds and perioral areas, then progresses to generalized superficial desquamation associated with fevers and malaise. This condition is caused by bacterial toxin rather than drug reaction. Educational Objective: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis are severe mucocutaneous drug reactions with high mortality rates. They are distinguished from each other by the amount of body surface area involvement, <10% for SJS and >30% for TEN, and common causes include beta-lactam antibiotics, anti-epileptics, sulfa-containing medications including trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and allopurinol. Treatment includes identifying and stopping the offending agent, supportive care, and wound management, preferably in a burn intensive care unit.
▶ Immune System Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome 1 questions
Source: 7A #44
An 11-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of fever, cough, and rash. He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. He has had frequent episodes of otitis media since birth and was hospitalized at the age of 6 months for meningitis. He is at the 10th percentile for length and 5th percentile for weight. His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 40/min, and blood pressure is 86/56 mm Hg. Examination shows an erythematous scaly rash with several weeping lesions over the trunk and extremities. There is bilateral scarring of the tympanic membranes and dried blood and crusty material in the nares. Decreased breath sounds are heard on the right. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL, Leukocyte count 12,400/mm³, Platelet count 75,000/mm³. An x-ray of the chest shows a right middle lobe consolidation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Chronic granulomatous disease B) HIV infection C) Severe combined immunodeficiency D) Thymic-parathyroid dysplasia (DiGeorge syndrome) E) Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
Correct Answer: E) Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is caused by a mutation in the WAS gene on the X-chromosome that encodes a protein essential for actin cytoskeleton rearrangement during interactions between T lymphocytes, antigen-presenting cells, and B lymphocytes, leading to impaired innate and adaptive immunity. The phenotype is variable, and patients present with the classic triad of eczema, thrombocytopenia, and recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria and opportunistic pathogens. This patient's clinical presentation is highly suggestive of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome: recurrent otitis media and meningitis from encapsulated bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae), eczematous rash with weeping lesions, and thrombocytopenia (platelet count 75,000/mm³). The growth failure and hypotension also reflect severe immunocompromise. Choice A (Chronic granulomatous disease): Caused by NADPH oxidase deficiency resulting in impaired intracellular killing. Presents with recurrent pyogenic infections and infections with catalase-positive organisms (Staphylococcus, Burkholderia cepacia, Nocardia, Aspergillus). Diagnosis by dihydrorhodamine test or nitroblue tetrazolium reduction test. Does not typically present with thrombocytopenia or eczema. Choice B (Acute HIV infection): Typically presents with systemic inflammatory symptoms including fever, chills, night sweats, fatigue, weight loss, and sore throat. Does not characteristically present with thrombocytopenia or the classic eczema seen in this case. Choice C (Severe combined immunodeficiency): Results from numerous mutations causing severe impairment in both B- and T-lymphocyte function with recurrent bacterial, viral, and fungal infections. Usually presents earlier in infancy (typically by 3-4 months) with failure to thrive and severe infections. Does not classically present with thrombocytopenia or eczema. Choice D (Thymic-parathyroid dysplasia/DiGeorge syndrome): Caused by 22q11 deletion leading to thymic aplasia and hypocalcemia with cardiac and craniofacial defects. Patients are susceptible to viral and fungal infections but do not typically present with thrombocytopenia or eczema. Diagnosis requires fluorescence in-situ hybridization. Educational Objective: Patients with Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome typically present with recurrent infections by encapsulated bacteria and opportunistic infections, thrombocytopenia, and eczema. The combination of recurrent otitis media and meningitis (suggesting defective response to encapsulated bacteria), thrombocytopenia, and eczematous rash in an 11-month-old boy is pathognomonic for Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.
▶ Male Reproductive Testicular Cancer 1 questions
Source: 7A #45
A 16-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination. Six months ago, he noticed a lump in his right testicle after participating in a soccer game, during which he sustained a kick to the groin. Ultrasonography 2 days later showed a cystic lesion consistent with trauma. He was advised to avoid contact sports for 2 weeks and was told that the lesion would resolve without treatment. The patient reports that since that time, the lump has increased in size and has become firm. He also reports facial acne, swelling of his breasts, stretch marks over his abdomen, and a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight gain despite eating no more than usual. He has not had respiratory, gastrointestinal, or urinary symptoms. He appears well. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows facial acne. There are striae over the lower abdomen. A firm, fixed, 6-cm, nontender mass is palpated in the right testicle. There is no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Measurement of which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Serum alkaline phosphatase activity B) Serum CA 125 concentration C) Serum α-fetoprotein and β-hCG concentrations D) Serum prostate-specific antigen concentration E) Urine homovanillic-vanillylmandelic acid
Correct Answer: C) Serum α-fetoprotein and β-hCG concentrations
Testicular cancer most often occurs in those assigned male at birth, either during adolescence or before age 40 years. It presents with a painless, firm nodule in the testis, which is commonly asymptomatic, although it can also present with a dull ache in the surrounding region. Patients may report first noticing the lesion following testicular trauma. Testicular tumors are categorized as germ cell tumors and non-germ cell tumors. Germ cell tumors comprise most testicular cancer and include seminoma, choriocarcinoma, teratoma, yolk sac tumor, and embryonal carcinoma. Non-germ cell tumors are often sex cord-gonadal stromal tumors originating from Sertoli or Leydig cells. Risk factors for the development of germ cell tumors include cryptorchidism, family history, seminiferous tubule dysgenesis (Klinefelter syndrome), and heavy marijuana use. Laboratory evaluation will often reveal increased concentrations of LDH, α-fetoprotein, or β-hCG, the last of which can cause gynecomastia (explaining this patient's breast swelling), depending on the subtype of testicular cancer. Ultrasonography is the initial step in evaluation of a palpable testicular mass. Malignant neoplasms will show a heterogeneous mass with solid or cystic components, sometimes including calcifications. Initial metastatic spread is commonly to the para-aortic lymph nodes. Treatment requires orchiectomy with possible retroperitoneal lymph node dissection and chemotherapy depending on the presenting stage of disease. Choice A (Serum alkaline phosphatase activity) is a useful test in the evaluation of biliary disease and bone disease but is not specific for testicular cancer. Choice B (Serum CA 125 concentration) is a tumor marker closely associated with ovarian cancer and has poor specificity and positive predictive value for cancer, as it can be increased by several benign gynecologic processes such as menstruation and pregnancy. Choice D (Serum prostate-specific antigen concentration) is increased in benign prostatic hyperplasia, prostatitis, and prostate cancer but is not relevant for testicular cancer evaluation. Choice E (Urine homovanillic-vanillylmandelic acid concentration) is increased in catecholamine-secreting tumors such as neuroblastoma and pheochromocytoma, not testicular germ cell tumors. Educational Objective: Testicular cancer often presents as a painless, firm nodule in those assigned male at birth, either in adolescence or before age 40 years. Germ cell tumors comprise most testicular neoplasms and laboratory results often reveal increased serum LDH, α-fetoprotein, or β-hCG. Treatment requires orchiectomy with possible retroperitoneal lymph node dissection and chemotherapy depending on the presenting stage of disease.
▶ Musculoskeletal System Achondroplasia 1 questions
Source: 7A #47
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because of a bowleg deformity that has become more noticeable during the past year. He was adopted at the age of 8 months. The birth parents were told that he had hypotonia as a newborn, but no other medical history was provided. He sat upright at the age of 12 months and walked at the age of 24 months. He is at the 3rd percentile for height and 20th percentile for weight. Examination shows frontal bossing and a small nasal bridge, a normal trunk, short limbs, and increased lumbar lordosis. There is genu varum of both knees. X-rays of the lower extremities show metaphyseal flaring, inverted V-shape distal femoral physis, and a disproportionately long fibula. The most likely explanation for these findings is a defect of which of the following? A) Cartilage oligometric matrix protein B) Fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 C) Sulfate transport protein D) Type 1 collagen E) Type 2 collagen
Correct Answer: B) Fibroblast growth factor receptor 3
Achondroplasia is the most common skeletal dysplasia and is most commonly associated with mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) gene. This mutation causes constitutive activation of FGFR3, leading to downstream effects that inhibit endochondral ossification required for normal development of long bones. The clinical presentation is characteristic: patients have macrocephaly with frontal bossing and a depressed nasal bridge, short stature secondary to decreased length of upper and lower limbs, varus deformity (genu varum), and hypotonia in infancy. The developmental milestones are typically delayed (sitting at 12 months, walking at 24 months). Radiologic findings include metaphyseal flaring, inverted V-shape of the distal femoral physis, and a disproportionately long fibula relative to the tibia. Most mutations are spontaneous in origin, though achondroplasia is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern when present in families. Diagnosis is made based on characteristic clinical and radiologic findings. Choice A (Cartilage oligometric matrix protein) is an extracellular matrix protein present in cartilage that may be used as a marker for cartilage turnover, but is not involved in achondroplasia development. Choice C (Sulfate transport protein) is present in developing and mature cartilage as well as several other organs, but is not associated with achondroplasia. Choice D (Type 1 collagen) is found in bones, skin, tendon, and dentin. Defects in type 1 collagen are associated with osteogenesis imperfecta, which presents with multiple fractures following minimal trauma in infancy, characteristic blue sclerae, and conductive hearing loss—a distinctly different clinical picture. Choice E (Type 2 collagen) is found in cartilage, the vitreous humor, and nucleus pulposus. Defects in type 2 collagen have not been associated with achondroplasia development. Educational Objective: Understand that achondroplasia results from mutations in the FGFR3 gene causing constitutive activation and inhibition of endochondral ossification required for normal longitudinal bone development. Recognize the characteristic clinical features including short stature, macrocephaly, frontal bossing, varus deformity, and hypotonia in infancy, along with specific radiologic findings. Recognize the distinctive presentations that differentiate achondroplasia from other genetic skeletal dysplasias and collagen disorders.
▶ Uncategorized Müllerian Agenesis 1 questions
Source: 7A #49
A 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 1-week history of constant severe abdominal pain. During the past year, she has had 10 episodes of cramps; each episode lasts 3 to 5 days. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She has never had a menstrual period. She is sexually active with one male partner and uses condoms inconsistently. She is at the 80th percentile for height and weight. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg. Breast and genital development is sexual maturity rating stage 5. Abdominal examination shows moderate tenderness. A mass is palpated in the suprapubic region. On examination of the external genitalia and lower vagina, the cervix cannot be visualized because of bluish bulging vaginal tissue that obscures the upper vagina. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis? A) Karyotype analysis B) Urine culture C) Intravenous pyelography D) Pelvic ultrasonography E) Laparoscopy
Correct Answer: D) Pelvic ultrasonography
A transverse vaginal septum occurs when there is failure of canalization of the vaginal canal, preventing the excretion of menstrual blood. This condition presents with primary amenorrhea, cyclic pelvic pain, and a bulging pelvic mass in an adolescent with otherwise normal sexual development (sexual maturity rating stage 5 in this case). Significant accumulation of menstrual blood products may give the bulging septum a blue appearance on physical examination, a condition known as hematocolpos. The bluish bulging vaginal tissue obscuring the cervix in this patient is pathognomonic for hematocolpos. Diagnosis is made by pelvic ultrasonography, which will confirm the presence of fluid accumulation above the obstruction. Treatment involves transvaginal incision and drainage with resection of the septum and evacuation of accumulated blood. Choice A (Karyotype analysis) is not necessary. While karyotype abnormalities such as gonadal dysgenesis 45,X (Turner syndrome) can cause amenorrhea, they are typically associated with other physical manifestations not present in this patient, including short stature, webbed neck, and swelling of the hands and feet. The clinical presentation of hematocolpos makes transverse vaginal septum the most likely diagnosis. Choice B (Urine culture) would be useful for diagnosing urinary tract infections, which commonly present with dysuria, urinary frequency/urgency, and suprapubic pain. A UTI would not explain the patient's cyclic cramping pattern or the hematocolpos findings on examination. Choice C (Intravenous pyelography) is used to evaluate abnormalities of the genitourinary system including lesions of the kidney, ureters, bladder, and urethra. It is not used in the evaluation of primary amenorrhea, and this patient has no urinary symptoms to suggest its use. Choice E (Laparoscopy) can aid in diagnosis of multiple intra-abdominal pathologies such as endometriosis, which presents with chronic dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, dyschezia, and infertility. This patient exhibits none of these symptoms and has no intra-abdominal signs or symptoms to justify an invasive procedure.
▶ Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Herpes Zoster 1 questions
Source: 4A #1
A 6-year-old girl in remission of acute lymphoblastic leukemia has had pain in her right shoulder for 2 days. She is receiving maintenance chemotherapy and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii (formerly P. carinii) pneumonia. She has a 4 x 1-cm, erythematous patch beneath the right scapula with six to eight superimposed, small, clear fluid-filled vesicles. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this rash? A) Coxsackievirus B) Herpes simplex virus C) Herpes zoster D) Leukemic relapse E) Toxic drug reaction
Correct Answer: C) Herpes zoster
This patient's immunocompromise and dermatomal vesicular eruption is consistent with reactivation of varicella zoster virus (VZV, also known as human herpesvirus-3 or HHV-3) in the form of herpes zoster infection. VZV is transmitted via respiratory secretions and direct contact with infected skin lesions, causing two diseases: varicella (chickenpox) and herpes zoster (shingles). Herpes zoster results from reactivation of dormant VZV from the dorsal root ganglion of a spinal nerve. It classically presents as a unilateral, dermatomal erythematous patch with overlying clear to yellow, grouped vesicles. The thoracic and trigeminal nerves are common sites of reactivation. The patient's immunosuppression from chemotherapy significantly increases risk for herpes zoster reactivation. Neuropathic pain often precedes and can outlast the rash, though post-herpetic neuralgia is more common in elderly patients. Treatment involves guanosine analogs such as acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir, which inhibit viral DNA polymerase. Choice A (Coxsackievirus) causes hand, foot, and mouth disease with painful oval-shaped vesicles on palms, soles, and oral mucosa, or herpangina affecting the posterior pharynx. This does not match the dermatomal distribution seen in this patient. Choice B (Herpes simplex virus) presents with genital herpes, herpes labialis, herpetic whitlow, or systemic manifestations. While HSV can cause cutaneous vesicles, the dermatomal distribution of this patient's lesions is characteristic of herpes zoster rather than HSV. Choice D (Leukemic relapse) can present with leukemia cutis from infiltration of epidermis and dermis by leukemic cells. However, leukemia cutis typically presents with firm papules or subcutaneous nodules, not vesicles. Choice E (Toxic drug reaction/Toxic epidermal necrolysis) is a severe cutaneous reaction characterized by large areas of dusky erythema with epidermal desquamation. The confinement of small vesicles to a single dermatome without spreading is highly uncharacteristic of toxic drug reactions. Educational Objective: Herpes zoster is caused by reactivation of dormant varicella zoster virus infection in the dorsal root ganglion of a spinal nerve. It most commonly presents with grouped clear to yellow vesicles on an erythematous base in a dermatomal distribution, particularly in immunocompromised patients.
▶ Musculoskeletal System Juvenile idiopathic arthritis 1 questions
Source: 4A #2
A previously healthy 6-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents because of intermittent right knee pain for 2 months. The pain typically occurs in the morning and after naps. She has not had fever, rash, or symptoms in any other joint. She plays soccer twice weekly but has not had any injuries. Her parents recall that she had a sore throat for 2 days prior to the onset of her knee pain. There is no family history of osteoarthritis. She is at the 25th percentile for height, 70th percentile for weight, and above the 97th percentile for BMI. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). Examination shows slight bowing of the lower extremities. The right knee is larger than the left knee. There is tenderness of the right knee to palpation. Range of motion of the right knee is decreased. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 45 mm/h. X-rays of the knees show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Acute rheumatic fever B) Juvenile arthritis C) Septic arthritis D) Tear of the anterior cruciate ligament E) Tibia vara
Correct Answer: B) Juvenile arthritis
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) occurs before the age of 16 and is the most common rheumatic disease among children. The disease has an autoimmune cause and is characterized by joint pain and inflammation. The clinical presentation in this case is consistent with oligoarticular JIA, which involves fewer than five joints (typically large joints such as the knee) and is associated with antinuclear antibody (ANA) positivity. Patients commonly exhibit extra-articular manifestations such as uveitis, lymphadenopathy, and rash. Diagnosis is based on a combination of characteristic clinical findings and suggestive laboratory tests, such as ANA, rheumatoid factor, anti-citrullinated peptide, and inflammatory tests such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). There is no single confirmatory laboratory test for JIA. Treatment modalities include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, disease-modifying antirheumatic medications such as methotrexate, and biologic agents. Choice A (Acute rheumatic fever) is a late complication of under- or untreated Streptococcus pyogenes (group A) infection characterized by carditis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea, and migratory polyarthritis. Although the patient had a preceding sore throat, she lacks the characteristic manifestations of acute rheumatic fever, and the monoarticular (single joint) presentation is inconsistent with the typical migratory polyarthritis pattern. Choice C (Septic arthritis) presents acutely with fever, joint swelling, erythema, pain, tenderness with range of motion, inability to bear weight, and leukocytosis. Arthrocentesis typically shows bacteria on Gram stain and leukocyte count ≥50,000/mm³ with neutrophilic predominance. This patient lacks fever and has a chronic 2-month course, making septic arthritis unlikely. Choice D (Tear of the anterior cruciate ligament) commonly presents as an acute injury in athletes attempting rapid changes in direction upon a planted foot. Patients typically report an audible pop and experience acute onset of pain, swelling, and instability. This patient has insidious onset with no reported injury. Choice E (Tibia vara) refers to an outward-bowing deformity of the tibia commonly occurring in children with vitamin D deficiency (rickets) or Blount disease. It does not typically manifest with joint swelling or tenderness. Educational Objective: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is the most common rheumatic disease in children under age 16 with an autoimmune etiology. It presents with chronic joint pain and inflammation, often affecting large joints in oligoarticular disease. Diagnosis requires a combination of clinical findings and laboratory tests including ESR, ANA, rheumatoid factor, and anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies, as there is no single confirmatory test.
▶ Human Development Gynecomastia in adolescents 1 questions
Source: 4A #4
While being evaluated for a cardiac murmur, a 12-year-old boy is noted to have bilateral gynecomastia. His sexual development is Tanner stage 3. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step? A) Measure serum corticosteroid concentrations B) Measure serum gonadotropin concentrations C) Evaluate his brothers for this finding D) Privately tell his parents about the finding E) Reassure him that this is normal
Correct Answer: E) Reassure him that this is normal
Gynecomastia refers to an increase in the amount of glandular breast tissue in males. Pubertal gynecomastia is a benign proliferation of glandular breast tissue that is common in boys aged 12 to 14 years old, typically when they have a sexual maturity rating of Tanner stage 3, as in this patient. It is caused by a disruption in the normal balance of androgens and estrogens during puberty, with increased estrogen resulting from conversion of androstenedione and testosterone to estrone and estradiol. On physical examination, gynecomastia may be tender to palpation. Laboratory studies will show results within reference ranges in physiologic pubertal gynecomastia. The condition typically self-resolves, though medical (such as aromatase inhibitors) and surgical (liposuction) options exist for symptomatic patients. Since this patient has no signs suggesting pathologic gynecomastia, reassurance is the most appropriate next step. Choice A (Measure serum corticosteroid concentrations) may be useful in evaluating Cushing syndrome or Addison disease, but neither presents with gynecomastia as a direct finding. Cushing syndrome presents with weight gain, fatigue, truncal obesity, fat redistribution, hirsutism, and abdominal striae, while Addison disease presents with hypotension, hypoglycemia, hyperpigmentation, and abdominal pain. Choice B (Measure serum gonadotropin concentrations) may be useful in evaluating hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, such as Klinefelter syndrome, which can present with gynecomastia. However, patients with Klinefelter syndrome typically have testicular atrophy, tall stature, and long extremities, which this patient does not exhibit. Additionally, laboratory values are normal in physiologic pubertal gynecomastia. Choice C (Evaluate his brothers for this finding) may be useful if gynecomastia were caused by a hereditary disorder such as partial androgen insensitivity or aromatase excess. However, this patient is presenting with mild gynecomastia associated with puberty, making physiologic gynecomastia more likely. Choice D (Privately tell his parents about the finding) is inappropriate because the condition is benign, and the patient should be included in health conversations regarding his body.
▶ Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Congenital Nevus 1 questions
Source: 4A #5
A 4-month-old girl is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. She is breast-feeding successfully and has been in good health. She is able to roll from her stomach to her back, and she looks around with curiosity, coos, and orients to voice. Her parents are concerned about a lesion on her left thigh that has become darker since birth. The patient appears well. She is at the 50th percentile for length and weight. Examination of the left thigh shows a brown lesion. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Congenital melanocytic nevus B) Hyperpigmented macula C) Macular stain D) Port-wine stain E) Superficial hemangioma
Correct Answer: A) Congenital melanocytic nevus
Congenital melanocytic nevus (CMN) is a benign proliferation of melanocytes that is present from birth. Compared to normal skin, melanocytes within a nevus are clustered into nests located in the basal layer of the epidermis, in the dermis, or both. Compared to acquired nevi, CMN are often larger and darker. CMN are classified by size: small (<1.5 cm), medium (1.5-20 cm), large (20-40 cm), and giant (>40 cm). Large and giant CMN carry increased risk for malignant transformation. In this case, the CMN is symmetrical, uniform in color and thickness, with a rough texture and hair present on the inferior aspect—a common finding in CMN. CMN should be routinely monitored by a dermatologist, and any area that develops increased thickness or color change should be biopsied to evaluate for melanoma. While CMN are benign if they do not develop melanoma, they can cause psychological morbidity if located in cosmetically sensitive areas. Surgical excision of large or giant CMN is usually impossible, but particularly bothersome areas may be excised for improved function and cosmesis. Choice B (Hyperpigmented macula/café-au-lait spot) presents as a tan to dark brown uniformly pigmented macule or patch, representing focal increased melanin production rather than increased melanocytes. This lesion is a dark brown plaque with hair, potentially asymmetrical with irregular borders, making it inconsistent with a café-au-lait spot. Choices C, D, and E are all vascular lesions that appear red to purple rather than brown to black. Macular stain (Choice C), also called nevus flammeus, are red patches typically on the forehead and posterior neck at birth. Port-wine stain (Choice D) and nevus flammeus are capillary malformations. Superficial hemangioma (Choice E) is a benign proliferation of capillary-sized vessels that may ulcerate and bleed. Both port-wine stains and superficial hemangiomas can be treated with laser therapy; nevus flammeus on the forehead and eyelids commonly resolves, while those on the posterior neck usually fade but do not completely disappear. Educational Objective: Congenital melanocytic nevus (CMN) is a benign proliferation of melanocytes present from birth that is often larger and darker than acquired nevi and may have hair present. Large or giant CMN have increased risk for malignant transformation and require regular dermatologic monitoring.
▶ Immune System Selective Immunodeficiency (IgA) 1 questions
Source: 4A #7
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a follow-up examination 2 weeks after being treated for an ear infection. He has had recurrent ear infections, sinusitis, and two episodes of bacterial pneumonia since birth. Over the past year, he has undergone placement of two sets of tympanostomy tubes for otitis media.
