His mother is HIV negative. He currently takes no medications. He is at the 25th percentile for height and weight. Examination shows no abnormalities except for small anterior cervical lymph nodes. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of disease? A) Antibody deficiency B) Impaired chemotaxis C) Impaired respiratory burst D) Splenic dysfunction E) T-lymphocyte dysfunction
Correct Answer: A) Antibody deficiency
IgA deficiency is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms. Selective IgA deficiency describes a decreased or absent concentration of circulating IgA with normal concentrations of IgG and normal or increased concentrations of IgM. IgA is critical for immune health and functions in two primary ways: first, IgA binds pathogen surface antigens targeting them for opsonization, complement activation, and phagocytosis; second, IgA coats mucosal surfaces and prevents colonization, adhesion, and invasion by pathogenic microorganisms. Immunoglobulins are produced by plasma cells, which are terminally differentiated B lymphocytes, so causal deficiencies are hypothesized to be related to B lymphocyte abnormalities. There is clinical heterogeneity in the severity of IgA deficiency—some patients remain asymptomatic while others suffer from recurrent sinopulmonary infections or otitis media as in this patient. In younger patients with severe deficiency, failure to thrive is common. Anaphylactic reactions to blood products such as plasma are classic but uncommon; such severe reactions are most common in patients with undetectable concentrations of IgA and occur because of preformed antibodies against IgA. Impaired chemotaxis (Choice B) describes syndromes such as hyperimmunoglobulinemia E syndrome, where patients have abnormal Th17 T-lymphocyte function and impaired IL-17 release, presenting with recurrent abscesses with minimal inflammation. Impaired respiratory burst (Choice C) describes chronic granulomatous disease, caused by NADPH oxidase deficiency. Patients present with recurrent pyogenic infections with catalase-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus, with normal leukocyte and immunoglobulin concentrations. Splenic dysfunction (Choice D) can result from splenectomy or diseases such as sickle cell disease. This predisposes to infection with encapsulated organisms such as Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. IgA deficiency is the more likely diagnosis for this patient. T-lymphocyte dysfunction (Choice E) describes numerous disorders affecting T-lymphocyte maturation, survival, or function such as SCID or DiGeorge syndrome, resulting in near absence of T lymphocytes with recurrent viral and fungal infections. These patients present with severe and recurrent invasive infections early in life. Educational Objective: Selective IgA deficiency describes a decreased or absent concentration of circulating IgA, an immunoglobulin critical to mucosal immunity. Patients may be asymptomatic or present with recurrent sinopulmonary infections, otitis media, and failure to thrive. Anaphylaxis following blood transfusion due to preformed anti-IgA antibodies can occur. Immunoglobulin concentrations demonstrate decreased or absent IgA with normal or high IgG and IgM.
▶ Immune System Common Variable Immunodeficiency 1 questions
Source: 8A #41
A 12-year-old girl with chronic sinusitis is evaluated for cough for 4 days. She had pneumococcal pneumonia 5 months ago that was treated. She is at the 50th percentile for height and weight. Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), heart rate is 105/min, and respirations are 30/min. Breath sounds are decreased on the lower right. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 21,000/mm³ Segmented neutrophils 70% Bands 15% Lymphocytes 15% Platelet count 140,000/mm³ CD3+ T-lymphocyte count 1500/mm³ (N=820-1900) CD4+ T-lymphocyte count 1000/mm³ (N≥2500) CD8+ T-lymphocyte count 400/mm³ (N=250-650) Serum IgA 20 mg/dL IgG 150 mg/dL IgM 30 mg/dL Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Common variable immunodeficiency B) Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease) C) Severe combined immunodeficiency D) Systemic lupus erythematosus E) Transient agammaglobulinemia of infancy F) X-linked agammaglobulinemia
Correct Answer: A) Common variable immunodeficiency
The most likely diagnosis is common variable immunodeficiency (CVID). The exact cause and pathogenesis are unknown; however, the disease is characterized by combined T- and B-lymphocyte defects, dysfunction in B-lymphocyte differentiation, and a decrease in serum concentration of all immunoglobulins, as demonstrated by this patient's markedly reduced IgA (20 mg/dL), IgG (150 mg/dL), and IgM (30 mg/dL) levels. The patient also shows moderately reduced CD4+ T-lymphocyte count (1000/mm³, well below normal of ≥2500). CVID commonly presents in the second to fourth decades of life with recurrent upper respiratory, pulmonary, and gastrointestinal infections, as evidenced by this patient's chronic sinusitis and recent pneumococcal pneumonia. Patients may develop bronchiectasis as a result of recurrent airway infection and inflammation. CVID is also associated with persistent diarrhea as a result of chronic Giardia lamblia infection. Physical examination may show lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. The mainstays of treatment include intravenous immunoglobulin replacement therapy and antibiotics. CVID is strongly associated with lymphoma and autoimmune conditions. Choice B (Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome/Kawasaki disease) is a multisystemic vasculitic disease resulting in acute arteritis with risk for coronary artery aneurysms. It is characterized by fever for at least 5 days, bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, polymorphous rash, lymphadenopathy, erythema and edema of hands and feet, and erythema of mucous membranes with dry, cracked lips. This patient lacks these characteristic clinical features. Choice C (Severe combined immunodeficiency) results from various mutations and commonly presents with recurrent bacterial, viral, and fungal infections due to severe impairment in both B- and T-lymphocyte function in infancy. The age of this 12-year-old patient makes this diagnosis unlikely, as SCID typically presents much earlier in life. Choice D (Systemic lupus erythematosus) is an autoimmune disease resulting in fever, rash, photosensitivity, kidney disease, and nonerosive arthritis. The characteristic malar rash spares the nasolabial folds. This patient's laboratory findings are inconsistent with SLE and show immunodeficiency rather than autoimmunity. Choice E (Transient agammaglobulinemia of infancy) is characterized by a drop in IgG concentrations greater than the expected physiologic hypogammaglobulinemia during the first 6 months of life as maternal antibodies are replaced by the infant's own. IgA and IgM concentrations are typically normal, and IgG returns to normal by age 6 years. This patient is 12 years old and has low IgA and IgM in addition to low IgG, making this diagnosis unlikely. Choice F (X-linked agammaglobulinemia) is caused by mutations in the BTK gene encoding a tyrosine kinase essential for B lymphocyte development and proliferation. Patients lack functioning B lymphocytes and normal immunoglobulin concentrations. It nearly always presents within the first 18 months of life with recurrent infections and is more common in males given X-linked inheritance. This patient's later presentation at age 12 makes this diagnosis less likely. Educational Objective: Common variable immunodeficiency is a primary immunodeficiency syndrome that classically presents in the second to fourth decades of life with recurrent sinus, pulmonary, and gastrointestinal infections. Laboratory studies reveal low concentrations of all immunoglobulins and may show moderate T-lymphocyte abnormalities.
▶ Cardiovascular System Cor Pulmonale 1 questions
Source: 4A #10
A 13-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis is brought to the physician because of a 6-month history of progressive difficulty breathing. Her mother says that her daughter's hands and feet have appeared swollen during this period. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 124/84 mm Hg. Examination shows dusky nail beds and clubbing of the fingers and toes. There is nasal flaring and moderate intercostal retractions. Bilateral crackles and rhonchi are heard on auscultation. S2 is loud and split in the second left intercostal space. The liver edge is palpated 5 cm below the right costal margin, and the spleen tip is palpated 1 cm below the left costal margin. There is bilateral pitting edema over the dorsum of the hands and feet. Laboratory studies show: Na+ 126 mEq/L, Cl- 84 mEq/L, K+ 4.1 mEq/L, HCO3- 36 mEq/L, Albumin 2.8 g/dL, Urine protein 1+. Pulmonary function tests show a decrease in forced vital capacity from 75% to 30% of predicted value over the past year. An x-ray of the chest shows marked hyperinflation with coarse nodular infiltrates bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's edema? A) Cirrhosis of the liver B) Cor pulmonale C) Inferior vena cava obstruction D) Lymphedema E) Nephrotic syndrome F) Protein-losing enteropathy G) Vitamin E deficiency
Correct Answer: B) Cor pulmonale
This patient with cystic fibrosis is presenting with findings of volume overload in cor pulmonale. Patients with cystic fibrosis may develop pulmonary hypertension as a result of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and fibrotic remodeling in chronically hypoventilated and inflamed pulmonary parenchyma, leading to increased vascular resistance. If severe, this process can lead to cor pulmonale, which refers to isolated right heart failure secondary to chronic pulmonary pathology with increased pulmonary vascular resistance and right-sided heart pressures. Right heart failure typically presents with venous congestion, seen as jugular venous distention, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly, and splenomegaly with or without ascites. The clinical findings in this case—progressive dyspnea, bilateral crackles and rhonchi, loud split S2 (indicating pulmonary hypertension), hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and bilateral pitting edema—are consistent with cor pulmonale. Circular of the liver (Choice A) occurs secondary to many causes, most commonly alcoholic and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. While cirrhosis presents with ascites, anasarca, jaundice, increased transaminases, low albumin, and impaired hepatic synthetic function, and right heart failure may cause secondary cirrhosis, this patient has only some consistent findings and lacks the typical markers of primary cirrhosis. Inferior vena cava obstruction (Choice C) causes obstruction of venous drainage from the lower body, often related to underlying malignancy with mass effect, thrombosis from an indwelling catheter, or compression by a gravid uterus. This patient lacks a history suggestive of any likely cause of IVC obstruction. Lymphedema (Choice D) refers to swelling secondary to abnormal lymphatic drainage of a region, often secondary to surgery, radiation, or invasive parasitic disease. This patient lacks the appropriate history for these causes. Nephrotic syndrome (Choice E) results from many causes and typically presents with proteinuria, edema, hyperlipidemia, and a hypercoagulable state. While this patient does have low albumin and trace proteinuria, cystic fibrosis does not commonly cause nephrotic syndrome. Protein-losing enteropathy (Choice F) refers to gastrointestinal pathology resulting in protein loss, which may present with abdominal pain, diarrhea, and peripheral edema. Causes include inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, and amyloidosis. While cystic fibrosis may cause steatorrhea, this does not explain the current clinical presentation. Vitamin E deficiency (Choice G) presents with hemolytic anemia and generalized muscle weakness, with a similar presentation to vitamin B12 deficiency including posterior column and spinocerebellar tract demyelination. This does not explain the patient's acute presentation. Educational Objective: Cor pulmonale refers to isolated right heart failure secondary to chronic pulmonary pathology with increased pulmonary vascular resistance and right-sided heart pressures. Patients with cystic fibrosis may develop pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale as a result of chronic alveolar hypoventilation with reactive pulmonary hypoxic vasoconstriction and vascular remodeling.
▶ Blood Lymphoreticular System Methemoglobinemia, congenital 1 questions
Source: 4A #15
A previously healthy 10-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents because of a 2-hour history of increasing headache, dizziness, and nausea. His father is a butcher and says his son ate a new batch of sausage shortly before he became ill. Earlier today, the patient was given the task of cleaning out the garage. On arrival, the patient is alert and is not in respiratory distress. His pulse is 136/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 104/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 73% that increases to 80% when 15 L/min of oxygen is administered via face mask. Examination shows profound central cyanosis. The pupils are equal and reactive to light. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. His methemoglobin is 40.5% of his total hemoglobin. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows: pH 7.37, PaCO2 42 mm Hg, PaO2 48 mm Hg, HCO3- 24 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Administration of atropine B) Administration of deferoxamine C) Administration of methylene blue D) Administration of naloxone E) Administration of pyridostigmine F) Hyperbaric oxygen therapy
Correct Answer: C) Administration of methylene blue
Methemoglobinemia occurs when an abnormal fraction of heme iron in the blood exists in the ferric (Fe3+) form (methemoglobin). Methemoglobin cannot effectively bind oxygen, which impairs tissue oxygen delivery. Most cases of methemoglobinemia are acquired, typically via exposure to an oxidant stressor such as an anesthetic (e.g., benzocaine), nitrate, or dapsone. In this case, the patient likely was exposed to nitrates from the sausage or another oxidant during garage cleaning. Symptoms include shortness of breath, fatigue, lethargy, lightheadedness, and in severe cases, arrhythmia, seizure, and multisystem organ failure. Vital signs typically show reduced oxygen saturation, and examination may disclose cyanosis. Characteristically, blood appears darkened on gross visualization, although hemoglobin concentration and erythrocyte morphology are normal. Treatment includes supplemental oxygen plus the intravenous administration of methylene blue, a reducing agent that donates electrons to heme. The reduction of heme iron to the ferrous (Fe2+) form restores the ability of hemoglobin to bind, carry, and deliver oxygen to tissues. Choice A (atropine) would be indicated in cases of symptomatic bradycardia or organophosphate poisoning. This patient's pulse is tachycardic at 136/min, making atropine administration inappropriate. Choice B (deferoxamine) is indicated in the treatment of hemochromatosis or iron toxicity. It binds free iron in the serum and promotes elimination in the urine, not applicable here. Choice D (naloxone) is indicated in cases of opioid overdose, characterized by respiratory depression. This patient's hypoxia is caused by methemoglobinemia, not respiratory depression. Choice E (pyridostigmine) is used in the treatment of myasthenia gravis as an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor and is not relevant to this condition. Choice F (hyperbaric oxygen therapy) can be helpful in decompression sickness and carbon monoxide poisoning, not methemoglobinemia. Educational Objective: Methemoglobinemia occurs when heme iron exists in the ferric (Fe3+) form. Treatment includes supplemental oxygen plus intravenous methylene blue, which donates electrons to reduce ferric iron back to the ferrous (Fe2+) form, restoring hemoglobin's oxygen-binding capacity.
▶ Social Sciences Healthcare-Associated Infections 1 questions
Source: 4A #16
A 10-day-old male newborn is admitted to the hospital for treatment of indirect hyperbilirubinemia due to isoimmune hemolysis. He is placed in a room with a 2-month-old female infant with dehydration secondary to rotavirus gastroenteritis. Two days later, he develops vomiting and diarrhea, and a stool specimen is positive for rotavirus antigen. This nosocomial infection is most likely caused by failure of caregivers to do which of the following? A) Dispose of diapers and other waste items properly B) Observe gown and glove precautions C) Observe hand-washing techniques D) Place the patients in a reverse airflow room E) Restrict visitors to the room
Correct Answer: C) Observe hand-washing techniques
Proper hand-washing technique is the most effective strategy to limit the spread of nosocomial enteric viral pathogens such as rotavirus. Hand washing should involve rubbing the hands together with soap for at least twenty seconds before rinsing. Individuals often neglect to scrub the entire surface of the hands despite adequate duration of hand washing. Viral shedding in stool can occur prior to symptom development, potentially allowing asymptomatic patients to become vectors for disease, and viral shedding persists until after symptom resolution. The newborn likely acquired infection after caregivers contacted surfaces contaminated by feces from the other infant and then touched the younger child without proper hand washing. Alcohol-based hand sanitizers are not as efficacious as soap and water for removing enteric viruses, though bleach-based cleaning agents are effective. Choice A (Disposing of diapers properly) is important since rotavirus is shed in stool, but adherence to this measure is typically higher among caregivers than simple hand washing. Direct acquisition through contact with contaminated diapers is less likely than transmission through contaminated surfaces touched by caregiver hands. Choice B (Gown and glove precautions) is an important part of contact precautions for viral gastroenteritis; however, proper hand washing must occur before and after donning and doffing protective equipment and is the fundamental preventive measure. Choice D (Reverse airflow room) would have little effect on rotavirus transmission since this pathogen is not transmitted by aerosolized particles. Negative pressure rooms are reserved for airborne pathogens such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis and measles. Choice E (Restricting visitors) decreases the number of potential vectors but proper hand washing is more effective at reducing infection spread regardless of visitor numbers. Educational Objective: Proper hand-washing is the most efficacious measure in preventing the spread of enteric pathogens and should be observed judiciously, with particular attention to scrubbing all hand surfaces for at least twenty seconds with soap and water.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Hypothermia 1 questions
Source: 4A #19
A 6-hour-old female newborn has had cyanosis of her arms and legs since birth. She was born at 38 weeks' gestation following an uncomplicated pregnancy and cesarean delivery for breech presentation. She weighed 3090 g (6 lb 13 oz) at birth. She has been breast-feeding well. She is alert and is not in acute distress. Her rectal temperature is 36.2°C (97.2°F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 36/min, and blood pressure is 80/45 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 96%. Examination shows cyanosis of the upper and lower extremities but no circumoral cyanosis. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Capillary refill time is mildly delayed. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Placement of the newborn under warming lights B) Blood culture C) Chest x-ray D) Echocardiography E) Intubation and mechanical ventilation
Correct Answer: A) Placement of the newborn under warming lights
This neonate presents with a slightly decreased body temperature of 36.2°C (97.2°F) with cyanosis of the extremities and delayed capillary refill time, which are manifestations of mild hypothermia. Neonates, particularly preterm neonates, have a high body surface area relative to their mass, making them prone to rapid heat loss and hypothermia development. The normal respiratory rate (36/min), normal oxygen saturation (96% on room air), and normal cardiopulmonary examination findings indicate this is not respiratory distress or cardiac pathology. Neonatal hypothermia requires prompt correction as it is associated with increased mortality. Hypothermia increases oxygen consumption and metabolic demands on the neonate, which can lead to less successful resuscitation efforts if needed. Temperature regulation measures include increasing delivery room temperature, skin-to-skin contact with mother immediately after birth, radiant heaters during resuscitation, and swaddling after drying. Choice B (Blood culture): While hypothermia can be a sign of systemic illness such as sepsis, this neonate has relatively mild hypothermia and an otherwise normal course in the first 6 hours after delivery, making systemic illness unlikely. Blood culture is unnecessary at this time. Choice C (Chest x-ray): This infant's cyanosis is due to the vasoconstrictive response to the cold environment, not respiratory distress or congenital heart defect. The normal respiratory rate and oxygen saturation do not warrant chest imaging. Choice D (Echocardiography): There is nothing to suggest a congenital heart defect as the cause of cyanosis, so echocardiography is not indicated at this time. Choice E (Intubation and mechanical ventilation): The normal cardiopulmonary examination and vital signs do not indicate respiratory compromise requiring mechanical ventilation. Educational Objective: Neonatal hypothermia may develop after delivery as a result of rapid heat loss of the neonate. Cyanosis of the extremities and delayed capillary refill time are manifestations of hypothermia rather than primary cardiac or respiratory pathology. Neonatal hypothermia requires prompt correction as it is associated with increased mortality and increased metabolic demands.
▶ Immune System Anaphylaxis 1 questions
Source: 4A #23
A previously healthy 8-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of difficulty breathing 10 minutes after being stung by a bee. His temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), pulse is 130/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 65/50 mm Hg. Examination shows wheezing, audible stridor, and a generalized urticarial rash. Epinephrine and methylprednisolone are administered. Administration of which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Cromolyn sodium B) Dopamine C) Fluids D) Lidocaine E) Norepinephrine
Correct Answer: C) Fluids
Anaphylaxis is a severe type 1 hypersensitivity reaction that presents following allergen exposure (in this case, a bee sting). It is caused by widespread IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation resulting in histaminergic responses across multiple organ systems, leading to flushing, angioedema, bronchospasm, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, and vasodilation that can result in airway obstruction and circulatory collapse. Anaphylaxis represents a form of distributive shock characterized by a primary reduction in systemic vascular resistance (SVR) secondary to IgE-mediated histamine and cytokine release. While cardiac output initially increases to compensate for low SVR, untreated anaphylaxis progresses to decompensation with progressive hypotension and insufficient organ perfusion. This patient has already received epinephrine (first-line therapy) and methylprednisolone. The next critical step is fluid resuscitation to increase intravascular volume and support adequate organ perfusion. The patient's hypotension (65/50 mm Hg) indicates distributive shock requiring volume expansion. Choice A (Cromolyn sodium) is a mast cell stabilizer used in asthma and allergic rhinitis to prevent degranulation, but it is not indicated in acute anaphylaxis. Choice B (Dopamine) is a vasopressor used in shock management, but intravenous fluids should be administered first prior to vasopressor therapy to support adequate perfusion. Choice D (Lidocaine) is an antiarrhythmic and local anesthetic agent that has no role in anaphylaxis management. Choice E (Norepinephrine) is a catecholamine that increases SVR and can be considered as adjunctive vasopressor therapy if the patient remains in shock despite maximal epinephrine and fluid resuscitation, but it is not the immediate next step. Educational Objective: Anaphylaxis is a distributive shock with primary SVR reduction. First-line therapy consists of intramuscular epinephrine followed by aggressive fluid resuscitation to restore intravascular volume and support end-organ perfusion. Vasopressors are reserved for refractory hypotension despite these interventions.
▶ Respiratory System Community-Acquired Pneumonia 1 questions
Source: 4A #24
A 2-year-old girl is brought for a follow-up examination 2 days after initiating amoxicillin therapy for a right lower lobe pneumonia. She had been healthy prior to onset of the pneumonia. She continues to have fevers and cough, and she now has right-sided chest pain. Her immunizations are up-to-date. She appears ill and is tachypneic. Her temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 140/min, and respirations are 45/min. Repeat x-rays of the chest show a large dense consolidation in the right lower lung field and a fixed right-sided effusion. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism? A) Enterobacter cloacae B) Haemophilus influenzae type b C) Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare D) Pseudomonas aeruginosa E) Staphylococcus aureus
Correct Answer: E) Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is the correct answer because this patient presents with pneumonia that has failed to respond to amoxicillin therapy, a beta-lactam antibiotic. Staphylococcus aureus commonly expresses beta-lactamases, which confer resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics such as amoxicillin. This resistance explains the clinical failure despite appropriate initial antibiotic coverage. The patient's age (2 years), up-to-date immunizations, and clinical presentation with consolidation and effusion are consistent with S. aureus pneumonia. In pediatric patients aged 2-5 years, the common bacterial causes of pneumonia include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Staphylococcus aureus. Viral pneumonia is actually most common overall in this age group. The clinical failure of amoxicillin monotherapy is a key diagnostic clue pointing toward a beta-lactamase-producing organism. Choice A (Enterobacter cloacae) is a Gram-negative, facultative anaerobe that comprises part of normal gut flora. While it can cause respiratory infections, it is primarily associated with immunocompromised patients and would be an unusual cause of community-acquired pneumonia in this otherwise healthy child. Choice B (Haemophilus influenzae type b) is an encapsulated, Gram-negative coccobacillus and historically was a common cause of pediatric pneumonia. However, widespread childhood immunization programs have significantly reduced the risk of H. influenzae type b infection. This patient has up-to-date immunizations, making this diagnosis less likely. Choice C (Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare) is a non-tuberculous acid-fast bacillus that may cause pneumonia when organisms are inhaled from the environment. It is more commonly associated with immunocompromised patients and would be an unusual cause in this otherwise healthy child. Staphylococcus aureus remains a more common pathogen. Choice D (Pseudomonas aeruginosa) is a Gram-negative bacillus ubiquitous in the environment. While it causes various infections including hospital-associated and ventilator-associated pneumonia, it is characteristically associated with cystic fibrosis. Community-acquired pneumonia from Pseudomonas in otherwise healthy children is rare. Educational Objective: Pneumonia is common in the pediatric population and is typically caused by respiratory viruses, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Staphylococcus aureus. Immunization programs against Haemophilus influenzae type b have significantly reduced the prevalence of this disease. Beta-lactamase-producing Staphylococcus aureus should be suspected when pneumonia fails to respond to beta-lactam monotherapy, and combination therapy with a beta-lactamase inhibitor (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanic acid) or other appropriate anti-staphylococcal therapy is recommended.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Glycogen Storage Disease 1 questions
Source: 4A #26
A 6-day-old girl is brought to the physician because of vomiting for 2 days. She has not had fever. She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy, labor, and delivery. Results of newborn screening are pending. She was discharged at the age of 1 day. She is exclusively breast-fed and is feeding every 3 hours. She is at the 50th percentile for length and head circumference and 5th percentile for weight. Examination shows generalized jaundice. The liver is enlarged and firm. Her serum total bilirubin concentration is 14 mg/dL, with a direct component of 8 mg/dL. Test of the urine for reducing substances is positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Galactosemia B) Hereditary fructose intolerance C) Mucopolysaccharidosis II D) Type I glycogen storage disease E) Tyrosinemia
Correct Answer: A) Galactosemia
Galactosemia is the most likely diagnosis in this exclusively breast-fed patient with hepatomegaly and the presence of reducing substances in the urine. Normal metabolism of lactose involves separation into glucose and galactose by lactase. Free glucose can be used for cellular energy production while galactose must be converted to galactose-1-phosphate by galactokinase and then subsequently converted to UDP-galactose and then glucose-1-phosphate by galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT). Classic galactosemia results from deficiency of GALT, an autosomal recessive disorder. Breast milk contains galactose, which patients with galactosemia are unable to break down. Early complications include jaundice, vomiting, hepatomegaly, diarrhea, lethargy, and occasionally sepsis with Gram-negative organisms. Coagulopathy and easy bruising may also occur. Diagnosis is made by assessing for the presence and activity of GALT in erythrocytes by radioimmunoassay. Reducing substances are molecules that can convert cupric to cuprous ions in the urine and include glucose, lactose, pentose, and galactose. The presence of these substances (galactose) can suggest the diagnosis but is not specific. Additionally, while galactosemia is detected on newborn screening, manifestations of the disease can occur before the results of screening are available. Treatment requires eliminating dietary galactose and providing necessary supplements; however, this may not reverse neurologic sequelae of the disease, such as infantile cataracts and intellectual disability. Choice B: Hereditary fructose intolerance is caused by a deficiency in aldolase B, an enzyme important in the metabolism of fructose. Deficiency results in increased concentrations of fructose-1-phosphate and fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, causing a deficiency of available phosphate, which inhibits gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. Patients present with hypoglycemia only after fructose is introduced into the diet. Choice C: Mucopolysaccharidosis II, also known as Hunter syndrome, is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by a deficiency in iduronate-2-sulfatase, which results in the deposition of heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate. Within the first year of life, patients develop coarse facial features, hepatosplenomegaly, hernias, and dysostosis multiplex. Choice D: Type I glycogen storage disease is caused by glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency. This enzyme is located in the liver and functions in gluconeogenesis to convert glucose-6-phosphate to glucose for its release into the blood. Impaired gluconeogenesis can lead to severe hypoglycemia during periods of fasting. It is characterized by excess glycogen in the liver, hepatomegaly, and fasting hypoglycemia. Choice E: Tyrosinemia can refer to one of several disorders in which enzymes required for the metabolism of tyrosine are deficient. In its most severe form, it can present with liver disease and renal tubular acidosis, but hypophosphatemia, bone mineralization disorders, and aminoaciduria are also potential findings. Educational Objective: Galactosemia refers to defects in enzymes that metabolize galactose. Classic galactosemia results from the deficiency of GALT, which converts galactose-1-phosphate to UDP-galactose and then glucose-1-phosphate. Early manifestations include jaundice, hepatomegaly, hypotonia, and sepsis. Reducing substances in the urine are often present but not specific.
▶ Renal Urinary System Renal Artery Stenosis Due to Atherosclerosis 1 questions
Source: 4A #28
A 3-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after the onset of lethargy. There is no history of trauma, and she has not had fever, diarrhea, or vomiting. She was born at 27 weeks' gestation and required 2 months of ventilatory support and a 2-week course of dexamethasone therapy for respiratory distress syndrome of the newborn and bronchopulmonary dysplasia. She had an umbilical arterial and venous catheter in place during the first 2 weeks of life. Her temperature is 36.7°C (98.1°F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 110/85 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Cardiac examination shows no abnormalities. Doppler ultrasonography shows renal artery thrombosis. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's hypertension? A) Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease B) Idiopathic intracranial hypertension C) Increased renin production D) Prematurity E) Prolonged use of corticosteroids
Correct Answer: C) Increased renin production
Renal artery thrombosis is a rare complication of umbilical artery catheterization that can present up to several weeks after catheter removal. Other risk factors include sepsis, volume depletion, and patent ductus arteriosus. Occlusion of the renal artery by thrombus results in decreased afferent blood flow to the affected kidney, which triggers increased renin production from the juxtaglomerular apparatus. Overstimulation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system results in secondary hypertension. Treatment includes systemic anticoagulation and volume resuscitation, with unilateral nephrectomy reserved for refractory hypertension. Choice A (Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) can result in pulmonary hypertension from chronic hypoxia and vascular remodeling in adults but would be unlikely in a 3-month-old patient. Choice B (Idiopathic intracranial hypertension/pseudotumor cerebri) presents as increased intracranial pressure without identifiable cause, most commonly in younger females with risk factors including obesity and use of vitamin A, oral contraceptives, or danazol. It typically presents with holocephalic headache and blurry vision, not the acute presentation described. Choice D (Prematurity) is a risk factor for surfactant deficiency and neonatal respiratory distress syndrome but does not directly explain hypertension. Choice E (Prolonged use of corticosteroids) can cause hypertension through fluid retention from mineralocorticoid effects; however, dexamethasone is a potent glucocorticoid with minimal mineralocorticoid effects and is unlikely to produce significant hypertension, especially weeks after exposure. Educational Objective: Impaired perfusion to one or both kidneys is a potential cause of secondary hypertension. Renal artery thrombosis, a rare disorder associated with umbilical artery catheterization, causes decreased afferent blood flow to the affected kidney, triggering increased renin production from the juxtaglomerular apparatus and resulting in secondary hypertension via activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
▶ Nervous System Special Senses Epidural Hematoma 1 questions
Source: 4A #29
A 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of vomiting for 20 hours and lethargy for 4 hours. Earlier that day, she fell and struck the side of her head on a coffee table while demonstrating a new dance step; she did not lose consciousness at that time. Vomiting began approximately 4 hours after she hit her head. On arrival, she is sleepy but oriented. Her pulse is 76/min, and blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg. There is a 4-cm round soft area of swelling over the left parietal bone. Optic fundi are difficult to examine, but there are no obvious hemorrhages. A CT scan shows a lens-shaped extracerebral density underlying the parietal swelling. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Cerebral contusion B) Concussion C) Diffuse axonal injury D) Epidural hematoma E) Intracerebral hematoma F) Shaken baby syndrome G) Subdural hematoma
Correct Answer: D) Epidural hematoma
Epidural hematomas are most commonly associated with trauma to the middle meningeal artery causing accumulation of blood between the dura and the skull, which is bound by dural sutures. They classically present following head trauma with initial loss of consciousness followed by a brief period of lucidity before later developing altered mental status, headache, emesis, lethargy, and signs of cerebral compression. Physical examination may disclose lateralizing signs such as hemiparesis or signs of increased intracranial pressure such as papilledema. Initial evaluation with non-contrast head CT scan shows a lens-shaped hyperdense lesion with adjacent cerebral compression and possible midline shift. Definitive management is surgical evacuation, and occasionally hyperosmolar therapy if there is impending cerebral herniation. Choice A (Cerebral contusions) are seen in acceleration or deceleration injuries, particularly in basal frontal and temporal areas, with imaging showing multiple small, diffuse hyperdense lesions rather than a single lens-shaped lesion. Choice B (Concussions) are mild forms of traumatic brain injury presenting with confusion, amnesia, headache, and dizziness, with MRI typically showing no abnormalities. Choice C (Diffuse axonal injury) is a severe form of traumatic brain injury presenting immediately with profoundly altered mental status or coma from shearing of white matter tracts, with neuroimaging showing small hyperdense lesions in white matter rather than a lens-shaped lesion. Choice E (Intracerebral hematoma) presents acutely with headache, altered mental status, hemiplegia, vision changes, aphasia, or coma, appearing as a hyperdensity within the parenchyma rather than near the cranial bones. Choice F (Shaken baby syndrome) typically presents with lethargy or altered mental status, seizures, and apnea, with physical examination disclosing injuries inconsistent with history and retinal hemorrhages, and neuroimaging showing cerebral contusions with potential subdural and subarachnoid hemorrhages. Choice G (Subdural hematoma) presents following trauma with blood beneath the dura from shearing of bridging veins, appearing crescent-shaped on CT scan rather than lens-shaped. Educational Objective: Epidural hematomas present following trauma with initial loss of consciousness followed by a lucid interval prior to developing altered mental status, headache, emesis, lethargy, and signs of cerebral compression. Non-contrast head CT scan shows an extracerebral lens-shaped hyperdense lesion bound by suture lines.
▶ Gastrointestinal System Giardia infection 1 questions
Source: 4A #31
A previously healthy 16-month-old boy is brought to the physician because of decreased appetite, poor weight gain, and intermittent diarrhea over the past 3 months. He has vomited once during this period. He has not had fever, and his activity level has been normal. At the age of 12 months, he was at the 50th percentile for length and weight. He is now at the 50th percentile for length and 20th percentile for weight. Examination shows mild abdominal distention. Test of the stool is positive for Giardia lamblia and negative for occult blood. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this child's failure to thrive? A) Hypermetabolic state B) Inherited disaccharidase deficiency C) Malabsorption of fats and carbohydrates D) Overgrowth of saprophytic organisms E) Utilization of nutrients by the parasite
Correct Answer: C) Malabsorption of fats and carbohydrates
Giardia lamblia is a flagellated, parasitic organism that causes giardiasis, typically acquired through ingestion of cysts in contaminated water that mature into trophozoites in the small bowel. Parasitic overgrowth of the small bowel leads to intestinal malabsorption of fats and carbohydrates, which is the primary mechanism underlying this patient's failure to thrive and malnutrition. Giardiasis presents with persistent diarrhea that is foul-smelling and fatty, along with abdominal pain, bloating, cramping, and weight loss. Children and infants are more likely than adults to present with dehydration and failure to thrive secondary to malnutrition from malabsorption. Diagnosis is made via stool culture, microscopy, or stool antigen testing, which characteristically shows flagellated, pear-shaped trophozoites with two large central nuclei and a medial axostyle. Metronidazole is first-line treatment. Incorrect choices: A) Hypermetabolic state can occur in hyperthyroidism, but Giardia lamblia does not cause perturbations in thyroid function. B) Inherited disaccharidase deficiency underlies lactose intolerance, but Giardia lamblia infection does not cause lactose intolerance. D) Overgrowth of saprophytic organisms is inconsistent with Giardia lamblia presence. Saprophytic organisms (molds and fungi) derive energy from decaying organic matter, and Giardia is neither a fungus nor saprophytic organism. E) While Giardia lamblia does utilize nutrients in the human small bowel, small bowel parasitic overgrowth leading to intestinal malabsorption—not direct nutrient consumption by the parasite—is the underlying cause of diarrhea and failure to thrive. Educational Objective: Giardia lamblia causes giardiasis presenting with persistent foul-smelling fatty diarrhea, abdominal symptoms, and failure to thrive resulting from small bowel parasitic overgrowth and malabsorption of fats and carbohydrates.
▶ Gastrointestinal System Biliary atresia 1 questions
Source: 4A #34
An otherwise asymptomatic 4-week-old boy is brought to the physician because of increasing jaundice for 1 week. He was born at term following a prolonged labor. One day after birth, he received phototherapy for jaundice and was discharged on the third day. He is exclusively breast-fed. Examination shows no abnormalities except for jaundice. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin concentration of 12 g/dL with normal red cell morphology, and a total serum bilirubin concentration of 12 mg/dL with a direct component of 8 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism of this patient's jaundice? A) Decreased biliary excretion B) Decreased hepatic glucuronosyltransferase activity C) Decreased hepatic Y and Z protein concentrations D) Decreased serum bilirubin uptake E) Increased serum bilirubin production
Correct Answer: A) Decreased biliary excretion
Neonatal jaundice with a preponderance of conjugated bilirubin, as indicated by an increased direct bilirubin (8 mg/dL out of 12 mg/dL total), is suggestive of biliary atresia. Biliary atresia is caused by abnormal underdevelopment of the extrahepatic biliary system. Affected infants are able to conjugate bilirubin normally in the liver but are unable to excrete bile into the gastrointestinal lumen due to decreased biliary excretion. Affected infants present with worsening jaundice caused by conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, along with pale stool, dark urine, poor weight gain, and in untreated cases, cirrhosis, coagulopathy, and portal hypertension. Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and therefore does not cause kernicterus. Treatment includes surgical portoenterostomy or liver transplant. Choice B (Decreased hepatic glucuronosyltransferase activity) underlies Gilbert syndrome and Crigler-Najjar syndrome, both characterized by defective hepatic conjugation of bilirubin with accumulation of unconjugated bilirubin (increased indirect bilirubin), not conjugated bilirubin. Choice C (Decreased hepatic Y and Z protein concentrations) would interfere with hepatic bilirubin conjugation by disrupting the cytosolic binding and transport of bilirubin to the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, but this leads to conjugation defects, not excretion defects. Choice D (Decreased serum bilirubin uptake) would occur in hypoalbuminemia, as circulating unconjugated bilirubin depends on albumin binding for transport to the liver. Choice E (Increased serum bilirubin production) is suggestive of hemolytic disease such as sickle cell disease, characterized by increased indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase, and decreased haptoglobin. Educational Objective: Biliary atresia results from abnormal underdevelopment of the extrahepatic biliary system, causing inability to excrete conjugated bilirubin. Affected infants present with worsening jaundice due to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, pale stool, dark urine, poor weight gain, and in untreated cases, cirrhosis, coagulopathy, and portal hypertension.
▶ Respiratory System Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome 1 questions
Source: 4A #35
A 4-year-old boy is hospitalized because of fever, shallow breathing, and unresponsiveness for 3 hours. His temperature is 40°C (104°F), pulse is 160/min, respirations are 60/min, and blood pressure is 60/35 mm Hg. Examination shows purpura over the lower extremities. He is intubated and mechanically ventilated. Blood cultures grow Neisseria meningitidis. Two days later, an x-ray of the chest shows bilateral patchy infiltrates. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism for these findings? A) Cholinergic hyperactivity B) Enzymatic deficiency C) Increased vascular permeability D) Mucosal inflammation E) Oxygen toxicity F) Surfactant deficiency
Correct Answer: C) Increased vascular permeability
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a severe complication associated with numerous causes, including sepsis, aspiration, pneumonia, trauma, and shock. This patient presents with sepsis from Neisseria meningitidis (evidenced by fever, purpura, hypotension, and positive blood cultures) complicated by ARDS. ARDS results from the effect of cytokines on the pulmonary parenchyma following direct or indirect lung injury. This leads to endothelial injury with increased vascular permeability, allowing exudative fluid to extend into the alveolar space, resulting in diffuse alveolar damage and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema. ARDS is characterized by respiratory failure with bilateral diffuse interstitial and airspace opacities (as seen on this patient's chest x-ray showing bilateral patchy infiltrates) from underlying diffuse alveolar damage and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. Mechanical ventilation is often required in the management of ARDS due to hypoxemia and hypoventilation. Choice A (Cholinergic hyperactivity) may result in cholinergic crisis from excessive stimulation of nicotinic and muscarinic receptors. In the lungs, this causes decreased lung compliance, bronchoconstriction, and increased bronchial secretions, but is not associated with the clinical presentation of sepsis and meningococcemia. Choice B (Enzymatic deficiency) is characteristic of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, which results in host tissue damage from neutrophil elastase in the lungs and liver, with imaging typically showing emphysematous changes in bilateral lung bases. This does not explain the acute presentation following infection. Choice D (Mucosal inflammation) occurs with direct lung irritation or injury, as in pulmonary infection, chemical pneumonitis, inflammatory lung disease, foreign body aspiration, and malignancy. However, ARDS is characterized by increased vascular permeability in the alveoli rather than mucosal inflammation. Choice E (Oxygen toxicity) is a complication of mechanical ventilation with high fraction of inspired oxygen and can lead to cell membrane oxidative damage and alveolar collapse with extensive pulmonary edema. However, this patient was otherwise healthy prior to his infection without pulmonary involvement, likely requiring a low fraction of inspired oxygen, making ARDS resulting from sepsis and increased vascular permeability more likely than oxygen toxicity. Choice F (Surfactant deficiency) is the underlying pathophysiology of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome caused by alveolar collapse from inadequate surfactant production. Surfactant deficiency may also result from drowning injury or aspiration, but does not explain the mechanism of ARDS in this septic patient. Educational Objective: Acute respiratory distress syndrome is a life-threatening inflammatory disorder characterized by increased pulmonary vascular permeability and diffuse pulmonary edema with a proteinaceous exudate. It is associated with numerous causes, especially sepsis, aspiration, pneumonia, trauma, and shock.
▶ Cardiovascular System Functional Murmurs 1 questions
Source: 4A #36
A 2-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother for a well-child examination. She is at the 50th percentile for length and weight. A grade 2/6, crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur with a musical quality is heard best at the lower left sternal border with no radiation. S2 is normal. Precordial activity and peripheral pulses are normal. There were no previous notations of a murmur in her medical records. An ECG shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Reassurance that this is a benign murmur B) Complete blood count C) Chest x-ray D) Echocardiography E) Antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures
Correct Answer: A) Reassurance that this is a benign murmur
A Still murmur is a benign, asymptomatic murmur heard in children characterized by a systolic, musical, grade 1 to 2 murmur best heard at the lower left sternal border. It is typically louder when the patient is supine than when sitting and most commonly self-resolves by adolescence. Benign murmurs are more frequently seen in children after one year of age, whereas pathologic murmurs are more common in infants under one year. This patient presents with classic features of a Still murmur: appropriate age (2 years), normal growth parameters, grade 2/6 systolic murmur with musical quality at the lower left sternal border, normal S2, normal precordial activity and peripheral pulses, normal ECG, and no prior documentation of murmur. Pathologic murmurs typically present with grade 3 or greater intensity, diastolic timing, maximal intensity at the left upper sternal border, holosystolic quality, harsh or blowing character, or are more intense in the upright position. They are also associated with symptoms such as dyspnea, diaphoresis, or failure to thrive. Complete blood count (Choice B) is not indicated as this patient has a benign murmur without signs of infection or anemia. Chest x-ray (Choice C) is used in evaluation of congenital heart disease but would show no abnormalities in a Still murmur and is not needed. Echocardiography (Choice D) is appropriate for concerning murmurs such as grade 3 or higher with diastolic components, but plays no role in evaluating this benign murmur. Antibiotic prophylaxis (Choice E) is reserved for patients with prosthetic heart valves, unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, repaired congenital heart disease with residual shunts or valvular regurgitation, or valve regurgitation in transplanted hearts—this patient does not meet these criteria. Educational Objective: A Still murmur is a benign, asymptomatic murmur of childhood that presents with a systolic, grade 1 to 2 murmur with a musical quality best heard at the lower left sternal border, requiring reassurance rather than further investigation.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Hyperthermia 1 questions
Source: 4A #37
A 13-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after the sudden onset of headache, nausea, and vomiting during football practice. Although practice was held in the evening, the temperature outside was 85°F, and the humidity was 80%. The patient reports that he had been drinking water frequently during practice. He had not eaten since breakfast. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He is at the 90th percentile for height, weight, and BMI. On arrival, he is alert, responsive, and severely diaphoretic. His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 100/min, and blood pressure is 110/77 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Genital and pubic hair development are Tanner stage 3. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's symptoms? A) Acute gastroenteritis B) Heat exhaustion C) Hypoglycemia D) Hyponatremic dehydration E) Malignant hyperthermia
Correct Answer: B) Heat exhaustion
Heat exhaustion is the correct answer. Athletes are at increased risk for heat exhaustion as a result of strenuous exercise in hot temperatures and increased humidity. Other risk factors include lack of acclimatization, obesity, dehydration, and poor physical fitness. During exertion, the body dissipates heat by increasing blood flow to skin and producing sweat to facilitate evaporative cooling. However, when ambient temperature is increased and humidity is high, these mechanisms are less effective at dissipating heat, resulting in heat exhaustion. Heat exhaustion is characterized by exercise intolerance, increased core body temperature, and the absence of neurologic disturbances (such as altered mental status, confusion, or seizure). It is associated with dehydration, tachycardia, lightheadedness, muscle cramps, and generalized weakness. Management involves removing the individual from the heat, removing excess clothing, and initiating cooling measures such as immersion in cool water or evaporative cooling. Incorrect choices: Choice A (Acute gastroenteritis): While this patient has nausea and vomiting, he does not have diarrhea, which is characteristic of gastroenteritis. Heat exhaustion is more likely given the clinical context of exercise in hot, humid conditions. Choice C (Hypoglycemia): Although the patient exercised after not eating since breakfast and would be at risk for hypoglycemia, healthy individuals typically maintain stable serum glucose through hepatic glycogenolysis during exercise and fasting. Furthermore, hypoglycemia would not cause hyperthermia and typically causes altered mental status rather than the alert, responsive presentation described. Choice D (Hyponatremic dehydration): While this can occur with severe vomiting and diarrhea, this patient lacks diarrhea. Hyponatremia develops due to loss of electrolytes and water with subsequent increase in antidiuretic hormone action, but this does not explain the acute presentation in the context of exertional heat exposure. Choice E (Malignant hyperthermia): This is caused by a genetic defect in the ryanodine receptor and presents with muscle rigidity, tachycardia, hyperthermia, and lactic acidosis when exposed to succinylcholine or volatile anesthetics. This patient has no anesthetic exposure and lacks muscle rigidity. Treatment would be dantrolene. Educational Objective: Heat exhaustion is characterized by exercise intolerance, increased core body temperature, and the absence of neurologic disturbances. It is associated with dehydration, tachycardia, lightheadedness, muscle cramps, and generalized weakness.
▶ Respiratory System Pneumothorax 1 questions
Source: 4A #38
A previously healthy 17-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 40 minutes after being stabbed in the left side of her chest with a pair of scissors. En route to the hospital, intravenous lactated Ringer solution was administered, and administration of oxygen (3 L/min) via face mask was begun. On arrival, she has severe chest pain. She is agitated and diaphoretic and is not oriented to person, place, or time. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 32/min and labored, and palpable systolic blood pressure is 80 mm Hg. Examination shows jugular venous distention bilaterally. The trachea is deviated to the right. Breath sounds are decreased on the left with hyperresonance to percussion. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management? A) Chest x-ray B) Insertion of an oropharyngeal airway C) Needle decompression D) Pericardiocentesis E) Cricothyroidotomy
Correct Answer: C) Needle decompression
Tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening condition that can occur as a complication of penetrating thoracic trauma. It develops when air enters the pleural space but is prevented from exiting, causing increasing amounts of trapped air to compress the lung parenchyma and prevent lung expansion. As the pneumothorax progresses, it causes tracheal or mediastinal deviation away from the affected hemithorax and compresses the pulmonary veins and superior vena cava, decreasing venous return. This manifests with hypotension, jugular venous distension, and obstructive shock. Tension pneumothorax is characterized clinically by absent breath sounds and hyperresonance to percussion due to increased air in the intrathoracic space displacing normal lung tissue. In an unstable patient presenting with these signs, immediate needle decompression is required to evacuate air from the pleural space, followed by tube thoracostomy. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis that does not require imaging confirmation before intervention in an unstable patient. Choice A (Chest x-ray) would delay critical treatment. Tension pneumothorax requires immediate clinical recognition and intervention rather than radiographic confirmation in an unstable patient. Choice B (Insertion of an oropharyngeal airway) is an airway adjunct used during bag-valve mask ventilation to open the airway, typically when the tongue obstructs airflow. It does not address the underlying pneumothorax. Choice D (Pericardiocentesis) is indicated for pericardial effusion or cardiac tamponade, which present with muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distention, hypotension, and possibly pulsus paradoxus. While this patient has jugular venous distension and hypotension, these result from tension pneumothorax with mediastinal compression, not pericardial tamponade. Choice E (Cricothyroidotomy) is an invasive airway access procedure indicated when endotracheal intubation fails in cases of airway compromise. This patient's primary problem is the pneumothorax causing shock, not airway obstruction. Educational Objective: Tension pneumothorax results from air entering the pleural space but being unable to exit, leading to progressive lung collapse and mediastinal mass effect. Clinical presentation includes respiratory distress, tracheal deviation, hypotension, jugular venous distension, decreased breath sounds, and hyperresonance to percussion. Management requires emergent needle decompression followed by chest tube placement. Diagnosis is clinical and should not be delayed for imaging in unstable patients.
▶ Behavioral Health Phencyclidine Intoxication 1 questions
Source: 4A #40
A 16-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by police because of a 5-hour history of hallucinations, profuse sweating, and intermittent yelling and flailing. He is striking out at those near him and requires leather restraints. His pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 150/85 mm Hg. Physical examination shows pallor, profuse diaphoresis, and recent bruising. Mental status examination shows incoherent speech, episodic screaming, and agitation. He is disoriented to person, place, and time. The most appropriate next step in management is administration of which of the following? A) Intramuscular lorazepam B) Intramuscular naloxone C) Intravenous 50% dextrose D) Intravenous flumazenil E) Intravenous 5% glucose and 0.9% saline
Correct Answer: A) Intramuscular lorazepam
Phencyclidine (PCP) is an illicit substance that acts on the central nervous system through multiple mechanisms: antagonism of NMDA receptors leading to excitatory neurotransmitter release, inhibition of reuptake of dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin, and stimulation of alpha-adrenergic receptors. Acute PCP intoxication presents with psychosis, bizarre behavior, agitation, aggression, rotatory nystagmus, and ataxia. Patients exhibit sympathomimetic effects including diaphoresis, tachycardia, and hypertension. The clinical presentation in this case—severe psychomotor agitation, hallucinations, profuse sweating, tachycardia, and hypertension—is classic for PCP intoxication. Control of psychomotor agitation is the first step in management for the safety of both patient and medical staff. Chemical sedation with benzodiazepines such as intramuscular lorazepam or midazolam is the appropriate initial intervention. Once adequate sedation is achieved, further evaluation can be completed to assess for traumatic injuries or complications including rhabdomyolysis, hyperthermia, seizures, encephalopathy, or comatose state. Choice B (Intramuscular naloxone) is indicated for opioid overdose characterized by respiratory depression, apnea, and hypoxia—not the severe agitation seen here. Choice C (Intravenous 50% dextrose) is for hypoglycemia, which would cause confusion and altered mental status but not hypertension and psychomotor agitation. Choice D (Intravenous flumazenil) is for benzodiazepine overdose, which presents with sedation and respiratory depression, not agitation. Choice E (Intravenous 5% glucose and 0.9% saline) represents maintenance fluids that would not address acute sedation needs.
▶ Blood Lymphoreticular System Anemia of chronic disease 1 questions
Source: 4A #43
A 7-year-old girl with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis is brought to the physician because of a 1-year history of progressive fatigue. She has had occasional fever and swelling and pain of the knees during the past month. She appears ill. Her temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse is 104/min, and respirations are 20/min. Examination shows pale conjunctivae. The spleen is palpated 2 cm below the left costal margin. The right knee is warm, erythematous, and mildly swollen; range of motion is limited. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL, Mean corpuscular volume 75 µm³, Leukocyte count 11,000/mm³, Reticulocyte count 0.5%, Platelet count 400,000/mm³. For each patient with anemia, select the most likely diagnosis. A) Acute lymphoblastic leukemia B) Anemia of chronic disease C) Autoimmune hemolytic anemia D) Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency E) Hemolytic uremic syndrome F) Hereditary spherocytosis G) Lead poisoning H) Red blood cell aplasia (acquired) I) Sickle cell disease J) Thalassemia K) Uremia of chronic renal failure
Correct Answer: B) Anemia of chronic disease
This patient with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) with fevers, fatigue, right knee effusion, and splenomegaly most likely has anemia of chronic disease (ACD). ACD is found in many autoimmune, infectious, and malignant disease states. Chronic inflammation results in increased hepcidin production, which leads to decreased responsiveness of the bone marrow to erythropoietin and retention of iron within the reticuloendothelial system (RES). This creates a state of functional iron deficiency despite adequate iron stores. Patients present with either normocytic (early) or microcytic (late) anemia with reduced reticulocytes, indicating inadequate bone marrow response. Laboratory findings include normal to slightly high ferritin concentration with decreased serum iron concentration and total iron-binding capacity (TIBC). Choice A (Acute lymphoblastic leukemia) is a pediatric malignancy presenting with malaise, fatigue, weight loss, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, anemia, and thrombocytopenia with circulating leukemic blasts on peripheral blood smear. Anemia results from bone marrow infiltration by malignant cells. However, this patient's WBC count is normal and no blasts are mentioned. Choice C (Autoimmune hemolytic anemia) results from autoantibody binding to RBC surface antigens leading to RES removal or intravascular hemolysis. Diagnosis requires positive Coombs test, unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, decreased haptoglobin, and spherocytes or reticulocytes on smear. This patient has a low reticulocyte count, which is inconsistent with hemolysis. Choice D (G6PD deficiency) causes oxidative stress and hemolysis upon exposure to medications such as sulfa drugs. No such exposure or hemolytic features are present. Choice E (Hemolytic uremic syndrome) is classically associated with E. coli O157:H7 infection presenting with bloody diarrhea, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. This patient lacks these features. Choice F (Hereditary spherocytosis) is autosomal dominant due to mutations in ankyrin, spectrin, and band proteins with spherocytes on smear. Treatment is splenectomy. This patient has no family history and the presentation is inconsistent. Choice G (Lead poisoning) inhibits ferrochelatase and ALA dehydratase, reducing heme synthesis. Manifestations include encephalopathy, cognitive dysfunction, peripheral neuropathy, hearing loss, renal tubular dysfunction, interstitial nephritis, vomiting, abdominal pain, and constipation. No exposure history is noted. Choice H (Red blood cell aplasia, acquired) is an autoimmune process destroying erythroid progenitor cells with low reticulocyte count and preserved other cell lines. While this patient has low reticulocytes, the clinical context of JIA with fever and splenomegaly points to ACD. Choice I (Sickle cell disease) results from β-globin mutations causing abnormal hemoglobin S polymerization in hypoxia. No sickling crisis or characteristic features are described. Choice J (Thalassemia) results from α- or β-globin gene deletions or mutations. Presentation ranges from asymptomatic carrier to severe transfusion-dependent anemia. No mention of ethnic background predisposing to this condition. Choice K (Uremia from chronic renal failure) interferes with platelet activity and predisposes to bleeding, though platelet counts are usually normal. No renal dysfunction is indicated. Educational Objective: ACD is common in patients with chronic inflammatory diseases because of increased hepcidin production. This results in increased retention of iron within the RES and impaired iron exportation for erythropoiesis. Ferritin concentrations are normal to high while serum iron concentrations, TIBC, and reticulocyte counts are decreased, reflecting the bone marrow's inadequate response to anemia.
▶ Gastrointestinal System Ulcerative colitis 1 questions
Source: 4A #44
A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of lower abdominal cramps and intermittent pain in her knees and hips for 6 weeks. The cramps are relieved by bowel movements. During this period, she has had 6 to 10 urgent, bloody bowel movements daily. Examination shows a swollen, mildly tender left knee joint. Her hemoglobin concentration is 14.5 g/dl, leukocyte count is 16,000/mm³, and platelet count is 790,000/mm³. Analysis of knee joint aspirate shows straw-colored, slightly turbid fluid with a leukocyte count of 2000/mm³ (40% segmented neutrophils). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Adenovirus gastroenteritis B) Chronic nonspecific diarrhea of childhood C) Giardiasis D) Henoch-Schönlein purpura E) Pseudomembranous enterocolitis F) Ulcerative colitis
Correct Answer: F) Ulcerative colitis
Ulcerative colitis is an inflammatory bowel disease that results in inflammation and ulceration of the colonic mucosa and submucosa, typically beginning in the rectum and advancing proximally in a continuous distribution. The clinical presentation in this case is classic: chronic abdominal pain relieved by bowel movements, prolonged bloody diarrhea (6-10 urgent bowel movements daily for 6 weeks), and extraintestinal manifestations including arthritis of the knees and hips. The laboratory findings show reactive thrombocytosis (790,000/mm³) and leukocytosis (16,000/mm³) typical of chronic inflammatory conditions. The knee joint aspirate with straw-colored fluid and mild inflammation is consistent with inflammatory arthritis associated with IBD. Diagnosis is confirmed by colonoscopy and biopsy demonstrating characteristic crypt abscesses. Imaging typically shows loss of haustral markings. Treatment includes immunomodulators, biologics, and steroids, with total colectomy being generally curative and eliminating colorectal cancer risk. Choice A (Adenovirus gastroenteritis) causes self-limited viral gastroenteritis with acute nausea, vomiting, and non-bloody diarrhea. It would not cause bloody diarrhea or persist for 6 weeks. Choice B (Chronic nonspecific diarrhea of childhood) is an idiopathic condition in otherwise healthy children that does not cause weight loss, abdominal pain, or bloody stools. Choice C (Giardiasis) presents with foul-smelling, fatty diarrhea and bloating, typically in those exposed to contaminated freshwater. It does not typically cause bloody stools. Choice D (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) is a small-vessel vasculitis presenting with gravity-dependent purpura (buttocks, legs, feet), arthralgias, hematuria, and abdominal pain including intussusception. While it can cause arthritis and abdominal symptoms, the prominent bloody diarrhea and chronic presentation are more consistent with ulcerative colitis. Choice E (Pseudomembranous colitis) is caused by Clostridium difficile and typically occurs as a hospital-acquired opportunistic infection following antibiotic use (especially ampicillin and clindamycin). Colonoscopy would show patchy white pseudomembranes, and there is no history of recent antibiotic exposure in this case. Educational Objective: Recognize ulcerative colitis as an inflammatory bowel disease presenting with chronic bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and extraintestinal manifestations including arthritis. Distinguish from other causes of bloody diarrhea and gastrointestinal disease based on clinical features and risk factors.
▶ Nervous System Special Senses Medulloblastoma 1 questions
Source: 4A #45
A previously healthy 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of progressively worsening headaches and difficulty walking over the past 6 weeks. Examination shows bilateral papilledema, right abducens palsy, and gait ataxia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Acoustic neuroma B) Dandy-Walker syndrome C) Medulloblastoma D) Optic nerve glioma E) Pinealoma
Correct Answer: C) Medulloblastoma
Medulloblastomas are the most common malignant brain tumor in children with peak incidence between ages 5-9 years. They are frequently located in the cerebellum and typically cause occlusion of ventricular drainage, leading to increased intracranial pressure. This patient's clinical presentation of progressive headaches, bilateral papilledema (indicating increased intracranial pressure), gait ataxia (from cerebellar disruption), and cranial nerve palsy is classic for medulloblastoma. Physical examination findings often include nystagmus, dysdiadochokinesia, dysmetria, and cranial nerve palsies. Diagnosis is confirmed with MRI and biopsy, typically obtained during surgical resection. Lumbar punctures are performed to evaluate for metastatic spread through cerebrospinal fluid. Treatment includes surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy. Choice A (Acoustic neuroma): A benign Schwann cell tumor of the vestibulocochlear nerve presenting with ipsilateral hearing loss, vertigo, and dysmetria. This patient lacks hearing loss, making this diagnosis unlikely. Choice B (Dandy-Walker syndrome): A malformation of the cerebellar vermis and fourth ventricle with cystic enlargement and hydrocephalus that typically presents early in life with developmental delay. This would be less likely in a previously healthy 7-year-old with acute symptom onset. Choice D (Optic nerve glioma): An astrocytoma of the optic nerve associated with neurofibromatosis type 1, presenting with gradual proptosis, vision loss, and occasionally hydrocephalus. This patient has relatively acute onset of ataxia and cranial nerve palsies without evidence of vision loss. Choice E (Pinealoma): Classically presents with paralysis of upward gaze (Parinaud syndrome), diplopia, and signs of increased intracranial pressure. Although this patient has increased intracranial pressure and abducens palsy, he lacks upward gaze paralysis. Educational Objective: Medulloblastomas are the most common malignant brain tumor in children, often presenting between ages 5-9 years with signs of increased intracranial pressure (headache, nausea, vomiting) and cerebellar signs (gait ataxia, incoordination). Management requires surgical resection followed by radiation and chemotherapy.
▶ Male Reproductive Torsion of Testis 1 questions
Source: 4A #46
A previously healthy 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of right scrotal pain and swelling for 3 hours. There is no history of trauma. He was sexually active 3 months ago, and he did not use a condom. Examination shows tenderness and edema in the region of the right testicle. The cremasteric reflex is absent on the right side. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings? A) Leukemic infiltration of the testis B) Malignant infiltration of the testis C) Persistent patency of the processus vaginalis D) Persistent patency of the urachus E) Twisting of the spermatic cord
Correct Answer: E) Twisting of the spermatic cord
Testicular torsion occurs when the testicle rotates about itself within the scrotal sac. The resultant twisting of the spermatic cord, which contains the gonadal artery, pampiniform plexus, and gonadal vein, results in vascular congestion and potential cessation of venous or arterial flow to the testis. Patients typically present with acute, severe testicular pain with diffuse tenderness and swelling. Patients may also exhibit nausea, vomiting, and lower abdominal pain. There is typically a negative cremasteric reflex with a high-riding, transverse lie of the testicle on physical examination. If not properly and expeditiously managed with surgical detorsion and orchiopexy, testicular torsion can result in testicular infarction as well as infertility. Choice A (Leukemic infiltration of the testis) is seen in acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Because of the blood-testis barrier, chemotherapy is less able to reach the testis. Testicular leukemia presents as painless testicular enlargement. Choice B (Malignant infiltration of the testis) can occur in testicular tumors such as seminoma, choriocarcinoma, teratoma, embryonal carcinoma, or yolk sac tumor. Presentation is variable depending on the type of tumor. Seminoma is the most common testicular tumor and presents as painless testicular enlargement. Choice C (Persistent patency of the processus vaginalis) can lead to the formation of a hydrocele if filled by peritoneal fluid, or hematocele if complicated by blood accumulation. It also increases the risk for an indirect inguinal hernia. Choice D (Persistent patency of the urachus) contributes to a persistent connection between the bladder and the umbilicus. Patients with a patent urachus can present with clear urine leaking out of the umbilicus. It can also be asymptomatic or potentially complicated by infection. The clinical presentation of acute severe pain, absent cremasteric reflex, and physical findings are pathognomonic for testicular torsion, which is a surgical emergency requiring prompt intervention to preserve testicular viability.
▶ Human Development Nutrition in infancy and childhood 1 questions
Source: 4A #47
A healthy 9-month-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents for a well-child examination. Her parents are concerned that she is not gaining enough weight. She is breast-feeding six times daily and taking small amounts of baby food from a spoon. She is at the 5th percentile for weight and 25th percentile for length and head circumference. Review of the growth chart shows that this growth pattern has been consistent since birth. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Reassurance that this growth pattern is within normal limits B) Increasing caloric intake by adding more baby food C) Replacing breast-feeding with soy-based formula D) Supplementing breast-feeding with whole cow milk
Correct Answer: A) Reassurance that this growth pattern is within normal limits
Growth charts display percentile curves of body measurements (head circumference, body weight, and length) used to evaluate normal growth, short stature, growth delay, failure to thrive, nutritional deficiencies, malabsorption, endocrinopathy, and other disorders. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides the international standard for infant growth charts. For infants less than 2 years of age, children are classified as having low weight or short stature only if they fall below the 2nd percentile for weight or length, respectively. This patient is at the 5th percentile for weight, which while lower, is still within normal limits and not a cause for concern. Importantly, her growth pattern has been consistent since birth, indicating normal constitutional growth variation. Further assessment and intervention for growth or nutritional problems should only be pursued if infants fall below the 2nd percentile or if there are significant changes in growth pattern. Choice B (Increasing caloric intake by adding more baby food) would not be appropriate since the patient's weight and length measurements are within normal limits. Such recommendations would only be warranted if weight were below the 2nd percentile and inadequate caloric intake was the identified cause of growth delay. Choice C (Replacing breast-feeding with soy-based formula) is inappropriate because breastfeeding is the standard source of nutrition for infant growth and healthy development and should be continued. Choice D (Supplementing breast-feeding with whole cow milk) would be harmful to the infant. Introduction of whole cow's milk prior to one year of age is associated with type 1 diabetes mellitus, increased risk for cow's milk allergy, constipation, and iron deficiency anemia. Educational Objective: Growth charts assess percentile curves of body measurements in children. For infants less than 2 years of age, concern for abnormal growth is indicated by measurements below the 2nd percentile for weight or length, or by significant deviations from established growth patterns. Constitutional growth variation in healthy infants with consistent growth patterns requires reassurance rather than intervention.
▶ Blood Lymphoreticular System Rh incompatibility 1 questions
Source: 4A #49
