A 9-month-old boy is brought to the physician 2 months after his parents noticed that he seemed to be ignoring them. On questioning, they note that he does not appear to be startled by loud noises. Growth and development have been otherwise normal. He was born at term to a 28-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1. His mother's blood group is A, Rh-negative, and his blood group is A, Rh-positive. He had a serum total bilirubin concentration of 25 mg/dL at the age of 2 days and received phototherapy for 2 days. He continued to be mildly jaundiced until the age of 1 month. Serum studies since then have shown no abnormalities. Examination today shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is most likely to have prevented this patient's current condition? A) Avoidance of breast-feeding B) Water supplementation C) Longer course of phototherapy D) Antibiotic therapy E) Exchange transfusion
Correct Answer: E) Exchange transfusion
This patient presents with sensorineural hearing loss (ignoring parents, not startled by loud noises) at 9 months of age, which is a classic long-term neurologic sequela of kernicterus. Kernicterus results from deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the brain, particularly in the basal ganglia, pons, and cerebellum. It typically presents acutely with poor feeding, lethargy, and seizures, and if untreated, causes permanent neurologic abnormalities including sensorineural hearing loss and gaze palsies. This patient had a peak bilirubin of 25 mg/dL at 2 days of life in the context of Rh incompatibility (Rh-negative mother with Rh-positive infant), indicating hemolytic disease of the newborn due to maternal anti-Rh(D) antibodies. Exchange transfusion is the most effective intervention for severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia caused by hemolysis, particularly Rh alloimmunization, because it removes both the offending antibodies and the circulating bilirubin, preventing bilirubin deposition in the brain. The patient received only 2 days of phototherapy, which was insufficient given the severity of hemolysis. Incorrect choices: Avoidance of breast-feeding (Choice A) addresses breast milk jaundice or breastfeeding jaundice, which typically cause mild hyperbilirubinemia and are not the etiology in this case. The diagnosis is Rh hemolytic disease. Water supplementation (Choice B) is not used to treat hyperbilirubinemia and carries risk of hyponatremia due to neonatal renal immaturity. Longer course of phototherapy (Choice C), while useful for mild-to-moderate hyperbilirubinemia, would have been insufficient for severe hemolytic disease; phototherapy converts indirect bilirubin to water-soluble forms but cannot remove the hemolytic stimulus or offending antibodies as effectively as exchange transfusion. Antibiotic therapy (Choice D) is for treatment of neonatal infections and has no role in preventing bilirubin-induced neurologic injury. Educational Objective: Kernicterus is caused by high concentrations of unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, commonly resulting from hemolysis due to Rh alloimmunization or glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. It presents with poor feeding, lethargy, and seizures acutely, and causes permanent neurologic sequelae including sensorineural hearing loss and gaze palsies if untreated. Exchange transfusion is the definitive treatment for severe hemolytic hyperbilirubinemia because it removes both antibodies and bilirubin.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Prader-Willi Syndrome 1 questions
Source: 8A #2
A 6-year-old girl is brought to the office by her mother because of compulsive eating since the age of 3 years. She was born following an uncomplicated pregnancy; delivery was complicated by breech presentation. During infancy, the patient had hypotonia. She began walking at the age of 2 years and talking at the age of 2.5 years. The patient lives with her mother and older sister. She is at the 52nd percentile for height and 98th percentile for weight. Physical examination shows almond-shaped eyes and a prominent nasal bridge. Examination of the extremities shows hypotonia. Mental status examination shows delayed speech and motor development. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Angelman syndrome B) Down syndrome C) Fetal alcohol syndrome D) Prader-Willi syndrome E) Rett disorder F) Williams syndrome
Correct Answer: D) Prader-Willi syndrome
Prader-Willi syndrome is a rare genetic disease caused by the lack of expression of paternal genes in the chromosome region 15q11-13. It is inherited in a sporadic pattern and may result from mutations or deletions in the paternal alleles, errors in the genetic imprinting of these alleles, or their complete absence in the case of maternal uniparental disomy. The syndrome has several characteristic features that match this patient's presentation: Hypotonia is common and can lead to abnormal uterine position of the fetus and complicated labor (as seen with the breech presentation), as well as feeding difficulties and failure to thrive in infancy. Developmental delays, intellectual disability, and disruptive behavioral patterns are commonly observed. It is associated with growth hormone deficiency and short stature. Hyperphagia and obesity are hallmark manifestations, explaining the patient's compulsive eating and 98th percentile weight. Individuals tend to have distinct facies with almond-shaped eyes, strabismus, and a wide, flattened nasal bridge, all present in this patient. The prognosis is good, as patients tend to do well into adulthood. Angelman syndrome (Choice A) is a similar genetic disorder caused by loss of expression of the maternal gene UBE3A in the chromosome region 15q11-13, but key distinguishing features include hyperactivity, excitability, uncontrolled laughter, sleep disorders, and puppet-like ataxia with characteristic hand-flapping. Down syndrome (Choice B) results from trisomy of chromosome 21 and presents with characteristic physical features including broad, flat facial features with prominent epicanthal folds and a single palmar crease. While patients may have obesity, the syndrome does not typically present with the specific combination of hyperphagia and the distinctive facial features seen in Prader-Willi syndrome. Fetal alcohol syndrome (Choice C) is associated with intellectual disability, developmental delay, and physical malformations such as microcephaly, facial dysmorphia, limb deformities, and congenital heart disease, along with a history of maternal alcohol use during pregnancy, which is not described here. Rett disorder (Choice E) results from sporadic mutations in the MECP2 gene on the X chromosome and affects those assigned female at birth. Symptoms typically appear in the first 18 months of life with progressive motor impairments, developmental delays, and significant scoliosis and kyphosis, not the hyperphagia and obesity seen in this case. Williams syndrome (Choice F) is characterized by distinct elf-like facies, verbal and social skills that often mask intellectual disabilities, and an extremely friendly demeanor. Supravalvular aortic stenosis is common. It results from a microdeletion on chromosome 7 that includes the elastin gene and does not present with hyperphagia or obesity. Educational Objective: Prader-Willi syndrome is a genetic disorder characterized by hypotonia, intellectual disabilities, behavioral issues, hyperphagia, and obesity. It is caused by absent expression of paternal genes in the chromosome region 15q11-13 and is a well-known example of a disorder associated with genetic imprinting and uniparental disomy.
▶ Cardiovascular System Bacterial Endocarditis 1 questions
Source: 8A #4
An asymptomatic 14-year-old boy is brought for a well-child examination. He has had a murmur since 4 years of age. A grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur and an early diastolic murmur at the midleft sternal border are heard. Echocardiography shows a bicuspid aortic valve with mild gradient. For which of the following conditions is this patient at greatest risk during childhood? A) Bacterial endocarditis B) Brain abscess C) Congestive heart failure D) Dissecting aortic aneurysm E) Syncope
Correct Answer: A) Bacterial endocarditis
Bicuspid aortic valves may be inherited or sporadic. As a result of their geometry and abnormal leaflet excursion, they are subject to more blood flow turbulence (generating the murmur) and shear forces. This leads to increased local tissue inflammation and calcification compared with trileaflet valves. Bicuspid valves are more prone to the development of early aortic stenosis or aortic regurgitation. Abnormal valve architecture can also present a nidus for infection; hence, patients are at increased risk for bacterial endocarditis. There is also a small risk for systemic thromboembolic disease from clots that form on the valve. Congenital and hereditary conditions associated with bicuspid aortic valves include Turner syndrome, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, coarctation of the aorta, patent ductus arteriosus, and ventricular septal defects. Choice B (Brain abscess) is a potential complication of infective endocarditis due to septic emboli, but a bicuspid aortic valve is not a direct risk factor for brain abscess. Choice C (Congestive heart failure) is a long-term complication of an untreated bicuspid aortic valve that may result due to chronically increased left ventricular afterload or severe valvular disease. Patients with bicuspid valves should be monitored regularly to allow for prompt surgical intervention if needed to prevent progressive heart failure. Choice D (Dissecting aortic aneurysm) occurs more frequently in patients with bicuspid aortic valves compared with the general population, and a large percentage of patients develop an enlarged aorta susceptible to aneurysm formation. However, aneurysm dissection is a less common complication than infective endocarditis. Choice E (Syncope) may result from one of the conditions associated with a bicuspid aortic valve, such as advanced heart failure, but is not a directly correlated risk. Educational Objective: Patients with a bicuspid aortic valve, or another structural abnormality of the cardiac valves, are at much greater risk for infective endocarditis than the general population.
▶ Blood Lymphoreticular System Cyclic neutropenia 1 questions
Source: 8A #5
A 2-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 2-day history of fever and mouth sores. His mother says he has been fussy and refused to eat but that he is beginning to feel better. He has a 1-year history of recurrent infections. Growth and development are appropriate for age. His temperature is 38.4°C (101.2°F), pulse is 120/min, and respirations are 20/min. Examination shows scattered aphthous ulcers in the oral cavity. The skin is clear, and there is no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL Leukocyte count 4000/mm³ Segmented neutrophils 4% Lymphocytes 84% Monocytes 12% Platelet count 250,000/mm³ Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Chédiak-Higashi syndrome B) Cyclic neutropenia C) Dyskeratosis congenita D) Fanconi syndrome E) Hypersplenism F) Leukemia G) Severe congenital neutropenia H) Viral illness I) Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency
Correct Answer: B) Cyclic neutropenia
Cyclic neutropenia is a rare inherited immunodeficiency syndrome characterized by periodic episodes of neutropenia and infection. Most cases follow a cyclic pattern that recurs every 21 days and typically lasts for 3 to 6 days. The disease is associated with mutations in the gene encoding neutrophil elastase. Classic symptoms include fever, malaise, and ulcers affecting the oral mucous membranes. Patients may also develop pharyngitis and chronic periodontal disease resulting in early tooth loss. During episodes of neutropenia, patients are at increased risk for bacterial infections involving the respiratory tract, gastrointestinal tract, urinary tract, or skin. Diagnosis is confirmed by monitoring neutrophil count several times weekly for at least 6 weeks, with genetic testing for mutations in the neutrophil elastase gene also recommended. Acute management involves treating infections with appropriate therapies and maintaining good oral/dental hygiene. Long-term therapy with human granulocyte-colony stimulating factor is effective in keeping neutrophils at normal concentrations. Chédiak-Higashi syndrome (Choice A) is caused by mutations in the LYST gene and presents with frequent bacterial infections, oculocutaneous albinism, peripheral neuropathy, and progressive neurologic dysfunction. Dyskeratosis congenita (Choice C) is characterized by a triad of skin abnormalities (reticular hyperpigmentation pattern, pale-gray macules, areas of atrophy), dystrophic nails, and oral leukoplakia, with pancytopenia. Fanconi anemia (Choice D) causes bone marrow suppression, pancytopenia, and recurrent infections, also characterized by short stature, microcephaly, developmental delay, and café-au-lait skin lesions. Hypersplenism (Choice E) involves splenomegaly and cytopenias of all three cell lines due to sequestration, not the isolated periodic neutropenia seen here. Leukemia (Choice F), especially acute lymphoblastic leukemia, presents with malaise, fatigue, weight loss, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and circulating leukemic blasts on peripheral blood smear. Severe congenital neutropenia (Choice G) is typically more severe with infections in the first few months of life and high risk for transformation to acute myeloid leukemia, unlike the cyclic pattern. Viral illness (Choice H), including parvovirus B19, EBV, CMV, HIV, and dengue, can cause bone marrow suppression with cytopenias but does not follow a cyclic pattern. Vitamin B12 deficiency (Choice I) results in megaloblastic anemia with macrocytosis and is associated with chronic alcohol abuse, gastric bypass, Crohn disease, or malabsorptive disorders.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever 1 questions
Source: 8A #6
A previously healthy 6-year-old girl is brought to the physician in June because of a 4-day history of persistent fever and severe headache and a 1-day history of rash over her hands. She lives in a rural area and is frequently bitten by mosquitoes. One month ago, she was treated with corticosteroids for poison ivy. She appears ill. Her temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 110/min, and respirations are 22/min. Examination shows bilateral, nonpurulent conjunctival injections and scattered petechial lesions over the palms and distal aspect of the upper extremities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Dengue fever B) Erysipelas C) Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) D) Exanthema subitum E) Measles F) Meningococcemia G) Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease) H) Rocky Mountain spotted fever I) Typhoid fever
Correct Answer: H) Rocky Mountain spotted fever
Rocky Mountain spotted fever is a tick-borne disease caused by Rickettsia rickettsii, which are gram-negative, obligate intracellular organisms. These organisms target endothelial cells, triggering vascular injury and permeability. This illness is most common in the early spring and summer, following a tick bite in an endemic area (e.g., Mid-Atlantic/Southeastern United States). Incubation occurs 2 to 14 days after exposure and manifestations include fever, headache, and petechial rash. Other manifestations include conjunctivitis, seizures, encephalitis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, cardiac arrhythmias, and coagulopathy. Laboratory testing shows thrombocytopenia, hyponatremia, increased liver enzymes, increased partial thromboplastin, and prothrombin times. If there are concerns of central nervous system involvement, lumbar puncture is recommended. Serologic testing for IgM and IgG antibodies against Rickettsia is the most used test, and patients are most often treated with doxycycline therapy. Empiric treatment should be initiated when clinical suspicion is high, as early treatment improves the prognosis, and laboratory assays are not perfectly sensitive or specific. Dengue fever (Choice A) presents with febrile illness, associated headache, retro-orbital pain, and marked bone and muscle pains lasting approximately 1 week, with possible hemorrhagic complications. It is transmitted by Aedes egyptii mosquitoes in tropical and subtropical climates, inconsistent with this patient's presentation. Erysipelas (Choice B) is a superficial skin infection with fiery-red color and ridge-like, sharp borders commonly seen on the face or lower extremity, most commonly caused by group A streptococcus. Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) (Choice C) is associated with parvovirus B19 infection and presents with pink patches on bilateral cheeks giving a "slapped cheeks" appearance, potentially followed by a lacy, macular eruption on trunk and extremities. It typically affects otherwise asymptomatic school-aged children. Exanthema subitum (Choice D), or roseola infantum, is caused by human herpesvirus 6 infection and presents with several days of fever sometimes accompanied by seizures. As fevers subside, a characteristic blanching macular eruption forms on the neck and trunk, spreading to the face and extremities. It is typically a benign, self-limited condition. Measles (Choice E) is caused by the highly contagious paramyxovirus and characteristically presents with prodromal fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and a confluent maculopapular rash starting at the head or neck and spreading to the trunk, excluding the palms and soles. Meningococcemia (Choice F) is caused by Neisseria meningitidis and presents with fever, nausea, vomiting, myalgias, and headache, potentially followed by neck stiffness and altered mental status. Patients may develop an initial petechial or purpuric rash that may progress to complications including disseminated intravascular coagulation and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome. Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease) (Choice G) is a multisystemic vasculitic disease characterized by fever for at least 5 days, bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, polymorphous rash, lymphadenopathy, erythema and edema of hands and feet, and erythema affecting mucous membranes with dry, cracked lips. Complications include coronary artery aneurysm. Typhoid fever (Choice I) is associated with bacterial infection by Salmonella Typhi and presents with pain, fever, chills, and diarrhea, most common in children in endemic settings. Educational Objective: Rocky Mountain spotted fever is a tick-borne illness associated with fever, headache, and petechial rash that starts days to weeks following a bite from an infected tick. Patients may develop life-threatening complications including encephalitis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, cardiac arrhythmias, and coagulopathy-related complications. Diagnosis is made by immunoglobulin testing. Patients rapidly respond to treatment with tetracyclines, such as doxycycline.
▶ Blood Lymphoreticular System Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency 1 questions
Source: 8A #10
A 5-day-old boy of Mediterranean descent is brought to the physician because of a 2-day history of progressive jaundice. He has had five yellow, seedy stools daily during this period. He was born at term to a 32-year-old primigravid woman. During the third trimester, his mother took an old prescription of sulfamethoxazole for cystitis without consulting the physician. The blood group of the mother and the newborn is O, Rh-positive. He receives 2 ounces of a cow's milk-based formula every 2 hours. Examination shows no abnormalities except for jaundice from the head to the upper thighs. His hematocrit is 33%, and total serum bilirubin concentration is 20 mg/dL with a direct component of 0.9 mg/dL. Direct and indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) tests are negative. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's jaundice? A) Dehydration B) Enzyme deficiency C) Milk protein allergy D) Physiologic jaundice E) Sepsis
Correct Answer: B) Enzyme deficiency
Neonatal jaundice is defined as an increased bilirubin (>5 mg/dL) that results from either increased hemolysis (bilirubin generation) or decreased bilirubin conjugation or excretion. This patient presents with anemia and indirect (unconjugated) hyperbilirubinemia in the first few days of life, suggesting a pathologic hemolytic process. The negative Coombs test excludes immune-mediated hemolysis, and his Mediterranean background is a key clinical clue. The most likely diagnosis is glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. G6PD is an enzyme in erythrocytes that catalyzes the conversion of NADP+ to NADPH. An inadequate supply of NADPH leads to decreased concentrations of glutathione, which is a critical scavenger of reactive oxygen species within erythrocytes. Increased oxidative stress, particularly with exposure to sulfa-containing compounds (such as the sulfamethoxazole the mother took during pregnancy), results in hemolysis of fetal red blood cells and neonatal jaundice. Choice A (Dehydration) can result in jaundice due to increased enterohepatic circulation and concentration of bilirubin, but this patient's findings are more consistent with hemolysis given the anemia and elevated indirect bilirubin. Choice C (Milk protein allergy) may present with IgE-mediated or non-IgE-mediated manifestations such as anaphylaxis, urticaria, angioedema, reflux, enterocolitis, or enteropathy, but does not explain the hemolytic picture with low hematocrit. Choice D (Physiologic jaundice) occurs in nearly all newborns and is caused by increased breakdown of red blood cells, immature liver metabolism, and increased enterohepatic circulation. Features include development after 24 hours of life, a bilirubin increase rate of less than 0.5 mg/dL daily, a maximum peak of 14-15 mg/dL, and predominantly indirect bilirubin (>90%). This patient's bilirubin of 20 mg/dL and low hematocrit indicate pathologic causes rather than physiologic jaundice. Choice E (Sepsis) can cause indirect hyperbilirubinemia and presents with irritability, lethargy, and poor feeding, but the clinical presentation is more consistent with G6PD deficiency triggered by sulfa exposure. Educational Objective: NADPH is produced from NADP+ by glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) and is required for the reduction of glutathione, which scavenges reactive oxygen species in erythrocytes. G6PD deficiency results in increased oxidative stress that leads to hemolysis when patients are exposed to certain medications such as trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and other sulfa drugs. This condition is particularly common in individuals of Mediterranean, African, and Asian descent.
▶ Endocrine System Androgen insensitivity syndrome 1 questions
Source: 8A #12
A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her mother because she has not yet had a menstrual period. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She appears in no distress. She is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 54 kg (120 lb); BMI is 19 kg/m². Breast development is present and appropriate for age, but she has minimal pubic and axillary hair development. Pelvic examination shows normal external female genitalia. The cervix is not visible, and no pelvic masses are palpable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Follow-up examination in 6 months B) Karyotype analysis C) Measurement of serum estrogen concentration D) MRI of the pituitary gland E) Estrogen therapy
Correct Answer: B) Karyotype analysis
Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS) is caused by a defect in the androgen receptor complex resulting in a genotypic 46,XY person developing phenotypic female or atypical genitalia and female secondary sexual characteristics. Testes are present and produce testosterone normally, but the absence of a functioning androgen receptor prevents hormone binding and thereby prevents the development of secondary male sexual characteristics. Patients present with female external genitalia, scant pubic and axillary hair, absent uterus and fallopian tubes, and a rudimentary vagina. Menses does not occur because of the lack of cyclic progesterone and estrogen, and the lack of a functional uterus with endometrial lining. Patients show increased concentrations of testosterone, estrogen, and luteinizing hormone on laboratory evaluation. Diagnosis is made with karyotype analysis showing XY chromosomes in a patient with phenotypically female characteristics. Choice A (Follow-up examination in 6 months) would be inappropriate as early recognition and diagnosis of androgen insensitivity syndrome promotes clinical intervention where possible. Additionally, evaluation for causes of primary amenorrhea is generally indicated if menarche has not occurred at or before age 16 years. Choice C (Measurement of serum estrogen concentration) will show an increased concentration of estrogen, but it would not show the specific diagnosis of androgen insensitivity syndrome, which is diagnosed via karyotype analysis. Choice D (MRI of the pituitary gland) can identify a pituitary tumor, which is associated with gynecomastia, galactorrhea, and amenorrhea when prolactin is functionally produced by the tumor. Other signs of a pituitary tumor include features related to its mass effect in the sella turcica with loss of other pituitary hormones, or damage to the optic chiasm resulting in bitemporal hemianopsia on examination. Choice E (Estrogen therapy) would be inappropriate, as patients with androgen insensitivity syndrome show increased concentrations of estrogen. Educational Objective: Androgen insensitivity syndrome occurs because of a defect in the androgen receptor and results in persons with genotypically male chromosomes developing phenotypically female characteristics. Diagnosis is made with karyotype analysis.
▶ Uncategorized Peripartum Herpes Simplex Virus Infection 1 questions
Source: 8A #15
An 8-day-old newborn is brought to the emergency department 10 minutes after she developed weakness and stopped breathing while being bottle-fed. On arrival, she is intubated and stabilized. During stabilization, she has a 3-minute episode of bicycling movements of the lower extremities and deviation of the eyes to the left. Phenobarbital is administered. Her pulse is 160/min. Physical examination shows poor response to stimulation and decreased muscle tone. Deep tendon reflexes are brisk. Babinski sign is present bilaterally. A lumbar puncture is performed. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows: Glucose 55 mg/dL Protein 65 mg/dL Erythrocyte count 350/mm³ Leukocyte count 70/mm³ Segmented neutrophils 20% Lymphocytes 80% Treatment with antibiotics is begun, and she is admitted to the intensive care unit. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism? A) Cytomegalovirus B) Escherichia coli C) Group B streptococcus D) Herpes simplex virus E) Toxoplasma gondii
Correct Answer: D) Herpes simplex virus
This newborn with seizures, lethargy, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with lymphocytosis and increased erythrocytes has a presentation concerning for encephalitis caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV). Neonatal infection with HSV can occur via the placenta or through direct inoculation as the newborn passes through the birth canal of a mother with active lesions. Infection with HSV can cause both cutaneous herpetic lesions and systemic manifestations such as meningoencephalitis. Patients may present with altered mental status, headache, fever, seizures, and focal neurologic deficits. In newborns, lethargy may be the primary presenting sign. Lumbar puncture should be performed in all patients with suspected HSV encephalitis and often shows mildly increased protein, normal or mildly decreased glucose, increased erythrocytes, and increased leukocytes with a lymphocytic predominance. Definitive diagnosis requires polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing to detect HSV in the CSF. Treatment requires intravenous acyclovir. Choice A (Cytomegalovirus): CMV in a newborn manifests as hearing loss, seizures, a petechial rash, intracranial calcifications, organomegaly, and lymphadenopathy especially if contracted through vertical transmission prior to birth. Choice B (Escherichia coli) and Choice C (Group B streptococcus): Both are common causes of neonatal meningitis. Patients may present with lethargy and seizures, but the CSF would contain decreased glucose, increased protein, and a markedly increased leukocyte count (often >1000/mm³) with a neutrophilic predominance, which differs from this case's findings. Choice E (Toxoplasma gondii): Can be transmitted from mother to fetus through the placenta. Patients with congenital toxoplasmosis often present with chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications. Educational Objective: Patients with herpes simplex virus encephalitis may present with headache, lethargy, seizures, and fever. Cerebrospinal fluid findings include mildly increased protein, normal or mildly decreased glucose, increased erythrocytes, and increased leukocytes with a lymphocytic predominance, as well as a PCR test positive for HSV. Treatment is with intravenous acyclovir.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Dehydration 1 questions
Source: 8A #16
A previously healthy 10-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of profuse watery diarrhea, frequent vomiting, and poor feeding. He usually breast-feeds well but refused all feedings today. Growth and development are appropriate for age. He appears lethargic. His respirations are 48/min, and blood pressure is 68/54 mm Hg. Examination shows mild abdominal distention. Capillary refill time is 4 seconds. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management? A) Oral rehydration B) Continuous infusion of fluids at maintenance doses C) Intravenous administration of dopamine D) Intravenous administration of fresh frozen plasma E) Intravenous bolus of 0.9% saline
Correct Answer: E) Intravenous bolus of 0.9% saline
This infant presents with signs of moderate to severe dehydration secondary to gastroenteritis, evidenced by tachypnea (48/min), hypotension (68/54 mm Hg), lethargy, poor feeding, and prolonged capillary refill time (4 seconds). Dehydration is categorized as mild, moderate, or severe based on presenting signs and symptoms. Mild dehydration presents with normal vital signs, normal mental status, and normal urine output. Moderate to severe dehydration presents with tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, delayed capillary refill, lethargy, sunken fontanelles, and decreased urine output. The treatment of choice for moderate to severe dehydration is an initial bolus of 20 cc/kg of intravenous crystalloid (normal saline or lactated Ringer's) for volume expansion. Patients with severe dehydration and hypovolemic shock can rapidly decompensate to cardiovascular collapse without adequate resuscitation and require frequent re-evaluation with additional fluid boluses as needed. Choice A (Oral rehydration) is appropriate only for mild dehydration in children tolerating oral intake. This patient's vomiting, poor feeding, and signs of significant dehydration require intravenous resuscitation. Choice B (Continuous infusion of fluids at maintenance doses) would be appropriate only after adequate volume resuscitation has been achieved and euvolemia restored. Maintenance fluids are not sufficient for a dehydrated, hypotensive patient requiring resuscitation. Choice C (Intravenous dopamine) can be used in cardiogenic shock, though norepinephrine or dobutamine are often preferred. At low doses, dopamine causes renal vasodilation; at intermediate doses, it increases cardiac output via increased stroke volume; at higher doses, it increases mean arterial pressure through vasoconstriction. However, high-quality studies do not clearly demonstrate these dose-dependent effects, and dosing variability plus arrhythmogenicity limit dopamine's clinical use. More importantly, this patient needs volume resuscitation first, not vasopressor support. Choice D (Intravenous fresh frozen plasma) contains clotting factors, fibrinogen, antithrombin III, and other plasma proteins. It is used to replace clotting factors in coagulopathic patients, not for volume resuscitation in dehydration. Educational Objective: Patients with moderate to severe dehydration may present with tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, delayed capillary refill, lethargy, sunken fontanelles, and decreased urine output, and require initial volume resuscitation with intravenous crystalloids (20 cc/kg bolus), followed by maintenance fluids and ongoing reassessment for additional boluses if needed.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Kawasaki Disease 1 questions
Source: 8A #18
An 18-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of increasingly rapid breathing and irritability. Two months ago, he had a high-grade fever, "pink eye," red swollen hands, enlarged lymph nodes, and cracked red lips; these symptoms resolved spontaneously within 14 days. He is in obvious discomfort. His temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 150/min, respirations are 60/min, and blood pressure is 60/40 mm Hg. Examination shows no other abnormalities. An x-ray of the chest shows cardiomegaly. An ECG shows right-axis deviation, left ventricular hypertrophy, and ST-segment depression in leads II and III. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's tachypnea? A) Chronic inflammatory interstitial lung disease B) Congestive heart failure C) Mitral valve obstruction D) Pericardial effusion E) Thickened internal layer of pulmonary arterioles
Correct Answer: B) Congestive heart failure
This patient's prior illness and current presentation are highly concerning for congestive heart failure caused by mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease). Kawasaki disease is a multisystem vasculitis in children characterized by fever for at least 5 days, bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, a polymorphous rash, lymphadenopathy, erythema and edema of the hands and feet, and erythema affecting the mucous membranes with dry, cracked lips. To diagnose Kawasaki disease, fever for 5 days or more plus four of the remaining criteria are required. Laboratory studies may show thrombocytosis and increased ESR. Complications of Kawasaki disease include coronary artery aneurysms, and if untreated, can lead to aneurysmal expansion, rupture, myocardial infarction, and/or congestive heart failure. The patient's cardiomegaly on chest x-ray, ECG changes showing left ventricular hypertrophy and ST-segment depression, hypotension, tachycardia, and tachypnea are all consistent with congestive heart failure from cardiac complications of prior Kawasaki disease. Children suspected of having Kawasaki disease require immediate evaluation with ECG and echocardiography, treatment, and monitoring for progression or complications. Treatment of Kawasaki disease involves high-dose aspirin and intravenous immunoglobulin, and is the only widely accepted indication for aspirin use in febrile children due to the risk for Reye syndrome. Kawasaki disease is one of the most common pediatric vasculitides and a cause of pediatric heart disease. Choice A (Chronic inflammatory interstitial lung disease) is rare in childhood and presents with progressive dyspnea, nonproductive cough, and tachypnea with interstitial fibrosis on imaging. The prodromal illness and subsequent findings are consistent with Kawasaki disease, which does not typically involve the lungs. Choice C (Mitral valve obstruction) would result in pulmonary edema from impaired forward flow of blood, presenting with progressive dyspnea, nonproductive cough, and tachypnea with congested pulmonary vasculature and increased interstitial markings on imaging. A murmur of mitral stenosis would likely be present on examination. Kawasaki disease is associated with mitral regurgitation, not obstruction. Choice D (Pericardial effusion) typically presents with hypotension, tachycardia, increased jugular venous pressure, and pulsus paradoxus when severe or causing tamponade. While it is a potential complication of Kawasaki disease, the findings in this case are more consistent with congestive heart failure. Choice E (Thickened internal layer of pulmonary arterioles) is not likely to explain this patient's symptoms, as Kawasaki disease rarely involves the pulmonary vasculature. Educational Objective: Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease) is a multisystemic vasculitis resulting in acute arteritis with a risk for the development of coronary artery aneurysms. Untreated disease can result in severe cardiac complications, including aneurysmal expansion, rupture, myocardial infarction, and congestive heart failure.
▶ Musculoskeletal System Myositis, infective 1 questions
Source: 8A #19
A 12-year-old boy is brought to the office because of a 2-day history of severe bilateral calf pain. One week ago, he had a dry cough, sore throat, headache, and fever, which resolved with ibuprofen therapy after 5 days. Currently, he is not taking any medications. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). Examination shows marked tenderness to palpation of the calves. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Dermatomyositis B) Influenza-induced myositis C) Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease) D) Parvovirus B19-induced arthritis E) Rheumatic fever
Correct Answer: B) Influenza-induced myositis
Influenza-induced myositis is a common cause of viral-induced myositis triggered by influenza A or influenza B infection. Most patients report associated viral symptoms such as fever, anorexia, and arthralgias. Myositis may occur during active infection or after the infection resolves, with symptoms including myalgias and tenderness to palpation. Additional symptoms can range from mild weakness to quadriparesis. Laboratory analysis may show increased creatinine kinase activity and myoglobinuria. Testing for influenza virus is diagnostic when combined with appropriate clinical signs and symptoms plus supporting laboratory features. Choice A (Dermatomyositis) presents with both cutaneous and musculoskeletal manifestations including heliotrope rash, Gottron papules on the dorsal hands, and shawl distribution rash, along with proximal muscle weakness. This patient lacks characteristic skin findings. Diagnosis requires clinical findings and serologic testing including antinuclear antibodies and specific myositis antibodies. Choice C (Kawasaki disease) is a multisystemic vasculitic disease characterized by fever lasting at least 5 days, bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis, polymorphous rash, lymphadenopathy, erythema and edema of hands and feet, and mucous membrane involvement with dry cracked lips. This patient lacks these characteristic features and has normal temperature. Choice D (Parvovirus B19-induced arthritis) presents with acute, symmetric arthritis or arthralgias often affecting smaller joints of the hands, wrists, and feet, and may be associated with the classic "slapped cheek" appearance. Symptoms typically resolve within 3 weeks. This patient's calf tenderness is more consistent with myositis than arthritis. Choice E (Rheumatic fever) is a sequela of untreated Group A Streptococcus infection with an autoimmune reaction against host proteins similar to streptococcal M protein. Manifestations include carditis, arthritis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, and Sydenham chorea. The patient's viral prodrome and acute myalgia presentation are not consistent with rheumatic fever. Educational Objective: Influenza-induced myositis is associated with influenza A or B infection and commonly presents with viral symptoms including fever, anorexia, and arthralgias. Myositis may occur during or after infection, with symptoms ranging from mild weakness to quadriparesis. Diagnosis is confirmed by positive influenza testing and elevated creatinine kinase levels in the appropriate clinical context.
▶ Female Reproductive Breast Candidiasis of the Vulva or Vagina 1 questions
Source: 8A #21
A 5-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her mother because of a 5-day history of progressive burning with urination and redness in the vaginal area. Her mother also noticed a small amount of yellow discharge on the patient's underwear. The patient has not had fever, vomiting, or diarrhea. She has no history of serious illness and receives no medications. There is no history of sexual abuse. Vital signs are within normal limits. Genitourinary examination shows moderate erythema over the vagina and entire perineum, including the perianal area. No vesicles or pustules are noted. There is a small amount of white discharge at the introitus. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Results of a culture of the vaginal discharge are pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy? A) Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin B) Oral acyclovir C) Oral amoxicillin D) Oral metronidazole E) Topical nystatin
Correct Answer: E) Topical nystatin
This pediatric patient with vulvar erythema and white vaginal discharge most likely has vulvovaginitis caused by Candida albicans, a fungal pathogen that causes a variety of infections including vulvovaginitis, urethritis, thrush, and sepsis. Patients with candidal vulvovaginitis present with an erythematous rash, vaginal itching, and thick, white discharge. Diagnosis is confirmed via pseudohyphae on microscopy. Common risk factors include diabetes mellitus and recent antibiotic or corticosteroid use. Treatment of superficial cutaneous candidiasis is with topical antifungal medications such as nystatin. Choice A (Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin) are antimicrobial agents used for empiric treatment of suspected Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis infections. Vaginitis caused by these organisms is sexually transmitted and typically presents with mucopurulent discharge, not the thick white discharge seen in this case. Choice B (Oral acyclovir) is used to treat herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection. Genital herpes is a sexually transmitted infection most often caused by HSV-2 and presents with multiple painful vesicles on an erythematous border. This patient has no vesicles. Choice C (Oral amoxicillin) combined with clavulanate can treat bacterial cystitis, which presents with dysuria and urinary frequency. White vaginal discharge and an erythematous rash over the vulva and perineum are more consistent with fungal vulvovaginitis. Choice D (Oral metronidazole) can be used to treat systemic fungal infections, but topical agents are preferred for superficial cutaneous infections like vulvovaginitis. Educational Objective: Vaginal candidiasis involves overgrowth of normal vaginal Candida flora. Symptoms include pruritus, erythema, and white discharge. Treatment is with topical antifungal agents such as nystatin.
▶ Respiratory System Sinusitis 1 questions
Source: 8A #22
A previously healthy 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his mother because of a 5-day history of runny nose and mild cough. His mother says his nasal discharge was clear at first but has been yellow for 24 hours. He had a low-grade fever for the first 2 days of his illness but has not had fever for 3 days. The patient's father recently had a cold. The patient is at the 50th percentile for height and weight. His temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 96/62 mm Hg. Examination shows a moderate amount of yellow-to-white discharge from both nostrils. There is no periorbital edema or erythema. Multiple 1.5-cm, freely mobile, nontender nodules are palpated in the anterior cervical area bilaterally. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Allergic rhinitis B) Allergic sinusitis C) Bacterial sinusitis D) Cervical lymphadenitis E) Viral rhinosinusitis
Correct Answer: E) Viral rhinosinusitis
This patient with rhinorrhea, mild cough, low-grade fever, and bilateral cervical adenopathy has a presentation consistent with viral rhinosinusitis. Acute rhinosinusitis (ARS) is defined as symptomatic inflammation of the sinuses and nasal cavity lasting less than 4 weeks and can be classified as either viral or bacterial. Most cases of ARS are viral in cause, with rhinovirus, influenzavirus, and parainfluenza virus being the most implicated pathogens. Patients with viral rhinosinusitis may present with cough, nasal congestion, clear or purulent nasal discharge, and facial pain that is worse when leaning forward. In viral rhinosinusitis, fever, if present, typically resolves after 24 to 48 hours, as occurred in this patient. Physical examination may show tenderness to percussion over the sinuses. Treatment of viral rhinosinusitis involves supportive care with over-the-counter analgesics, antipyretics, saline nasal spray, and oral or intranasal decongestants. Antibiotics are not indicated unless bacterial infection is suspected. Choice A (Allergic rhinitis) commonly presents with rhinorrhea, sneezing, cough, and nasal congestion, and is often associated with allergic conjunctivitis and asthma. These conditions do not present with fever or lymphadenopathy. Choice B (Allergic sinusitis) can develop when chronic nasal obstruction leads to impairment of sinus drainage. However, like allergic rhinitis, this does not present with fever or lymphadenopathy. Choice C (Bacterial sinusitis) has signs and symptoms that overlap those of viral rhinosinusitis, making them difficult to distinguish. However, bacterial sinusitis is much less common than viral sinusitis, and symptoms typically last more than 10 days. Symptoms typically present following viral upper respiratory infection, and patients may present with worsening of symptoms following an initial period of improvement. This patient with mild symptoms and fever that resolved after 2 days most likely has a viral infection. Choice D (Cervical lymphadenitis) presents with enlarged, inflamed, and tender lymph nodes in the neck and may be either unilateral or bilateral. Bilateral cervical lymphadenitis often occurs secondary to viral upper respiratory infections, while unilateral cervical lymphadenitis is often bacterial in cause. Importantly, this patient's lymph nodes are nontender, making primary lymphadenitis unlikely. The lymphadenopathy is reactive to the viral upper respiratory infection. Educational Objective: Acute rhinosinusitis is usually viral in cause, and patients may present with cough, nasal congestion, clear or purulent nasal discharge, and facial pain that is worse when leaning forward. If symptoms persist beyond 10 days, a bacterial cause is more likely.
▶ Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Tinea Corporis 1 questions
Source: 8A #24
A 14-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 1-week history of a mildly pruritic rash on his left arm. He has mild asthma that is well controlled with an inhaled corticosteroid. He plays several sports and currently participates on the school wrestling team. His family lives on a farm in North Dakota. They have had a pet dog for 5 years; the dog is in good health and has no skin lesions. The patient appears well. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). Examination shows a 3-cm lesion over the left forearm. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy? A) Topical clotrimazole B) Topical mupirocin C) Topical nystatin D) Oral cephalexin E) Oral itraconazole
Correct Answer: A) Topical clotrimazole
Tinea corporis is a common superficial dermatophyte infection caused by direct inoculation of the skin from affected individuals or animals, including dogs and cats. This patient's exposure to wrestling (skin-to-skin contact) and a farm dog makes tinea corporis the likely diagnosis. Trichophyton species are a common cause. Microscopic examination of skin scrapings with potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation shows branching septate hyphae. Tinea corporis is treated with topical azole antifungals, such as clotrimazole, which inhibit conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol in the fungal cell wall by the enzyme 14-alpha demethylase. Topical mupirocin (Choice B) is used for superficial bacterial infections such as Staphylococcus aureus and does not have antifungal properties. Topical nystatin (Choice C) is a polyene antifungal used specifically for mucocutaneous Candida infections, which typically present with a beefy red appearance, often in intertriginous regions, and may be associated with satellite pustules. Nystatin binds cell membrane sterols and is not appropriate for dermatophyte infections. Oral cephalexin (Choice D) is a cephalosporin antibiotic used for gram-positive bacterial infections and has no antifungal properties. Oral itraconazole (Choice E) is an azole antifungal with a similar mechanism to clotrimazole; however, due to risks of serious side effects such as congestive heart failure and hepatotoxicity, it is reserved for systemic fungal infections such as blastomycosis, histoplasmosis, and aspergillosis. Additionally, azole antifungals inhibit cytochrome P450 3A4 enzyme. For superficial dermatophyte infections like tinea corporis, topical azoles are the first-line treatment.
▶ Gastrointestinal System Salmonella species gastrointestinal infection 1 questions
Source: 8A #28
A 3-week-old girl is admitted to the hospital because of a 1-day history of fever and irritability and a 2-day history of diarrhea that has become bloody during the past 6 hours. She was born at 39 weeks' gestation; pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. History of cow milk-based formula. The family occasionally eats out at fast-food restaurants. There are two pet lizards at home. The patient is at the 25th percentile for length and weight and 50th percentile for head circumference. Her temperature is 39.1°C (102.4°F), pulse is 170/min, and respirations are 40/min. Capillary refill time is less than 2 seconds. Her hemoglobin concentration is 16 g/dL, leukocyte count is 18,000/mm³, and platelet count is 260,000/mm³. Serum electrolytes, urea nitrogen, and creatinine are within the reference ranges. After 24 hours, blood and stool cultures grow gram-negative rods. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism? A) Campylobacter jejuni B) Escherichia coli O157:H7 C) Listeria monocytogenes D) Salmonella enteritidis E) Shigella sonnei
Correct Answer: D) Salmonella enteritidis
Salmonella enteritidis is a motile, gram-negative bacillus that is a major cause of diarrhea worldwide. In the United States, it is most associated with undercooked poultry, eggs, or meats, and has been associated with pets such as turtles, reptiles, and chickens—a key finding in this case with the pet lizards at home. The incubation period typically ranges from 8 to 72 hours, after which patients develop diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and fever. Bloody stools are common in children. Salmonella gastroenteritis is usually self-limited, with fevers resolving within 2 to 3 days and diarrhea resolving in approximately 1 week. Supportive care, including oral rehydration, is the cornerstone of management, and antibiotics are not generally recommended in immunocompetent individuals with mild to moderate infections. Stool studies may show gram-negative bacilli. Choice A (Campylobacter jejuni): A gram-negative rod causing bacterial diarrhea associated with consumption of undercooked poultry or meat. Patients typically present with watery diarrhea self-limited to 1 to 3 days, managed with supportive care. Choice B (Escherichia coli O157:H7): Associated with Shiga toxin and outbreaks of bloody diarrhea. Serious complication of hemolytic uremic syndrome may develop, presenting with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and kidney failure. This patient's labs do not show the expected thrombocytopenia or anemia pattern. Choice C (Listeria monocytogenes): An aerobic, gram-positive bacillus (not gram-negative as cultured) associated with unpasteurized dairy products or deli meats. Incubation period is approximately 24 hours with fever, watery diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting. Self-limited within 2 days. Notably, it poses risk for transplacental transmission in pregnant women. Choice E (Shigella sonnei): A gram-negative bacillus associated with initial watery diarrhea followed by bloody diarrhea, fevers, abdominal distention, and cramping. While similar presentation, Shigella is more typically associated with person-to-person transmission rather than pet reptile exposure. Educational Objective: Salmonella enteritidis is a gram-negative bacillus and major cause of diarrhea worldwide, most commonly associated with undercooked poultry, eggs, meats, and pet reptiles. Clinical presentation includes bloody diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and fever with typical symptom resolution in 1 week. Diagnosis is confirmed by stool culture. Management is supportive care with oral rehydration, and antibiotics are not recommended for immunocompetent patients with mild to moderate disease.
▶ Pregnancy Childbirth Puerperium Neonatal Conjunctivitis 1 questions
Source: 8A #29
A 2-day-old full-term newborn is brought to the physician because of bilateral eye discharge. He was delivered at home by his father and has not yet been examined by a physician. He appears well. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows marked swelling of the eyelids; there is profuse yellow discharge from both eyes. The conjunctivae cannot be visualized because of the swelling. No other abnormalities are noted. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? A) Allergic conjunctivitis B) Chemical conjunctivitis C) Chlamydial conjunctivitis D) Gonococcal conjunctivitis E) Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease)
Correct Answer: D) Gonococcal conjunctivitis
Gonococcal conjunctivitis is the result of direct inoculation of bacteria from the genital canal to the newborn's eyes during the process of delivery. The clinical presentation includes erythema, profuse purulent discharge (often yellow as described in this case), eyelid swelling, and lymphadenopathy. Gram stain of purulent discharge will show gram-negative diplococci. Newborns diagnosed with gonococcal conjunctivitis should be hospitalized, cultures should be obtained, and patients should be provided systemic antibiotics, particularly ceftriaxone. Patients may also be provided artificial tears until their condition improves. In the hospital setting, erythromycin eye drops are provided to newborns at the time of delivery to prevent gonococcal conjunctivitis. Choice A (Allergic conjunctivitis) presents with erythema, pruritus, and watery discharge (not purulent) involving bilateral eyes. Treatment involves avoiding allergens and using topical antihistamine or alpha-1 agonist eye drops. Choice B (Chemical conjunctivitis) results from chemicals meeting the conjunctiva. Symptoms include erythema, redness, pruritus or pain, and watery discharge. Once the chemical has been washed from the eye, symptoms improve. Chlorine is a common self-limited cause. Choice C (Chlamydial conjunctivitis) typically occurs 5 to 14 days following delivery (not at 2 days), presents with initial watery discharge that becomes mucopurulent over time, and may produce bloody discharge. Nucleic acid amplification tests are the gold standard for diagnosis, and azithromycin is the preferred treatment. Choice E (Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome/Kawasaki disease) is a multisystemic inflammatory disease characterized by fever for at least 5 days, bilateral nonexudative conjunctivitis (not purulent), polymorphous rash, lymphadenopathy, erythema and edema of the hands and feet, and mucous membrane involvement with dry, cracked lips. Educational Objective: Gonococcal conjunctivitis results from inoculation from the maternal genital canal during delivery and is associated with erythema, profuse purulent discharge, eyelid swelling, and lymphadenopathy in newborns. Newborns diagnosed with gonococcal conjunctivitis should be hospitalized and provided systemic antibiotics such as ceftriaxone. Prophylactic erythromycin eye drops are provided to all hospital-delivered newborns to prevent this condition.
▶ Multisystem Processes Disorders Vitamin K Deficiency 1 questions
Source: 8A #31
A 5-day-old newborn has hemorrhagic disease due to vitamin K deficiency. He is bleeding from the nose, mouth, and gastrointestinal tract and into the subdural space. In addition to vitamin K therapy, administration of which of the following is the most appropriate next step? A) Cryoprecipitates B) Factor VIII concentrate C) Fresh frozen plasma D) Lactated Ringer solution E) Platelets
Correct Answer: C) Fresh frozen plasma
Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin that plays an important role in the synthesis of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as proteins C and S. Primary sources of vitamin K include leafy green vegetables and endogenous production by intestinal bacterial flora. Vitamin K deficiency is common in newborns due to poor placental transfer of vitamin K, low concentrations of vitamin K in breast milk, immature neonatal intestinal flora, and poor absorption. Vitamin K deficiency presents with signs and symptoms of bleeding (also known as hemorrhagic disease of the newborn), which may include cutaneous bleeding (bruising, petechiae, oozing from venipuncture sites), hematomas, epistaxis, or gastrointestinal, retroperitoneal, or intracranial hemorrhage. All newborns should be administered prophylaxis with intramuscular vitamin K. Newborns with evidence of bleeding should be treated with oral or intravenous replacement of vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma (FFP). FFP contains all coagulation factors, as well as fibrinogen and proteins C and S, making it the ideal immediate treatment for this patient's active bleeding. Choice A (Cryoprecipitate) contains concentrated fibrinogen along with factors VIII and XIII, and von Willebrand factor. While useful for treating coagulopathic states with decreased fibrinogen and factor VIII such as disseminated intravascular coagulation, it does not contain the vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, and X or proteins C and S that are deficient in this patient. Choice B (Factor VIII concentrate) is useful for bleeding disorders characterized by factor VIII deficiency, such as hemophilia A and von Willebrand disease, but does not address the multi-factor deficiency seen in vitamin K deficiency. Choice D (Lactated Ringer solution) is a crystalloid solution useful for intravascular volume repletion in hemorrhage. While volume replacement may be helpful, correcting the underlying coagulation factor deficiency with FFP is the more important step to address the patient's bleeding disorder. Choice E (Platelets) is incorrect because vitamin K deficiency does not result in thrombocytopenia; it affects only coagulation factor synthesis, not platelet production or number.
▶ Skin Subcutaneous Tissue Diaper Rash 1 questions
Source: 8A #33
A 4-month-old female infant is brought to the physician because of a rash in the diaper area for 5 days. The infant has had two episodes of otitis media treated with oral antibiotic therapy but has been otherwise healthy. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F). Physical examination shows a red, confluent rash with sharply demarcated borders, pustules, and satellite papules in the diaper area. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy? A) Topical mupirocin B) Topical nystatin C) Oral cephalexin D) Oral ketoconazole E) Intravenous amphotericin B F) No pharmacotherapy is indicated
Correct Answer: B) Topical nystatin
Candida species are part of the normal skin flora but commonly cause infection in intertriginous areas such as the diaper area in infants, as well as genital and inframammary regions in adults. Candida infections present clinically with beefy red patches favoring skin folds, accompanied by satellite papules and pustules. This clinical presentation is characteristic of candidiasis and is the key diagnostic finding in this case. Topical nystatin is a polyene antifungal agent that is the first-line treatment for mucocutaneous candida infections. Nystatin works by disrupting fungal cell membrane integrity and is particularly effective for topical cutaneous infections. Choice A (Topical mupirocin) is an antibacterial agent used for superficial bacterial infections such as Staphylococcus aureus. It works by binding bacterial tRNA synthetase and inhibiting RNA and protein synthesis. Mupirocin is not effective against fungal pathogens and therefore is not appropriate for candidiasis. Choice C (Oral cephalexin) is a first-generation cephalosporin antibiotic effective against gram-positive and some gram-negative organisms. As a bacterial antibiotic, it has no antifungal activity and is not indicated for candida infections. Choice D (Oral ketoconazole) is an azole antifungal agent that was historically used for systemic fungal infections but is rarely used in modern clinical practice due to severe side effects including hepatotoxicity and QT prolongation. While topical azoles are widely used for cutaneous fungal infections, oral ketoconazole is not appropriate given the associated toxicity and the availability of safer topical alternatives like nystatin for localized cutaneous disease. Choice E (Intravenous amphotericin B) is a systemic polyene antifungal reserved for serious systemic fungal infections. It binds and disrupts ergosterol in fungal cell membranes. However, it carries significant toxicity including fever, chills, nephrotoxicity, and life-threatening arrhythmias. Amphotericin B is not indicated for cutaneous candidiasis when topical agents are effective and safer. Choice F (No pharmacotherapy is indicated) is incorrect because pharmacotherapy is clearly indicated. Topical antifungal treatment with agents such as nystatin is standard and effective for candida diaper dermatitis.
